en: *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Three, Part Two.
Compiled by the Sramana Tae-hyeon of Cheonggyu.
*Record of Studies on the Treatise on Consciousness-Only*, Volume One (Commentary on 12b).
This treatise is briefly analyzed through three sections: first, the section on revealing the tenets and identifying the essence; second, the section on analyzing the title;
and third, the section on explaining the meaning of the text.

Regarding the term "Exposition of the Tenets" (*Siddhāntavyākhyāna*), there are, for now, two schools of tenets. The first is that of Bhāviveka and others, who expound the words of the *Prajñāpāramitā*: conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena exist conventionally, while their ultimate nature is emptiness.
As stated in the *Tattvārthāvatāra-kārikā* (The Verse on the Jewel in the Palm): "In its true nature, conditioned phenomena are empty, because they arise dependently like illusions."

The unconditioned has no reality; its non-arising is like a flower in the sky. Regarding this, Dharmapāla and others, relying on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, maintain that all phenomena have both emptiness and non-emptiness, as stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā*:

"The false discrimination exists; within it, these two are entirely absent. Herein there is only emptiness, and therein also exists that [discrimination]. Some say that these two are substantially existent and argue over them.
Treatise: As stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, after one thousand years, disputes regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*astitva*) arose within the Mahāyāna;

this refers precisely to that. How did these disputes unfold? Regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Self and dharmas do not exist, yet emptiness and consciousness are not non-existent.

By being free from both existence and non-existence, one accords with the Middle Way. This negates the grasped object (*grāhya*) while preserving the remaining two natures (*svabhāva*). This is the position of the [Yogācāra] masters.

The *Ratnakośa-śāstra* states: "Just as one says that [the self] is non-existent in order to abandon the fault of falling into the extreme of eternalism, one also says that this [eye and so forth] exists in order to abandon the fault of falling into the extreme of nihilism.
That is to say, the eyes and other faculties produced by the power of causes and conditions are subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and exist by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*).
They are not like a flower in the sky, which is entirely a non-entity; rather, they are established [as existing] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*)."
It is empty; this exists conventionally, while in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), all is empty. Furthermore, regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there are two differing explanations.
According to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla’s response to the school of Bhāviveka, the two emptinesses are themselves the ultimate reality (*tattva*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"The nature revealed by the two emptinesses is not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is by nature free from existence and free from non-existence. This is the position of the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka in response to Dharmapāla.

The Dharma-system is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness. The *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā* (Pal-zhen lun) states: "True Suchness is established as that which is merely the absence of all that is grasped.
Thus, not only do the two explanations regarding the essential nature differ, but they also conflict concerning whether the ultimate exists or does not exist.

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "If this consciousness did not exist, then conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) would not exist. Since conventional truth does not exist, ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) would also not exist.
To deny these two truths is 'badly grasped emptiness' (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*). The *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā* (or *Lakṣaṇaṭīkā*, known as the *Zhenzhenglun* / *Pal-zhen-lun*) states:

"The Buddha speaks of the existence of nirvāṇa from the perspective of the conventional, just as the Buddha speaks of the existence of spontaneously born sentient beings (*upapāduka-sattva*). Because we accept this existence, there is no fault of contradicting our own tenets. However...
Based on this, the negation of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*) serves as the proof.

Regarding this, there are traditional accounts by Cien and others asserting that there was indeed a dispute between the two masters; however, some say there was no dispute at all. This is because Bhāviveka did not accept [the existence of] non-existence (*abhāva*) in the ultimate sense.

As stated in the *Tarkajvālā* (The Blaze of Reasoning): "This statement 'it is not existent' merely negates the nature of existence; its function is exhausted there, and it does not further signify non-existence, just as in worldly convention..."

This was stated provisionally; it was not said that silk is not [produced] from itself, for it is not necessarily the case that those words directly denote blackness. Furthermore, he addresses the objection:
Moreover, what he says—that if one considers the ultimate nature (*tattva*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are utterly non-existent—is the meaning of his formal thesis (*pakṣa*).

This immediately constitutes a denigration of all those who follow false views. The intended meaning here is that it refers to the specific categories of the gateway of empty, natureless, and illusory manifestation;
it does not mean that everything is denied as non-existent in every respect. Even Dharmapāla does not accept [the existence of things] in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
As the *Śata-śāstra* states: "Even the present does not exist in the ultimate sense, because it arises from conditions. Just so...
Regarding illusions and the like, it is further stated that the expression "emptiness" is a negation (*pratiṣedha*) rather than an affirmation (*vidhi*). It is not merely that emptiness exists;
rather, it is even the "emptiness of emptiness. This is explained at length. The masters of the *Saṃprayukta-śāstra* refuted by the *Tattvasaṃgraha* were not the Dharmapāla school.
For the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, in his *Śataka-vṛtti*, refutes the *Saṃprayukta* masters for reasons identical to those [of Śāntarakṣita]. This serves as proof to support the view of Jñānagarbha.

The Master [Vasubandhu] and others transmit the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*. Some say that these two terms—“dispute” (*vigraha*) and “argument” (*vivāda*)—have the same meaning. This is like the dispute regarding a stūpa being coarse at the bottom and fine at the top;

it necessarily arises because one must first grant the opponent’s position before one’s own can be established. In the school of Dharmapāla, one must certainly cite what is grasped as an object of attachment (*parikalpita*).

Since the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), emptiness, existence, and so forth are all objects of attachment, both natures (the imagined and the dependent) are wondrously existent and are not entirely non-existent.

Therefore, it is said that the two kinds of emptiness are not the ultimate truth. Emptiness refers to one extreme; nor is there non-empty existence, for when both paths are cut off, it is called *tathatā* (suchness).
Thus, the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka cites conventional existence to exclude all forms of non-existence and to distinguish it from absolute non-existence.

The conventional also does not exist, for the two natures are wondrously non-existent; this is because there is nothing to be apprehended. If one were to merely eliminate existence, one could then attain non-existence;
yet since non-existence is also eliminated, it is said that "there is nothing to be apprehended. That which has nothing to be apprehended is free from the meaning of the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*).
As the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All four extremes are subsumed under the grasping of dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). Based on this correct principle, Master Wonhyo...

The preceding arguments regarding speech are similar in intent. Because those of dull faculties in the final age rely on such disputations to artfully produce their own interpretations, I shall now take the three—object, practice, and fruit—as described by Dharmapāla in his *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* as the tenet of this treatise.
This is subsumed within the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Regarding the exposition of its essential substance (*svabhāva*), Master Ji establishes four gates:

first, subsuming characteristics into their nature, which is the substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*); second, subsuming the remainder into the substance of consciousness, which is "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*); third, subsuming the provisional to follow the real substance, which is sound;

and fourth, discussing the substance of the nature and its functions separately, which refers to the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*). Master Ce establishes five gates, adding further to the preceding [four].

Section Three: The Gate of the Essential Substance of the Three Dharmas (This has no separate substance, as the preceding four [sections] are subsumed within the three categories as appropriate). The Three Treasuries have eight gates: 1. The Gate of Subsuming Delusion and Returning to Truth; 2.

The Gate of the Distinction between Truth and Delusion. This also has two parts: a. The Gate of Subsuming Characteristics and Returning to Consciousness; b. The Gate of the Distinctions among the Characteristics of Consciousness.
The latter [of these two] also has two parts: a. The Gate of Subsuming the Provisional and Following the Real; b. The Gate of the Distinctions between the Provisional and the Real.
A separate section. The latter section also has two parts: first, the section on the essential substance of the three dharmas;

second, the section on the extraction of the substance from the enumeration of dharmas (this also lacks a separate substance apart from the four, and thus Master Ji’s [classification] of four [types of] "dull" and "pure" is adopted). Within the discussion of the substance in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the *Nirabhilāpyadharmatāśāstra* states:
"That which appears as a collection upon the consciousness of the listener is called the substance of the teaching, because it directly produces understanding. A summary verse says:

One should not abandon what precedes the sutra for what follows it, nor should one arbitrarily fix the names of the characters. Regarding the single character in the sutra, there are many applications;
it is not the case that the new simply follows the old.

This is as described by Ji (Jizang) in his *Ce* (Investigation), among the various scholars' commentaries. Each of the four lines of this verse presents a difficult point regarding a specific meaning. That is to say, some have said:
When one hears the teaching that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, the four types of determinate consciousness (*niścaya-citta*) each newly acquire three characteristics.

These characteristics successively flow into one another and coalesce, such that the subsequent rate-er consciousness (*sātaka-jñāna*) seeks its object without relying on names. This seeking is accompanied by the five [sense] faculties;
because it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it seeks the object of the preceding rate-er consciousness. That [opponent’s] claim is not so, for it does not abandon the preceding [object].

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): because it follows upon the subsequent mind, what is heard or practiced arises abruptly; since it arises in a state of distraction, its principle carries along with the preceding object—why must it necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

This position is also consistent with taking the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) as a well-stated doctrine. Therefore, since it is not a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it should likewise take names (*nāman*) as its object.
Some say that seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*) is not direct perception, and thus it also takes names as its object. The four types of seeking are as follows: [text continues].

Next, one attains the three nines and the twelve four-character marks. Some say: "Regarding 'existence' and 'non-existence,' when one hears them and seeks them out impulsively (*sāṃketika*), it is the same at all times.
Because the mind continues to seek after the impulse has passed, and because the existence and non-existence have not yet been determined.

[They claim that] regarding hearing, practice, and constant application, there are three [stages] for each plus the meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Both of these views are irrational, for there is determination regarding names and words.

Because the mind is concentrated. It is not so; there would be no basis for subsequently understanding the meaning of the phrases. One should not say that many [moments] arise suddenly at the end, except for the meaning of the phrases, because they have nothing upon which to depend.
Furthermore, when it says, "the five must necessarily seek after," this is stated to show that these five do not continue in succession;
it does not exclude the possibility that the five definitely arise immediately thereafter regarding an object with which one is well-accustomed. In such cases, they are indeed determined.
Therefore, as it is said that the mental consciousness arising immediately after the five sensory consciousnesses is either investigative or determinative;

some say there are four "sudden" (*saterila*) moments of mind, and that these also take names and words as their objects, such that the ear-consciousness and the mental consciousness together comprise eight moments of mind.

That claim is incorrect, for when the four syllables are uttered, each requires many movements [of the vocal organs], and thus a single sudden moment of mind would be separated by a vast interval. Some say:

Some maintain that there are two types of *manasikāra*: first, that which arises spontaneously (*sahaja*) when seeking; second, that which arises from resolve (*niścaya-manasikāra*). Others maintain that there is one type, namely the mind of resolve (*niścaya-citta*);
and yet others maintain that there is none at all, namely the mind of seeking (*paryeṣaṇa-citta*). Finally, some maintain that there are always three, namely the latter three minds.
This is not correct, for when a new object appears before one, there is no spontaneous [arising]. Now, I shall set forth an alternative interpretation. The verse says:
The first syllable has three moments of mind; the second is exclusively *saṃtīraṇa* (investigation); the third and fourth are the same as that.
The first moment does not constitute a "name" (*nāman*). Commentary:

Regarding the various [syllables] having three [moments], it means that immediately after *saṃtīraṇa*, there arises determination (*niścaya*). This is because [syllables] such as *dha* and others are worldly...
Because it is habituated, although it determines the name, it subsequently seeks out its referent. This mind of determination is also called "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*).

There are two types of hearing and application: sudden and determined. When listening, there is no such thing as [sudden] hearing; hearing is always like application (or when it is possible to apply, one also seeks out the phrases and meanings).
Among these, the sudden [moment] cannot be called a name, because a sound of a single moment lacks expressive power; it only attains the first [moment].
The various activities [of the mind] undergo transformations until they reach the stage of definitive determination (*niścaya*), at which point they first attain their established names.
In total, there are fourteen dharmas that are determined in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), each attaining three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) because they increase the meaning of the phrases.

Nevertheless, while the preceding objects manifest as a flow for the succeeding moments of mind, in reality, the four names each have their own specific referents; however, for the sake of the designating terms (*vācaka*), we speak of them as being so many. Question:
If one asks what intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) these various names signify: the answer is that conventional designations signify the conventional, and non-existence signifies non-existence;
however, any meaning that is not shared [with others] is termed "intrinsic nature. Briefly stated, these names clarify the tenets and reveal the essential substance.

Regarding the second title, "The Chapter on Analysis" (*Vibhaṅga-mukha*): according to the *Juyao* and other sources, Vasubandhu’s original verses are titled the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
A separate note beneath the title states that it is also called the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, because the teachings of the *Triṃśikā* establish *vijñaptimātra*.
However, as for the term "establishment" (*siddhi*) used here, the commentary explains that the three parts [of the treatise] establish *vijñaptimātra*.
It is so called because it is "established" (*siddhi*). As explained by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla in his commentary on the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, titled the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ṭīkā*:
"The term 'vijñaptimātra' (consciousness-only) is a name for that which is established; it excludes external objects and retains the internal mind.

Because this is the primary tenet of the treatise, both the teachings and the principles of the root text are termed 'vijñaptimātra,' while the teachings and principles of the commentary are collectively termed 'siddhi' (establishment)."

How is this known to be so? Having already established the meaning of the nature and characteristics of *vijñapti-mātratā* based on the sacred teachings (*āgama*) and correct reasoning (*yukti*), it is clearly understood that the means of proof (*sādhana*) applies to both scripture and logic.

Since it is stated that "the nature and characteristics of *vijñapti-mātratā* have been established," and because the initial statement says, "I shall now explain what was taught therein," it is clearly understood that the object of proof (*sādhya*) likewise applies to both scripture and logic; for they are established through mutual dependence. Thus, there are four [points].
The *Śūyao* (Essential Pivot) explains the ten meanings of the *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra); it is prolix and lacks essential points. To summarize:

"Vijñaptimātra" (Consciousness-only) is named using the *adhikaraṇasaptamī* (locative determinative compound), because "only" (*mātra*) is identical to "consciousness" (*vijñapti*). It may also be explained as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

Some explain it as being like "non-greed" (*alobha*), but this is incorrect, as it would not be subsumed under the six types of compounds. Otherwise, one would have to conclude that the term "non-greed" refers merely to the absence of greed. As for the treatises, they rely upon the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Compassion. It should be understood as usual that this is based on the wisdom of yoga. Regarding the statement "composed by the Bodhisattvas Dharmapāla and others":
nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was an ordained bodhisattva named Vasubandhu, which translates as "World-Kinsman.
When he was nearly eighty years old, he composed these root verses (*mūlakārikā*). At that same time, there were only two others: Bandhuśrī and Yaśomitra.

The Great Master composed this commentary on the verses. One thousand one hundred years later, there were eight other masters; among them, the most eminent was Dharmapāla, which in Chinese is translated as Hufa (Dharmapāla).
Jì states that he was the son of a king in the city of Kāñcī in the country of Draviḍa in South India (Cè states he was the son of a minister).
At the age of twenty-nine, he practiced dhyāna and paid homage beneath the Bodhi tree.
At that time, he composed this commentary on the treatise. He passed away at the age of thirty-two.
He appeared contemporaneously with Bhāviveka and was the most eminent among the ten commentators. These and others are the ten masters of the treatises, as detailed in the two sub-commentaries.
Third, regarding the section on explaining the meaning of the text: the treatise consists of three parts. First, the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching;

second, the section on the correct exposition of the holy teaching; third, the section on concluding the title and dedicating the merit. The first part has two sections: namely, the verses and the prose commentary. The verses themselves have two sections:
the first half concerns taking refuge, and the second half concerns the purpose for which it is done. As for the term "khai" (稽), it refers to the one who is capable of showing reverence.

Regarding the phrase "prostration" (*praṇāma*), it refers to the essential nature toward which one turns, as expressed by terms such as "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). It is called "prostration" because one touches the head to the ground. By means of the body’s prostration, one expresses reverence through the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind].
Its essence consists of faith (*śraddhā*) and a sense of shame (*hrī*); for, in the presence of those possessing virtue, one honors and respects them through pure conduct.

Regarding the essence of that which is revered, there are three essential explanations. The first states that one reveres only *nirvāṇa*, because it is... [self-]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a Buddhist treatise, likely concerning the opening homage of a text. The translation reflects the technical terminology and the structure of the original.)

Because its nature is eternally supreme. This means that the essence of the four types of nirvāṇa is all *tathatā* (suchness). When one correctly attains the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), it is called "complete purity" (*paripūrṇa-viśuddhi*).
"Part" (*bhāga*) refers to a stage (*avasthā*). As for the nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātratā*), it is the "naturally pure nirvāṇa" (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*).

The others—the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder)—are called "complete purity" because they are realized only when the fruition is perfected (for in the ten stages, the afflictions and the characteristics of suffering have not yet been exhausted). This is the "part."
Regarding "purity": it refers to non-abiding *nirvāṇa*, because it is admitted that this has already been realized during the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

(This is because its function of not abiding in the two extremes already exists; there is scriptural evidence for this in the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*). Furthermore, the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles is merely a conventional analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and possesses only a single liberation.

Great *parinirvāṇa*, however, is the perfection of three things. Regarding these three things, there are two senses: first, they consist of one essence with three names as the three things; second, they consist of three meanings.

There are three names for three things: the wisdom capable of contemplation, the Dharma-body which is the object of contemplation, and the analytical cessation that is the state of being free from fetters.

These are the three things in terms of name and substance. Regarding the one true *tathatā*: its nature as wisdom is called *prajñā*; its manifestation of virtue is called the *dharmakāya*; and its freedom from bondage is called liberation (*vimukti*).

These are the three things in terms of name and meaning (the other two [categories] should be understood accordingly). According to another interpretation, there are three things in terms of substance: the essence of wisdom itself is called *prajñā*; its being free from the two obstacles is called liberation; and its collection of manifold virtues is called the *dharmakāya*.

Because it is taught as the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) which is the wisdom of suchness (tathatājñāna), analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) in its essential nature is called liberation (vimukti). The fruit obtained by wisdom is called prajñā. The two types of abandonment and the two types of wisdom are called bodhi. Therefore, because it encompasses all virtues, it is called the Dharma-body, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

All conditioned merits of the Tathāgata are subsumed under the category of "with remainder," whereas his unconditioned merits are subsumed under the category of "without remainder. Nevertheless, it is solely by virtue of the nature of non-abiding, which is eternally perfect and quiescent, that these three matters together are termed Great Nirvāṇa (as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*).

One interpretation states: One reveres only Bodhi because the Bodhisattva seeks wisdom rather than parinirvāṇa. Through the sublime contemplation of equality, although the causes have already been attained, one reveres the four wisdoms of the fruit;
these are called "complete purity" or "partial purity," while the two wisdoms of the cause are included as well.
"Vijñaptimātratā" (the nature of consciousness-only) refers to the object realized; however, the intention is to revere that Bodhi which realizes it, because it possesses efficacy.
One interpretation states that both Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are revered together: Vijñaptimātratā is the basis of Nirvāṇa, and while its essential nature is pure, it is not said to be "perfected";
perfected purity is Bodhi. This is because two [aspects] are attained during the causal stage, and four are perfected in the fruit. As it is said:
The ninth [verse] states: "The intent of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is that sentient beings attain the two types of *parāvṛtti* (transformation) of enlightenment and *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding this, the sub-commentary provides four interpretations: 1. Reverence for the Dharma, not the person, because the Dharma is what all Buddhas take as their teacher. 2. Reverence for the person, not the Dharma, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (64):

"If one wishes to compose a treatise, one should first pay homage to the two teachers. This refers to reverence for the person. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full passage would likely continue with further interpretations regarding the dual reverence of both person and Dharma, or the transcendence of both.)

Out of reverence for the Dharma; out of respect for the original master of the treatise (the Buddha); and out of veneration for the meaning [of the Dharma], one pays homage to the masters who opened and elucidated it (the Bodhisattvas).

Regarding the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), there are three pairs of persons and dharmas to be revered: the completely pure original masters and the partially pure Bodhisattvas. As for the dharmas, they are that which is to be followed and maintained.
Because it is through persons that the Way is propagated; because they are the basis for the treatise; because the nature of consciousness is the Dharma-jewel;

because the perfected purity constitutes the Buddha-jewel and the partial purity constitutes the Sangha-jewel; and because the teachers of the root verses are included as those who can give rise [to understanding].

Although there are these seven interpretations, the Tripiṭaka masters explain in detail that "respecting persons" is superior. According to the rules of phonology (*śabdavidyā*), among the seven case-endings (*vibhakti*), this refers to all objects of veneration.

All [traditions] explain this by means of the fourth case (the agentive). However, the Sanskrit original explains the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) by means of the seventh case (the locative), which expresses the objective sphere.

Here, "consciousness-only" functions as the differentiator (*viśeṣaṇa*), while "perfectly pure" (*pariśuddha*) functions as the differentiated (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, we now pay homage specifically to that which is perfectly pure within the nature of consciousness-only.
Since the nature of consciousness-only is the objective sphere expressed by the seventh case, according to the ninth chapter of the treatise, there is a brief [explanation].
There are two natures: first, the nature of falsity (*abhūta-parikalpa-svabhāva*), which refers to that which is universally admitted as being grasped (i.e., the purity of what is to be eliminated);

second, the nature of reality (*tathatā-svabhāva*), which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) (i.e., the purity of what is realized). Furthermore, there are two natures: first, the conventional (*saṃvṭti*), which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) (i.e., the purity of what is to be abandoned);

second, the ultimate (*paramārtha*), which refers to the perfected nature (i.e., the purity of what is attained). The *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot) analyzes these three natures and two truths into many categories; [this would be] too prolix.

And yet it is not desired. Regarding that which is pure therein, one should know what is to be revered. Among those who explain [the purpose], some say it is solely for the sake of the endurance of the Dharma and for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, because the intention abides in the Dharma.
Others say it is solely for the sake of benefiting people, even though they interpret that explanation as meaning the intention is to benefit others.
According to the true meaning, it is for both people and the Dharma, for both self-benefit and the benefit of others; this refers to the explanation.
He says: "In order to cause the Dharma to abide, and because the abiding of the Dharma benefits others—which serves as one's own benefit—I shall explain the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
'I' refers to the provisional person; Kuiji [the base] says it is Sthiramati, while Cecheng [Mei] says it is Dharmapāla.
His teaching is that of the fully perfected pure ones. However, regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya*..."

Whatever is undertaken [in this treatise] should all be subsumed under the purpose of this discourse. The meaning of benefit and happiness is explained in detail elsewhere, such as in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Now, this treatise is composed so that [the reader] may give rise to correct understanding.
The commentary states: The preceding verses indicated the intent of composing this exegesis; now, the intent of Vasubandhu’s composition of the treatise is clarified.
The text consists of three sections: first, those such as Sthiramati [composed it] so that others might generate understanding, sever obstructions, and attain the fruit;

second, according to Cien, those such as Nanda, and according to Jiqian, those such as Huibian, [composed it] to sever obstructions, realize emptiness, and awaken to the characteristics of Vijñaptimātra; third, those such as Dharmapāla [composed it] to refute [opposing views].

To reveal the principle of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) by means of various refutations of false attachments, there are likewise three stages: first, the generation of understanding prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*); second, the severance of hindrances upon the stages;
and third, the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood. This refers to the first stage. The word "now" (*idānīm*) specifically indicates the time when Vasubandhu composed these verses.

Regarding the "two emptinesses" (*dvayaśūnyatā*), they are the emptiness of persons (*pudgalaśūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*). As in the various attachments discussed below, all are described as being deluded and erroneous; for within both persons and phenomena, there is no self (*ātman*).
To cling to existence is an error; to fail to realize non-self is called delusion.
By generating understanding, one severs [delusion], and as that obstacle is severed, it follows that [the other] is severed.
The commentary states: "The second [stage] is the severing of obstacles. The term "heavy obstacles" is a word of reproach; each of the two obstacles has its own light and heavy aspects.

Because it is a weighty category, there is an anticipated objection stating: "Only the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) in our system directly obstructs the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*);

what proof is there that the realization of these two emptinesses universally severs the remaining obstructions? In response, this statement is made: since the two attachments are the root from which greed and the other afflictions arise, as one realizes emptiness, the remaining obstructions are universally severed.
(Cai [Mei] says: "Although the attachment to phenomena is pervasive, here it is explained in terms of the specific characteristics of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). *Shuyao*).

[It is said: According to the school of Sthiramati, it is not taught that the five [consciousnesses] or the eighth [consciousness] possess the grasping of a sentient being (*sattvagrāha*), nor is it taught that the seventh [consciousness] possesses only the grasping of a living being (*jīvagrāha*).

If one speaks of the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses], their afflictions are termed "heavy" because their conceptual attachments are profound; those within the five consciousnesses are "light," because they are induced by others and lack the grasping of a living being.
If one speaks of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the sixth [consciousness] is termed "heavy" because its comprehension is profound and vast; the five... [are light].
The eighth is called "light" because its conceptual clinging is shallow. Thus, through the presence of both heavy and light obstacles, one realizes emptiness and abandons the heavy;

the remaining light ones are extinguished accordingly (the various scholars' elaborate explanations all converge on this meaning). Alternatively, it is said that active manifestations are called "light" and habitual seeds are called "heavy";

they are abandoned according to the abandonment of the heavy, which should be understood by analogy with what precedes. The former explanation is superior, as it maintains that both manifest and seed forms of grasping and obstruction coexist. As it says:

What kind of habituation is called "heavy" and what kind of manifestation is called "light"? Therefore, the former [habituation] is superior. Furthermore, it is said that there are nine grades of obstacles for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
If the first eight grades are merely obstacles while the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) has not yet been severed, how can the remaining obstacles arise and be severed in accordance with their grasping?

Moreover, it is objected that according to Sthiramati, with the exception of the seventh consciousness, all others consist of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). If so, how could the "companions of harm" be eliminated in the fifth stage?

The sixth and seventh stages and so forth are called "feeble" (*karśa*) and so on. The commentary explains: regarding the first [stage], it is simply stated that the obstacles arise from grasping (*grāha*);

when grasping is severed, the obstacles are extinguished. It does not say that the extinction of all derivative obstacles follows the severance of their primary grasping. To resolve this later objection, it is said:

although all are attachments to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), because there are primary and derivative forms, those that are closely associated with the [fourth stage] grasping are called "harmful companions" (*sahāya-hantr-ākhyā*), while those that are distant are called "feeble."

This is inferior. It is not so; for the sūtras concerning the "harming of companions" and so forth clarify only afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), not cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). To correlate these with the three types of transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) and so forth is both prolix and unnecessary.
"Severing hindrances in order to attain Great Bodhi. The commentary states:
"The third [section] concerns the attainment of the fruit; its headings and explanations should be understood. Regarding 'supreme fruit' (according to Cè), there are four permutations:

first, that which is supreme but not a fruit—namely, the wisdom and abandonment of a Bodhisattva; second, that which is a fruit but not supreme—namely, the wisdom and abandonment of an Arhat; third, that which is both supreme..."
It is also a fruit; namely, the two fruits of a Buddha. Four cases are neither superior nor fruits: ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*).

To distinguish these from the other three categories, it says "superior fruit. If both fruits of a Buddha are termed "superior," why does the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* state that the liberation of the three vehicles is identical?

And why does the *Mūlamahāyāna-karmasiddhi-sūtra* state that the name "Vajra" refers to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)? [The answer is that] their essence as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is identical. Because...

It is capable of realizing supremacy. Just as the "non-abiding path" reveals the supremacy of non-abiding, the liberation of the Tathāgata is superior to that of the two vehicles because it realizes the wisdom that is capable of [realizing] the remainderless state—whereas for the two vehicles there is still a remainder and they have not yet escaped manifest suffering—and because it has severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, the Tathāgata’s liberation is superior to that of the two vehicles because he has severed the habitual tendencies. Regarding the term "Equal Enlightenment" (*Samyaksaṃbodhi*), it means equality in one respect. Within this, there is a statement concerning the "True... [nature].

[Their] wisdom is equal to that of a Buddha; however, because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is inferior, [the distinction remains]. The Tripiṭaka Master says: "The uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) both sever the same single obstacle;

therefore, the word 'equal' is used, but it does not mean their liberations are identical. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, at the end of the twenty-fifth fascicle, states: "A Buddha is named for clearly seeing the Buddha-nature (*buddha-dhātu*);
a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage has not yet seen the Buddha-nature, and thus it is not clear. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle fifty...

Because there is a distinction of superiority and inferiority between Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vibuddha-bodhi*), [the former] is a secondary function of abandonment. What is meant by "Equal Enlightenment"? It is the meaning of "according to reality" (*yathābhūta*), as explained in the *Mātṛkā*.

Regarding "true liberation": there is that which is liberation but not true; this refers to partial nirvana (*pradeśa-nirvāṇa*), because it is attained through suppression (*vibhava*). There is that which is true but not liberation;

this refers to the True Suchness of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā-tathatā*), because it is neither the path nor the fruit. There is that which is both true and liberation; this is the nirvana of the three vehicles (*triyāna-nirvāṇa*).
Because it is eternally free from bondage, there are two cases that are neither: excluding the three aforementioned characteristics, these distinguish it from the remaining three propositions.
Regarding "true liberation" and "great enlightenment" (*mahābodhi*): there is that which is great but not enlightenment, namely the wisdom of ordinary beings, *śrāvakas*, and *bodhisattvas*;

there is that which is enlightenment but not great, namely the noble wisdom of *arhats*; there is that which is both great and enlightenment, namely the wisdom of the Tathāgata; and there are two cases that are neither, namely: [The remainder of the passage follows.]

In general, when studying the wisdom of the two vehicles of the noble ones, it is based on the fact that both obstacles [the afflictive and the cognitive] equally obstruct wisdom and must be abandoned; however, because we are now addressing the preeminent [cognitive obstacle], we speak of abandoning the wisdom-obstructing [obstacle] specifically.
Furthermore, this is for the purpose of providing instruction so that one may come to know things as they truly are.
The commentary states: This is the second section, which severs attachments, realizes emptiness, and awakens to the characteristics of Vijñaptimātra.

Whereas previously there were three points, here there are two points, so as to enable the attainment of the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional (as Ji says). It is for the sake of opening the way for beginners and providing instruction for those who have practiced for a long time.

Now, regarding those among the non-Buddhists who specifically postulate a self—such as the Sāṃkhyas and others—they each maintain distinct theories apart from the aggregates. They postulate [a self] separately.

As for "Dharma," it refers to the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), the six categories (*padārtha*), and so forth (which include the aggregates, elements, and bases, as they should be subsumed herein).

Regarding those within our own Buddhist tradition who specifically postulate a self (*ātman*), the *Siddhāntabhedoparacanacakra* states: "The Vātsīputrīya, the Mūlasarvāstivāda, the Saṃmitīya, and others."

All [of these] maintain the existence of a self (*ātman*). Those who specifically maintain the existence of dharmas include the Sarvāstivādins, the Mahīśāsakas, and others (those who have wrongly grasped emptiness, etc., should be included herein).
These followers of both internal and external paths are deluded regarding the nature of the ultimate and the conventional.

To provide an opening for the external paths and to demonstrate [the truth] for the internal paths, one causes true wisdom to penetrate the reality of True Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), because subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) cognizes the characteristics of consciousness-only. Question: Regarding the Vātsīputrīya Arhat...
"Why does the view of self arise? Ce (Ceci) says: "The Tripiṭaka master explains that this conception arises because they have not yet attained arhatship;
it is discussed here because it was previously mentioned, referring to the tenets of that school. The same applies to the Sautrāntikas and others, as they were originally non-Buddhists.
Alternatively, it refers to what the disciples of that school conceive, even when they are not yet non-Buddhists, as in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. That school offers this defense: 'Our school...'"
Because he did not recite the *Pudgalapratiṣedhaprakaraṇa* Sūtra, the Upādhyāya said: "Although he had attained arhatship, he still possessed the same dharma-attachment as my own view of a self;
due to the strength of his habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), such an attachment arose."
"Furthermore, there are those who are deluded and mistaken... [up to] ...just as consciousness is not non-existent. The commentary states:
This is the third section, which refutes various false attachments and gives rise to correct understanding. Within this, there are two parts: first, the presentation of four types of calculations;
second, the summary of these divergent attachments. Regarding the four types of calculations: first, the Sarvāstivādins and others maintain that [the object] exists outside of the mind.

Regarding the claim that objects exist as truly real in the same manner as the mind, Master Ji’s formal inference (*pramāṇa*) states: "The self exists as a determinate reality apart from the mind and its objects;

for it is admitted that [the self] is not non-existent once [the mind and objects] are excluded, since it is subsumed under one or the other of the two factors—the mind and its objects—just like the mind and mental factors.

(This contains the fallacy of uncertainty, as there are cases where neither the mind nor its objects exist, yet they are still subsumed under one or the other. One might ask: "Are the mind and so forth necessarily truly real, or are they something else, such as a jar, which is not truly real? This fallacy is disregarded here). Master Ce’s formal inference states: "External objects..."

It is not non-existent, because it is subsumed under either the grasper (*grāhaka*) or the grasped (*grāhya*). As the Master of the Treatise [Dignāga] states regarding internal consciousness, there are two fallacies in this inference:

first, the fallacy of confusion between self and other; and second, the fallacy of the lack of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). Regarding the first: if the subject (*dharmin*) were an external object, that would be an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*); if the similar instance were the Master himself, that would be an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). It is impossible for a single inference to be both self-referential and other-referential. Why? If it were purely an inference for others, then since it is something the proponent himself does not accept, there is the fallacy of lacking a similar instance within an inference for oneself.

Consequently, the mention of the "Master" in the example would be useless. Regarding the second: even if this were free from fault for the Sarvāstivādins, there is still the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because they all admit that minds can arise by taking non-existence as their object. The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Observation) states: "This..."
Regarding the internal consciousness as an analogy: if one were to employ the internal and external consciousnesses of our own school (svatantra), the Master would not accept it.

Because [the reason] depends on another [school], the analogy fails to be established for both parties. (Since all agree that consciousness exists, the concordant example can be established; however, it is unnecessary to address such fallacies of similarity in detail, and thus these elaborate explanations will not be taken up hereafter).

The Master Śubhagupta states: "As I have explained, external objects are not non-existent, because—excluding non-entities—they are subsumed under either the apprehended or the apprehender within the duality of subject and object.

This is like the internal consciousness of the Proponent of Consciousness-Only (Vijñānavādin). [Response: Although this formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), it nevertheless suffers from the aforementioned fallacies of confusion regarding self and other.

Since internal consciousness is universally admitted to possess substantial reality (*dravyasat*), the dispute concerns only whether that object exists externally or not; why then labor over the internal consciousness distinguishing between self and other? [Question: Excluding the words of the Proponent of Consciousness-Only, can "other" be established?
[The opponent] objects: "How does the Mahāyāna dispel that attachment? The proof [of our position] states: It contradicts the distinct characteristics of phenomena (*dharma*).
The internal refutation through a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: Your external object is neither separate from consciousness nor non-existent;

this is because you admit it is subsumed under one or the other of the non-existent subject or object of cognition (*grāhya-grāhaka*), just like internal consciousness. This contradicts the intended distinction within your own doctrine regarding the thesis.

The term "consciousness" (vijñāna) also includes mental factors (caitta). Therefore, there is no lack of determination (aniyata), as there are indeed dharmas that possess their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa); otherwise, they would contradict their own nature. Furthermore, those [external objects] are not established as having the nature of external entities.
Thus, it is better to interpret this category [of consciousness] alone; for the spurious explanations in the subsequent treatise are but a proliferation of empty words.
Alternatively, some maintain that internal consciousness, like its objects, does not exist.
[The author] comments: This is the second position. Jñānasena says: Masters such as Bhāviveka and others, by asserting that all phenomena are empty, thereby negate the very substance of the mind.
Their formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is: You assert that internal consciousness, like its objects, does not exist, because you admit it to be an object of cognition, just like your external objects.

In the case of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), there must be a subject (*dharmin*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), both of which you [the opponent] yourself [must accept]. The term "thesis" (*pakṣa*) is like an object; the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is useless. One may simply state the thesis: "consciousness is not existent. The proof states:

Because there are three types of inconclusive reasons (*anaikāntika*)—those that are self-inconclusive, other-inconclusive, and both-inconclusive—it is as follows: if one says "like my *tathatā*," it is other-inconclusive; if one says "like your conventional mind-object," it is self-inconclusive;
and if one says "like your conventional truth," since you admit that *tathatā* exists and I also admit that it exists, it is both-inconclusive.

Since it is "other" [in the sense of being external], it is only "other" and thus inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). It is certainly impossible for that which is "other" to serve as an example for that which is "self," and therefore inconclusive. Furthermore, the conventional cannot be inconclusive with respect to the ultimate; thus, an inconclusive reason based on common consensus (*sādhāraṇa-anaikāntika*) is also unreasonable. This is because, from the perspective of ultimate truth, one would doubt whether things are empty or non-empty.

[The argument] would only then become inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Since [the object] exists in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), it is not truly existent; therefore, existence does not [apply to both sides of the dichotomy]. To explain, let us first refute [the opponent's position] as follows: "Since you admit it is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), is it like external objects, which are empty in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-śūnya*), or is it like the mind and mental states, which exist conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*)?
They must answer: "Like conventional minds and mental states, they are merely empty in the ultimate sense. Thus, there is no inconclusiveness. Master Ce’s formal inference (*pramāṇa*) states:

"Internal consciousness is non-existent, because it is subsumed under one or the other of the grasped (*grāhya*) or the grasper (*grāhaka*), just like external objects" (What is the intended meaning? If it were empty and non-existent, it would contradict the sacred teachings; the *Prajñāpāramitā* does not teach that [consciousness] is non-existent).

This is because of the meaning [of the term]. If emptiness were not non-existent, there would be the fault of establishing what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If this were an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), it would also be indeterminate (*anaikāntika*) due to *tathatā* (suchness) being present in other cases; the same applies if it were a common inference (*sādhāraṇa*), as it is traditionally taught that all common inferences regarding one's own property (*svadharma*) are indeterminate.

Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master [Kamalaśīla] offers another interpretation: Bhāviveka establishes the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) but does not establish the vision (*darśana*). For instance, when visual consciousness perceives blue and so forth, the mind itself is distinct from the blue and so forth;
there is no separate perceiving subject external to it. This extends even to the realization of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), where there is no wisdom external to it.

Although, in the conventional sense, both object and mind exist together such that the object is real while the mind is unreal—and since reality pertains solely to the object—the Vijñānavādin masters subsume the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) back into the mind.

Their intention is this: when true wisdom realizes suchness, the wisdom itself is unreal as it merges with the object; the same applies to other states of mind. Mental activity resembles the object, whereas the object does not resemble the mind.

It is clearly understood that the mind is unreal and undergoes transformation in accordance with the object; thus, one cannot say that bondage and liberation arise from the mind. Since the mind and the object are fundamental, let it not be that the mind is both bound and liberated by wisdom. Because wisdom is the sovereign, even if it has not yet attained benefit, it is able to lead one toward the Path; therefore, this is designated as "conventional."
The five consciousnesses do not exist; there is no need for further refutation regarding the marks of the world.
Alternatively, some maintain that while the functions of the various consciousnesses differ, their substance is identical.
The commentary states: this is the third position. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "There is a class of teachers who assert that there is but one consciousness. They...
That [mind] undergoes transformation and acquires various names, just as in the case of mental karma (*manas-karman*). The *Śāstra* states:
"A certain class of Bodhisattvas cites three sūtras as evidence: first, the *Dharmapada-sūtra*, because the mind travels far and wanders alone;

second, the *Sūtra on the Five Faculties Producing Consciousness*, because the mind is able to individually experience the objects traversed by the five faculties; third, the *Sūtra on the Twelve Bases*, which subsumes the six consciousnesses as a whole."
Because it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Cè (測) says: "It merely speaks of the six consciousnesses as being a single mental consciousness;

it does not speak of the seventh and eighth, nor do they have a separate substance. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "There is no other consciousness apart from the mental consciousness, except for the existence of a separate ālayavijñāna.
By this, one should know that the seventh [consciousness] also has a separate substance. However, the eighth consciousness relies upon and grasps the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*).

Fearing that this might overextend to the six consciousnesses, he specifically singles them out for exclusion. The commentary states: In the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Mind, Thought, and Consciousness" of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, only the six consciousnesses and the *ādāna-vijñāna* are clarified.

This is because the masters who maintain that there is only one consciousness fundamentally do not believe in the existence of the *manas-vijñāna*, and thus they exclude only the eighth [consciousness].
This passage also refutes the master of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Regarding the eighth [consciousness], he says: Five...
Within the cave-like gate, the monkey stirs and acts.
Some maintain that apart from the mind (*citta*), there are no separate mental factors (*caitta*).
The commentary states: "This is the fourth position. Cè says: "This refutes the doctrine of Buddhatrāta, as in the *Vibhāṣā* (140)."
Second, it is said: The Venerable Buddhadeva asserts as follows: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*):

first, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and second, the mind (*citta*). That is to say, there is no derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) apart from the primary elements, and there are no mental factors (*caitasika*) distinct from the mind.

All material forms are merely specific differentiations of the primary elements, and all non-material phenomena are merely specific differentiations of the mind. Alternatively, this is the position of the Sautrāntika school.
There are two [positions]. As stated in the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise Following Reasoning), volume eleven:

"The Dārṣṭāntikas assert that there is only mind and no separate mental factors (*caitta*)—this being the view of Buddhatrāta, who maintains that the person consists of six parts and that defilement and purification arise from the mind. Those who maintain that mental factors exist engage in much debate:

some say there are only three, namely feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*), because the sūtras speak of the five aggregates; others say there are four, by adding contact (*sparśa*); and others say there are ten."
That is to say, there are ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). Some say there are fourteen, adding greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.
Now, this treatise is composed in order to refute those [factors] as they are respectively absent in various [mental states], and to exclude such [erroneous] views.
The commentary states: The second section extensively refutes divergent attachments. Previously, four positions were presented:
namely, the sequence of Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna, and Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. However, the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot) states that these apply to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

The first is Mahāyāna, referring to the school of Bhāviveka, which relies on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and maintains that objects exist external to the mind. The second is the Hīnayāna position of the Ekavyāvahārika school. First.

All phenomena are merely provisional designations. Third, regarding the master of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) of the Lesser Vehicle: as stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, "mind, thought, and consciousness are one.
Fourth, regarding the Mahāyāna according to the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*: they maintain that "only mind" appears as greed and so forth, or as faith and so forth;

these correspond respectively to the grasping of objects and the grasping of mind, or the grasping of the subject and the grasped, which is neither empty nor existent. It is not [the case that] mind grasps the object.
For the most part, they are not different. The *Vyākhyāyukti* (the *Shu*) analyzes the relationship between the object and the mind through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Bhāviveka follows the Lokāyata; for them, there is the object but no mind (the Lokāyata claims that all phenomena are composed of the primary elements). The Madhyamaka and Mahāyāna maintain that there is the mind but no object. The Sarvāstivāda and others hold that there is both the object and the mind.
The Vaitulika and Ekavyavahārika schools maintain that there is neither object nor mind. By citing these, one includes the various views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); therefore, it is said:

Regarding these various differing interpretations, the initial statement "I now compose this treatise" and the concluding statement "therefore I have composed this treatise" both apply to each of the three structural sections.
"If there is only consciousness" (up to) "it is said that there is a self and dharmas.
Commentary: This is the second section, the formal exposition. There are both the root text and the commentary; the commentary may follow the root text. The root text consists of three sections:
the first twenty-five verses clarify the objective realm of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*); the next four verses clarify the practice of consciousness-only; the final one...

Verse: Clarifying the Result of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*). This section also has three parts: first, one and a half verses on the gate of revealing the doctrine and extracting its essence;

second, the extensive explanation of the gate of Consciousness-Only; third, the concluding explanation that resolves external objections. The first part also has two sections: first, raising the inquiry by way of a question;
second, providing the formal answer by citing the verse. This is the former. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya*, among the five questions, this is the fifth.

[The question is: "How do you bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings? Baso (基) says: Since this treatise takes Consciousness-Only as its central tenet, how could it not contradict worldly teachings?
[For those teachings state that] "self and dharmas fundamentally do not exist, like the horns of a rabbit," and thus various things should arise without causes. Therefore, [the question is asked].
"By means of the provisional designation of self and dharmas... and the consciousness that discriminates objects. [Commentary:
Regarding the second part, the formal response presented in verse, there are two sections: the verse itself and its explanation. This is the first. Within the verse, there are two parts:
the first three lines resolve the objection and clarify the tenet; the final three lines briefly set forth the essential nature.
That [school] says: "The 'I' (ātman) is the dharma; consciousness is the self-substance (*svabhāva*); that which is transformed is the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*).

This 'transformer' refers either to the transformer of these aspects and the seeing, or to this self-substance itself as the transformer; both explanations are acceptable. Regarding the statement "only three":
although the transformations are of infinite kinds as described below, the types of transformers are three.
The Treatise says: [Up to] "Dharma means that which provides a norm and sustains.
The Commentary says: There are two parts to the explanation of the verse. First, the explanation of the first three lines, which addresses general objections and establishes the fundamental tenet.

Second, from "The aspects transformed by consciousness, though of immeasurable kinds," onwards, the explanation of the last three lines, which sets forth the characteristics of the transformer. The first part also has two sections. The first is the direct [explanation].
This is because it explains the verses and extensively refutes the attachments of outsiders. The formal explanation has three parts: first, the explanation of two lines;

second, the explanation of the third line; and finally, the various categories. This is the first line. Regarding "by way of conventional designation": since the grasped self and dharmas do not exist, they are not external;

since consciousness appears as a semblance of self and a semblance of dharmas, they are not external; and since nothing real exists apart from consciousness, it is said to be "by way of conventional designation."
I have two meanings: sovereignty and severance. Because it is sovereign, it is called "lord" (*pati*); because it severs, it is called "ruler of phenomena" (*dharma-adhipati*).

It has two further meanings: producing understanding and maintaining intrinsic nature. That which causes beings to produce understanding is called "guidance" (*viniyaka*); that which can maintain its own nature is called "maintenance" (*dhṛti*).

Each and every one of these penetrates all *ātman* and *dharma*. Ce (Cecheng) says: "In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 52, it states that both that which possesses a rule (*dhāraṇa*) and meaning (*artha*), as well as that which lacks a rule and meaning, can all give rise to the mind;
thus they are all called *dharma*. It is clearly understood that all things possess the meanings of 'rule' (*niyama*) and 'retention' (*dhāraṇa*). Ji (Jizang) says:
"'Rule' applies only to existent phenomena (*dharma*), while 'retention' extends to non-existent phenomena (*adharma*). This is incorrect, for [non-existent phenomena] can also give rise to the mind.
To resolve this, the Master [Sthiramati] offers a defense: "If the cognition arises from the actual object (*bimba*), it is merely a reflection (*pratibimba*);

thus, the object itself would not be the basis for the cognition. However, the cognition of a non-existent thing arises fundamentally from the cognition itself; it does not arise from a reflection as a real entity. As the Blessed One said:
"My noble disciples truly know what exists as existing, and truly know what does not exist as non-existing."
"Both of those possess [the notion of self], yet there is a distinction in their conventional designation.
Commentary: This explains the second phrase. "Sentient beings," "living beings," and so forth, are the notion of self in the world.

"Stream-enterers," "once-returners," and so forth, are the notion of self in the Noble Teaching. "Substance," "qualities," "actions," and so forth, are worldly phenomena. [The categories of] aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)...

These are the teachings of the Noble Dharma. That is to say, based on correct or incorrect modes of reflection (*vitarka*), one establishes various distinct categories—such as "sentient beings" and so forth—as conditions according to their respective aspects.
For example, [one might designate someone as] a "self" (*ātman*) because they possess consciousness or because they possess a life-span;

or again, as a "conventional person" (*pudgala*) because they have entered the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*) or because they possess the remaining single existence (*ekabhavika*). It is by means of such doors of correct or incorrect meaning that these [designations] are established as conditions.

It is the provisional designation (*prajñapti*) of the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*). Such characteristics [continue] until they are provisionally designated.

[The commentary] states: This explains the third phrase. First a question is posed, then an answer is given: "If all selves and phenomena are merely provisional designations... [The text continues: "Provisional..."

"It must necessarily rely on the real. [Question: "Upon what does it depend for its establishment? The answer consists of two parts; this is the first, which provides a general response. *Ce* (Yinming Jushuzhongshu) says:

"It is established based upon the appearance and seeing (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*) transformed by consciousness. *Ji* (Weishi ershi lun shuji) says: "It is universally established based upon the self-substance (*svabhāva*) transformed by seeds (*bīja*)."
"Consciousness (vijñāna) refers to discernment (*vijñapti*)... because it is associated with meditative concentration. The commentary states:
In the subsequent detailed response, there are two parts: [discernment] as consciousness and [discernment] as transformation. This is the first.

"Discernment" (*vijñapti*) refers to the function of the eight consciousnesses in discerning objects, just as in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, where "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are differentiated names for this same thing. [An opponent] objects: "The mind..."
If it is not that which is transformed by consciousness, how can it be "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) in the same way as form (rūpa)? To explain this:

its nature as that which transforms is subsumed under the term "consciousness" because it is invariably associated [with mental factors]. This means that while all mental factors (caitta) each transform their own objects, because the inferior is hidden and the superior is manifested, one does not say they are "only objects."
"Transformation refers to the substance of consciousness" (up to) "because there is nothing upon which it relies.
The commentary states: Next, in explaining transformation, there are two [types]: because it is threefold and because it is twofold. This is the first [type]. The Tripiṭaka Master says:

Sthiramati establishes only the single self-cognizing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*); Dharmapāla and Śubhagupta establish only the image and seeing divisions (*nimittabhāga* and *darśanabhāga*). This excludes [the former].

Regarding those three [divisions], other masters provide a collective explanation. Although Dharmapāla and Prabhākaramitra establish four divisions, they provisionally rely on the three divisions accepted by common consensus, as Dignāga’s third division subsumes the fourth.
Jñānasena states: "The characteristics of the perceived (nimitta-bhāga) and the perceiving (darśana-bhāga) seeds may be either the same or different.
If they are of the same seed, then a single consciousness-substance transforms and arises appearing as the two divisions of the perceived and the perceiving, just as..."

A single snail transforms and produces two horns. If these were seeds of a distinct nature, then the substance would transform to resemble the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), and the transforming seed of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) would likewise arise resembling the image.

Since they are reckoned not to be real, the name "resembling" (*pratibimba*) is established for the image-part. If there were separate seeds [for each part], how could they be called the transformation of consciousness?

Because the aspect (*nimitta*) arises through the conceptualization of the mind, both [the aspect and the seeing] depend upon the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). It is clearly known that the substance of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) depends on it, and that the aspectual manifestation arises from the cognition of the division [of subject and object].

Regarding the seeds of these three factors, the *Shuyao* states: "The correct doctrine of Dharmapāla holds that the substance, the manifestation, and the three [aspects]—these three natures (*trisvabhāva*)—do not necessarily have identical seeds, as they correspond to what is appropriate. Thus, the verse says:
The objective realm does not follow the mind; the solitary image arises solely from the seeing-part. The "image with substance" applies to both the mental object and the fundamental nature;

these categories, according to their respective applications, encompass all objective realms. There are three types: first, the objective realm consists of the true entities of all phenomena, which are termed "fundamental nature" (svabhāva).
Regarding the object: form is true form, and mind is the real mind. This true dharma is not necessarily determined by the three natures of the mind.

For example, the five sense-objects as they truly are possess only the nature of being ineffable (*avaktavya*), because they do not follow the five consciousnesses that take them as objects—which can be of all three natures—nor do they follow the mind in being bound to the same realm (*dhātu-bandhana*), as the eighth consciousness is bound to only one realm.

The objects of the seeds [of the eye and ear consciousnesses] pertain to all three realms. When one’s body is in a lower realm and one gives rise to the two supernormal powers (abhijñā), they take the divine eye and ear as their objects.
When the body is in a higher stage, the two consciousnesses of the eye and ear perceive objects of the desire realm;

from the second dhyāna upward, the eye and ear consciousnesses take both their own and other stages as objects, and these consciousnesses are bound by the dhyāna [in which they arise], while the objects are bound to their respective stages. (The Commentary provides two interpretations: one is as stated here; the other holds that in the first dhyāna, there are three consciousnesses.)

One apprehends superior colors and so forth; because they do not differ from their realm (dhātu), they are bound by the same level as the first dhyāna. Such categories likewise do not arise from a single type produced by the mind, because the characteristics (*nimitta*), seeds (*bīja*), and individual substances (*svabhāva*) are each distinct.

[Commentary: Among the five aggregates of phenomena—mind, mental factors, and matter—these phenomena sometimes possess actual utility; therefore, they must necessarily have their own distinct, *dharmatā*-based seeds.

When the mind takes them as its object, they appear clearly before it without requiring deliberation, nor do they belong to the past or future. They are able to produce the substance of their own seeds and objective parts (*nimittabhāga*) without opening up other seeds; this is termed a "nature-object" (*xingjing*). Although the reflections within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) lack [substantiality], [the nature-objects are real].

That which is functionally effective and arises from its own causes is called a "real entity" (*dravyadharma*). Although the later section of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that objects in other stages lack their own intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*), according to this present passage, consciousness still arises from distinct seeds. Since the objects of the first dhyāna are bound to their own stage, such binding does not follow the mind; this is certain because of this text.

If those [objects] did not take other dharmas as their substantial basis (*ālambanapratyaya*), what would they see? For there is no intrinsic substance of one's own. That is to say, even when one is born in a higher realm and does not enter meditative absorption or supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), one can still clearly perceive the various forms of lower realms.
This is because the forms of the lower realms are not the result of karma or the fruit of meditative absorption and supernatural powers.

The second is the realm of solitary images (*kevala-pratibimba*). Because their nature, their connection to seeds, and their status as objects are all invariably identical to the perceiving portion (*darśana-bhāga*), they are like the sixth consciousness taking as its object such things as a tortoise’s hair, flowers in the sky, the son of a barren woman, or unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) belonging to other realms.

Or, in the case of all such types of objects, they invariably follow the mind and possess no separate essence or function; because they are subsumed under the category of provisional objects (*prajñapti-viṣaya*), they are so named.

Regarding "solitary shadows" (such as the hair of a tortoise and other non-existent dharmas): if there were such a thing as a "dharma-nature seed" (*dharmatā-bīja*), it would have to be like form (*rūpa*) and other phenomena, capable of arising at times because it would produce its own fundamental dharma.

According to ancient tradition, the seeds perfumed by the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of visual consciousness can, depending on conditions, occasionally give rise to the visual and mental consciousnesses; yet the objective aspect of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is fundamentally non-existent and does not arise. One should know that those shadows likewise lack a dharma-nature seed.

Because they lack a dharma-nature, there are no newly perfumed seeds either, for new seeds must rely upon the perfuming of a dharma-nature. The same applies to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). Although other realms of phenomena may potentially arise, when a lower defiled state conditions a higher one, it is necessarily indistinct; it is merely a matter of conceptual investigation and deliberation, lacking the power to trigger the production of a shadow from a higher seed.

It is merely like a reflection established by conceptual discrimination. Since the seeds arise from the seeing [consciousness], their nature and their association are likewise the same. It does not take the upper [level] as an object for the lower, because it apprehends [its object] with clarity. Among these, there is the grasping of a self apart from the aggregates; the types of objects, whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), are numerous.

Therefore, it is said that they are equal. Regarding the six meanings of seeds inducing their own fruits, this refers exclusively to the primary gate (*mukha*) and not to secondary derivations; thus, there is no contradiction.

Third is the "境 with a real substrate" (*sadravyālambana*). This means that this reflected image possesses a real underlying substrate (*bimba*), such as the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) transformed by the seventh consciousness within the causal state.
Consequently, it may be classified as non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) according to its substrate, and likewise according to its perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*).

That which is subsumed under the "obscured" (nivṛta) may also be said to arise from seeds of the objective aspect (nimittabhāga), and it may also be said to arise from seeds of the subjective aspect (darśanabhāga).

Because its meaning is not fixed—it is produced by the power of inferential investigation rather than being a directly perceived object—it is said to be "obscured" by way of its subjective aspect; yet, because it arises resembling the objective aspect, it possesses that objective aspect.

Therefore, from the perspective of the substantial seeds (*dravya-bīja*), they are said to be "unobscured" (*anivṛta*), because they obtain the substantial seeds that serve as the basis for renewed existence (*punarbhava*). Question: Since the images (*pratibimba*) that can be "repeated" (*ābhāsya*) pertain to both natures (wholesome and unwholesome), the seeds (*bīja*) that are "repeated" should likewise pertain to both. Furthermore, among the six characteristics, if the nature of the seed and the manifest (*pravṛtti*) are identical, would they not produce the same category of result?

Could they then also pertain to the "obscured" (*nivṛta*)? Answer: Only from the perspective of the substantial portion (*dravyāṃśa*) do the seeds of the "repeated" exist, and not otherwise. From the perspective of the aspect of seeing (*darśanāṃśa*), it is like a solitary image (*kevala-pratibimba*); that is to say, because it arises from the seeds of seeing, it does not repeat the substance. This is because it does not resemble the seeing itself, nor does it [repeat] the other.

[Regarding the "heavy" (adhimātra) type: Seeing its unobscured aspect, it arises resembling its substantial object from the seeds of that very substance, thereby obtaining a [re-]birth as a substantial object. It is not clearly determined whether this applies to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses; however, because they lack a corresponding objective reality, they are termed "solely projected" (*kevala-pratibimba*).

As for the eighth consciousness, it is not so, because it does not plant seeds of a similar nature. Although its mode of activity (*ākāra*) follows the pattern of a reflection having a substance, since it lacks any corresponding reality whatsoever, it would be unreasonable [to classify it as such].
Regarding the phrase "according to the nature-seed (*prakṛti-gotra*) and so forth, as appropriate": "as appropriate" is not a fixed definition; there are two ways in which it is applied.

First, regarding the manifestation of meaning through the three objects: within the arising of various mental aggregates (*citta-kalāpa*), there may be one, two, or three [objects] combined within a single aggregate.
