That there is only one has already been explained previously. That there are two combined is, for example, when the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) takes dispersed objects of its own stage as its cognitive domain.

The object of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is the original nature-object (*mūla-svabhāva-viṣaya*). The objects of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are solitary-image objects (*kevala-chāyā-viṣaya*).

[Regarding why the objects of the mind and mental factors are solitary-image objects: They spontaneously respond to karma and evolve in accordance with consciousness. Since their coarseness and subtlety are equal and they lack superior auxiliary conditions, they arise as something resembling that [original object] solely from their own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). [This differs from the five consciousnesses, whose self-nature is coarse and active, and which possess superior auxiliary assistance—namely, the sense organs (*indriya*) that share the same objective field and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that shares the same focal point—which strike and activate the seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), causing the manifestation of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) of one's own mind.

If these seed-images were able to arise directly from the seeds, they would have to be actual manifestations (*pravṛtti*); however, since they do not resemble [the manifest state], they are merely images. Since they are similar [to the original object], [they are established as solitary-image objects].

Because they arise from the mind as distinct [objects], according to these five categories, they are exclusively "solely projected" (*kevala-pratibimba*) objects; this is the intention of this master. The objects of the five consciousnesses—the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of their own level—are "original-nature" (*mūla-svabhāva*) objects.

They may also be said to be "substantially accompanied" (*sadravya-sahita*) objects, just like the sixth consciousness when it takes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the past or future as its object, which is a "solely projected" object and may also be said to be a "substantially accompanied" object, as it perfumes seeds and gives rise to the fundamental [consciousness].

Because they possess substantial reality (*dravya*), the objects of the five consciousnesses are, in actuality, only "objective realms" (*dharmatā-viṣaya*). They necessarily rely upon a primary "substantial essence" (*mūla-dravya*); thus, they are metaphorically termed "conjoined with substance" (*sopādhi*). Although called "conjoined with substance," their natures do not intermingle; they are clearly and directly realized without requiring inferential search. They arise solely from their own seeds and do not proceed from the [defiled] seeing-consciousness.

When taking past or future aggregates as objects, no present substantial essence exists; these are therefore metaphorically termed "solitary images" (*kevala-pratibimba*). Yet, because they arise from the seeds of a past or future substantial essence and produce a subsequent cognition of that same class, they are subsumed under the category of "conjoined with substance.

However, due to the power of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), they are not called "objective realms. For example, the cognitive image of an object manifested by the Diamond-like Mind (*vajropama-citta*) has no present substantial essence and is thus called a "solitary image. It arises from the seeds of the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) according to the natural law (*dharmatā*), yet because it also produces a subsequent cognition of its own kind, it is likewise called "conjoined with substance. As the Master [Xuanzang] testified: "By virtue of..."

Because the eight [categories of] present contaminated phenomena serve as the five conditions for the future, one obtains the seeds of the stainless mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the water-like wisdom (*samatā-jñāna*). If there were no present phenomena of their own kind, it would not be the case that those seeds are not [reproduced]. Since contaminated phenomena serve as the objective basis (*ālambana-pratibimba*) for the reproduction of stainless seeds, they are contradictory [to the nature of the stainless].

Furthermore, since mental factors such as wisdom (*prajñā*) in the category of the eighth consciousness lack a present objective basis, they should not [be reproduced]. It is also illogical for a "solitary image" (*kevala-pratibimba*) produced by the seeds of the mental consciousness to reproduce the eighth consciousness; therefore, another dharma serves as the objective basis.

There are three types of combined objects (*sābhāsālambana*): for example, when the eighth consciousness takes the matter produced by meditative concentration (*samādhi-nirmāṇa-rūpa*) as its object; when mental factors take a mere image (*pratibimba*) as their object;
and when the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) takes a real nature (*dravyasvabhāva-viṣaya*) as its object, which may also be described as an object bearing substance (*sadravyālambana*).

This is because the matter produced by meditative concentration transformed by the sixth consciousness serves as the primary substance (*mūla-dravya*); thus, the images of gold, silver, and so forth, which arise according to what is contemplated in meditation, [are based upon that substance].

The resulting form arises accordingly; it is conventionally designated as "bearing a substrate" (*sābhāsā*). Some say that a single type [of form] simultaneously produces both the objective field and its result, and these two forms are called "bearing a substrate.

This is incorrect, because it would imply that the image within visual consciousness and its substrate do not arise from different seeds—since they are termed "objective fields by nature" (*svabhāvaviṣaya*)—and furthermore, it would mean that the results induced by uncontaminated meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) must necessarily arise from different seeds and thus could not be called "bearing a substrate. Although the category of things produced by karma takes another thing as its substrate, their seeds are not distinct; therefore, they are not called "bearing a substrate. The results of meditative concentration are not like this, for the form of the result is produced again from the objective field of the concentration.
Secondly, regarding the phrase "according to the respective nature, seed, etc.": this clarifies that the three aforementioned types of objects apply according to their specific circumstances.

It may be so. Or, while their nature (*svabhāva*) is the same, the connection (*pratisaṃyukta*) and the seed (*bīja*) differ, such as when the divine eye or ear belonging to a lower stage takes an object in a higher realm.
Or, while the connection is the same, the nature and the seed differ, such as when the five consciousnesses take the five objects of their own realm.

Or, while various factors are the same, the connection differs; from the perspective of an aggregate (*rāśi*), it exists, but from the perspective of a single dharma (*dharma*), it does not exist. As for example:
In the eighth consciousness-aggregate, the objects of the mental factors (*caitta*) are of the same nature as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*);

however, the objects of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) have different modes of connection (and so forth). [Question: What serves as proof for the existence of these three types of objects? Master Tz’o says: Although there is no scriptural authority (*āgama*), correct reasoning (*yukti*) serves as the measure. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 73, states: "Furthermore, there are two other kinds of characteristics:

those produced by prior conceptualization and those produced by the characteristic itself, which together constitute the characterized. What is the characteristic of the image (*pratibimba-lakṣaṇa*)? It refers to that which appears through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) arising from pervasive conceptualization; it does not abide in its own original nature. [Commentary: "Produced by prior conceptualization" refers to the subjective perceiver.

The "aspects" (nimitta) and that which is produced from the aspects constitute the nature-realm (svabhāva-viṣaya). That which is accomplished through commonality is the "aspect-bearing" (sanimitta). The "image-aspect" (pratibimba-nimitta) is the "solitary shadow" (kevala-chāyā). It arises solely from other seeds; it is said not to abide in its own original nature. Cei states:

"The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and the aspect-part (nimitta-bhāga) are definitely produced from distinct seeds, because they are perfumed separately. The *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* further states:

"This refers to the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors, as well as the aspects and seeing-parts they transform, along with their natures, realms, and stages—with the exception of the wholesome [states] of the Buddha-fruit and the most inferior indeterminate (nivṛta-avyākṛta) states."

[The Master Zhong] states that the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) gives rise to its own kind [of seeds]. (The Former Master [Xuanzang] explains: "This treatise speaks of general characteristics and not in minute detail. Furthermore, regarding nature (*dhātu*), realm (*dharmadhātu*), and so forth, there is no separate substance for the seeds;

rather, through the power of the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), the body itself has a lateral function that can take seeds as its object. Thus, nature and realm are not separate. The *Śāstra* says: "When taking all non-existents as objects, the hundred dharmas must have a real substance that is necessarily 'non-existent,' because it is distinct from form (*rūpa*) and the other [aggregates].
It must not be of the same substance as the seeing-part. This is because the mind that forcefully discriminates takes non-existent things as its objects."

The manifested *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) must necessarily possess four characteristics. Since it arises from its own seeds, how could it be produced from [the seeds of] what is seen? This is not logical.

If the shadow of a non-existent dharma were produced from the seeds of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it would not be a shadow of a non-existent thing. If it were a non-existent dharma, the shadow would necessarily lack power, as it would not be capable [of producing itself]. Even if a shadow were produced, what fault would there be in the nature of things (*dharmatā*)?

This would arise from the perfuming of its own seeds; consequently, an Arhat would have to possess the seeds of defiled dharmas. However, because the Buddha has exhausted those seeds when perceiving *saṃsāra* and the teachings of the Two Vehicles, it is merely called a "solitary shadow" (*kevala-pratibimba*), for at that time there is no capacity to produce an objective aspect.
"Or again, [the view that] internal consciousness [exists] while external objects truly exist.

The commentary states: This is the second interpretation, that of the "Two-Part" school (*dvibhāgavāda*). Master Ji says: This refers to the doctrines of Nanda, Bandhuśrī, and others. Their position is that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is difficult to establish as a basis;

rather, it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) because one perceives this transformation, and not "object-only. Based upon this objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), one clings to [the existence of] external [objects].

"Self and dharmas" refers to that which is not external but appears as if it were external, because the mind clings to them as being outside. Regarding "the power of the habitual perfuming of the discrimination of self and dharmas," Ce (測) says:

"This arises from the sixth and seventh consciousnesses perfuming the eighth. Alternatively, one may interpret it such that the view of self is called the "perfuming of self," while the factors of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) and names-and-words (*nāma-vyañjana*) are called the "perfuming of dharmas.
The phrase "like a dream" clarifies that these are what are grasped based on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). [The] Sarvāstivāda school...

Although it is granted that the dreaming mind has an object, it is not the case that the father [in the dream] is actually the father; therefore, it serves as a valid analogy. The Sautrāntikas maintain that dreams take non-existent things as their objects, thus establishing the analogy.
"Affliction" refers to a disease or visual impairment, such as the cataract known as kāmalā and the like.
"Even that which is accepted by the foolish exists as ultimate reality. Commentary:

The third section consists of various analytical gateways, which contains three parts: first, the gateway of distinguishing the provisional from the real; second, the gateway of distinguishing existence from non-existence;

and [third], the refutation of exaggeration and diminution. Regarding the refutation of exaggeration: it is to refute the exaggerated attachment to the existence of external objects apart from the mind. It is to refute diminution...
Because they grasp at the non-existence of internal consciousness and so forth, there is the third gate: the inclusion of the two truths. External objects that are grasped are merely conventional;

internal consciousness, being dependent nature, is also the second [truth], the ultimate. This is because neither is included in the second conventional [truth] (the fourfold two truths should be understood as explained below).
"How should one know [this]... because it is unattainable? The commentary states:

This second section extensively refutes the attachments of outsiders. Within it, there are three parts: the general question and answer, the specific question and answer, and the concise establishment of the sūtra.
Herein, the non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles pose the general question, and the Master provides the general answer.
"How does the real self [exist], up to the point that it experiences suffering and pleasure?
The commentary states: The second section, the specific refutation, has two parts: [the refutation] of the self (*ātman*) and of phenomena (*dharma*).

The first part also has five sections, because there are two types of threefold conceptions, as well as the refutations of the subtle and the refutations of objections. Regarding the first three conceptions, both non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and followers of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) hold them.

The statement "There is a self" refers to those who pose the question. Within the response, there are two parts: that which is based on their tenets and that which refutes them. This is the first part.
Regarding this, the first [position] is the calculation of the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools. Both masters maintain the two meanings of being eternal and omnipresent.

However, the Sāṃkhya school maintains that [the self] is solely the experiencer, because it experiences the phenomena produced by the three *guṇas*, just as a king enjoys sovereignty while remaining inactive.
The Vaiśeṣika school maintains that the self (ātman) is both the agent and the experiencer; however, they hold that it only experiences and does not act, because it lacks sovereignty.

How, then, can its permanence and omnipresence be known? Therefore, the commentary explains both points by stating: "Because one experiences pleasure and pain according to the karma one has created, [the self] is always found to be acting and experiencing in all places.
Since a permanent entity lacks the principle of arising and returning, the *Shuyao* states: "The Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools establish the self."

The proponent says: (Now it is said: these three types of valid cognition do not [apply] to the Sāṃkhya school. Since they themselves admit that space (*ākāśa*) and fire are impermanent through transformation, they cannot serve as valid examples. "The self (*ātman*) and its nature are eternal, because it is admitted to have no beginning or end, like space and so forth.
(Now it is said: among the reasons, one must exclude non-existent things; one should use a rabbit's horn to demonstrate the fallacy of being inconclusive.

Furthermore, "the substance of the self is all-pervading, because it is admitted to be eternally abiding, like space and so forth. The substance of the self is eternal and pervasive, yet it is admitted to follow the body in performing karma.

Because it experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth, it is like great empty space. Regarding the first syllogism, there is the fault of contradicting the specific characteristics of existing phenomena (*dharmas*):

[the self] should not be dependent on the body, because it acts as the agent and experiencer of the self. Regarding the second syllogism, there is the fault of contradicting the specific characteristics of the action:
[the self] should not be the agent or experiencer, because its essence is eternal and omnipresent. Regarding the third syllogism, the cause for being dependent on the body...

First, the fallacy of non-establishment (*asiddha*): [the reason] exists neither in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), space, nor in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), the pot; it is absent in both. As the *Śāstra* states: "Since this is admitted, there is no fault of being present in only one [of the two]."

The "Unshared Indeterminate" (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*). [The Proof states: "The characteristics of the unshared indeterminate are difficult to understand. It is commonly accepted that the substratum of space (*ākāśa*) is eternal and omnipresent; this [subject] is not so. That [space], by following the body, acts as a recipient; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is neither eternal nor omnipresent.

This means that among all categories, there is never a single phenomenon that follows the body to act as a recipient. This is the 'unshared indeterminate' of that [reason]. Is it not the case that a single thought-moment, acting as a recipient following the body, exists in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)? Because it does not perish first and arise later, it is not a single cause. [The Proof states:

"In the *Śūyao* (Essential Summary), all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) contain contradictions regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*), just as in the case of the Great [Elements]."

"Space is not of the nature of self. (According to the tradition of this master, within the intended tenet system, that which is common to all phenomena is called a "differentiation of non-dharma" (*dharmanirviśeṣa*). That which applies to only a single phenomenon is called a "differentiation of dharma" (*dharmaviśeṣa*); this is not the case here. Later generations should not rely on this.

Whether it is pervasive or non-pervasive, if it contradicts the intended tenet system within the context of a statement concerning a phenomenon (*dharma*), it is called a "differentiation of dharma. If it contradicts the intended tenet system within the context of a statement concerning a locus of a phenomenon (*dharmin*), it is in all cases called a "differentiation of dharmin" (*dharminirviśeṣa*)).
"Second, they cling to a self (up to) because it has the capacity for contraction and expansion.
The commentary states: This is the second calculation. Formerly called *nirgrantha*, it is now called *nirgranthaputra*.
This is called the son of the one who has abandoned fetters (*Nirgrantha*). They hold that clothing constitutes a "fetter" and being naked constitutes "freedom from fetters.
Because they are naked and without shame, they are also called "the unfettered" (*Anāśrita*). Their founder is called the "Fettered One," and his disciples are called "sons. The *Shuyao* states:
Their own [logical] measure says, "The self as it is described does not reside fixedly within the body, because it belongs to the body, just like a shadow and so forth. Therefore, below...
The refutation says: "I" should be subject to destruction, because it is grasped as something accompanying the body; therefore, it is like a shadow and so forth.
Thirdly, [the self is grasped] because it performs actions.

The commentary states: This is the third calculation. In Sanskrit it is called *Vṛṣabhadhvaja*, which here means "Lord of Beasts. He constantly wears red garments and is thus also named "Red-Robed One.
Master Ji says: Furthermore, there is a non-Buddhist sect known as the "Pervasive Manifesters" (*Vyāpaka-nirgata*), who are able to distance themselves from worldly affairs.

Because they frequently renounce the world, and because they consider their own [views] to be minor, they exercise light and independent mastery over the various faculties, performing functions such as seeing.
This describes the three types of tenets held by the five teachers; the remaining ninety kinds do not differ from these three.
"First, it is irrational... [up to] ...to create various karmas. The commentary states:
The refutation consists of three parts; the first refutation also has two parts: because it is a direct refutation and because it is a refutation of the subtle. This is the first.

This refutes both masters simultaneously: Your conceived self should not follow the body, because you conceive it as permanent, just like space (here, "because it is permanent" applies specifically to the Vaiśeṣika, while the reason "because it is omnipresent" applies to both masters). To refute the Vaiśeṣika separately:
Your conceived self should not be able to perform various karmas in accordance with the body, because you conceive it as permanent and omnipresent, just like space. Jī says:
If you establish that "I" should be immovable because you admit it is permanent and omnipresent like space,

there is the fallacy of contradicting your own position (*abhyupagata-doṣa*). Since the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* states that [the self] has no activity, the phrase "immovable" now definitively establishes the reason based on what you yourself have admitted.
Furthermore, regarding the self that is clung to [up to] "because of its conjunction with the self," the commentary states:

This is the second subtle refutation. First, it is refuted by showing commonality; later, it is refuted by challenging the tenet of difference. Although True Suchness (tathatā) is possessed in common, it is not an agent or an experiencer;

therefore, it should be understood that this does not serve as a valid analogy. As for the claim that "because they mutually pervade one another, their essences must be intermingled," [this is also untenable].

There are two traditions regarding this: one says it is refuted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the other says it is refuted by logical objection (*codya*). Regarding the refutation by objection, as the *Ki* commentary states:

"Because they mutually pervade one another, it is difficult for them to constitute a single entity; this does not necessarily require a formal proof," and so on at length. If the opponent were to offer a defense, saying:
"Just as with forms that occupy the same location and are inseparable, although many forms pervade [the same space], they do not constitute a single [entity]; I too..."
This is also not the case. [If one were to claim] "I" is truly real, there would be the fault of confusion with form (*rūpa*), because form is illusory.

Master Ce also said: "The intention of the Tripiṭaka master is this: [the self] is dependently established and conventionally distinct according to conditions; 'I' am substantially real. If it were pervasive, there would be a real confusion [with all things]. Some say that the seven substances are distinct categories and thus have no confusion."

"No, that is not so. For the two types of sentient beings would have to intermingle with the objective realm and the vessel-world, as they would be identical in their transformations. This is the intention of the Master [Śubhagupta]. Regarding the formal proof (*pramāṇa*) used to refute this, Śubhagupta says: (Note: "When establishing the formal proof, he uses distinct terminology for each case. [The proof is: "If one were to say... [The refutation follows: "Śubhagupta says..."
The self of all sentient beings and the self of Devadatta should be one in essence, because you admit that they are both permanent and omnipresent, just like the self of Devadatta.

The treatise says "intermingling" (*saṃkīrṇa*), intending that they enter into one another to become a single entity. [Śāntarakṣita] says: This statement is irrational. It would be redundant to say that all sentient beings have one self, as it was already stated previously.

Rather, it refers to many selves within a single body being intermingled; this is not the case. Since they admit these selves are distinct, it is difficult to make them one, so there is no fault of redundancy. They admit that many selves dwell intermingled within a single body, which results in the fallacy of contradicting their own position.

Although it is said that "mutual pervasion" (anyonya-saṃsarga) occurs, the intended meaning is "constant pervasion" (nitya-saṃsarga). If it were merely mutual pervasion, there would be no analogous example [for this doctrine]. (For two things are called "mutually pervasive" only when they are both dharmas of an Ārya;
otherwise, Devadatta’s self would [absurdly] be mutually pervasive with his own [body]). Cè states: "Devadatta’s true self and Yajñadatta’s self would then have to be essentially intermingled."

Because they mutually pervade one another. For example, in the case of "being produced by effort" (*kṛtakatva*) as a general characteristic serving as a reason, both [the subject and the predicate] possess the sense of pervading others. This interpretation is superior. (The commentary states: Both "I" [the self] and "mine" possess the meaning of pervading others.)

This is in accordance with the *Śāstra*. Ji (Jizang) says: "The [reasons] 'eternal' and 'pervasive' contradict the *Śāstra*. However, Master Ce’s first reason should state: 'Because they are of the same kind (*sajāti*), without increase or decrease, and mutually pervasive. The term 'of the same kind' excludes the seven substances; 'without increase or decrease' excludes the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

Although these are conventionally non-mixed, there is still the fault of being 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*). Alternatively, since either of the two selves would be included because they are mutually pervasive, there would be no inconclusiveness.

If that were so, the first reason would still remain inconclusive, for the second self—the form-body of self-enjoyment—is of the same kind as its objects, without increase or decrease, and is mutually pervasive without being mixed. However, regarding external inference, the internal inconclusiveness violates the rules of Hetuvidyā; therefore, the inconclusiveness regarding the seven substances and so forth is useless. Guan (Fazang) says: "First..."
In my treatise, it is stated that "similarities are mutually pervasive" (the proof states: "It is not so; for a single entity cannot be said to be mutually pervasive"). Fan says:
"The selves of all sentient beings must be one in essence, because you admit they are closely joined and pervasive, like great empty space.

This term 'closely joined' excludes matter occupying the same location, for empty space is not 'closely joined' and thus does not constitute a single [unified] entity. (The proof asks: "What is the meaning of 'closely joined'? If it means forming a single composite, it contradicts your thesis.")

There is no distinction. Since they are conjoined yet not one, they occupy the same location; therefore, the term "intimate conjunction" (saṃyoga) is used [but] it adds nothing to the underlying principle. As for the statement that [the self] should be called the "experiencer of all that is produced," etc.:

When one person performs and experiences [karmic actions] through the three types of karma, it should be called "the performance and experience of everything belonging to my self," because each of the three types of karma is joined with all selves.
Consequently, when even a single body attains liberation, all persons and selves should attain liberation.
This is not like various lights, which each belong to separate lamps; for my self does not arise from separate bodies.
The middle [position] is also irrational (up to the point where it is said) "like the play of a child. The commentary states:

In refuting the existence of an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for those free from fetters (*vītarāga*), there are four difficulties: first, refuting expansion and contraction by means of permanence; second, refuting permanence by means of expansion and contraction;

third, [refuting it] because it follows the body and is subject to bending; and fourth, because that which is subject to bending is not a single entity. The logical measures (*pramāṇa*) are easy to understand, yet the child does not comprehend them.
This is trivial. It is like the play of a slave; there is nothing to be recorded.
Furthermore, it is irrational because [the objects] are not constant or uniform. The commentary states:
"To refute the proponents of the 'animal-mind' (獸主) and others. Jizang says: "The intent of the refutation is that [the mind] cannot move universally across all objects within a single kṣaṇa."
Because it is extremely minute, like an atom (*paramāṇu*). [The opponent] defends by saying: "It is not that we maintain the movement occurs over a long duration;

rather, because it is so rapid, it appears to move everywhere in a single moment. [The author] refutes this, stating that it is not a single, permanent entity, because it involves coming and going, like a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*).
Furthermore, regarding the self that is clung to as being neither identical to nor separate [from the aggregates], the commentary states:
Of the three subsequent views, this is the first, because it involves two types of clinging and is subject to refutation. The aforementioned three types of views are as follows.
Among the four types of yoga, the latter three are all subsumed under this "separation from the aggregates" (*skandha-vivikta*). "Separation" means being distinct [from them].

The Sāṃkhya notion of a self (*ātman*) involves volition (*cetanā*), yet it is not included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), because although it possesses volitional thought, it is asserted to be eternal.

The fourth [type of yoga] does not include this third conception; however, regarding the self-clinging of non-Buddhists, the *Four Essentials of the Pivot* (*Catuḥ-prakaraṇa-śāstra*) explains it thus. The third is the Vātsīputrīya school.

This is translated as "Vatsīputra" (The Calf). [In ancient times, there was a rishi who lived in a secluded mountain retreat. His lustful mind was insatiable, and he eventually consorted with a mother cow. A son was born, from whom the clan originated; this is one of the lineages of the Brahmins.]
"First, the self as the aggregates (up to) the real self is not established.

Commentary: This is the second refutation. There are four parts to the refutation of the self as the aggregates. "Lightning and so forth" serve as metaphors. The remaining formations and matter refer to the matter of the six external bases that are dissociated [from mind].
Since their logical measures (*pramāṇa*) are easily understood, they are not explained here. It is said that they are "inexpressible," whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Vātsīputrīya masters establish five dharma-treasuries: namely, the three time periods, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the inexpressible treasury (*avaktavya-kośa*).

Because the true self (*ātman*) cannot be definitively described as either conditioned or unconditioned, [Seng]fan says: "It is difficult to refute; there is no need to refute it through formal inference."
It is not permissible to say it is "not-self," for that would contradict the intended meaning. Jì (基) says: One may formulate the syllogism as follows:
"Your 'self' should not be said to be 'self,' because you admit that it is neither spoken of as conditioned nor unconditioned, like a tortoise's hair.
Cè (測) says: "'Self' refers to one's own self; 'not-self' refers to what is not another's self. This does not accord with the literal meaning of the text.
Furthermore, all that is clung to [up to] "both are unestablished.
The commentary states: This is the second major section, the subtle refutation. It has three parts; this is the first. Refuting the Sāṃkhya school:
[The Sāṃkhya claims] "the self possesses thought. [The response is: Your self must be subject to transformation and impermanence, because you admit that it does not possess thought at all times.
It is like the root of the mind. Ji [Kuiji] says: "Your self-substance must be subject to transformation and impermanence, because its activity sometimes arises and sometimes does not.
This is like [the case of] mahat and so forth. Such arguments for refuting the Vaiśeṣika school and others are easily understood through formal logic (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding all that is clung to [up to] "both are unestablished":

the commentary states that this refers to the second atom (*paramāṇu*). Jizang says: "There is no teacher who maintains that the self (*ātman*) is entirely useless; rather, it is according to what is appropriate.
One should understand that the Sāṃkhya school admits the absence of the function of movement and transformation, and these should be refuted individually.
Furthermore, regarding the self that is clung to [which leads one] to sink and wander in birth and death:

the commentary states that within the third subtle point, there are three [sections]: because it is difficult to refute, because it is refuted by formal inference (*pramāṇa*), and because it is the primary explanation. This is the first.

The intention of those authoritative scriptures is that although the view of self conforms to its objective referent, it is nonetheless a perversion because it conforms to defilement; therefore, there is no self.

The opposite is true. It is just like our own school [of thought]: although there is *tathatā* (suchness), if one conceives of it as being existent, this still constitutes attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

However, the "self" (*ātman*) they postulate is held to possess a real ontological essence (*svabhāva*), which differs from *tathatā*, whose nature is free from both existence and non-existence. Therefore, such is the tenet of that school.
The mental state and its object are contradictory.
Furthermore, regarding all views of a self (up to) "like other phenomena," the commentary states:

this is the second refutation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). An external opponent objects: "You take the true mind as your object, but you do not take true suchness (*tathatā*) as your object. There is [this objection].

Because of the object of cognition (*ālambana*). Just as when one cognizes other minds, the mind that cognizes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) does not cognize the storehouse consciousness itself.

The reason and the example are as stated previously. The formal inference (*sādhana*) is judged as follows: True Suchness (*tathatā*) and true gnosis (*jñāna*) are free from subject and object; therefore, they are not within the reach of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [since the cognition of an image would merely result in a circular argument].

Regarding the difficulty of cognizing the storehouse consciousness, the proof states: This is what is accepted by the Mahāyāna; thus, it commits the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for there is not even the slightest phenomenon [that exists independently].
Because it can apprehend others (there are further difficulties; those that are useless are not recounted).
Therefore, from the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) up to the arising of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).

[The] commentary states: This third section is the formal explanation; the text is clear and may be understood accordingly. Regarding "the arising of the marks of one's own mind," there are two explanations in the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot).
First, the characteristic of the image; second, the characteristic of that which is grasped. Although it lacks substantial reality, it appears before the mind;

because it is subtle, it is difficult to sever, as it is severed only upon its manifestation. Regarding the grasping associated with the manas, tradition holds there are two views. One says: first, the ālayavijñāna.
Because there are nine grades according to the karma that can induce [rebirth], the *manas* that takes this as its object has nine grades, totaling eighty-one grades.
However, this tenth [grade] is said to be "without coarse or subtle" because it is taught that the single path is severed based on the power of the hindrances.

One interpretation states that it belongs to a single stage and a single grade; it is called "without coarse or subtle" because this category of dharma has no distinct sub-grades, and karma merely causes it to be superior.

Inferior. Because it does not allow for coarse or subtle [distinctions], it is difficult to abandon through a single path; because it requires many skillful means, it is said to be "repeatedly" [abandoned], rather than being abandoned "repeatedly" [in the sense of multiple stages].
Regarding the view of self in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there are five Western (Indian) explanations.

First, it is said that because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is subtle—whether taking objects collectively or individually—it is suddenly severed by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), despite having nine grades. Second, it is said that collective objects are as previously described, while individual objects pertain to the [nine] stages (*bhūmi*).
1. [Some say] it is abandoned by the ninth path of the [final] stage (*bhūmi*), because its activity is subtle. 2. A third [view] says: collectively, as before;

individually, each of the nine grades of each stage is abandoned separately. 3. A fourth [view] says: both collectively and individually, each stage is abandoned by the ninth path. 4. A fifth [view] says:

both collectively and individually, each of the nine grades of each stage is abandoned separately. However, among these, the fourth is superior according to the Dharmapāla school. If it were like the first three, how could there be an Anāgāmin?

Because the fault of not exhausting the nine grades [of afflictions] would persist; for when a noble one (*ārya*) is born in a higher realm, they retrogressively sever those of the lower realms (this contradicts the seventh fascicle, which excludes only the *manas*).

If it were as the fifth master asserts—that subsequent non-outflow wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-anāsrava-jñāna*) should have no capacity to sever obstacles—then since there are distinct grades of delusion regarding the principle (*tattva*), correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) must universally sever them (this would contradict the *Yogācārabhūmi*’s distinction between mundane and supramundane paths of abandonment; the fifth master’s reconciliation that subsequent wisdom abandons refers only to the assistance provided by the Bodhisattva’s diamond-like concentration to the severance by correct wisdom). If one says...
That which is innate (*sahaja*) is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Why, then, does the *Laṅkāvatāra* state: "There are two kinds of view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*":

namely, the innate and the conceptualized (*parikalpita*)"? It continues: "Because the two kinds of conceptualized view of a self have first been abandoned, doubt regarding the Dharma does not arise. Cè (Ce) says:

"The statement that the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) abandons the innate [view of a self] is spoken in terms of its suppression and abandonment (*vibhava-prahāṇa*). Jǐng (Jing) says: "The Tripiṭaka Master examined the Sanskrit manuscript of the sūtra, and it indeed contains [the following]:..."

Regarding the middle character [of the term "anāgāmin"]: if translated literally, because the two kinds of views (*dṛṣṭi*) have been severed through discrimination (*vikalpa*), doubt regarding the Dharma does not arise;

one transcends the grasping of the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the *anāgāmin*. According to the five explanations in the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot), the first—the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—is the correct interpretation:

it involves the immediate and sudden severance of both the discriminative and the innate [afflictions], as well as their associated companions. (The other four are not mentioned here, as they lack any meaningful application. This is what is meant by "and so forth" (*yādi*).

Regarding "discrimination" (*vikalpa*): even if one hears the correct teaching, one generates a false understanding. For example, upon hearing that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is discriminated as and grasped as a self, [one might think] it exists only in the sixth consciousness.
This is because the other consciousnesses are shallow and subtle, and because they are continuous; whereas discrimination is coarse and violent, and characterized by interruptions.

Regarding the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) as taught in false teachings, Master Ji says: "This refers to the calculation based on the aggregates," for false teachings take the aggregates to be the self.
Regarding the "self-characteristic" (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) taught in the [non-Buddhist] teachings, Jñānaprabha states that it is a conceptualization [of a self] apart from the aggregates (*skandha*).

However, concerning the "reflection apart from the aggregates," the Tripiṭaka Master explains that it is like the reflection of a self that is omnipresent according to the Vaiśeṣika school and others; or it is the form of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu-rūpa*), because it is all-pervasive;

or it is the consciousness of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vijñāna*), as when one speaks of the two aggregates [of feeling and perception], excluding feeling, perception, and formations—one should reflect upon this accordingly. Furthermore, it manifests within the mind.

This refers to the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). Yuance states: "Although there are three interpretations, the *sabhāgatā* of empty space and matter is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) because it is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

Therefore, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is stated to be the correct meaning. [This is not accepted by us]. Even the reflection of a non-existent thing can function as an object-condition; how much more so the reflection of a conventional designation, which possesses substantial reality?

Furthermore, although the blue color of the space-element is indeed a real form, it is established under a distinct name and is thus termed a "conventional form" (*prajñapti-rūpa*), just like sunlight. That which is transformed from the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) serves as the objective substrate (*nimitta*) for the five sensory consciousnesses and possesses practical efficacy. It is also separately perceived as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

It does not take other stages as its object. Why? Because one wishes to see the consciousness that takes the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) as its object; therefore, [the ālayavijñāna] cannot be relied upon [as such]. Guanding says:

Since the locus of true attachment is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and its activity conditions are boundless, taking it as the self (through the view of self-discrimination) does not necessarily mean it takes that [consciousness] as its object. For instance, according to the Sāṃkhya school, they reckon the self to be volition (*cetanā*); since it is not constant deliberation, how could it be the fundamental consciousness?

However, that which the *manas* and other [minds] ultimately cling to is called the "locus of true attachment. Jñānagarbha says: "The shadow of a self apart from the aggregates is designated as the 'substantial basis' (*pratibimba*).

The mental aspect transformed by the mind is subsumed under the 'homogeneous class' (*nikāya-sabhāga*). Whether it is pervasive or non-pervasive, according to what each individual conceives, the similar aspect of a self appears to the minds of all sentient beings;

because it is neither matter nor mind yet manifests within the mind, it is called 'homogeneous. This interpretation is superior. Regarding the observation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), Jñānagarbha says: "This is explained in reliance upon the two vehicles and their modes of practice. As for the term 'persons'..."

[The Bodhisattva] abandons them. The Bodhisattva also universally abandons them by means of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). [Regarding the Bodhisattva’s Path of Seeing: if one names it according to its predominant function, it is called the "knowledge of the emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*), which universally abandons both obstacles; if one relies on its mode of activity (*ākāra*), [it is so named].

It must be understood that because one relies on the power of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) to sever [afflictions], it is said—based on its mode of activity (*ākāra*)—that they are severed by the emptiness of persons; this does not mean that the function of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is used to sever afflictions. The *Shuyao* states:

"Regarding the two views arising from heterodox teachings and heterodox thought, which are severed first among the three minds of the path of seeing? There are four interpretations. (This question is useless;

all afflictions are severed by the first mind, all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are severed by the second mind, and the third is liberation, wherein only the residual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are abandoned. Thus, the answer is likewise useless. As for the statement that "it may exist or may not exist":

Master Ki said: "The innate [self] definitely exists; the conceptualized [self] is not fixed. That which exists within the aggregates has substance; that which is apart from the aggregates lacks substance.
The sūtras speak of it based on its shadow, yet all take the aggregates as their object."
"If a real self does not exist... [up to] ...it is not within our own school.
Commentary: This is the first of the three sections in the third major division, which explains external objections. It consists of four formal inferences (*prayoga*).
In the later period, you would have no memory of past events, because the essence [of consciousness] would be no different [from before], just as it was in the earlier period.
Conversely, in the second case, mental activity would be eternal, because it is not separate from the essence, just as the essence itself is eternal.

Conversely, in the fourth case, as for the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), the locus of its teaching differs; it is either based on self-realization or the power of conceptualization, each relying on one side [of the argument].

By the power of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), one recollects the original object of focus. Consequently, at a later time, a mind associated with mindfulness (*smṛti*) recollects the preceding mind.

This recollection occurs entirely through the force of perfuming (*vāsanā*). Although the preceding phenomena are distinct, they serve as the basis for the subsequent mental state through skillful means;
even if the subsequent mind is distinct, it recollects other phenomena because there is a corresponding perfuming of both the object and the subject as appropriate.
"If there were no real self" (up to) "there is no contradiction in principle.

[The] commentary states: This is the second [point]. Regarding the meaning of the second formal argument (*pramāṇa*), Jñānagarbha says: "If the activity undergoes transformation, the substance must be impermanent."
"If I [do not truly exist]... [up to] ... falsely grasping it as a self.
Commentary: This is the third [point].
How can there be consciousness outside [of the object], since the principle [that such exists] is non-existent?
The commentary states: In the second major section, "Refuting Attachment to Dharmas," there are three parts, as they provide general and specific conclusions. This is the first.
[It concerns] that which is grasped by non-Buddhists (up to) what is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The commentary states: There are two distinct categories: [those of] non-Buddhists and those of the Hīnayāna. Each of these also has two parts: direct refutation and refutation by analogy.
The first of these also has two parts: the adherence [to the view] and the refutation [of it]. This is the former. That is to say, at the beginning of the kalpa, there were non-Buddhists.
He is named Kapila (formerly transcribed as Kāpila, which is erroneous). This means "yellowish-red," because his hair, beard, and facial complexion were all yellowish-red.

Later, his chief disciple was named Vārṣagaṇya (meaning "Rain"), so called because he was born during the rainy season; his followers were known as the Vārṣagaṇya heretics. In Sanskrit he is called Sāṃkhya, which is translated here as "calculation" (*saṃkhyā*). Calculation refers to the calculation of wisdom;
by calculating and measuring all phenomena, he gave rise to a treatise (*śāstra*) based on that calculation. Thus it is called Sāṃkhya.

Because it can produce the categories (*sāṃkhya*), it is called *Sāṃkhya* (the Fundamental Teacher’s Dependent Origination; as recorded in the *Yuanqi ji*). Those who compose the treatise and its auxiliary works are called Sāṃkhya masters (*sāṃkhyika*).

That school establishes twenty-five principles (*tattva*). The verse says: Self-nature (*prakṛti*), the Great One (*mahat*), ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*), the eleven faculties (*indriya*), and the true self (*puruṣa*).
Twenty-five; four, three, and two. Among these, the triad of *sattva* and so forth is called the principle of self-nature (*prakṛti-tattva*).

Formerly it was called "dark nature" (*mingxing*). When about to produce the "Great One" and the rest, it is also called "supreme nature" (*pradhāna*). It is called "supreme" because it is preeminent and ancient. It is capable of...
The root of birth and death is called the three *guṇas*. The *Sāṃkhyakārikā* states: "Joy is the essence of *sattva*; passion (*rajas*) is the essence of sorrow;
and darkness (*tamas*) is the essence of delusion" (that is, pleasure, pain, and equanimity). These constitute the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which truly exists, yet is subtle and invisible.
The opponent asks: "If it is invisible, how do you know it exists? The answer is: "One perceives the cause by means of its effects," referring to the effects such as the *mahat* and so forth.

Because it possesses three qualities (*guṇa*), one infers by analogy that its own nature (*svabhāva*) likewise possesses three qualities. Just as seeing blue clothing, one knows there are blue threads;
or as when the three years have increased [in intensity], it is able to subdue the other two, just as the intense light of the sun can subdue the stars and so forth.

When the Self (*ātman*) gives rise to volition (*saṃkalpa*) with the desire to enjoy objects, although it does not explicitly state "it is needed," the primal nature (*prakṛti*) transforms immediately. At first, there is a coarse aspect, which is called...

It is the Great Truth (*mahat-tattva*). At that time, there is as yet no differentiation of form and so forth. Once gross characteristics arise, it knows what the Lord requires and transforms the characteristics of form and so forth according to its own desire;
because it grasps the intention of the "I," it is called the "grasping of the I" (*ahaṃkāra*). It is also called "intellection" (*buddhi*) and so forth, because it grasps the intention of the "I.
Accordingly, it transforms color, sound, smell, taste, and touch; these are called the five *tanmātras*. "Only" (*mātra*) means...
"Definitive" means having a fixed limit; there are only five objects, neither more nor less, and thus these five are "only-objects.
The remaining sixteen arise because they must necessarily be experienced by the sense faculties and so forth. These are the five great elements (the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space).

The five faculties of cognition (*pañca-jñānendriya*)—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. What is their essence? The eye is composed of fire derived from form; the ear is composed of space derived from sound (and since both sound and space are unobstructed); the nose is composed of earth derived from fragrance; the tongue is composed of water derived from taste; the skin is composed of wind derived from touch.

The five faculties of action (*pañca-karmendriya*). As stated in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*: "Tongue, hands, feet, the organ of generation, and the organ of excretion. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Hands, feet, mouth, male, and female. The faculty of mental equilibrium (*manas-samatendriya*).

One interpretation says it is the consciousness-mind, for the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* states: "That which is capable of discernment is the mind (*citta*). Another interpretation says it is the internal mind, for it can take pure and subtle forms as its objects of contemplation. Some say the mind is composed of earth. Others say...
It is said that all five great elements are capable [of this]. When I contemplate a superior object, the three *guṇas* undergo transformation; I then experience it and am bound by that object.
Later, through wearying of the world and practicing the path, when I no longer contemplate, the *prakṛti* does not transform; being free from bonds, I attain liberation.

As for the statement "twenty-five, four, and three," the extensive version consists of twenty-five, the intermediate version consists of four propositions, and the abbreviated version consists of three; thus [it is called] the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*.
Treatise. The verse says: The fundamental nature is without transformation; the "Great" (mahat) and so forth are both fundamental and transformed;
the sixteen are only transformed; the Knower is neither fundamental nor transformed. Commentary: As for "fundamental nature," it is called such because it can give rise to all things.

Since it does not arise from anything else, it is not a transformation. The "Great" (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the five sense-objects—these seven are both fundamental and transformed. That is to say:

Because it can produce others and is produced from others. As for the sixteen that are merely transformations—namely, the five great elements and the eleven faculties—the "knower" is not originally a transformation;
this means that I cannot produce others and am not produced from others, as it differs from the preceding three.

The three [reasons] for this brief statement are: its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), its transformation (*vikāra*), and the fact that "I" know it. They maintain that the three entities, such as the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth, are substantially real (*dravyasat*).

This is like the Sarvāstivāda school’s theory of atoms (*paramāṇu*) forming the sense faculties (*indriya*). According to their system, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists of the five physical faculties, such as the eye, and the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) as its nature.
"That position is irrational" (up to) "it is not a synthesis of three. The commentary states:
In the second refutation, there is a general negation followed by a counter-question, which may be understood from the text. There are three specific refutations:

because of the refutation of the object to be established (*sādhya*), because of the refutation of the means of establishment (*sādhana*), and because of the refutation of both the means and the object. This is the first [of these]. There are three formal arguments (*prayoga*). Regarding that:
Regarding the thesis that jars and the like, although they are composed of many constituent parts, are not separate from them; therefore, they are real and not merely conventional.

Forests and the like, being separate [from their constituents], are accepted as conventional examples. The second formal argument states: "Your 'wholeness' (*mahat*) and so forth are not obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they are conventional, like an army or a forest.
Since the previous argument has already established this, it serves as a valid reason (*hetu*). In their own system, such entities can never be objects of direct perception.

It is obtained as a designation (*prajñapti*). It is not the same as the fixed nature of dharmas, for its objective condition (*ālambana*) is also a designation. Since it is established through inference from others, there is no fault of being indeterminate.

Master Ce, in discussing colors such as length and so forth, cites two interpretations from the West: one says they are subsumed under the real *dharmāyatana* and are not the objects of visual consciousness;

the other says they are like what is taught regarding the *rūpāyatana*, which is the object of visual consciousness (yet, in taking the actual principle, it is as explained in the *Mātṛkā*). Furthermore, he asks: "Based on..."

[Objection: Since the physical dimensions such as length and so forth are established based on the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), and names are likewise established based on sound, they should also belong to the sense-base of sound (*śabdāyatana*).
[Response: Among the twelve sense-bases, physical dimensions depend upon a single base, whereas names depend upon many bases; therefore, they are compatible [with the sense-base of visible form].

For example, the mindless meditative absorption (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) both depend upon the seeds of both mind and mental factors, yet they are classified as dissociated (*viprayukta*). [This argument is not logical,] as explained in the *Mātṛkā*: since the principle of length and so forth applies to the first ten sense-bases, and since the manifest [action] (*vijñapti*) already pervades both visible form and sound, [the same should apply here].
Because they are not associated [with one another]. The first and last two measures (*pramāṇa*) are not explained because they are easy [to understand].
Regarding the three, such as *sattva* and so forth, up to their synthesis into one:
the commentary states that within the second refutation of the "establisher," the first measure follows from the preceding [argument] to cause the three to be synthesized. Transformation is not...
Regarding the statement that "the same applies to the constant paradigm": according to that school, the three *guṇas* are the very substance of the *mahat* and so forth.
While the three *guṇas* are eternal, the *mahat* and so forth are impermanent; their impermanence consists solely in transformation (*pariṇāma*).

As for seeking that which is without arising or ceasing, the *Saptati-śāstra* (Seventy Verses on Sāṃkhya) states: "When opposing conditions are yet to come, it remains stationary for a time, like a mountain or a tree before a fire has reached it."

At the time of calamity, these [elements] temporarily cease to exist. If the fire-calamity has not yet arrived, at that time the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) dissolve into the five subtle potentials (*tanmātra*).
The five subtle potentials dissolve into the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), the ego-principle dissolves into fire, and the great elements dissolve into primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Therefore, the great elements and so forth are impermanent; primordial nature is not like this, for it is eternal and lacks dissolution. Herein lies the intended objection: "If [the self] were likewise..."
The three [elements], such as *pradeśa* (the locus), are non-eternal because they are transformations of the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*), just like the Great Elements themselves.
This is how the thesis (*pakṣa*) is established by combining the three examples. In the third section, the refutation through the relative nature of essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*kāritra*):

since the essence is the capacity (*śakti*), it should be manifold, just like the function (for in their own school, they admit that essence and capacity are identical, whereas our own school holds them to be neither one nor different). Briefly stated, as with the essence, the function should also be one (since they admit each is one...).

Transformation twenty-three (due to its manifold functions). Fourth, regarding the refutation through the relative opposition of place and time: when this substance transforms into this color at this location, it should likewise transform at other locations, because its essence is not distinct;
it would be just like this current location. Fifth, regarding the refutation through the relative opposition of the essence and its characteristics:

first, there is a direct general negation; second, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established as follows: "It is not logical that [the substance] should transform into a single characteristic at the time of conjunction. With...

Because their essence is no different when they have not yet conjoined; just as in the state prior to conjunction (according to that school), one [quality] increases its capacity to suppress the other two, just as the intense light of the sun suppresses the stars and so forth.

Therefore, it is incorrect to suppress this objection by treating it as a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). To subsequently refute it would constitute the fault of contradicting one's own tenet (*siddhāntavirodha*). One should understand that the identity of essence and characteristic (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-tādātmya*) is established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, these three are distinct [up to] being conceptually constructed (*vikalpya*) as existing.
The commentary states: In the third section, which provides a dual refutation of both the subject and the object, the initial general refutation says:

"Since the three virtues (*guṇas*) and the one Great One (*mahat*) are identical in essence and characteristic, the Great One should not be one, and the virtues should not be three. Following this, after a detailed refutation, they are successively negated and dismantled.

If you claim that these three factors originally possess two aspects—such that they are perceived as one in their totality, yet remain three when distinguished—and that the aspect is identical to the substance, such that the substance itself ought to be threefold, then how do you know that the three factors are distinct?

Your *sattva* and so forth would not be *sattva* and so forth, because they would possess all three aspects, just like *rajas* and the others. Furthermore, each individual quality (*guṇa*) would consequently become matter (*rūpa*) and the other elements.

Because they possess the three characteristics, just as when the three [factors] conjoin. If it is argued that possessing the characteristics is impossible because the substance is lacking, then each substance would have to be threefold, since the substance is identical to the characteristics.
As with the characteristics, the rest of the text is easily understood.
"Regarding what is grasped by the Vaiśeṣika school (up to) that which is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Commentary: The second [section], the refutation of the Vaiśeṣika, has two parts: the presentation of their tenets and the refutation thereof. This is the first.

It refers to the end of the *vivartakalpa* (the aeon of formation), when the human lifespan was immeasurable. A non-Buddhist appeared—[as stated in the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra*, fascicle 2: "These are all inconceivable bodhisattvas"]—named Uḍra.
Rūka—this is translated as "owl. During the day, he avoids the five desires and hides away in mountain forests; at night, when his sight and hearing have ceased, he then goes out to beg for food.
People of the time called him the Owl Ascetic (Rūka-ṛṣi). His hair was disheveled and his appearance was hideous; those who saw him were struck with terror and lost their wits.
Therefore, during the night watches, he sought rice from the husks and sustained his life by eating only that; this is also called the "Rice Vow" (*taṇḍulika*) or *Vaiśeṣika*.
This is translated as "Excellence Treatise" (*Shenglun*), for its discourse on the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) excels and differs from others.

He attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), which is to say he realized *bodhi*. As he was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he sought a successor to transmit the Dharma who possessed seven virtues. Jiji (Daoxuan) says: [text follows].
He is named Maṇava, which here means "Scholar-Child" (Routong). The Scholar-Child is also called Upatiṣya, which here means "Five-Crested.
This is because he has five crests on his head, as his hair curls in five directions. Cè states that the Scholar-Child had further disciples.

It is called the *Pañcaśikhīya* (traditions differ regarding its name). His wife was difficult to convert; the Rishi waited for her faculties to ripen, and only after nine thousand years did he finally convert her.

He composed the *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra-alaṃkāra-śāstra* to explain the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*): 1. substance (*dravya*), 2. quality (*guṇa*), 3. activity (*karman*), 4. generality (*sāmānya*), 5.

particularity (*viśeṣa*), and 6. inherence (*samavāya*). Although it has not yet been translated, according to the Tripiṭaka, the category of "substance" refers to that which possesses substantial reality.

The self-substance (*ātman*) is the basis for qualities and activities, as it can act as the sovereign. This consists of nine factors: earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, direction, the self, and the mind.
Of the four great elements, there are two types: subtle and coarse. The subtle ones are eternal in substance; they disperse during the kalpa of emptiness.

During the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*), two atoms (*paramāṇu*) combine to produce one "son" [a dyad]. This son enters into the measure of two atoms. Two sons produce a grandson, which gradually forms the great earth.
At the time of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*), it is gradually extinguished and returns to abide within its original atoms. "Space" (*ākāśa*) refers to the element of space (*ākāśamahābhūta*).
"Time" (*kāla*) refers to temporal periods. "Direction" (*diś*) refers to the ten directions. "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the true self. "Mind" (*manas*)—in Sanskrit, *anu-manas*.
This is called "subtle meaning. It is capable of producing cognition and so forth; it repeatedly revolves within the gates of the five sense faculties.

Its substance possesses physical obstruction and is incapable of cognitive reflection. Regarding the term "quality-phrase" (*guṇapada*): "quality" refers to the quality of the Path, the quality of the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
Because it possesses superior power, there are twenty-one such qualities: form, sound, odor, taste, touch, number, quantity, unity, difference, conjunction, disjunction, and beauty.

Ugliness; suffering and pleasure; aversion and attachment; folly and wisdom; diligence and indolence (on the land of the Snowy Mountains there was a master of treatises named Prajñācandra who composed the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*, asserting twenty-four virtues;

as these are not relevant to the present discussion, they are not recorded here). Action refers to the performance of karma; this is of five kinds, because of the movements of grasping, releasing, contracting, extending, and walking.

There are those who claim that "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) is a single dharma capable of causing real entities to possess their essential nature (the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* calls this the "Sentence of Identity").

Regarding the "Sentence of Similarity and Difference," there are many eternal dharmas capable of causing real entities, etc., to possess similarity and difference (the masters of the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* divide this into four).

1. The term "identity-and-difference" (ekāneka-pada) serves to differentiate dharmas. 2. The term "capacity" (samarthya-pada) assists the term "conjunction" (saṃyoga-pada) by enabling causes to produce their respective effects. 3. The term "incapacity" (asamarthya-pada) precludes the production of other effects. 4. The term "shared-characteristic" (ubhaya-bhāga-pada) is present throughout substance, quality, and action.

Because they are both identical and different, that which has not yet arisen and that which has already ceased do not meet with one another; they are ultimately non-existent in five ways. That treatise establishes this as the tenth "inexpressible category" (*avyākṛta-pada*), because there is no substance to be expressed. It is not included among the six categories, for those six exist only as [conventional] entities.
Regarding the "conjoined phrases" (*saṃyukta-pada*): there is one eternal dharma that causes the real entities (*dravya*) and so forth to be connected and inseparable.

As for the statement that "many have the nature of being real and are obtained through direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*), although there are many interpretations, let us take two meanings for now. First, it is said:

although all six [categories] are real, within the category of "real" (*dravya-pada*), because armies and forests are conventional (*prajñapti*), only the first five categories are obtained through direct perception; thus, they are common [to both].

This refers to "many. One interpretation states: "Many [attributes] belong exclusively to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they are obtained solely through the synthesis of one [attribute] with inference (*anumāna*) (among the ten categories, those of substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity are obtained through direct perception; whereas difference, inherence, capacity, and incapacity are not obtained through direct perception). The verses on the various positions refuted in this treatise state:

'The gross, the subtle, the great, the object, the obstruction, the gross, the great, the quality, the action, and transience (transience having the meaning of impermanence); the subtle, the self, and permanence.'"
Produced fruits (*janyaphala*). Other dharmas are the opposite of this. This fourth phrase applies generally to the preceding three.
That is to say, among the six phrases, the coarse four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the mind (*manas*) are obstructive (*sapratigha*); other dharmas are the opposite (all are non-obstructive).

Only the coarse four great elements and *dharma*, *karman*, and the impermanent are [produced]; the rest are all permanent. The subtle four great elements and the self (*ātman*) are permanent and produced fruits; the rest are not.
(The following section critiques the opponent's position; it should be explained accordingly).
Why is their tenet irrational? The commentary states:
Within the second critique, there are three parts—a general refutation, a counter-question, and an extensive refutation. This [passage] constitutes the first two.
"Among the various categories [of existence], up to [the category of] things such as rabbit horns.

[The commentary] states: Within the third extensive section, there are three parts: a general refutation of all categories, a specific refutation through mutual comparison, and a brief summary of the inversions.
The first part also has two sections. This is the first: the gate of whether permanent phenomena produce or do not produce effects; that is to say, "permanent."
That which abides in the dharma and is capable of producing an effect is the subtle four great elements (*mahābhūta*) in the state of true origination.

If there are auxiliaries, they consist of the conjunction of the mind (*manas*), the Great Existence (*mahāsattā*), and the specific universals (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). The inference is as stated in the text. (If one relies on the ten categories, those ten types of qualities that are generally permanent can also produce effects; however, they are not what is being addressed here, as they are not among the six [categories] under discussion.

That which is permanent and does not produce an effect consists solely of space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), and direction (*dis*). If it does not originate truly, although it may be associated with the Great Existence and the universals, it remains so.

They are different yet in harmony. However, since the reason (*hetu*) in the preceding formal argument stated that [the object] exists as a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and possesses causal efficacy, it refutes both the primary and the secondary positions.

Otherwise, that reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). (Tse says: "If the thesis were truly stated as 'it is not substantially existent,' one would immediately commit the fallacy of inconclusiveness by using *tathatā* [Suchness]. Therefore, it says 'apart from consciousness' [to avoid this]. )

No. Within his inference (*parārthānumāna*), there is no "unestablished" (*asiddha*) reason for himself; rather, he merely uses it to establish the meaning of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), stating that [objects] are not separate from consciousness.
"Regarding all that is impermanent... [down to] having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Commentary:
This is the second [section], the gate of the obstructed and the unobstructed regarding impermanence. That is to say, the coarse four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are impermanent and obstructed.

Virtuous deeds are unimpeded. He [the opponent] maintains that jars and the like are as real as the great earth, whereas armies, forests, and so forth, being divisible in substance, are not real and thus serve as analogies.

In the refutation of non-obstruction, with the exception of cognitions and the like, the remainder constitute the subject (*dharmin*); therefore, there is no fault of "contradiction with the thesis" (*pratijñā-virodha*).
Furthermore, regarding their attachment [to the elements] up to "real earth, water, fire, and wind," the commentary states:

The second section, which provides a specific refutation through relative analysis, consists of two parts: the refutation of their substantial existence and the refutation of their being apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The first part also has four sections: (1) the refutation of real qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karman*); (2) the refutation of the category of existence (*sattā*); and (3) the refutation of sameness and difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

Fourth, the refutation of the harmonious union (*saṃghāta*). There are three difficulties in the first [section]. This first one is the difficulty regarding the non-inclusion of real qualities (*guṇa*).

They maintain that solidity (*khara*) and so forth are distinct from earth (*pṛthivī*) and the other elements, yet they are included within the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) and are the domain of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

*Vyākhyāyukti* states: "The atoms of the parents are the sons of two atoms; they are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* states: "Only the son produced by three atoms is coarse and heavy."

"Concordance with qualities. The following explains concordance with coarse qualities, as these are apprehended by the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*). Cè states: "With the exception of [the quality of] conjunction (*saṃyoga*), all others are obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Zēng states: "Cè’s view is superior. That school does not claim that only what is apprehended by the material sense-faculties constitutes the object of direct perception.

For example, among the qualities (*guṇa*), such things as the cognition of pleasure and pain are not apprehended by the material sense-faculties, yet they are objects of direct perception. This is so.
Now, it is said that what is touched by the body-faculty (kāyendriya) only destroys coarse objects; since the subtle is categorized as being like the coarse, it should likewise be so.

To illustrate this refutation of the category of "substance" (dravya): earth, water, and fire should not be included within the category of "obstructive substance," because they are visible to the eye, just like the color blue and so forth. This should be understood through repeated application.
Furthermore, regarding their tenet [extending] to earth, water, fire, and wind:

the commentary states that this second pair concerns the difficulty of [proving] permanence for that which possesses resistance. If something possessing resistance were permanent, it would be difficult to establish as impermanent—this refers to the subtle four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the mind (*manas*).

As for that which lacks material resistance yet is apprehended by the sense organs of form, it is difficult to establish because of its commonality with qualities (*guṇa*), activities (*karman*), substances (*dravya*), and generality/particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

There are obstructions. In that school, the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are subsumed under the category of substantial entities (*dravyapada*): the eye-faculty is fire; the ear-faculty is space (Master Ji says:
when it perceives sound, it exerts its function within the body, and is thus called the "space-ear-faculty"); the nose-faculty is earth; the tongue-faculty is water;
and the body-faculty is wind (their subtle natures are all eternal).
Furthermore, that which they grasp [is like] empty flowers and so forth. The commentary states:

This is the third pair of arguments concerning the difficulty of [proving] the lack of intrinsic nature apart from consciousness. However, with the exception of cognition and so forth, other phenomena are taken as the thesis.

If one posits [the categories] such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth, it is a case of proving what is already established. Regarding "not being real qualities" (*na dravyaguṇāḥ*), with the exception of the first [category], the remaining five are the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Regarding "not being real substances and so forth" (*na dravyādyarthāḥ*), with the exception of the first [category], the remaining five are the thesis. The first thesis should be stated as: "Cognition and so forth are not real;
the other dharmas, such as qualities, must not have a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) existing apart from consciousness. As for the latter thesis, it may be stated as follows:

It is not the case that there are [terms] such as "cognition" (*buddhi*) and so forth among the remaining categories such as "substance" (*dravya*). However, for brevity, the distinctions regarding cognition, pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth have not been examined individually.
