By excluding each one in turn, there are six types of inference (*anumāna*). If two, three, and so forth are excluded, then there would be many types of inference;

however, since the force of the argument applies universally to refute all six, two types of inference are established by excluding the first [category], namely "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "nature" (*svabhāva*).
"That which they grasp as existing" (up to) "is merely a false conceptual construction.

[The Commentary] states: Next, the refutation of *mahāsattā* (Great Existence) is twofold: by means of formal inference (*pramāṇa*) and by means of logical objection (*codya*). Regarding the phrase "separate from reality," etc.:
One apprehends the conjunction of similarities and differences among qualities and activities; because this is a collective apprehension, there is no fallacy of uncertainty (*anaikāntika*).

The two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are as stated in the text. Next, the refutation is presented: "Just as your 'Great Existence' (*mahāsattā*), its essence is not non-existent, yet there is no separate entity that causes it to have the nature of existence.

The same should apply to [categories such as] substance (*dravya*) and so forth, since their own essences are not non-existent. If, apart from the dharma that possesses existence, there were a separate [entity] that..."

There is the nature of existence (*sattā*). It should be distinct from the five kinds of non-existence; otherwise, there would be no separate nature of existence [apart from those five] (as the Sarvāstivādins do not establish a nature of existence external to the Great Existence, but rather establish the "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) based on phenomena such as form, yet they do not establish a homogeneity upon that homogeneity; therefore, this is refuted by analogy). Paramārtha says: This is a refutation by means of inference (*pramāṇa*). That is to say:

Your "real existence" and so forth have no separate nature of existence, because you admit they are not non-existent, just like the nature of existence itself. Consequently, the five kinds of non-existence should also possess a separate nature of existence. There is.

Because within non-existence (*abhāva*), each is subsumed by one of the two [categories]. For example, as with "reality" (*tattva*) and so forth. (In this case, there are two faults: it does not accord with the treatise, and the logical reason (*hetu*) is fallacious.

That is to say, it would imply that the five kinds of non-existence possess distinct natures, which contradicts your own tenet; furthermore, the reason of being "subsumed by one of the two" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because, among existence and non-existence, each is subsumed by one. Would reality and so forth have distinct natures, like "existence" and "sameness-and-difference"? Or would they lack distinct natures?)

The Master [Kuiji] says: "If you claim that 'existence' (sattā) possesses a further nature, then there must be a distinct nature for that existence, because you admit it is not non-existent, just like real substances, qualities, and so forth.

One might argue that this is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) by applying the category of 'sameness and difference' (*tādātmya-tadutpatti*), but since this is not universally established, there is no inconclusiveness.

Furthermore, according to your tenth proposition, one would have to posit a distinct nature outside of non-existent phenomena; yet, apart from 'Great Existence' (*mahāsattā*) and the like, existence and non-existence are two mutually contradictory phenomena."

Therefore, [the opponent argues that] the qualities and activities as they truly are—[this is also not the case]. Even in a common inference (*sādharmya-anumāna*), one may encounter uncertainty due to other factors; how much more so in the present case of an inference based on difference (*vaidharmya-anumāna*), where there is uncertainty regarding identity and difference?

Thus, the subsequent refutation of the five types of non-existence is subsumed under the tenth category, which does not contradict our own school’s tenets and should constitute a valid inference (*anumāna*). However, because the five types of non-existence would render even "non-existence" itself non-existent, this contradicts the intended tenet and fails to constitute a valid inference (as the *Śāstra* text merely presents this as a point of refutation).

Master Ki explains the intent of the objection: Although the subject (*dharmin*) is not non-existent, it does not exist of its own accord; therefore, an existent must be posited. Yet, it follows that a non-existent phenomenon (*abhāva-dharma*) would not [be established].

"Non-existence" does not exist [as a thing]; one does not establish "non-existence" as something separate from the absence of phenomena. This objection remains constant; by what means can it be dispelled?

The master [Dharmakīrti] refutes this, saying: "The essence of an existent phenomenon is not non-existent; because it exists, it possesses the nature of existence. The essence of a non-existent phenomenon is not existent;

because it is non-existent, it lacks the nature of existence. Since these two are mutually exclusive, this response remains distinct [from the objection]. How then can you refute another? Therefore, in the present treatise:

"However, [the opponent] attempts to refute [the position] by means of a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) (which we now maintain is incorrect. For example, because there is no 'nature of non-existence,' existence exists; since there is no 'nature of non-existence,' it conversely proves that existence exists.

Just as when one objects that because there is no 'nature of non-existence' there must be a 'nature of existence' and thus existence is established, even though non-existence lacks a 'nature of existence,' it is only through having a 'nature of non-existence' that it is non-existent. This refutation is consistently uniform; how could there be no power to refute? Therefore, the present objection is a refutation, not a refutation by means of establishing a formal syllogism).

The *Shuyao* says: 'In the statement refuting existence, there are four [types]: first, contradiction with the self-characteristic of the dharma, etc. (This is incorrect, for it is one who has poorly formulated the syllogism who himself points out the fault). The *Guan* says:"
Apart from the five kinds of non-existence, there is no separate nature of non-existence, because it is subsumed under one or another of the categories of existence or non-existence.

For example, [the category of] substance (dravya) and so forth [as established by the opponent] is not established, because substances and the like are admitted to have no separate nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, that which they grasp [up to this point] should be understood according to this principle.

The commentary states: In the refutation of "sameness and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), there are two parts: refutation by means of formal inference (*pramāṇa*) and refutation by means of logical challenge (*codya*). This is the first. This consists of two examples:

the first is the refutation of "nature" (*svabhāva*) by means of "dharma. Regarding the distinct natures of "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth, termed "categories of sameness and difference," they formulate the following inference:

The nature of substance (*dravyatva*) is not substance, because it is different from substance, just like a quality (*guṇa*). The nature of quality is not quality, because it is different from quality, just like an action (*karma*).

The nature of action is not action, because it is different from action, just like substance. The Master of the Treatise [Dharmakīrti] refutes this in its entirety, stating that it is logically untenable;

let it not be so, for all these [arguments] would incur the fallacy of contradicting the self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*). The contradictory proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is as follows: According to your own admission, the nature of substance must not be [substance].

[The opponent argues: "Because it is different from reality (*satya*), [reality] is not of the nature of reality, just like a quality (*guṇa*). The same applies to qualities and activities (*karman*).

Furthermore, you do not accept that these three natures—reality and so forth—are not of the nature of reality and so on because they are different from reality and so forth. Secondly, [the argument] refutes the phenomenon by means of its nature (*svabhāva*):

namely, as with the previous reason, it not only contradicts the establishment of the nature of reality and so forth, but also causes reality and the others to lose their inclusion within the three propositions (*trikoṭi*). This is the formal inference (*pramāṇa*).

It is said: "You [the self] truly are not a real entity (dravya), because you differ from the nature of reality (tattva), just like qualities (guṇa) and so forth. Qualities and activities (karma) are likewise treated as mutual analogies;

thus, three categories are cited. Regarding the mention of "earth" and so forth: there are nine dharmas in the category of real entities, twenty-one in the category of qualities, and five natures in the category of activities.
Each is contrasted with its own essence (svabhāva) to refute the nature by means of the dharma, and to refute the dharma by means of the nature, following the previous method.
It should be understood. Question: Since you refute phenomena by means of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), stating that "earth is not earth," does this not contradict your own tenet?

Answer: There is no fault, because the "earth" you have conceptualized is not the actual locus (*pada*) of earth. Thus explains [Daoshi] the *Ji* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*). (The *Shuyao* further establishes the fallacies of *viruddha-hetu* [contradictory reason] and *viruddhāvyabhicārin* [counter-balanced contradictory reason].)
[The discussion] outside of the text regarding other theories is not what is required here.
[Regarding the passage from] "suchness" (*yathābhūtatva*) up to "merely a conventional designation" (*prajñaptimātra*):

the commentary states that this is the second refutation. On top of the conventionally established nature (*prajñaptidharma*), one does not establish a separate nature; it follows that there would be no [nature] at all on the level of reality (*tattva*).

[The category of] distinct nature (*anyathātva*). The same applies to qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karman*). If, apart from substance (*dravya*) and so forth, there were no real nature of "manifestation" (*vyakta*) and so forth, then apart from qualities and so forth, there should likewise be no real nature of "negation" (*pratiṣedha*) regarding substance and so forth. Since there is no separate manifestation, how could there be a difference? (This follows the meaning of the text). Cè says:

You claim that substance and so forth must lack a distinct nature, because you admit the existence of "sameness-and-difference" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). [Yet] it is like the nature of sameness-and-difference itself; you do not [admit] that substance and so forth are [merely] that.

There must exist the nature of being non-real and so forth, because within the categories of real and non-real, one must be subsumed under the other, just as with the nature of being real and so forth.

Since there is no distinct nature of negation (*pratiṣedha*) apart from the nature of affirmation (*vidhi*), we shall now establish its existence as a separate entity by means of formal inference, using the nature of affirmation as the illustrative example.
The Master [Kuiji] also establishes a formal inference (pramāṇa). (The meaning is the same as in the *Ceshu*).
Furthermore, that which they grasp [as existing] up to [the point mentioned] is also not substantially existent (*dravyasat*).

The commentary states: regarding the refutation of the phrase "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), the statement "because it is not subsumed under such dharmas as 'not being substantially existent' and so forth" does not refer to the Great [Element].
Because the five categories, beginning with "substance" (dravya), encompass all phenomena (dharma). The subsequent reference to "the reasoning mentioned above" refers precisely to this.
However, those [categories] such as substance, up to [the category of non-existence], are like the hair of a tortoise and so forth.

The commentary states: The second [section], the refutation of that which is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), has two parts: first, the refutation of the object apprehended; second, the refutation of the subject that apprehends. This is the first.
It is asserted that the six categories, such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, are objects of direct perception that exist externally to consciousness as real self-natures (*svabhāva*).

However, those five [objects] do not exist apart from consciousness; therefore, citing "tortoise hair" to establish that they are not objects actually establishes the opposite: that they are merely conditions not separate from consciousness.

The characteristics of the five sense-faculties and aggregates are not objects of direct perception (*pramāṇa*) and the like, yet they are omitted here and instead established through inference (*anumāna*).

Ciming says: "Excluding the 'feeling' category within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), such as the experiencing of pleasure and pain, he also admits that these are not separate from the mind."
Therefore, if one establishes [the thesis] by making it partially concordant with that [opponent's view], or if one avoids such partial concordance, there remains concordance with the following:

the thesis states that "reality and so forth are not only obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a real self-nature existing apart from consciousness. This is because the opponent admits that cognitions such as those perceiving pleasure and so forth also take reality and so forth as their objects;
they do not maintain that such cognitions obtain their objects solely by taking something apart from consciousness as their object. Thus, it is common [to both parties].
Because it excludes one portion of that which is apprehended as a whole, the term "total" (*sāmānya*) refers to that which is "separate from consciousness," rather than "only" (*kevala*).

This being so, this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) relies on either the apprehension of external objects alone or the total apprehension [of both internal and external]; by excluding one portion and taking as its object that which is separate from consciousness, it functions as a valid cognition.

Thus, there are no logical fallacies. (The views of Ki and Ce are identical. Furthermore, their commentary states: "If one did not say 'apprehending that which is separate from consciousness,' then it would belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), thereby incurring the two fallacies of contradicting one's own tenets and being redundant.")

This is an analysis based on a *karmadhāraya* compound; therefore, the term "cognition of the word" (*māna-ālambana-śabda*) is not essential. If one follows this precedent, then all forms of inference (*anumāna*), except for those that transcend verbal expression, would result in an infinite regress.
"Furthermore, [it refers to] the wisdom that takes reality as its object (yathābhūta-jñāna), up to the wisdom that accords with reality (yathārtha-jñāna)," etc.
The commentary states: This second section refutes the "attainer" (the subject). That which is attained is a single measure, while the attainers are six measures;

each has both general and specific aspects, and their manifestation should be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "arising through provisional conjunction," Master Ji says: when true wisdom arises, it conjoins with and takes reality as its object.
There is both similarity and difference. All cognitions that take qualities (guṇa) as their objects arise through conventional combination;

therefore, they should be understood like those [cognitions of universals], and are not subsumed under real cognition (*bhūtārtha-jñāna*). If one interprets it in this way, there is no cognition that takes a quality as its sole object that can serve as an analogy.

Because they must combine with conditions, there is "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and so forth; because there must necessarily be that which exists and that which is combined. Now, I shall explain this further:

"arising through provisional conjunction" (*prajñapti-saṃghāta-ja*) reveals that cognition arises only by depending upon multiple conditions. For example, when taking a real object as a condition, a provisional self (*ātman*) is produced;

this is because it arises from a multitude of conditions such as phenomena (*dharma*), non-phenomena (*adharma*), conduct (*caryā*), and so forth. According to the previous interpretation, the object must necessarily be manifold before [cognition] can arise.

Wisdom arises; it is subsequently understood that the object may be a single entity, yet it arises by depending on multiple conditions, and is thus called "arising through provisional combination" (both Cien and Mesei offer two interpretations:

one says it refers to the provisionally combined object of cognition, the other says it refers to the provisionally combined conditions for arising; the latter does not admit the former). The proof states: according to the first interpretation, it is simply from the primary conditions that it is termed "knowledge of existence" (*samvṛti-jñāna*).

Since it does not arise from multiple conditions, there is no fault [in this]. (The Master Ji raised an objection, but he did not understand the intent of the treatise and fabricated baseless arguments; therefore, his remarks are not recorded here.
When the treatise says "up to" (*yāvat*), it indicates that the refutation applies to all six [causes]; the concluding text is self-evident.
There are those who maintain [the position] from one [extreme] up to all [extremes], and all are refuted in this same manner.

The commentary states: This third refutation concerns the theory of a single cause. They assert that this celestial realm is the Dharma-body, which is eternal and omnipresent, and has no separate dwelling place;

whereas its Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) has distinct locations of residence. As for those things that are not eternal, they necessarily lack omnipresence. This refers to what was stated previously.

The proof has already been established. [If you argue that] "impermanence is the cause," the same applies to non-pervasiveness. Although the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body) is pervasive, it is not permanent;

how could there not be an "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reason here? Now, entering into their own school, we establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*); therefore, there is no such inconclusive reason.
As for the claim that "all phenomena must arise simultaneously in all places and at all times": since it is pervasive, why does it not arise in all places? Since it is permanent, why...
It would have to arise at all times and in all places where it does not currently arise, because its essence is without distinction [from that which arises].
If you claim that it does not arise all at once because it must depend upon desire (*chanda*) and conditions (*pratyaya*), this contradicts your own school’s tenets (Paramārtha says:

"the desire of Maheśvara"; Ji says: "the desires of sentient beings"; the former follows other treatises, while the latter holds that when conditions are present, Maheśvara initiates desire, and only then do phenomena arise). Even if one were to admit dependence on desire...

Regarding conditions (*pratyaya*): desire arises all at once as its condition, because that cause—Īśvara—is eternally and constantly present. As for the term "original limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*), it refers to the very beginning of the past.
Furthermore, there are not only causes such as prior karma (*pūrvakṛta-hetu*), but others as well; thus the treatise says "and so forth" (consulting the *Śata-śāstra-vyākhyā* and other works).
However, the names of the eight teachers who assert Īśvara and the like as the sole cause, along with their respective doctrines, are as found in Master Cè’s commentary.
There are others who hold biased attachments... [up to] ...because it depends upon various conditions. The commentary states:
This fourth section refutes the proponents of sound (*śabdavādin*). Regarding what is called the *Vidyā* (Knowledge), it was previously referred to as the *Yiṭuo* (Veda) treatise;
now it is called *Veda*. This means "knowledge. Because it explains the reality of all things, its principles are not fixed; other sounds contain errors and are not eternal.

Regarding the fixed measure: the Brahmins hold such a view. They claim that the one who recites [the Vedas] is Brahmā, but he is not their creator; only those of the Brahmin caste may orally recite and maintain them.
There are no separate written scrolls, and they do not permit members of other castes to recite them, even if they were to do so correctly. If they do recite them, it is not considered authentic.

Those who maintain that sound is manifested dependent on conditions are the proponents of the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti-vāda*). Those who maintain that sound is produced dependent on conditions are the proponents of the theory of production (*utpatti-vāda*).

Regarding the two types of manifestation theorists, one school maintains that each individual entity possesses its own eternal sound, similar to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as described by the Sarvāstivādins.

Second, the calculation that upon all things there is a single, common, and permanent sound—whether internal or external, in its entirety or in part—as in the *Yinming shu* (Commentary on Logic), which states:
"Because it is admitted to be a signifier (*vācaka*). Although the nature of sound is permanent, because it is not a signifier, there is no fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).
Regarding the phrase "other sounds," this refers to the remainder of the treatise. Ji says: "The nature of sound combined with [other factors] is called 'other sounds. One must not..."

Because the nature of sound is indeterminate, the thesis states: "Your sound is not the permanent essence of sound, because it depends upon various conditions and arises in response to manifesting agents;
the term 'only' refers to its dependence on conditions."
There are non-Buddhists who cling [to the view that] the substance [of things] truly exists.
The commentary states: Within the fifth section, the refutation of the Lokāyata (Worldly) doctrine, there are two parts: the presentation of their tenets and the refutation thereof.
This is the first. As stated in the second fascicle of the *Śata-śāstra*: "The Lokāyata non-Buddhists speak thus: 'All phenomena and their referents are the primary elements (*mahābhūta*')."

It is of the nature [of consciousness]. Apart from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is no other distinct entity (Cai says: "The essence within the four great elements is capable of cognitive reflection (*ālambana-cintā*); it is like the light of a lamp and so forth, unlike other things").

Regarding the statement that "words do not transcend the measure of causes": fundamentally, two atoms (paramāṇu) are eternally subtle; when they abide in conjunction at their sides and edges, they produce a single coarse form (rūpa).

Since these forms interpenetrate within the two atoms, it is said that [a new entity] does not arise. This is similar to the Vaiśeṣika school, yet it is also refuted therein, because below [the text] cites the categories of qualities (guṇa) and measures (pramāṇa) as a defense.
However, while the Vaiśeṣikas allow for other entities, this [system] maintains there are only the four great elements (mahābhūta).
This constitutes a difference between two schools (the Lokāyata school asserts that because there are only the great elements, at the time of death they return to the four great elements).
That too is irrational, [as it leads] to the permanence of atoms.
The commentary states: Regarding the second section on refutation, it is not difficult to understand through inquiry. There are three distinct modes of refutation:

by way of cause, by way of effect, and by way of both. This is the first. Cè (Cèlù) says: "Although the atoms of the Vaiśeṣika and the Lokāyata schools are minute, they possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*);

since their respective schools maintain this view, the initial [refutation] is a direct refutation, while the subsequent [refutation] is a refutation by means of logical measurement. Jī (Jì) says: "Both masters [Vasubandhu and Yaśomitra] maintain that atoms have no spatial dimensions."

Only the [Vaiśeṣika] system maintains that they are perfectly round; therefore, the former [passage] refutes this by way of negation, while the latter [passage] provides the formal proof for the refutation. Kuiji says:
"The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that atoms have no spatial parts (*digbhāga*), because the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra* states that they have no spatial parts.

However, the Lokāyata school does not necessarily hold the same tenets as the Vaiśeṣikas. (I now say: Ji’s interpretation is likely correct. Why? If the Lokāyatas maintain that all atoms possess spatial parts, how could the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) produced from them be admitted to lack spatial parts? If they did possess spatial parts, then the analogy cited in the treatise would be [inapplicable].)
[The reason] is not established.
Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the location where the produced fruit reaches. [Commentary:
Regarding the second refutation of the effect, there are two parts: the refutation based on the statement and the refutation based on the thesis. This is the first.
Since it does not transcend its cause, it should be like a single atom (*paramāṇu*). They [the Vaibhāṣikas] maintain that a permanent atom is not apprehended by the physical sense faculties;

rather, it is only when the colors of the "initial seeds" (*prathama-puṭa*) and so forth aggregate that they become objects of the physical sense faculties (as recorded in the *Ji* and *Ce* commentaries). The *Guangshi lun* (觀) states: "According to the *Daśapadārtha-śāstra*, the qualities of magnitude (*mahattva*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), and virtue (*guṇa*) are designated as 'magnitude' only when present upon the effect of three atoms.
Therefore, we know that the 'seed-atom' is not apprehended by the physical sense faculties and is not termed 'gross' (*audārika*). This serves as proof.

[The opponent] says: Although [the definition] relies on ten phrases, it does not conform to this treatise. Since it is stated that "resultant matter does not exceed the dimensions of its causes," it should—like an atom—not be called coarse matter (*audārika-rūpa*) and should not be apprehended by the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*). This would contradict your own tenets. It is clear, therefore, that what is produced is not "difficult-to-grasp" matter (*duranubhava-rūpa*);

rather, in relation to its parents (the causes), it is termed coarse matter, but this does not necessarily imply a large magnitude. Alternatively, it may be used in accordance with worldly convention.
The ten phrases are not the same.
If it is claimed that the resultant form (phala-rūpa) [extends] to false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*), the commentary states:
"The second [point] refutes this based on the tenet (*siddhānta*). That is, a single resultant form pervades both parents; however, that which is pervaded is not [the same as the pervader]."

First: That which is capable of pervading is called "coarse" (*audārika*); it is so named because it does not exceed two causes. Herein, inference (*anumāna*) is not explained because it is easy [to understand].
Furthermore, regarding the result and the cause: below, the two causes of the fruit-and-cause [section] obstruct one another while still allowing for the fruit.
As for the phrase "medicine entering molten copper," Cè (Cèlún) says: "Mercury and the like enter the molten copper and become gold (a similar gold). Jì says: "Brass."
Because the medicinal stone enters molten copper, [the opponent] asks, "Who allows this? and so forth. *Kui* (基) says that this refutes the [opponent's] intention.

[The argument is that the stone] merely enters the empty interstices within the sandy copper and does not enter its subtle essence (*sūkṣma-ātman*). Thus, the analogy is not established. Even if one were to grant that it enters the essence, it would either have to be separate from it or undergo transformation.
The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: Water entering the substance of sand should be separate and not one, because it enters into the midst of it, just like two grains of sand.

Regarding the intermediate space: just as these subtle particles enter between their parents, each individual particle must be distinct from the others, for you admit that they enter into the interval.

It is like water entering sand. As for the two particles of medicine and copper, their substances do not interpenetrate; yet, although they occupy the intervening gaps, the medicine causes the copper to transform.

Likewise, the color of the result should also arise through the conjunction and transformation of the ultimate atoms, because their mixed dimensions are identical. This is just as the medicine transforms the copper.
This means that in your own school, the atoms of the parents [the cause] are not one because they are separate, like sand; nor are they permanent because they undergo transformation, like copper.

Regarding the statement "not permitting [this] would contradict reason," etc.: if you do not permit that by obtaining the eastern part one obtains the western part, then it contradicts the aforementioned principle that the two (east and west) are a single measure.
If, however, you permit that by obtaining one part one obtains the other parts, then it contradicts what is directly perceived in the world.
This is the actual matter. By refuting their [claim] that there is a truly singular entity, one does not contradict the fundamental tenet [of our school].

In the Mahāyāna, according to principle, there is no truly singular thing, even down to a single atom (*paramāṇu*), for these are merely conventionally established. Refuting [the opponent's position] correctly based on this tenet is called "advancing";
refuting their subsequent attempts at rescue is called "retreating. This serves to conclude what preceded.
"However, as for the various non-Buddhists (up to) the differences of blue, yellow, and so forth.
[The commentary] states: This is the second major section, the refutation by categories. Since there are four propositions that universally encompass each category, this is the first proposition.
That is to say, all non-Buddhists concede that all phenomena possess two natures: first, the general; second, the particular. "General" refers to...

All phenomena do not lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Distinct" refers to the distinct natures of phenomena themselves and others. The phrase "existence, etc. includes "distinct nature" by way of ellipsis.

Since those general and particular natures are precisely the phenomena such as the "great elements" (*mahābhūta*), it is stated that there is the fault of contradicting inference (*anumāna-viruddha*):
because your great elements and so forth possess an intrinsic nature, they ought to have no distinction; consequently, this also contradicts your own tenet (*siddhānta-viruddha*).

Furthermore, regarding the world: they [the opponents] assert that the twenty-three dharmas are identical in substance and universally pervasive, which contradicts your doctrine that the three *guṇas* (qualities) are distinct in nature.

This is because, when these four categories are compared with one another, their existence is likewise equal. In the refutation of their distinct natures, the phrase "the nature of form" (*rūpa-svabhāva*) refers to the nature of transformation and resistance (*bādhanā*).

According to your theory of the five *tanmātras*, there should be no such things as blue and so forth, because they would be of the nature of form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the claim that they possess the nature of beautiful form incurs three faults:

contradiction with inference (*anumāna*), with one's own tenets (*svasiddhānta*), and with common worldly consensus (*loka*). Question: In the Buddha’s Dharma, are these two natures not inseparable from phenomena (*dharma*)? Answer: [They are not.]

Although it does not depart from phenomena, it is merely a conventional designation; because its specific and general characteristics are neither identical nor different, the two types of grasping at phenomena [exist] (up to) as objects that are not the domain of the eye and so forth.

The commentary states: The second phrase also entails three fallacies, because it is asserted that there exists a distinct "Greatness" (*mahat*) and "Commonality" (*sāmānya*) apart from the dharmas themselves.
Now, apart from these six phrases, no essence can be found. Furthermore, the quality of non-obstruction is not the object of the eye; thus, [the category of] form (*rūpa*) is not established.
There is no contradiction with our own tenets; the other cases should be understood accordingly.
Third, the position that holds the subject (*dharmin*) [to exist] is logically untenable.

The commentary states: The third point concerns the son of Nirgrantha (the Jaina), who goes naked. The Buddha censured him, saying he was "shameless" (*anapatrapā*), thereby avoiding the partial error mentioned previously.

Therefore, this admission that the two natures (*dvaya-svabhāva*) are also distinct from the phenomena (*dharma*) is made. The Master [Vasubandhu] refutes this, saying: "This is identical to the previous two cases. If one offers a defense, saying:

"The previous case concerned a difference in substance (*dravya-bheda*). The current meaning of 'difference' is that the two characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are contradictory; therefore, their substance must be distinct, just as in the case of suffering and pleasure (*duḥkha-sukha*). If one further defends this by saying:

"In the case of suffering and pleasure, although the substance and function (*svabhāva-vṛtti*) are contradictory and the meanings of 'one' and 'different' are distinct, their substances are not mutually distinct."

Therefore, next, [the opponent's position] is refuted because it contradicts [logical principles]. Next, it is refuted as follows: "The identity of the one and the different is not established in either case.
As the *Śata-śāstra* (Extensive Hundred Treatise) states in refuting this attachment: "The two types, 'one' and 'different,' are contradictory in their essential natures and characteristics;

yet to claim they are identical in substance is logically untenable. If they were one, it would not be one, because it is identical with the different. Just as with the different, if it were different, it would not be different, because it is identical with the one."

Therefore, since their natures and characteristics are contradictory, even if one were to grant that they share the same substance, then all your phenomena (*dharma*) would necessarily share the same substance.
If, however, "oneness" and "difference" are established through distinct conceptual designations, then, like the Buddha's teaching, they are merely conventional and not real.
Fourth, regarding the adherence to the existence of phenomena (*dharma*), one must not erroneously grant [the opponent's position].
The commentary states: This refutes the fourth alternative. Internally, it serves as a wholesome basis for producing sentient beings; in meaning, it is not false speech.

Yet, desiring to preserve one’s own life, one deceitfully engenders the trust of others through slanderous words and perverse livelihoods. To avoid the fault of contradiction, the established statement is that both are non-existent. Treatise.

The Master [Candrakīrti] refutes this, saying: "It would revert to the same fault as before. If it were not a case of 'neither-nor,' then since there is something indicated, it would necessarily be fixed [as one or the other].
If it were contradictory to the tusk [of the elephant], then negation would necessarily not be affirmation, and affirmation would not be negation; thus, your words would contradict your own tenet.
If it were determinately real, it would have to be designated as being neither identical nor different."

"Because the principles grasped by other vehicles do not exist [in reality]. Commentary:
This is the second major section, which refutes the attachments of the Hīnayāna. It is divided into two parts: a general refutation and a specific refutation. This is the first.

Since the mind and mental factors are the very substance of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), they are not refuted for now. However, the attachment to consciousness as being real will be addressed later.
Refutation by Example.
Furthermore, the form (rūpa) you maintain [to exist] is not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

The commentary states: there are three distinct points: because it refutes form, because it is non-associated (*viprayukta*), and because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The first of these also has [subdivisions].

Three: because of being with resistance (*sapratigha*), because of being without resistance (*apratigha*), and because of refuting both. The first [of these] also has three parts: because of the actual refutation, because of resolving objections, and because of restating the correct position.
The first [of these] also has two parts: because of the attachment [to a view] and because of the refutation [of that view]. This is the first [of those]. The Sarvāstivādins say:

The five faculties and five objects constitute "resistant form" (sapratigha-rūpa). Non-informative form (avijñapti) is non-resistant (apratigha). According to the Mahāsāṃghikas and others, that which is resistant is as previously described;
they state that the non-resistant refers to bodily vigor (kāya-vīrya) and bodily pliancy (kāya-praśrabdhi). The Sthaviras [assert] non-informative form to be an internal sphere within the chest.
According to the Sautrāntikas, the form that is the object of meditative concentration (samādhi-gocara-rūpa) is termed non-resistant.
"Because that resistant form (rūpa) [up to] is not substantially existent.

The commentary states: There are two parts to this refutation: the establishment of the thesis and the formulation of the reason. This is the first [the thesis]. Now, regarding this distinction between the provisional and the real:

Jizang says: Regarding the four positions, the Sautrāntika school holds that the ten bases are coarse and conventional while being subtle and real; the Mahāyāna holds that they are conventionally coarse and real while being subtle and conventional;
the Sarvāstivāda and other schools hold that both the coarse and the subtle are real; and the Ekavyāvahārika and other schools hold that both the coarse and the subtle are conventional.

All resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) are certainly not substantially existent. Each of these positions is contrasted with the Sarvāstivāda; however, if contrasted with the Sautrāntika, [the latter] allows that both faculties and objects are conventional.

Because it contradicts the [accepted] tenets, it cannot establish that atoms are substantially real; this is unestablished for at least one party within the Sarvāstivāda school, as evidenced by the Sūtras, and is therefore established below.
That is to say, it is established that atoms (paramāṇu) do not exist as substantial entities.

The commentary states: Within the second reason for this proof, there are two approaches: the gate of resistance versus non-resistance, and the gate of having spatial dimensions versus being without them.
The Sautrāntika school says: "Atoms possess resistance and also possess spatial dimensions, because they are material form (*rūpa*).

Although there is no obstruction when the atoms of the four sense-objects occupy the same location and interpenetrate, there is nonetheless tactile resistance, because atoms from two locations come into contact with one another.
The Vaibhāṣika school says: "Atoms possess neither resistance nor spatial dimensions, because they are subtle and spherical. [When] the four sense-objects..."

The atoms each abide in their own distinct locations; although they do not touch one another, there is still obstruction, because one location cannot accommodate another. Although there are many schools of thought, they do not exceed these two paths.

The arguments refuted in the treatise should be assigned accordingly based on this principle. As for the objection regarding the emission of shadows: since the substance of the aggregate of moving matter consists of atoms (*paramāṇu*), it must necessarily have upper and lower parts, and so forth... [it continues] until... it reaches... (Note:

Regarding the statement that "entry would not constitute grossness," this refers to the verse from the *Viṃśatikā-śāstra*:

"If an atom were to join with six [other atoms], it would have to occupy six locations; if it were to occupy the same location as the six, then a composite aggregate would be identical to a single atom.

As for the phrase "if that were so, it would not be obstructive resistance (*pratigha-sapratigha*)," according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there are three types of resistance: first, resistance regarding the object of cognition (*ālambana-sapratigha*).

This refers to: (1) the resistance of mutual obstruction (*pratighāta-sapratigha*), which pertains to the mind and mental factors with respect to their own respective objects; (2) the resistance of spatial obstruction (*deśa-pratighāta-sapratigha*), which pertains to the ten material elements (*rūpa-dhātu*) being obstructed from arising in a location occupied by another;
and (3) the resistance of objective obstruction (*viṣaya-pratighāta-sapratigha*), which pertains to the twelve elements and a portion of the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*).
That is to say, regarding those dharmas that possess objects, with respect to objects such as visible form, they admit only the aggregate to be obstructive resistance (*sapratigha*);
[if so], how could the five consciousnesses lack atoms (*paramāṇu*) as their bases and objects? For atoms themselves do not constitute obstructive resistance.

The commentary states: In the second section, the "Explanation of Objections," there are three parts: the general, the specific, and the conclusion. This is the first. Various followers of the Hīnayāna ask:
"If resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is not established, how can the five sense organs and their objects not exist? The Master of the Treatise replies:

"Although they exist as transformations of consciousness—namely, the eighth consciousness—it manifests through the causal conditions of form as the semblance of the five sense organs, such as the eye. 8.

And as for the five consciousnesses: by the power of the seeds of form, they manifest as transformations resembling the five objects, such as visible forms, which serve respectively as their bases and their objects.
Now, regarding the eye-consciousness (and so forth):
The commentary states: There are two distinct explanations, based on the support (*āśraya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana*). This is the first.

That is to say, although the fundamental consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness and meditative concentration are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they are certainly not so apprehended by the mind when emerging from concentration or during a state of distraction.

Rather, their existence as entities is known through inference based on their functional capacity (*śakti*). This is merely a functional capacity resembling form (*rūpa*) upon consciousness itself; it is not something produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) external to the mind.

Regarding the fact that external resistant matter (*bāhyapratigha-rūpa*) is not established as manifest, Wonch’uk states: "The Sarvāstivādins maintain that atoms (*paramāṇu*) and their aggregates (*saṃghāta*) are both real.

The Sautrāntikas maintain that atoms are real while aggregates are conventional (*prajñapti*). The Dharmaguptakas maintain that aggregates are conventional from the perspective of the sense bases (*āyatana*), but are real in substance from the perspective of the aggregates (*skandha*).
The Ekavyāvahārikas maintain that there is only conventional designation (*prajñaptimātra*). Since these various false conceptualizations are logically untenable, [the Mahāyāna...]
The explanation is as stated in the fourth fascicle.
These consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, [function] as object-conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The commentary states: In explaining the object-condition, there are two parts; this first section establishes the correct position.
That is to say, it is that which can induce [the arising of consciousness] with respect to this object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The commentary states: In the subsequent refutation of erroneous views, there is a general determination followed by a specific refutation. With the exception of the Saṃmitīya school, this [refutation] is certain for the other schools.

These schools claim that all consciousnesses necessarily produce an aspect (*ākāra*) resembling the object (which is the *nimitta-bhāga* of the Mahāyāna), and that they are able to produce an aspect resembling the object.

Regarding "those with whom one is acquainted": you all collectively apprehend that object which resembles [the cognition]; this is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the cognition that resembles it, because it is not merely that which produces [the cognition], but is the objective condition [itself].

Ji says: From this point downward, there are four sections refuting [erroneous] attachments. First, the refutation of the Saṃmitīya; second, the refutation of the Sautrāntika; third, the refutation of the ancient Sarvāstivāda. This is the first.

They claim that one does not establish a "semblance-image" (sādṛśyākāra) but directly apprehends the external object. The object merely gives rise to the mind, and this is termed the "object-condition" (ālambanapratyaya). Ce says:
The Master of the Treatise recounts the positions of various schools, asserting that what he himself establishes is not the same as theirs.
[The Sautrāntika] asserts it is correct, lest causes and conditions (*pratyaya*) and so forth also become objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
The Tripiṭaka preserves this [distinction], because the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are able to produce [their respective] five consciousnesses.

The commentary states: This refutes the Sautrāntika school. Because the Sautrāntikas wish to distinguish themselves from the Saṃmitīya school, they assert that the five [consciousnesses] take only the provisional characteristics of the composite as their objects, and that consciousness merely resembles those composite characteristics; thus, real atoms do not serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Because there are no atoms (*paramāṇu*) as objective aspects within the five consciousnesses. That is to say, an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) must necessarily possess two characteristics:
first, it must have substantial existence and be capable of producing the mind; second, its aspect must appear within the mind.

Those other schools claim that since [the atoms] can induce the production of a consciousness resembling themselves, they constitute the object-condition by virtue of producing the mind and manifesting their aspect. However, the Sautrāntikas and others lack the logical grounds for this definition of a condition. This is because...
Because it lacks substantiality, the Sarvāstivāda and other schools lack the meaning of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), as their characteristics do not manifest.

For this reason, the Master [Vasubandhu], following the sequence of the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, refutes their tenets based on the contemplation of the object-condition. Regarding the passage "The characteristic of combination... and so forth:

the established doctrine is neither fixed nor definitive, for he himself admits that it is not substantially existent (*dravyasat*). As for the passage "Since that characteristic of combination is not real... and so forth, he then proceeds with...
Refutation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): Because that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot project a reflection as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

As the verse in the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states: "When combined with the five consciousnesses, even if it is an object, it is not a condition. (The word 'even if' [設] implies that although it is granted as a non-real, conventional object, it is the domain of the five consciousnesses;

hence 'even if' is used. Because its substance is truly non-existent, it is like a second moon (the appearance of a second moon seen by one with cataracts). [Yogācāra Master] Ji says: 'It is merely like the previous case where the five [consciousnesses] do not have it as a condition'; this is because their school does not admit that the five consciousnesses [perceive such an object]."
Regarding the second month, according to the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* commentary by Master Ghoṣaka, there are two interpretations.

One says that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) apprehends it (based on this, as previously stated, it is merely an analogy for the five [sensory consciousnesses] and does not constitute the sense of being an object-condition; it is not posited as an objective support). Another says that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) also takes it as its object.

However, it is only when grasping [the object] as real and so forth that it constitutes the mental consciousness (manovijñāna). (Based on these two analogies, Ke, She, Suo, Yuan, Ji, Ce, and Bing all state: "Dharmapāla holds the former view, as in the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra*."*)
"It is not the object of the ultimate [consciousnesses], nor is it the object of the five sensory consciousnesses.

Commentary: This refutes the original Sarvāstivādins who wish to differ from the Sautrāntikas; [it shows that] what lacks intrinsic nature cannot be an object-condition. This refers to the state of conjunction (*saṃnipāta*).
Each individual atom mutually assists the others, each acting as a support-condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*) because it possesses substantial reality; yet, it is not a scattered atom.
Therefore, we now refute the theory that [atoms] are the observed object (*ālambana*) of simultaneous perception. As their verse states:

"Atoms, with respect to the five consciousnesses, may be conditions but are not observed objects, because the aspect [of the atom] is absent from the consciousness, just like the eye-faculty and so forth. In the refutation of the attempted defense, [it says]: "The aggregate..."

Regarding the "combined aspect" (*saṃhata-lakṣaṇa*): a single gross characteristic arises upon the various atoms (*paramāṇu*). This is because the two stages of the process of breaking down [the object] are identical to the atom.
Some maintain that [objects such as] mountains and so forth are the objects of this consciousness.

The commentary states: There are two [reasons] for refuting the new Sarvāstivādins: because of their tenets and because of their logical fallacies. This is the first. That is to say, Saṃghabhadra says:
"When atoms are dispersed, they are not the objects of the five consciousnesses. When they are collectively assembled, they all possess two characteristics:

first, the spherical characteristic of the fundamental atom; second, the characteristic of the newly assembled aggregate. For instance, when seven atoms combine, each of those seven coarse characteristics..."

It is equal in size to seven subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*). However, the seven subtle atoms do not interpenetrate one another, whereas the seven types of coarse characteristics do interpenetrate one another, as in the Sautrāntika school’s doctrine of the mutual inclusion of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*).

Nevertheless, those coarse characteristics do not arise or cease as entities distinct from the subtle atoms, because they lack a separate substance. Furthermore, these coarse characteristics exist only in the present; they do not exist in the past or the future.

The specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not identical because they are coarse; since consciousness possesses these characteristics, they serve as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for its essence.
Their [the Vaibhāṣikas'] position is incorrect, because it does not apply to all objects.
The commentary states: This is the second refutation. Regarding the claim that "the substance and its characteristics are one," the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

"The characteristics of the state of aggregation are not the objects of the five [senses], because they are the characteristics of atoms, just like the characteristics of dispersed atoms. Next, the characteristics of cognition are refuted:

"Just as when observing objects such as jars or bowls, whether large or small, the number of atoms that constitute them is identical; therefore, the characteristics of the cognition perceiving them [are likewise identical]."

[The opponent argues: "There should be no distinction [between the subtle and the gross], because their arrangement (*anupūrvī*) differs. Since the gross characteristics all resemble the general characteristic of arrangement, [the gross is established].
Next, [the author] refutes this, saying: "In each case, the original subtle spherical form (*parimaṇḍala*) must be abandoned. If you say it is not abandoned, then the gross is not established.
Since you admit that the atom (*paramāṇu*) is a sense-object of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), how can a cognition of a gross characteristic take a subtle characteristic as its object? If...

To say that the coarse aspect (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*) is identical to the subtle aspect (*sūkṣma-lakṣaṇa*), and therefore the consciousness of coarse activity-aspects (*sthūla-kriyā-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna*) is called "taking the subtle as its object" (*sūkṣmālambana*), is also logically untenable.

Otherwise, the consciousness of color-aspects (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna*) would have to be called "taking sound as its object" (*śabdālambana*). In that case, a single consciousness would have to take everything as its object. (This refutation of the "aspect of cognition" [jñāna-lakṣaṇa] is a refutation by means of a logical argument [dūsana], not a refutation by means of a formal syllogism [pramāṇa].

An objection is raised against the Mahāyāna: "Although black and white are contradictory, you admit that visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) perceives them simultaneously. Likewise, why not admit that it perceives the coarse and the subtle simultaneously?"
Although they are not identical, what fault is there in their being common objects? Although there is a difference between coarse and subtle, they both reside within their own respective domains;

whereas sound and so forth each have distinct domains, how can you use the example of coarse and subtle to prove [your point]? It is argued: although blue and other colors differ from one another, they are all coarse objects perceived by visual consciousness.

Atoms, however, are extremely subtle; coarse and subtle objects are not perceived simultaneously. A single atom is not an object for the five [sensory] consciousnesses; it is only when they are aggregated that they become so.

[The opponent] says: "It can be said that sound is a condition (*pratyaya*) for [visual consciousness], though it is subtle and not an object of the eye. They support one another, so it can be called a condition. (This does not fully capture the principle.

If they attempt to defend this by claiming there are coarse and subtle modes of activity—just as the sixth consciousness cognizes both the coarse and the subtle—then why not ask why other consciousnesses should likewise cognize other objects? This question arises from a failure to understand the intent of the treatise. That is to say, although the consciousness that takes black as its object also takes white as its object, it does not take white as its own object by means of the mode of activity directed toward black.

However, the current objection is that because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) apprehends a subtle aspect while the object is coarse, one might object that the mode of activity directed toward color-form (*rūpa*) should likewise apprehend sound and so forth. This is the question raised because the mode of activity and the object are different).
"Even if one grants the existence of atoms (down to) real atoms.

The commentary states: This concludes the third refutation. Even if one were to grant the existence of atoms, it would still lead to the aforementioned faults; how much more so when considering the actual meaning, wherein no real atoms exist.
From this, it is known with certainty that [the object] is not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
[The commentary] states: In the third section of the preceding gate, the correct view is presented. That "seeing arises dependent upon them" clarifies the meaning of the condition (*pratyaya*).

That "because a mind arises having an existent entity, it bears their aspect" clarifies the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana*), because the aspect manifests within the mind. Thus, a single aspect manifests instantaneously.

This means it is conventionally designated as "one" to distinguish it from a collection of many atoms; it does not mean it is substantially one, because if one obtains this [side], one does not obtain that [side].
Since it is not substantially one, there must be a principle for establishing the existence of an atom (*paramāṇu*).

Therefore, it is a conceptual construction and is not included among the categories of error. (Based on this point of large and small, Master Ki extensively describes two Western interpretations: one says that visual consciousness also takes shape as its object, and because it conventionally relies on the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the location, it is considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); the other says it does not take it as an object, as in the case of facing [an object]).

[This is] a record of the Dharma (and thus is not recounted here). Regarding the statement that "it still possesses spatial dimensions" (*fang-fen*): Sthiramati says that "dimension" (*fang*) is identical to "part" (*fen*).

If one discusses minute divisions, there are dimensions but no parts. The Tripiṭaka Master says: The third chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the atom (*paramāṇu*) is provisionally established; in reality, it is not provisional.

It perfumes [the consciousness] to form seeds; it is not because atoms (*paramāṇu*) are analyzed through conceptual construction (*prajñapti*). This is merely a figurative explanation. Cè says: "The current interpretation follows the treatise.
This is a conceptual analysis of conventional designations. Apart from the eyes and so forth, there are no separate atoms, just as with length and so on.
Just as when perceiving length and so on, one must necessarily perceive blue and so on, so too when perceiving atoms, one must necessarily [perceive them in conjunction with other attributes]."

The coarse characteristics manifest. Ji (Jinagupta) says: "Break them down half by half, gradually eliminating the coarse. (I now maintain that the Tripiṭaka Master Ji’s explanation is superior; for although atoms are subtle, [they still possess parts]).

That is to say, it is subsumed under blue and so forth, because its substance is substantially existent. When one analyzes its mode of activity, it takes as its object a single category [of color], because [otherwise] it would contradict the principle of the aforementioned coarse and subtle [distinctions].
"Other non-obstructive forms... (up to) truly existent form-dharmas. [The commentary] states:
This is the second major section, refuting non-obstructive form. The general refutation is as before.

Since the Mahāsāṃghika, Sthavira, and Sautrāntika schools maintain that there are various unmanifest forms (*avijñapti*), the first formal argument (*pramāṇa*) says: "That which belongs to this category [is form], because it is subsumed under the aggregate of form. — Mece.

[The Master] says: "The real matter (*rūpa*) of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is the same as the Sautrāntika school: it is entirely non-obstructive (*apratigha*). Question: "When earth is transformed into ghee or curd, how can it be non-obstructive? Answer:
"There are two kinds of transformation through meditative concentration (*samādhi*): first, that which is obstructive; second, that which is non-obstructive.

If it is matter belonging to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), it is non-obstructive. If it is transformed into matter belonging to the spheres of form and so forth (*rūpādy-āyatana*), it is obstructive. (This explanation is irrational, for [the latter] is formless.)

Since the elements (*dhātu*) and tears possess visibility and resistance (*sapratigha*), those elements should necessarily possess the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), because they are of the nature of form. However, as stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the *Yogācārabhūmi* says that they lack visibility and resistance. (As recorded in the *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā*).
"Because neither informative nor non-informative matter (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) can be apprehended.
[The author] comments: The third pair refutes both the resistant (*sapratigha*) and the non-resistant (*apratigha*). This consists of two parts: first, based on reasoning;

second, based on scripture. The first part also has two sub-sections: informative and non-informative. Regarding the first, informative [matter], within the informative matter of the body, the initial term "shape" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to...
This is also the view of the Sarvāstivādins. They maintain that the actual form constitutes bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).

To further defend their position, they argue that although form can be analyzed and divided, the nature of the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) of length and so forth exists substantially; thus, when these atoms aggregate into a form, they are designated as "intimation. [We reply:

Your long atoms must be refuted, for they would possess the same nature as length, yet like short atoms, they are spherical (*parimaṇḍala*) in nature. This is just as when one examines the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

Because they are equal in being infinitesimal, distinctions of shape exist only conventionally. When those [objects] are reduced to their ultimate atoms, the cognition of them is necessarily abandoned.
If one were to say that this is motion, it would follow that [the object] should not be subject to destruction.
The commentary states: This refutes the Saṃmitīya school. They claim that when the matter of karma first arises, it is called "birth";
its subsequent exhaustion is called "cessation"; and the interval between is called "abiding. As long as the activity has not been completed, there is neither birth nor cessation;

therefore, at the time of performing the action, there is a real sense of motion (for according to their tenet, momentary destruction is definitively non-existent). Master Ji says: According to the authority of the treatises, they lack the sense of real motion; as soon as it arises, [it perishes].

[It] ceases. Therefore, mind and mental factors [cease] (for they maintain that mind and so forth perish at the very moment of their arising, as they lack the quality of motion). They do not accept this, saying: "Because one or the other would be unestablished.
Next, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is: You claim that karma perishes immediately upon arising without depending on a cause, just like mind and mental factors.

The opponent further attempts to rescue his position by saying: "In the Sarvāstivāda school, the destruction of dharmas awaits the characteristic of destruction (*vināśa-lakṣaṇa*) and does not depend on external conditions;

however, in our school, the destruction of form and so forth depends on external conditions, and therefore we do not admit [that destruction is an intrinsic cause]. The author then refutes this, saying:

"The destruction you have established should not be considered true destruction, because it depends on a cause, just like arising (*jāti*) and the other characteristics. (The intent of this objection is that arising is contrary to destruction: it arises depending on causes. Destruction is contrary to arising.)

It would follow that [the entity] perishes without cause. These latter two measures (pramāṇa) are employed by the Master [Vasubandhu] to refute the opponent's arguments as they are successively offered in defense; thus, the chain of arguments is completely shattered.
If one says that there is form (rūpa), [it follows that it] is certainly not substantially existent (dravyasat).
Jizang says: This was the refuter of the teacher who propounded the theory of the sun's emergence.

One hundred years after the Buddha-dharma had departed from the world, there was one named Kumāralāta—translated here as "Child-Head"—in the country of Takṣaśilā in Northern India, who composed the *Navasatika-śāstra* (Treatise in Nine Hundred Verses).
Some composed the *Dṛṣṭāntamālā-śāstra*, collecting wondrous metaphors and stories, and were thus called the Dārṣṭāntikas (Piyūshi).
During the fourth century, the Sautrāntika school first emerged; taking that as their primary tenet, it was known as the "Original Sautrāntika.

At that time, one master appeared in each of the five regions of India, such that contemporaries called them the "Five Suns Appearing Simultaneously," and they were known as the "Sunrise Masters" (*Sūryodaya-ācāryas*); these are the ones now being refuted (Master Cè held the same view). However, [Fǎ]fàn...
The Master said: "To say that 'the rising of the sun' refers to the Dārṣṭāntika school is incorrect. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (122) states:

'The Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that manifest and unmanifest karma have no substantial reality. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: 'The Dārṣṭāntika school allows only volition (*cetanā*) to be the substantial essence of karma.
How could this be the position refuted here? The *Karmasiddhi-prakaraṇa* states: 'The rising of the sun [refers to] manifest karma.'"

It truly exists. How could it be that this school [holds such a view]? (This interpretation is reasonable. As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* on Karma states: "The Sautrāntika school holds that bodily intimation has shape as its essence; it is merely conventional and not real, because bodily karma has volition (*cetanā*) as its essence.

Regarding the statement "it should be known that it is not like the categories of visible form, odor, or taste": visible form, odor, and taste are not informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*), because they lack the quality of making known [an intention], and because they are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*).
They are like the wind element within the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
"However, with the mind as the cause... [up to] ...it is conventionally designated as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).

Commentary: This indicates the correct view. It is based solely on blue and other colors; that which appears to move is designated as "intimation. Following the goodness or evil of the mind, it is in reality only indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

By specifying "the transformation of consciousness into hands and so forth," it distinguishes this from the Sarvāstivādins and others. By specifying "a continuous succession of arising and ceasing," it distinguishes it from the Saṃmitīyas and others. It is merely an appearance.
The movement indicates the departure of the army;
the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is likewise not [inconsistent], as there is no contradiction in principle.
The commentary states: Cè says that within the exposition of vocal intimation, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (fascicle 15) states: "Śrāvakas produce sound over many moments."

A single word can be expressed by a Buddha’s sound in a single *kṣaṇa*. Based on this foundation, one should understand that [the arguments] refute all other [non-Buddhist] theories, with the exception of the Buddha’s own voice, because [those others] necessarily consist of multiple moments (*kṣaṇa*) and must therefore be conventionally designated as a continuum (*saṃtati-prajñapti*). The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"A single momentary sound possesses name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*), and expresses all phenomena. This differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Jue (測) says: "This is according to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)."

It is not the case that vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates [action]. This is because volition is solely that which is manifested (*vijñapyate*), and is not itself the manifestor (*vijñapaka*).

Rather, it is by means of color-form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) that internal volition is manifested. Consequently, among the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the Tripiṭaka masters, the volition that manifests [action] constitutes the fourth proposition.
Since [the thesis] is in fact non-existent, there is no logical contradiction.

The commentary states: "The second [section] refutes the existence of avijñapti-rūpa, saying: 'Your avijñapti-rūpa is also not substantially existent, because it is subsumed under the category of rūpa;

for example, like vijñapti-rūpa' (this reason of being subsumed under one [of the categories] may also be applied). Within the presentation of the correct doctrine, first there is a general indication, stating: "thought" (cetanā).

Regarding "vow" (*praṇidhāna*): Cè (Cèyùn) states that in this context, volition (*cetanā*) constitutes the essence of the vow. (As stated below in Chapter Nine: "The perfection of vow is itself wisdom. Furthermore, it is explained that the three factors of desire, excellence, and mindfulness constitute its essence.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The mind of a bodhisattva has the characteristic of resolute aspiration. However, concentration, the path, and ethical discipline are volition but not vows; the prātimokṣa and so forth are both volition and vow.

To encompass both the concentrated and the distracted, they are collectively termed "volition and vow," distinguished solely according to whether they are wholesome or unwholesome and their respective timing.
[It is] restricted. It does not depend on the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because the inferior cannot surpass [the superior].
This means that it is established either based on the state of "attainment" (*prāpti*) or the state of "increase" (*vṛddhi*).

The commentary states: there are two distinct explanations. This non-manifest (*avijñapti*) discipline (*saṃvara*) depends on the wholesome; non-discipline (*asaṃvara*) depends on the unwholesome. As for the bases (*sthāna*):
Regarding the two [types] within the intermediate [category]: as for "surpassing body and speech," Master Ji says it excludes those [actions] that cannot induce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*);
Master Guan says it excludes intermediate karma (this is incorrect, for the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there is also non-informative matter in the intermediate category).

At the time of experiencing the wholesome or unwholesome, the seeds perfumed by the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates the action reach the point where, upon the completion of conditions, they possess the capacity to either cease evil or perform evil; accordingly, they are named "wholesome" or "unwholesome."

Regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) and its "increase": prior to attaining Buddhahood, this excludes both the preceding and subsequent stages. That is to say, at the time of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), the seeds have not yet increased;
and after they have been relinquished, the seeds no longer increase. It is only during the intermediate period that [the seeds] increase moment by moment.
The seven factors increase manifold. Regarding this, the Sarvāstivādins maintain that at the first moment there is only one set of the seven factors;
by the second moment, another seven factors arise. Although the factors of the preceding moment have fallen away into the past, they are still possessed [by the practitioner].
In this manner, through successive transmission until the seeds are not yet abandoned, one attains what was never before attained;
that which was previously attained is maintained without loss, yet it does not manifest. Regarding the three meanings of the Mahāyāna, according to the school of Nanda, Master Ji says:

"In every moment, the substance of the seeds is newly produced and doubles. (Master Ce says: That school has two interpretations. One is as stated above; the other is that 'what was never before attained' refers exclusively to growth. They themselves maintain that the theory of growth is superior. If [it is] the Moon...

Regarding the meaning of the "Treasury" (the *Abhidharmakośa*), Xuánzàng says: "Although its essence does not increase, its functional capacity doubles" (Master Cè agrees with this). As for the doctrine of Dharmapāla, the two masters' traditions differ. Xuánzàng says:

"One takes only the newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*) [seeds], and does not employ those that are innately present (*sahaja*). This is because the power of the latter is insufficient compared to the former.

Ce says: This applies generally to both the new and the old [types of seeds], because their powers are equal and they together act as causes and conditions to produce a fruit.
However, within the Dharmapāla school, two interpretations are formed. One states: there are three types of seeds for the volition that serves as the means of seeking precepts:

The third *karmavācanā* further gives rise to two types: newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*) and transmitted (*saṃtāna*). Based on the aforementioned five types, the seven branches are provisionally established.

Upon reaching the second moment of thought, another two types arise: newly perfumed and transmitted. Based on the aforementioned seven types, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) is provisionally established.

This continues until they are relinquished, as the function increases in every moment (*kṣaṇa*). Cè says: "Volition (*cetanā*) is of four kinds: first, deliberative volition (*tulanā-cetanā*), which is the remote preparation (*pūrvaprayoga*); second..."

The fourth, the volition of the moment (*kṣaṇika-cetanā*), operates simultaneously with body and speech; however, only the third is designated as "bodily and vocal karma," while the other three are "mental karma.

Because the fourth is inferior in its movement of body and speech, and because it is associated with the mental states of deliberation (*prekṣaṇa*) and determination (*niścaya*), it is called "mental activity" (*manas-karman*). Mind...

while the body and speech themselves have visible form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) as their intrinsic nature, the karma of body and speech has volition as its intrinsic nature because it is the volition that initiates them. Question:

If the volition that initiates body and speech is what constitutes karma, then between the informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) [karma], which one is included? Master Ki (基) answers:
It is neither manifest (*vijñapti*) nor unmanifest (*avijñapti*). It is not manifest because it does not indicate [an intention] to others;

and the names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*), which depend solely on matter; and the three [factors]—life-force (*jīvita*), the two types of non-mind (*acittaka*), and mental factors—which depend solely on the mind.
"This state is neither different [from the basis] nor does it exist as a real entity. The commentary states:

This refers to the first type of inference (*anumāna*). If one establishes the argument separately, asserting that speech is distinct from matter and distinct from mind, there is an uncertainty (*anaikāntika*) in each case.

Second, there is form apart from form, and there is mind apart from mind; he takes this [position] as its opposite. (This [refutation] is certainly not otherwise. If one relies on this meaning, there is nothing that is not so.)

As in the refutation of the Vaiśeṣika claim regarding the coarse four great elements: if they possess material resistance, they should be breakable and thus not real; if they lack material resistance, then like the mind and mental factors, they should not have a real intrinsic nature apart from these [elements]. All such lines of reasoning are refuted in this same manner.

The mind and its mental factors have distinct essences and functions; however, because they are established as a collective whole, there is no fault [in treating them as one]. This is the intended meaning of this measurement: it is not that the mind and its mental factors are entirely different from matter, for they are admitted to be subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), just like matter and the mind itself.

Regarding the objection that the specific characteristics of those phenomena contradict valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is argued: "This [entity] must truly exist, because it is admitted to be included within the aggregates (*skandha*), just like form (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*citta*).

[Response: This is not so. Regarding this thesis of true existence, upon what basis is the reason (*hetu*) established? Because of the [logical] measure (*pramāṇa*). However, there is no fault in taking only gross substantiality as the thesis, because other things such as matter are not subsumed under substantiality, just as an army or a forest is not a real entity (*dravya*). The *Pramāṇa* states: "Conditioned factors dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) definitely exist as real entities, because they are included within one of the five aggregates of phenomena (*pañcaskandha*).
