The commentary explains: Both [of these] measures possess the fallacy of the "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*) due to others, and the example is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the opponent.

This is because the Mahāyāna accepts that matter (*rūpa*), mental factors (*caitta*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are conventional (*prajñapti*). [This argument] does not fully accord with reason. If, within those reasons, one excludes the Mahāyāna’s conventional matter, mental factors, and so forth, then because the remaining five aggregates (*skandha*) are subsumed under any one of them, and because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*kāritra*) are distinct, there would be no uncertainty.

Thus, it should be treated as a contradictory determination (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) regarding the non-applicability of the conventional; the remainder, being real, are not subsumed [under the same category], yet they are accepted as not being non-existent, just like a jar (*ghaṭa*), a forest (*vana*), and so forth. This is real yet conventional; the materials of an army depend on conventionality, and because they are conventional, all may serve as metaphors).

The commentary states: In the second section, the specific refutation contains three parts. Jiji says: The first refutes the original fourteen [categories] of the Sarvāstivāda.

because of the general inquiry, because of the brief response, because of the extensive refutation, and because of the presentation of the correct view. These are the first two [of the six].

Because the phenomena within one's own continuum currently possess substantial existence, and because past phenomena never arise again, the subsequent attainment of those phenomena would likewise be useless. Non-acquisition is not [the same as] acquisition, because they are established as contradictory, just as acquisition is subsumed by either one [of its two types].

The fourth section presents the correct position. Regarding "dharmas that can be accomplished," this excludes the faculties of others, as well as those within one's own continuum that have already been suppressed or abandoned.

As for the term "already suppressed," it refers to cases such as suppressing defilements through meditative concentration, or suppressing wrong views that impair wholesome roots. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says:
It is both accomplished and not accomplished; for while its essence is accomplished, its function is not. The *Viśuddhacandra* commentary states: "The treatise speaks of coarse characteristics.

The subtle afflictions within the intermediate state are likewise both established and unestablished, as in the case of the nine types of arising craving and so forth (one should understand from this that self-love cannot be suppressed;

Regarding the phrase "abandoned" and so forth, it refers to the permanent destruction of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), as well as the fact that at the time of attaining Buddhahood, they are discarded because their substance is no longer established.

Or [it is] that which is abandoned at the time of attaining a fruit, or lost during the stage of progress (*pratipannaka*), or at the time of abiding in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), because its function is not established;

such cases are numerous. Having excluded these, one takes all remaining seeds within one's own continuum, as well as those produced from them—the self and others' bodies and the environment—and all their manifest activities (*samudācāra*) as appropriate, and names them the three kinds of possession (*prāpti*). Fifty-two [categories]. When seeds (*bīja*) are divided into two and the manifest (*samudācāra*) are combined into one, the *Xiányáng* (Exposition) reverses this.

(That is, if a dharma has already passed, or is yet to come, or is presently manifest, it is not a non-acquisition).
Regarding the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*): the Tripiṭaka masters state that it is so called because one takes birth while adhering to various divergent views.

Since those who equally realize noble wisdom are "noble ones" (*ārya*), they are termed "co-born" (*sahaja*). Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* refers to the two assemblies of ordinary and noble beings as the "assembly of the differently born" and the "assembly of the co-born," respectively.
Those who have not yet perfected the various noble dharmas—such as the fifty-six [factors]—are so designated because they have not yet given rise to all [of them].

Regarding the stages of the supramundane noble dharmas (*lokottara-āryadharma*), the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is established [in the sense that] none of these [dharmas] are attained therein. furthermore, even though one has not yet attained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one is still an ordinary person. The *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot) states:

[This implies that] regarding the obstacle to the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), both the seeds and the manifest states are unable to act as obstructions; thus, compared to those [obstacles], they are "unobscured" (*anivṛta*). The commentary states: The second [section] refutes the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). This refutation consists of two parts: first, the refutation of one’s own school (*svasiddhānta*); second, the refutation of what has not been admitted. Regarding the first, the school’s own position states:

There is no *sabhāgatā*. The Master of the *Nyāyānusāra* offers a proof to resolve the first objection, stating:

Since the characteristic of cessation is non-existent, what fault is there in depending on non-existence? (This demonstrates that the present non-existent phenomenon is conventionally established by depending on a previously existent phenomenon.)

[This is] not the case. It is not that the absence of meaning at present serves as the basis for the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), because that very absence constitutes the essence of the characteristic of cessation. The *Guān* (Contemplation) states:

"Although this interpretation avoids the error of [implying] a dependence on the basis of non-thought, it contradicts the treatise’s statement regarding 'subsequent non-existence' and the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

Since that which has already ceased is like a tortoise's hair, it should not be considered conditioned. [This is incorrect. This refers to the time of "non-existence" (*abhāva-kāla*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "First, there is the characteristic of arising within a single moment; subsequently, within that same moment, there is again the fourth characteristic of the conditioned. The *Śata-śāstra* says: "That which existed originally but is now absent is called..."

"Cessation" is not stated because it implies that what previously existed later becomes non-existent. However, this treatise refers to what was previously present as "later" based on its current absence; since this later non-existence is not permanent, how could it not be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)? As the *Nyāyamukha* states: "That which was originally non-existent now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence."

Existence and non-existence are not permanent; therefore, they are called "impermanent. Since things such as tortoise hair are not eternally non-existent, [the following is said]: regarding the statement that "arising manifests a phenomenon that previously did not exist," the proof, question, and answer state:

arising manifests that which previously did not exist; when it exists, it is termed a manifestation. Cessation manifests that which subsequently does not exist; when it exists, it is termed a manifestation.

Arising is termed "existence" (*bhava*); the time of existence indicates prior non-existence. Cessation is termed "non-existence" (*abhāva*); the time of non-existence indicates subsequent non-existence.

This means that at the time before cessation, [the entity] does not yet manifest. (According to Dharmapāla, since the points of reference differ simultaneously, the indications are different. This differs from Śrīlāta, who holds that even within a single present moment there are prior and posterior phases.)

As it is said, because atoms possess spatial dimensions, that which arises first abides later. At the time of the prior phenomenon, the subsequent phenomenon arises; arising and abiding are simultaneous, such that cause and effect are continuous. This is like the path of abandonment being in the phase of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), while the afflictions to be abandoned are in the phase of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, how is it known [that names and so forth do not exist], and what is the purpose of naming them?

The commentary states: The sixth section, which refutes the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, consists of two parts: refutation and establishment. The refutation also has two parts: general and specific.

This is the first [the general refutation]. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: Your actual names and so forth are not real designators, because they are distinct from sound and are not real.

Because they exist, just like form (*rūpa*) and so forth. If an opponent were to object: "Your [categories of] provisional names (*prajñapti*) and so forth should not be expressive (*vācaka*), because they are provisional and not separate from sound, just like the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth," the proof states: Names and so forth are provisionally established as the function of expressing through vocal sound.

We concede that, apart from sound, there is nothing else that can express. Since this is consistent with our position, we are without fault; whereas you do not accept sound [as the basis for expression].
This would contradict both the authoritative teachings and common worldly experience, namely that sound can produce the *nāma-kāya*, *pada-kāya*, and *vyañjana-kāya* once they have already arisen.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the Sarvāstivādins maintain two positions: first, that sound produces the *nāma-kāya*, *pada-kāya*, and *vyañjana-kāya*, just as the sense faculties produce consciousness;

second, that sound manifests the *nāma-kāya*, *pada-kāya*, and *vyañjana-kāya*, just as a lamp illuminates objects. For now, we shall refute the category of production (*utpāda*), as manifestation (*prakāśana*) is not established. (Ji)

[The opponent] says: You admit that sounds such as "birth" (*jāti*) necessarily possess phonetic inflection (*vaṅka*). Since this sound with its inflection is what expresses the meaning, what is the use of postulating something distinct from sound?
(Master Cè [Cien] also agrees; however, this is not a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa-vākya*). It is a proof established by the proponent, yet it does not accord with reason.)
If it is claimed that there exists a distinct substantial entity upon sound [and so forth], the following is a specific refutation.
The Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) offers this defense: because "curvature" (*kuṭilatva*) is identical to "name" (*nāman*) and so on.

This refutes your claim regarding the substantial entity of a distinct category of form (*rūpadharmāntara*) existing upon color, which would have to exist because it is the curvature upon the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Just as with the "crookedness" of sound, the intent of the treatise is to conversely demonstrate that there is no real entity (dravya) existing apart from the crookedness upon the sound itself;

this is because it is a crookedness upon the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). This is like the crookedness of form (the underlying principle is the same). The proof states: the subsequent inference commits the fallacy of a specific property of the subject (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*).

That is to say, if sound were crooked, it would follow that it is not included within the category of a nominal dharma (*prajñaptidharma*) distinct from sound, because the reason and example are as stated before. [Now, we say this is not so; although the crookedness depends on...]

Names and so forth are conventionally established; however, they are not the names and so forth themselves because they are curvatures. "Basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the state of the curvature of sound belonging to sound. Based on this, one further establishes the "expressive portion" (*vyañjanabhāga*). How is this known? For instance, a single [vowel] sound expresses nine distinct meanings, as it consists of nine divisions through its curvatures.

This meaning is established in detail as explained in the *Mātṛkā*. Since the curvature is a curvature of sound and is not dissociated from it, the Master’s formal argument (*pramāṇa*) does not commit the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*).
If it is argued that [the expression] from "upon sound" up to "certainly cannot denote," Ce (Cai) says:

To refute this, he offers a counter-argument: "Internal sound (*antaḥśabda*), being a form of flexion (*vaṅka*), should also be unable to denote, because it belongs to the category of flexed sound, like the sound of strings or pipes.
Ji says: The intent of that rebuttal is that this flexion is the very essence (*svabhāva*) of sound.
Just as the term "curvature" applied to form cannot express the essential nature of form itself, by this it is known that there exists something distinct called "name" (*nāman*) and so forth.
Guanding states: According to their final interpretation, there are two kinds of curvature; that which can produce curvature is sound (*śabda*).

That which is produced as a "flexion" (*kauṭilya*) is precisely what is called a "name," etc. [The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Since this treatise says that the production of names, etc., must necessarily involve flexion, it is clearly known that that which produces the flexion is sound.

Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* says: 'The flexion upon sound is itself the name, etc. Clearly it is known that what is produced is a non-associated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Now, I fear this is not so; since flexion is established as being like strings or pipes, it is known that his intention was that the name is not the flexion itself.

Therefore, the Sarvāstivāda school holds two general positions: first, that the flexion of sound is itself the name, etc.; second, that names, etc., are further produced upon the flexion. This [position] should be like the former: the sound is not produced separately.]
Regarding the phrase "names and so forth": The *Shuyao* states that the Master [Dharmakīrti] formulated this as a "contradiction of the qualification of the subject" (*dharmiviśeṣaviruddha*).

[The opponent's position is: "Internal sound, through its bending and curving, is capable of producing names and so forth; it does not fail to produce names and so forth, because it is a qualification of the subject. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

"This internal sound of yours should not produce names, because it is a bending and curving sound, just like the sound of strings or pipes. [The *Guan* states: "The qualification of the subject subsumes the specific production of names and so forth."]

It is not a signifier (*vācaka*), because it does not produce names and so forth; since it is not a signifier, it is not like a pivot [which functions as a basis]. Furthermore, who says that it is definitively incapable of signifying?
There are two interpretations. *Ki* (the commentator) says: The above refutes the position of Dignāga; this presents our own school’s tenet, namely the Sarvāstivāda.
The Sarvāstivāda does not admit that external sound has the function of signifying, whereas the Mahāyāna admits it. This is because, for example, in a Buddha-field, [sound] can indeed speak.

This is because of the nature of the Dharma, as explained in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*. The two types of karma—bodily and vocal—each have three varieties: those associated with one’s own body, another’s body, and that which is not associated with a body.

Mental karma has only two varieties, excluding that which is not associated with a body (it is still called "karma" because the volition of the agent proceeds toward an object of action). Master Ce says:

[This] repeatedly refutes the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, which states that sound has three types—namely, internal, external, and both—and that "both" refers to the strings [of a musical instrument].

The sounds of flutes and other instruments are merely admitted to be similar to designators (*abhilāpaka*); they are not truly capable of designating, because names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) are comprised within the category of sentient beings.

(The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* refutes this, saying: "Just as a single atom of form is not admitted to arise depending on two great elements (*mahābhūta*), so too should this sound be. The *Nyāyānusāra* rescues the position, saying: "Who says that a single atom is produced by two great elements? This is merely stated in terms of causes regarding auxiliary conditions for the simultaneous sound.

Thus, the *Śūyao* states: "If this person were to expose their body, the Buddha-dharma would condemn them as shameless; [the opponent] avoids the aforementioned partial error [by claiming the sounds are not truly designators]."

Therefore, this admission is made: that the two natures and the phenomena are both identical and different. The Master of the Treatise refutes this, stating that it remains the same as the previous two cases. Suppose they offer this defense:
"The 'difference' in the former case refers to distinct entities, whereas the 'difference' in the present case refers to a distinct meaning; therefore, [the fault does not apply].

Next, he refutes the notion that the internal curvature possesses the capacity for signification. Someone says: "Because one perceives the curvature of great sound, just as one admits of internal sound."
Regarding the claim that "if sound can signify," [it follows that] only speech can signify.
Jñānasena says: He further defends his position by saying, "I grant that internal sound can produce names (*nāman*) and so forth; therefore, it possesses the capacity for signification.
It is not every kind of sound [that does so]. Since you maintain that sound itself is what signifies, then sounds such as those from wind-chimes should also possess the function of signification."
The essential point of the Mahāyāna is that wind-bells and the like must possess the function of signification because they have the nature of sound, just like the sound of speech.

(In the *Ceshu*, the phrase "among the tenets" [宗中] lacks the qualification "one's own tenet" [自宗], which would result in a contradiction with one's own position. Regarding the statement "this should be like that," Cè says: "The Master of the Treatise refutes this by means of a counter-argument."
This internal vocal sound, like that external sound, does not separately produce real entities of name, phrase, and phoneme (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).

[The *Guān* commentary states: "This also contradicts the distinct characteristics of external inferential phenomena (*bāhyānumāna-dharma*). This is incorrect, because there is a distinction between the subject (*dharmin*). The *Zhèng* commentary states: "It contradicts inference (*anumāna-viruddha*). Because the subject is the same, these types of cases are all 'contradictions of equal force' (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). The conclusion below states:
"If one argues that although wind and speech are both sounds, names are produced only from the internal because of the distinction between internal and external."
Why is it not permitted? Because the internal and external are distinct; only internal curvature serves as the expressive signifier.
By what reasoning can one definitively know that it is the "Beloved of the Gods" (the *śabda*) and nothing else?

The commentary states: There are three aspects to the subtle nature [of the argument]. First, the refutation of the external subtle; second, the internal counter-objection; and third, the master’s resolution.

This means that speech is what expresses, as is commonly understood by both humans and devas. That which is capable of expressing is distinct from speech itself; this applies only to you and no one else. As for the term "lover of the gods" (*devānāṃpriya*): [The original text continues with the specific logical analysis.]
This is a case of playing with the name. Only that which is beloved by Heaven can endure. Furthermore, it is said: "The foolish person plays with words, calling 'Heaven' [a deity];
it is like referring to a slave as a 'lord'. It is a playful remark, saying: "O Heaven! You are truly worthy of respect," and thus it is called "Heaven-loved" (*tiān-ài*).
"Heaven" here simply means "loved" (*ài*). (Other meanings are as explained in the *Shù* and the *Shūyào*, etc.)
However, because the three [types of names] are provisionally established based on vocal sounds...

[the commentary] states: Second, the establishment of "correct" [names]. A name (*nāman*) expresses its own nature (*svabhāva*), meaning its essential body; it does not express its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), for words cannot reach that level.
For example, when one utters the name "fire," although it expresses the essential body, it applies universally to all fire because it is a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The statement that "speech is also not identical to sound" clarifies that it is established separately as a non-associated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). There is an objection:

"Since length and so forth are material form (*rūpa*), names and so forth should likewise be sound. This is not so. Why? Ji (基) and Ce (測) state: "This relies on the refutation found in the *Mātṛkā* regarding multiple dharmas."

Cè (Chè) says: "Because it is exclusively an object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)," but this is incorrect, for the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) would also have to be [exclusively objects of the mental consciousness].

Jī (Ji) says: "Because it is of the nature of instruction (*deśanā*)," but this is incorrect, for sound (*śabda*) is also instruction. Jì (Jì) says: "Because that which is expressed (*abhidheya*) is manifold," but this is incorrect.

"Do not [claim] that there are many objects of cognition, for the mind is likewise [single]. The proof states: "This is not so, because the characteristics and functions are superior," as refuted in the *Gāthā-ṭīkā*.
Other meanings are extensively discussed in the *Xinji-ji* (New Collection Commentary). Regarding "other Buddha-fields," Jì says:

"As stated by Vimalakīrti, one may [perceive them] through light, exquisite fragrance, taste, and so forth; or through the faculties of touch, thought, and enumeration—all of these can be designated as provisional."

The three categories, such as the establishment of names (*nāma-kṛtya*), are also subsumed under the dissociated (*viprayukta*). The Hīnayāna does not admit the existence of Buddhas in other directions.

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states: Apart from these three thousandfold world systems, there must also be the appearance of Buddhas in other directions at times to teach and transform sentient beings, because there exist sentient beings among humans and devas, just as in this land.
Regarding the proof, [the author] uses the kalpas of formation and destruction (*saṃvarta-vivarta-kalpa*) here.

[The opponent] raises the fallacy of the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*): [We say this is not so]. Because it is one's own inference (*svārthānumāna*), the reason (*hetu*) should state: "It is admitted that those [entities] possess names and so forth. Since the opponent does not admit this, [the reason is not inconclusive].

Furthermore, the Mahāyāna admits the manifestation of Buddhas through arising and passing away; what is said here is that there is the possibility of Buddhas manifesting at various times. Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness. The *Jīliàng* (基量) states:

"Even upon light and so forth, there exist names and so forth, because they depend upon the faculties and desires of sentient beings. Regarding such sounds, the proof by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) states: "Light, fragrance, and so forth definitely lack names and so forth."

Because it is not sound, like space and so forth. [The opponent’s reason] depends on the specific capacity and inclination [of the audience], and thus fails to be established for at least one party. However, when one states "as admitted by oneself" (*svayam-abhyupagata*), it can still function as a valid reason.

Although the Master [Dharmakīrti] repeatedly provides refutations based on contradictory characteristics, this is not logical, as explained in the *Mātṛkā*. Since the original Mahāyāna sūtras ultimately constitute the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), and since the Buddha taught the Dharma through fragrances and other such means, the former syllogism is superior.
There are those who maintain that the *anuśayas* (latent dispositions) are not dissociated [from the mind].
The commentary states: This is the second major section, refuting the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravādin, and Kaukkuṭika schools.
According to the Mahīśāsaka school, if an opponent were to raise this objection:

"The *anuśaya* (latent dispositions) of the Mahāyāna should not be seeds, because they are designated as 'greed' and so forth, just like manifest greed and so forth," the [text] provides a decisive rebuttal: "They are seeds, not manifest greed and so forth, because they produce their own results, just like the seeds of rice or wheat."
The [position] that there exists something distinct [from the aggregates], up to [the claim that] all [phenomena] should be negated—[this is] stated as follows:

the third example refutes [the views of] the Saṃmitīya school, who hold to "non-loss" (*avipraṇāśa*) and "increase" (*upacaya*) (which are synonyms for *prāpti*, acquisition), and the author of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

Regarding non-informative precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) and so forth, the masters of the *Nyāyānusāra* [assert] the nature of harmony (*sāmagrī*) and other such unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), up to their actual unconditioned nature. Commentary:
The third section, the refutation of the unconditioned, has two parts: the refutation of attachments and the establishment of the thesis. The first part also contains...

2. Because it is general and because it is particular; this is the first [point]. Regarding the "three kinds": they are established through real dharmas (*dravyadharma*), provisional designations (*prajñapti*), and inference (*anumāna*).

Jñānaprabha says: "The cognition that takes a jar and the like as its object is not subsumed under valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it does not newly apprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a dharma, because it is not a means of crossing over [to certainty], and because valid cognition does not require mere stubborn adherence" (as refuted in the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*). He establishes a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) to refute [this view], saying: "You [who hold this view] do not..."
Regarding "for the sake of the Dharma": one should not grasp [it] as being a truly existent unconditioned nature apart from form, mind, and so forth (this is the thesis).

This is because it is of the nature of an object of knowledge, or because it is a nature manifested by form, mind, and so forth (these are the two reasons). There are four ways of being manifested: first, by means of form, like a lamp illuminating an object;
second, by means of mind manifesting mind, like the knowledge of others' minds; third, by means of form manifesting mind, like a [verbal] expression [manifesting] internal [intention].
Mind. Fourth, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are manifested by the mind; just as the mind takes form as its object, so too does the unconditioned.

It is manifested from that [mind] and serves as the receptacle for form and the other aggregates, because it is manifested through the non-arising of afflictions once they have been severed. It is like the nature of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which serves as a cause based on a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

If you raise an objection from without, saying, "You should not cling even to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)," [we reply]: Unconditioned phenomena do not exist apart from form and so forth;

the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is as explained by the previous examples and thus suffers from the fault of being inconsistent with the facts. For our own school also maintains that it is precisely form itself [that constitutes this nature].
Furthermore, [if it were as you claim,] space and so forth would not be non-pervasive.

[The author’s] commentary states: There are three parts to this section. First, the refutation of the Sarvāstivāda position regarding the identity and plurality of the three substances; second, the refutation of other schools;

and third, a brief conclusion of the refutation. Regarding the Sarvāstivāda, there are two interpretations within their own tradition, as found in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, concerning the substance of the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

One [view] says there is one [space] for each; another says there are many for each. The former is taken as the correct position. Now, that correct position is refuted by the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):

Your space must be manifold, because where it is conjoined with one [atom], it is not conjoined with the others, just like [the atoms of] form (*rūpa*) and so forth. (The commentaries of Jikishō and Sōtatsu agree on this; according to the *Śāstra*, it is also possible that [space] is among those conjoined.

This is because it is subsumed under whichever one [it may be]. If you attempt to defend [your position] by saying this is not so, then at the place where it is conjoined with one, it would also have to be conjoined with the others. This is...
In that case, all phenomena would have to be mutually pervasive, which contradicts your own tenet that resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) are not pervasive.

If you argue that the Mahāyāna is subject to this same objection, the explanation is as follows: we do not establish the number "one" in the Mahāyāna based solely on conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Because the essence of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is neither one nor many, it is metaphorically designated as "one. Because it is not [literally] one, there is room for distinction.
Regarding the doctrine of the Sarvāstivādins: concerning the atom (*paramāṇu*), one [teacher] says that space does not pervade the atom because the atom is a substantial reality (*dravya*).
Another says that even a single [atom] can be pervaded, because in their school, space is non-obstructive (*anāvṛti*); the latter is considered correct.
The Master of the Treatise refutes both [positions]. *Ce* says: "To form a single entity together is called 'intermixture' (*saṃkara*);

thus, the substance of matter (*rūpa*) would not be one. *Ji Liang* says: "The substance of space within matter would then be identical to matter itself, because there is no distinction in their location.
This is like the matter in this place; it is incorrect to claim that matter which is non-separate from its location is indeterminate. Since you lack...
Because this is an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), one cannot charge it with the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by means of that [example].

This is because the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that "the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of all material forms (*rūpa*) abide separately," and thus there is no instance of material form occupying the same location to serve as an inconclusive counter-example. If an opponent were to raise an objection from the outside, they might say:

"The same applies to *tathatā* (suchness). To explain: *Tathatā* is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Apart from the true realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), there is no other distinct entity; *tathatā* and the phenomena...
They are neither identical nor different. Because they are not different, their mutual interpenetration is admitted;
because they are not identical, their natures and characteristics differ in category and class, for it is logically necessary that this be so.
The commentary states: While that school generally asserts the refutation of two types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), this [text] refutes them as being of a single essence.
"Schools" refers to the five schools, namely those consisting of the four truths and the categories abandoned through cultivation; these exist in all nine grades across each stage. Master Ji says:

If there were only one school and one grade, then at the time when the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of a particular grade are severed, one would have to obtain the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the fetters not yet severed within that same grade, because their essence is one. It is just like that.

It has already been established. This is known by inference rather than through analytical discernment (the Master [Xuanzang] extensively set forth that school’s doctrine regarding the two types of cessation; it need not be recounted here).
If its substance were manifold, it would not be able to universally accommodate all things.
The commentary states: The refutation of the doctrine of multiple entities should be understood through inference.
The tenets held by other schools—from [the point] "up to"—should be refuted according to the preceding method.
The commentary states: Next, the remaining [schools] are refuted by analogy; that is, the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Kaukkuṭika all establish nine [categories].

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) consists of eight categories: first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); third, space (*ākāśa*); fourth, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); fifth, the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); sixth, the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*);

seventh, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); and eighth, the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*). (The formless aggregates are subtle; distinct from them are the unconditioned phenomena.)

The nine factors of the noble path (which ensure that defilement and purity do not become confused). The Mahīśāsaka school also establishes nine: first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); third, space (*ākāśa*); fourth, the unshakable (*āniñjya*); fifth, the suchness of wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma-tathatā*); sixth, the suchness of unwholesome phenomena (*akuśala-dharma-tathatā*).

The seven indeterminate dharmas are the suchness of true reality (*tathatā*). The eightfold noble path is the suchness of true reality. Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the suchness of true reality.
The Sautrāntikas and Dārṣṭāntikas establish three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), which lack any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The Vibhajyavādins establish four unconditioned phenomena:

namely, the three beginning with space (*ākāśa*), and the unconditioned dependent origination (as stated in the sūtras: "Whether Buddhas appear or do not appear, the dharma-nature of dependent origination remains eternally present").
"Furthermore, all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)... [exist] apart from mind and so forth. The commentary states:
"This refutes [the views of] the aforementioned schools collectively. Regarding the Sarvāstivāda:

they assert that the three unconditioned phenomena are not obtained through the six causes; therefore, it is said they have 'no cause. They are not obtained through the five fruits; therefore, it is said they have 'no [fruit].'"
As for the fruit, this unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entity is itself both cause and fruit; it is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because it is the fruit of liberation.
The verse in the old *Abhidharmakośa* states, "The unconditioned is neither cause nor fruit," which is erroneous.

The verse in the new treatise states, "The unconditioned has neither cause nor fruit," which is correct (in the Mahāyāna, the unconditioned is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*), as it is the fruit of realization; as an efficient cause and so forth, it does not obstruct any fruits).
However, the sūtras state [that these] do not truly exist as fixed realities. The commentary states:

Regarding the second point, the establishment of the thesis concerning the manifestations produced by the transformation of consciousness, two interpretations are discerned. The first says that all are substantially existent;

for if they were merely adventitious reflections of their own seeds—being provisional phenomena like "non-existence"—they would not be causal conditions. The second says that only True Suchness (tathatā) is substantially existent.

The seeds of the reflected image (*pratibimba*) are perfumed. When taking space and so forth as objects, they necessarily carry a semblance (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), which differs from the *Shuyao* [Essential Points] that asserts they are exclusively "solitary images" (*kevala-pratibimba*).

The points regarding gain and loss are as previously stated. Question: If an image, though conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), is subsumed under the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in accordance with its original, then it should also follow that an image, though contaminated (*sāsrava*), is subsumed under the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) in accordance with its original.
Answer: Since their nature and characteristics are neither identical nor separate, it is said to be unconditioned in accordance with its original. [However, regarding] bondage...

The understanding of these matters is vastly different. According to what is seen, they are said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*); yet according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), Master Ji says:

"This very *tathatā*, being free from all obstructions, is therefore called 'space' (*ākāśa*). Regarding the phrase "ultimate realization," this reveals that the path of liberation is termed "ultimate.
Realizing the four propositions means that, moment by moment, the wisdom of dual contemplation severs delusions regarding both principle and phenomena.

All possess the four paths, as there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1. Realization by body (*kāyasaṃskāra*) but not realization by wisdom (*prajñāsaṃskāra*). This refers to the subsequently attained path of liberation (*prsthalabdha-vimukti-mārga*).

[This is because subsequent wisdom manifests as a reflected image and is not termed "realization. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The fundamental essence is called realization; subsequent wisdom is called attainment, because it involves something to be attained. 2. Realization by wisdom but not realization by body.

This refers to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the fundamental essence. [This is because the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of this specific category has not yet been realized. 3. Realization by both body and wisdom. This refers to the path of liberation of the fundamental essence. [At this present time...]

(4) The fourth is the realization that neither [of the two] exists, which is the subsequently attained path of uninterrupted realization (prsthalabdha-ānantarya-mārga). [In a single moment, these four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are all present;

it should be understood that multiple moments of a single path follow this same principle. Non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is of two kinds: first, non-arising by nature, which does not exist in other schools;

second, non-arising due to the deficiency of conditions. This latter kind is further divided into two: first, definitive non-arising, which is held in common with the Sarvāstivāda; second, subsequent re-arising, which exists only [in the Sautrāntika school].
Regarding the existence [of these] in the Mahāyāna, the *Shuyao* states: "Space is attained by both ordinary beings and noble ones through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

True Suchness (*tathatā*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*) are attained only by noble ones. Regarding the two types of 'immovable' (*āniñjya*), there are two explanations (as distinguished in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*). Question:

Why is there only one type of analytical cessation for the three realms, while the cessation of the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) is divided into two kinds? If one distinguishes them based on the two types of sensation (*vedanā*)...

The same applies to the stage of scattering (*vibhūmi*). Answer: It must be attained through the antidotes of the upper and lower stages. The two delusions of the immovable [attainment] (*āniñjya*) and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*) are established separately.

Because the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*) universally abandons the defilements of the nine stages, it is established as a single *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and *tathatā* (suchness).

Within these distinctions, the false apprehension of emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*) is excluded; it is definitively non-existent, and no one asserts its existence. This excludes the Mahīśāsaka school’s [assertion of] substantiality.

Some say that "emptiness" distinguishes the illusory nature of the dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva) from the "real," and that this reality differs from the false inversions of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), which is termed "true.
This is not the same as the Mahīśāsaka school’s assertion that there exists a separate, real, and eternal dharma.
"Non-Buddhists and other vehicles (up to this point) also possess attachment to dharmas.

The commentary states: Within the section on "Refuting Attachment to Dharmas," this is the third major division, which concludes the refutation of non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna. This section contains two parts:

refuting their attachments and demonstrating the correct [view]. This is the first part. First, it refutes form, the non-associated formations, and the unconditioned, according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
[The opponent] says: "If external objects do not exist, by what condition is the mind produced? Therefore, [the author] refutes this in turn, saying:

"Your claim that the cognition which apprehends those external objects does not have color and so forth external to that mind as its apprehended object is because, like the object of cognition of this very mind, it is itself the apprehender."

That which is "cognized" is a collective designation for all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). They [the opponents] raise this doubt: "If that is so, is the object of cognition real? Therefore, they also state a formal argument (*pramāṇa*):

"It is not substantially existent, because it is dependently originated (*paratantra*), like a magical illusion (*māyā-kṛta*); for all schools admit that a magical illusion is not real. [The author replies:
If that is so, since the mind and its objects are both empty and without distinction, why is it said that "there is only consciousness" (*vijñapti-mātra*)? As for the... [text fragment ends].

The commentary explains: To eliminate what is clung to while preserving the dependent consciousness as being substantially existent is itself a clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), just like clinging to external objects.
However, all such clingings to phenomena [are understood] to be like illusory things and so forth.
The commentary states: The second [section] demonstrates the correct [view]. An external doubt arises: "If there is no object, by what means does attachment arise?

This is understandable according to the text. Regarding the dual and single attachments, they shall be explained extensively later. Previously, the "original thought of self" was referred to as merely the "aggregates" (*skandha*);

now, the "original thought of phenomena" refers to the "bases" (*āyatana*) and "elements" (*dhātu*). Jiji says: Because the self has the sense of "activity," it is called an "aggregate"; the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) lacks this.

As for the term "use" (*yòng*), [the commentator] Jì considers it "small" and does not mention the *dhātu* (realms) or *āyatana* (bases). Jī’s position is not so; he merely maintains that there is a substantial entity (*tǐ*).
Regarding the statement "because it is a calculation of dharmas," Jī says: "The manas definitely exists, while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) may or may not exist.

That which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) definitely exists, whereas that which is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) is not fixed. As for the phrase "therefore the World-Honored One said," this refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
"Thus, the non-Buddhists (up to) 'therefore it evolves appearing as that'. The commentary states:

This concludes the third major section, which briefly summarizes the refutation of the grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*). It also has two parts: the summary of the conclusion and the resolution of difficulties.

This is the first [part]. Within this, there are three sections, consisting of three types of gradual abridgments for the purpose of establishing *vijñapti-mātratā*. First, in opposition to external [views]...

Regarding the object (*ālambana*): this briefly clarifies *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), meaning that external phenomena do not exist; this refers to the deficiency of the sense of "conditions.

If the functional operation of conditions must depend upon a substantially real entity, then even if one posits the existence of non-existent phenomena, they still possess a substantial body as a direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*), because their reflection appears before the mind, like a second moon;
thus, the objective referent is not negated. Next, regarding other aggregates, this briefly clarifies *vijñapti-mātra*. [As for] the Sarvāstivādins and others...
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is permitted [to exist], as it directly takes the present minds and mental factors of others as its objective support (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, according to the school of Sthiramati, the Buddha’s knowledge of others' minds directly illumines the minds of others, as well as the eight consciousnesses of the Buddha's own continuum, which serve as direct objective supports for one another (as evidenced by the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, where the treatise records that the Buddha directly illumines them).
Now, according to the school of Dharmapāla, from ordinary beings up to the Buddha, all [consciousnesses] transform into images; therefore, this [theory of] establishment [is maintained].

Refutation by means of measure (*pramāṇa*). The term "those aggregates" indicates the eight consciousnesses of other bodies as well as the various consciousnesses within one's own [stream] that belong to different aggregates, such as those that are not objects of perception, like the three liberations (*vimokṣa*) and so forth.
Subsequently, he clarifies the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) by gradually simplifying the discussion regarding those belonging to the same aggregate. *Cè* (Chè) says:

"This refutes the Dharmaguptaka school, which asserts that when the mind perceives an object, it also perceives the associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*). *Jī* (Jì) says: "This refutes the aforementioned..."

The Sthavira and Dharmaguptaka schools maintain that mental karma (*manas-karman*) is capable of taking other [factors] as its object. The Mahīśāsaka school refutes this, asserting that when the mind takes an object, there are co-existent factors (*sahabhū-dharma*).
The Western masters (the Vaibhāṣikas of the West) state that the five aggregates co-arising with wisdom (*prajñā*) are called co-existent factors.

Furthermore, the five consciousnesses have the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) as their co-existent bases, because within the body, matter and so forth belong to the same category as the faculties. They are capable of...
The mental consciousness that takes [an object] as its condition relies solely upon the immediately preceding mind (*manas*).

Its support is non-material and cannot take what is simultaneous with it as its object. This is because the material factors within the body belong to a category other than the sense faculties. (The Mahāsāṃghikas claim that when the mind perceives an object, it can cognize both itself and others, just as a lamp illuminates itself and also illuminates others.

Their view of "directly illuminating others" is the same as the Sarvāstivādins; their view of "illuminating itself" is identical to the Mahāyāna doctrine of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), and thus it is not refuted separately. The Vātsīputrīyas claim that the *pudgala* perceives objects but is not cognition. Since the self has already been refuted previously, it is not refuted here). — *Ji* (Commentary).

It is said: Regarding the two explanations in the Mahāyāna, one states that even if the Buddha’s mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) can manifest the images of wisdom, the factors associated with itself (*svasaṃprayuktadharma*) are not its objects (*ālambana*).

Nevertheless, because the self-substance of the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is fully exhausted, it constitutes omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), which is the object of the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*).

The mind and its associates must necessarily share the same object as the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), because it is admitted that they each perceive [the object] individually. One interpretation states:

"It is also admitted that the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is associated with [and perceives] its own objects. This merely implies universal and direct perception; it does not exclude indirect perception, for it is called "universal knowledge" (*sarvajña*) because it manifests images within its own vision.
However, the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) and the associated mental factors share the same object as the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*);

they are said to have the "same focal object" (*samālambana*) because it is not necessary for both to be seeing portions to have the same focal object (the three meanings of "as it is" are explained in the *Mātṛkā*). The cited verse is from the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*.
There is one who raises this objection [up to the point where it] "appears as if evolving as an external object.
The commentary states: This is the second explanation of the objection. Within it, there are three parts: the formulation of the objection, the refutation, and the conclusion of the correct position.
This is the first point. The Vaiśeṣikas and other schools raise this objection: "External objects do not truly exist; it is the mind that manifests as their likeness.
Just as one might say that cow-hair manifests as the likeness of tortoise-hair—yet that which is likened to does not exist at all—how can you say it is 'like that'?
The meaning of the analogy here is this: if a person is impetuous and fierce-minded, resembling true fire, only then can one say, "This person possesses great power."

The same applies to the statement regarding a person carrying a heavy load and the ox; since there are no truly existent internal or external *ātman* or phenomena outside of the mind, upon what basis could such a metaphorical designation (*prajñapti*) rely, and to what would it correspond?
That objection is irrational, as it has already been refuted previously.

The commentary states: Within the second section on refutation, there are two distinct parts: first, the refutation of non-Buddhists; second, the refutation of the Hīnayāna. The first of these also has two parts;
here, the first is the refutation of real entities, which was already established as untenable previously. Master Ji says:

"The transformed appearances of entities possess the dharma of selflessness, because both name and characteristic are absent from the *paratantra* (dependent nature). 'Dharma' refers to that which provides a standard and sustains itself; within the *paratantra*, there exists such a dharma."

"I" refers to a sovereign master (*adhipati*). Within that which is dependent on others, there is no self (*anātman*)—this [statement] does not fully capture the principle, for the treatises state that there exist things resembling a self and resembling phenomena (*dharma*). For this reason, *Ce* says: "The five aggregates, which are a conventional self, serve as the basis for the semblance of a self.
This means that what is not a self appears as a self, and what is not a phenomenon appears as a phenomenon; therefore, one cannot say that while phenomena exist, there is no self (*dharmanairātmya*).
This [interpretation] is excellent. In this context, what is called a "common phenomenon"? *Ji* says: that which possesses the function of being wholesome or unwholesome is called common.

Regarding "Dharma" (this refers only to the protection of Dharma): Ce says that what resembles permanence is called "common Dharma" (this refers only to the self). Guan says that the subject and object resembling the aforementioned [self] as a sovereign, a norm, and a sustainer are [the meaning here] (this applies to both self and dharmas).

This reveals that the tenet of this treatise holds that there is only the semblance and no reality; however, for the sake of those with worldly attachments, it is permitted to call it "common Dharma."
"Because [the reason] is unestablished both in terms of its class (*jāti*) and in terms of its reality (*vastu*).
Commentary: This is the first of two points regarding the refutation of the "pseudo-reason" (*sādharmya-sama*) and the "common property" (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*) within the second [section]. Kī says:
"Category" (*jāti*) refers to "nature" (*svabhāva*). This corresponds to the term "identity-and-difference. As for the term "existence" (*mahāsattā*), it is not accepted here. Why is this known?

Because, in the context below, "virtue" (*guṇa*) and "category" are mutually distinct; if "existence" were accepted, since it is a single entity that is necessarily non-distinct [from them], it would fail to function as a logical reason (*hetu*).
Master Ce had two interpretations: the first agrees with this [view]; the second says that "existence" is taken universally.
There is a distinction between them. "Generality" (sāmānya) is indeed the substratum of qualities; this is its nature as both universal and particular, whereas the others are not so.

One takes three [categories] and excludes three [others]. (The first interpretation is superior: there is one universal nature that does not involve separation, whereas "generality-and-particularity" (sāmānyaviśeṣa) consists of multiple entities and is likewise separate from qualities.)
"Based on categories, it is conventionally designated (up to: it is not established based on categories.

Commentary: There are two distinct explanations. This refutes reliance on categories; that is to say, according to our own school, one must rely on a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) before one can speak of the similarity between a person and fire.
That [opponent] likewise must rely on the power of the categories of identity and difference (*tattva-anyatva*) before they can speak of such similarity.
Therefore, the refutation is not established. This is because, according to the proponents of ultimate reality (*paramārthika*), a quality does not belong to a genus (*jāti*).

If one were to insist that although there is no common quality within the genus, human beings can still be said to resemble fire, then water should also be called "fire," since it likewise lacks a common quality with it.

If you argue that while the genus of water is separate from the qualities of fire, the genus of humans possesses those qualities and thus may be metaphorically so designated, this too is not the case. [This is because] it is urgent...

When a person is joyful, even though they are separated from fierce fire, one still refers to that person as "fire. This is a case of a dual application [of a term] for the purpose of refutation, as can be understood from the text.
This is a figurative designation based on reality (upādāya-prajñapti); it does not establish [the object] by relying on [that] reality.
The commentary states: This refutes [the view] that what depends on a real entity is not shared. The two qualities of "person" and "fire" each belong to their own respective real entities.
If they are not explained as connecting through a common category (*jāti*), then—just as two specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) lack the sense of being shared—they would be equivalent to water.

This explains the fault regarding fire and so forth. If it is argued that because two qualities are similar, one metaphorically says "the person is like fire," [we reply that] in the world it is not said that a quality is like a quality;
thus the objection is fully answered. (The elaborate explanations of Cè and others do not accord with the text.)
Furthermore, [the claim that] a designation must necessarily depend [on a real entity] up to [the point where it] would not accord with correct principle.

The commentary states: This is the second explanation, which addresses the objection of the Hīnayāna. "Dharma" refers to its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); "that" refers to the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).

Although they claim it is realized by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not within the reach of the verbal expressions of inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*). Question: When it is said that all dharmas are... [inference]...

The measure [of the object] is inexpressible. How, then, can the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) be apprehended through conventional cognition? Answer: It is because one merely excludes the attainment of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that verbal expression is said to apprehend the common characteristic.
That is to say, inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*) merely gives rise to an understanding in accordance with names regarding the common characteristic;

it is thus conventionally described as "attaining" it. For example, the word "blue" refers universally to all blue things; when this word arises, it gives rise to a general understanding of "blue. (This concerns the meaning of the particular and common characteristics.)
This is as explained in the *Nyāyānusāra* and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* (need not be repeated here). Nor is it the case that [the conventional] exists apart from this. Cè says:

"If one were to posit a self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as a basis for the conventional by means of some other expedient outside of the self-characteristics previously described, then one would have to say that the conventional must necessarily depend upon the real (*tattva*).
Since this is not so, the conventional depends only upon the semblance (*pratibimba*). Jī says: "It is not apart from..."

Conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*) and verbal expression have a distinct basis beyond [the object itself], which is established as its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); this is what is called conventional cognition.

It is the basis for linguistic designation (the former interpretation of the meaning being superior). That which is beyond the reach of sound refers to the own-characteristic, because there is no possibility of it being reached [by words].

This is so that inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*) might not arise regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*. Cè and others say: "In this treatise, 'self' (*ātman*) refers to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*)."

Treatise: Within the ultimate reality (*yathārtha*), both specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) each adhere to their own essence as specific characteristics.
This is because they are exclusively present objects that are free from verbal expression (*nāman*).

Regarding the claim that "both the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*) are not specific characteristics," it is because the signifier cannot [express] that specific characteristic, and the specific characteristic itself is not something signified by another. As for the statement "resembling" refers to superimposition (*samāropa*), Jñānaśrī says:
Upon the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), one superimposes a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) that is a distinct entity dependent on others;

that is, one imagines a single form-characteristic (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) as pervading all forms. Therefore, it is called "superimposition" (*samāropa*). Cè (Chè) says: "It does not mean that the grasping of what is spoken of is itself termed 'superimposition.

Common characteristics such as blue and so forth are themselves dependently originated (*paratantra*). (The intentions of these two masters are the same. Regarding the claim that there is a universal conceptual characteristic upon the mental image, Guān (Guān) says: "To include it within the 'homogeneous' (*sabhāga*) is incorrect. Zhèng (Zhèng) says: "The fundamental dharma..."

Regarding the statement that "impermanence is each attached to its respective substance," these are all dissimilar. It is not the case that they merely appear similar through the mind of inference (*anumāna*).

This is because, upon the fundamental dharma itself, there is only the absence of an added characteristic (*āropita-lakṣaṇa*); it is not that the characteristics attached to the substance are entirely dissimilar.

[To hold otherwise] would contradict the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) taught in the sūtras and would oppose the Buddha’s wisdom. (This point is refuted at length, as in the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*). Master Ji asked: "Why is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of something not considered a grasping (*abhiniveśa*)? That is to say:

Question: Should wholesome minds and the like involve clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*)? Answer: Although wholesome minds and the like do not correspond to the actual substance (*bhūta-rūpa*) when compared [to it], they do correspond to its reflected image;
therefore, they do not constitute clinging. Clinging occurs precisely because both [the mind and the object] fail to correspond to the actual substance and its reflection.
"However, based on the transformation of consciousness (up to) the provisional designation of self and dharmas.
The commentary states: This third section is the concluding summary, consisting of the *Gāthās of the Ornament of the Mahāyāna*.

Although there are no real entities of self and dharmas external to consciousness, in contrast to the imagined state of mind which conceives of a self and dharmas as existing, one provisionally designates what appears as resembling them based on the aspects of the seeing and seen portions of consciousness.
"The aspects transformed by consciousness" (up to) "combine to form a single kind.
The commentary states: There are two parts to the explanation of this verse. The first three phrases have already been explained; now, the latter three phrases will be explained.

This involves briefly presenting the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Within this, there are two [sections]: because it determines the number and because it explains the meaning. This is the first [section]. Regarding the object...
Although the manifestations of its appearances are each of infinite kinds, its classifications by way of its own essence are only three.

Since the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) has many names, why is it specifically called "maturation" (*vipāka*)? It is because maturation is its predominant nature. To explain: this fundamental consciousness exists in three states.

First, the stage of being clung to as "I" (*ātma-grāha-ālaya*): with the exception of those on the eighth stage and above and the Arhats of the two vehicles, all other stages are called *ālayavijñāna*.
Second, the stage of the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma: excluding only the Tathāgatas, this applies to all sentient beings.

Third, the stage of maintaining the continuity [of existence] (*saṃtati-parigraha*): this applies to all stages and is called *ādānavijñāna*. Since the latter two apply to all three [stages], they are said to be "many."
Furthermore, the explanation in the sutras that "the three realms are mind-only" is intended to dispel the predominant attachments of sentient beings;
it refers to the intermediate state, excluding the states of expansion and contraction. In Sanskrit this is called *manas*, which is translated here as "mind" (*yi*). Its meaning is "to cogitate.

It is both constant and discerning, and thus specifically receives the name "mind. The eighth consciousness is only constant; the sixth is only discerning; and the five sensory consciousnesses possess neither quality.
Because there are four propositions (catuṣkoṭi), [the text] contains many meanings; [those that are unnecessary are not taken].
These three are all termed "perfuming so as to cause growth. The commentary states:

Within the explanation of the meaning of transformation (*pariṇāma*), there are two [aspects]: from the perspective of the cause and from the perspective of the fruit. This is the first. Although the causes are manifold, [this refers to the primary one].
Now, only the seeds [of the view of self] serve as the cause, because they are immediately capable of transforming and producing manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).
Neutral states lack the power [to do so] and are not retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*), for retribution is remote and difficult to induce. Master Ji says:

"The seeds of the perfuming of the view of self are not mentioned because, apart from these two [types of seeds], there is no separate entity; they are excluded from conventional designations and do not separately induce karmic retribution."
"The second is the fruit-as-transformer (not implying all).
[Commentary: This refers to the second fruit. Jì (Jinaputra) says: "This means that there is transformation based on conditions which is not the same as transformation based on causes;

that is, because the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) transforms into the image-division (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-division (*darśanabhāga*). The 'fruit' is thus the transformer; this is also an *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (locative determinative compound). The image and seeing that are transformed consist of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)."

It is not one; therefore, there are various kinds [of transformation]. (In this context, "causal transformation" (*hetu-pariṇāma*) correctly refers to the meaning of seeds producing actualities, while "resultant transformation" (*phala-pariṇāma*) correctly refers to the meaning of the actual consciousness transforming into the aspects and the seeing-part. Question:

When actualities infuse seeds, and when seeds produce seeds—within these two types of transformation, to which are they subsumed? Answer: Both the production of seeds from seeds and the production of actualities from seeds are subsumed under causal transformation, because seeds possess the capacity for transformation.

Both the production of actualities from actualities and the production of seeds from actualities are subsumed under resultant transformation, because actualities possess the capacity for transformation.

Regarding "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), although there are distinct meanings—wherein seeds are also causes for the manifest and the manifest is also a cause for seeds, each possessing two types of transformation—because these would become confused, the Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang] retained the former as the correct interpretation.

Based on this, Kuiji states that the mention of the "seventh and sixth [consciousnesses] perfuming" is intended to clarify that the perfuming agents are also causes of transformative manifestation; this is not the primary meaning. (Treatise Record). Next is the realization of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). This is discussed in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and other texts. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

If they were to offer this defense: "The intent of the cited teaching is that it is called a causal condition because the perfuming causes [the seeds] to increase; thus, wholesome and unwholesome karma manifest so as to bring about their fruit."
"Various seeds increase. Good, evil, and indeterminate [dharmas] should have causes and conditions.

Below this, there are five points refuting Nanda. First, because he challenges the fundamental tenet; second, because he refutes divergent theories.

Therefore: (1) to state the correct principle; (2) to refute the opponent's position; (3) to apply the correct principle three times; (4) to resolve contradictions; and (5) to provide a summary. This is the first [point]. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states:
Your initial untainted state (*anāsrava*) should not arise, because it lacks causes and conditions, like a rabbit’s horn, etc. [The opponent] offers this defense:

This reason is unestablished in at least one respect. [The opponent argues that] the contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors perfumed by the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Because it is subsumed under either the outflowing (*sāsrava*) or the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), just like the non-outflowing. If one were to allow that the non-outflowing gives rise to the outflowing, there would be two faults:
first, the fault that a Buddha gives rise to what is outflowing; second, the fault that the wholesome gives rise to the unwholesome. Jñānagarbha says:
The opponent says: Not so. Because of superiority and inferiority, that which is inferior can serve as the cause for that which is superior; it is not because [the cause] is non-inferior.

If that were the case, then the unwholesome (*akuśala*) would have to be the cause of the wholesome (*kuśala*). Furthermore, if things that are contradictory could serve as causes, then the wholesome and so forth would have to be the seeds of the unwholesome and so forth.

This is universally illogical. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: The first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) should be an untainted seed, because it acts as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The entity that arises is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it is subsumed under the untainted (*anāsrava*). This is like the subsequent case of the "contradictory certainty" regarding the characteristics of realization of the untainted.
It is said that the first arising of the untainted is not from untainted seeds, because it is subsumed under the initial arising of either the tainted (*sāsrava*) or the untainted.

It is like the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*). [Now it is said: This argument commits the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon; since the first arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*) arises from seeds of the same nature, the reason and the example are like that. "Because they are [those who] engage in conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*), they are called 'Primordial Purity' (*mūla-viśuddhi*).
The commentary states: "The second [section] refutes divergent doctrines. Master Ji says: All false conceptualizations are termed *Vibhajyavādin*;
this is translated as 'Proponents of Conceptual Analysis. These consist of four schools: Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Gokulika."

(The *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra* states: "These four [schools] hold the same view as the Vibhajyavādins, that the nature of the mind is originally pure. Cè says: "The *Mahāvibhāṣā*, fascicle 27, mentions the Vibhajyavādins."
The defilement and purity of the mind are like those of copper vessels and the like; they are states of impurity and purity.

Since there is no pure perfuming, yet [defiled states] arise from causes, the Master of the Treatise now cites [the opponent's position] together with a refutation to prove his point, stating: "All that is incorrect is termed conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);

[The school’s] calculation is entirely identical to that [opposing] tenet. In refuting the notion that the mind is pure within [the state of] defilement, there are four fallacies: First, the fallacy of contradiction regarding the essence itself: if the characteristics are defiled while the nature is pure, they would be identical in their transformation, which implies permanence.

Second, the fallacy of the confusion between the two natures (parikalpita and paratantra): because they share the same pure nature, it would follow that what is spoken of as being like a "defiled mind" and so forth would not have a nature that is non-outflow (*anāsrava*).
As for the claim that its nature is not non-outflow, that has already been established previously; thus, the nature of all minds is not [merely] non-outflow.

[Otherwise, there would be] the fault that the uncontaminated cause would be identical to the three contaminants, because they would share the same contradictory nature. [Furthermore, there would be] the fault that ordinary beings and sages would be indistinguishable;

for if that school admits the existence of uncontaminated seeds, why would it require the actualization of the intrinsically pure nature as the cause? Cè (Cè) says: "In that school, there are two causes:
first, the causal nature (*prakṛti-hetu*), which is the uncontaminated seed; second, the triggering cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), which is the intrinsic nature of the mind. (However, that...)

It is not permitted that the seeds of the eighth consciousness exist without a basis. The proof states: Since those minds of the three natures are currently defiled, they are not untainted (*anāsrava*);
yet, because their fundamental nature is pure, the seeds perfumed by them become untainted. These seeds can produce both the tainted and the untainted;

when the untainted first arises, it takes these as its cause (for although those originally pure seeds have previously produced the tainted, the newly perfumed seeds are perfumed by the tainted, and the initial path lacks [the capacity for] direct [production]).
The uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) causes and conditions are refuted by analogy with the position of Nanda. The *Shuyao* states: "The Mahāsāṃghika and other schools do not establish seeds (*bīja*).

Here, we refute the doctrines of certain teachers of the Mahāyāna. Alternatively, the Mahāsāṃghikas may hold that the state of being about to arise (*utpatsyamāna*) constitutes the 'seed,' which differs from the Sautrāntika view that there is a distinct entity called a seed.
Or perhaps they refer to non-associated latent dispositions (*viprayukta-anuśaya*) as 'seeds'—this is incorrect, for [the text] speaks in contrast to the Vibhajyavādins."

Regarding your treatise: how do you know that this refutes the meaning of the Mahāyāna masters? Although the fundamental purity of the mind is the same for all, what fault is there in the fact that the Sautrāntikas differ [from others] regarding the existence or non-existence of seeds? Alternatively, if that which is about to arise is called a "seed," why speak of it as a seed [at all]?

The nature of their manifestation is identical; by using the manifest as an illustration for the seeds, it is clearly known that they cause [the fruit] to arise. This is because that which is to arise is purely untainted (*anāsrava*). Alternatively, if the seeds of those afflictions are called "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*), how could untainted seeds be called latent tendencies?

Therefore, one should know that this refutes the fundamental masters of the [opposing] schools. The three interpretations in the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot) are all untenable. Regarding the two meanings explained in the sutras: first, the mind of the *dharmatā*, as in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
Second, it relies on the minds of others, as in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Explanation: Regarding the phrase "experiencing a superior maturation" (*vipāka*), the Sarvāstivādins state that it only brings about a distinct retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*).

Because it serves as an antidote to that [obstruction], it is metaphorically designated as a "ripened fruit" (*vipāka-phala*).

By means of this accumulation (*saṃbhāra*), it perfumes other impure (*sāsrava*) completing karmas, causing them to bring about ripened results. However, the reason why sixty-seven [types of wholesome states] are designated solely as the Truth of Origination is that they augment the seeds of merit-based virtue, thereby causing retribution to be brought forth. These briefly summarize six meanings; although their synthesis and analysis differ, their significance remains consistent. To state it briefly, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* speaks of six kinds [of characteristics], of which this is the first.

This negates the non-Buddhist views that take such things as a primal nature (*svabhāva*) or a self (*ātman*) as eternal causes, as well as the views of the Mahīśāsaka school and others who regard dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"Both fruits coexist" (up to) "coexisting with the giving of the fruit.
