Because the body and its name are a composite, [the text] excludes past and future [bodies] as well as the bodies of others. Ji says: "Manifest" (pratyutpanna) means appearing;

it is called "manifest" because there are three meanings of manifestation in the present. For this reason, in a person who lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the seventh consciousness is not termed a "seed."
Because the fruit does not manifest. "Manifestation" excludes the seventh [consciousness]. "Present" excludes what precedes and follows. "Existing" excludes provisional phenomena.
Its essence is substantially existent because it functions as a seed. As for excluding the seventh [consciousness], the manas-āśraya must possess these six characteristics;
that is to say, it is momentary-perishing, up to and including the fact that it draws forth its own fruit. Since it does not [possess] the fruit of being perfumed...
[The opponent claims: "It manifests as a result; it lacks the two meanings [of being both cause and result] simultaneously. Now, we say this is not so.

Regarding the third meaning in the treatise, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) have already been excluded, because they shift between realms and stages and are not constant. Furthermore, the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is not excluded as the support for seeds.

Even when not currently arising, it is still called a "seed. If that were the case, the manas would lack constancy and should also be called a seed. This objection is not valid, for it is possible for it to produce a result.
Because they exist together, it is said that [the mind] possesses six characteristics; this does not mean that every moment of mind possesses all six.
Some say that a preceding seed gives rise to a subsequent manifest state. How can they interpret the meaning of this sacred teaching? [Vasubandhu] says:

As the Sthavira school maintains, the mind has two moments—its prior cessation and its subsequent arising—which both exist simultaneously in the present. However, there is the obstacle that two [distinct] destinies cannot be established concurrently. Thus he speaks.
Regarding the statement that "those which are mutually contradictory in sequence cannot coexist," *Ce* says:
If one allows that seeds produce simultaneous seeds, then those producing seeds must also necessarily have causes, because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), just like the seeds produced.

In this manner, the succession would extend infinitely within a single moment (since they cannot coexist, the preceding and succeeding moments are contradictory). If this is so, how can it be that by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), new [seeds] arise simultaneously?
Regarding the perfuming of seeds, there are two explanations in Master Ji’s commentary (*Shu*). One states: "These do not occur simultaneously;

rather, the preceding moment—by its inherent nature (*dharmatā*)—and the present [moment] acting as causes and conditions, produce a newly perfumed seed. The other states: "The original [seed] anticipates the new one and does not act as a cause and condition."

Because the manifest functioning acts as a perfuming cause (*paribhāvaka-hetu*) [for the seeds], [the first interpretation is difficult to understand]. Since the time when the subsequent perfuming arises is not fixed, how could it be that by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), new seeds are always pre-emptively grasped?

If they were not pre-emptively grasped, then when a perfuming suddenly arises, the seeds would lack their causal conditions and thus could not be produced. The latter interpretation is also difficult: when a substantial entity arises, it should be like its manifest functioning because of its inherent nature (*dharmatā*). Although a single substance (*ekabhāva*) necessarily flows through successive stages, what fault is there in the simultaneous production of distinct substances (*pṛthagbhāva*) as seeds?

Just as a new and an old seed together produce a single manifest result, so too do the perfuming and the [seed] inherently co-arise as a single type, functioning according to conditions; this is not a matter of pre-emptive grasping. Since it is a cause...
That which exists simultaneously with its fruit is the arising of the manifest activity (*samudācāra*). That which does not exist simultaneously is the seed that arises subsequently.

This is because it possesses the function of both immediately producing the manifest activity and projecting the seed. Since it produces two fruits, it is termed a "seed" (*bīja*) in relation to the manifest activity;

this is as explained in the *Anabhāvavāda-śāstra* (Treatise on Non-nature), where the non-arising of seed and fruit is called "genus" (*jāti*), whereas at the time of producing the manifest activity, it is called a "seed. (This is like necessarily establishing the name "seed" in relation to what is possible.)
"Third, they constantly follow and transform (up to) producing their own kind.
The commentary states: This is the third section among the seven meanings [of seeds]. They also act as causes for the intrinsic nature of subsequent moments. Regarding "until the ultimate stage":
first, in the case of the seeds of defiled dharmas, this refers to the stage when the antidotes such as the Path of Seeing arise; as for other impure (*sāsrava*) dharmas...

Up until the attainment of nirvāṇa, and even until the exhaustion of the future [aeons]— as Vasubandhu and Asvabhāva state, this refers to the manifest characteristics— the actual [seed] should also exclude the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*),
because these also possess the quality of shifting between realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*). Nevertheless, regarding the substratum upon which the seeds depend, no such exclusion is made.

The commentary states: Among the seven meanings subsumed [here], the sixth concerns the correspondence of functional capacity (*kāritra*). [It shows that] these five depend upon various conditions (up to the point where they do not arise constantly or simultaneously).
The commentary states: Among the seven points summarized here, the fourth concerns the acquisition of conditions (*pratyaya*), and the fifth concerns transformation (*anyathātva*).

According to the Sarvāstivāda school, since objects exist throughout the three periods of time, there is the fault of [cognition] arising all at once. Even if one attempts to defend this by claiming that while the substance (*svabhāva*) exists, its activity (*kāritra*) has not yet arisen, [we reply that] such activity would necessarily be constantly arising.

Because it does not depart from its essence and because it always possesses an object of cognition. The Mahāyāna is not like this; therefore, it demonstrates that its own school [of thought] does not maintain that [cognition] arises perpetually and instantaneously.
(6) It leads to its own result, up to: they act as mutual causes and conditions.
The commentary states: Among the seven meanings subsumed [in this section], the seventh is "conformity" (*saṃprayoga*).

This excludes the non-Buddhists such as Maheśvara, as well as the Sarvāstivādins who assert that the wholesome form and the four aggregates act as mutual causes and conditions for one another (Master Cè cites the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* on this point; here I explain that text according to its record in that treatise).
"Only within the fundamental consciousness... [they are] not real seeds.

The commentary states: This is a summary that distinguishes and maintains the essential points. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and its two commentaries state that both internal and external [seeds] possess six characteristics.

Here, however, in distinguishing and maintaining the essentials, it is said that real seeds are exclusively internal, while external [seeds] are merely designated as such because they are transformations of consciousness.
Regarding the term "repeatedly" (*gù*): Jì says it indicates "repeated transformation. This means that internal seeds are also transformations of consciousness and should therefore not be real seeds.
The answer is: once internal seeds have been transformed by consciousness, they subsequently produce wheat and so forth; these wheat and other grains are then again transformed by consciousness.
Because they undergo repeated transformation (since the seeds produced by the transformation give rise to further transformations), [they are not real seeds].
This capacity of the seed [continuing] until [the result arises] is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
The commentary states: This is the eighth section, the Gate of Projecting Birth. Herein there are two gates. First, the gate of the relative proximity and distance.

For instance, with respect to the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), they are the cause for the arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the projecting cause for the arising of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); whereas external seeds are the cause for the arising of the sprout and the projecting cause for the arising of the stalk.
The first is the gate of the mutual relationship between the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the completing cause (*paripūraka-hetu*).

For example, according to Vasubandhu’s treatise, external seeds from the time they reach the ripening of the fruit, and internal seeds up until the limit of the life-span, act as the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), which includes the subsequent withering and so forth;
the remains after death act as the projected cause (*ākṣepa-phala*). Vasubandhu explains only the latter, whereas this treatise and Asvabhāva fully distinguish both types.
"Internal seeds must [exist] because of the fruit produced by [the conditions]. Commentary:
This is the ninth section on the four conditions; it follows that internal causal conditions are analogous to external dominant conditions.
Regarding the meaning [of the passage] from "In dependence upon what meaning" up to "not the mental concomitants (*caitta*) and so forth," the commentary states:

Within the tenth section on the gate of perfuming (*vāsanā*), there are three parts: because of the brief question-and-answer, because of the extensive question-and-answer, and because of the summary conclusion.

Within the extensive section, there are two parts: that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*) and that which perfumes (*bhāvaka*). Within the four types of that which is perfumed, the first is "stable" (*sthira*).

Regarding the phrase "abiding nature" (*sthiti-svabhāva*): it refers to the fact that during the course of a single lifetime, [the storehouse consciousness] necessarily functions without interruption. Regarding the phrase "excluding the evolving consciousnesses" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna-pratiṣedha*), Wonch’uk says: "This excludes the seven evolving consciousnesses.

If it were admitted that they hold the seeds, then at the Bodhisattva’s Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), all contaminated seeds would be lost [since the manas undergoes transformation during that single period].

Wonch’uk further states: "The term 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*) also includes mental factors (*caitta*). Che says: "The third case particle [in the compound] serves to distinguish it from the mind [itself]" (this is consistent with the favorable meaning below).

Regarding "sound, wind, and so forth," the phrase "and so forth" includes all forms (*rūpa*). These are cited as representative examples to illustrate the category of sense faculties and their objects.

This is to distinguish them from the Sautrāntika position that both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are susceptible to perfuming (*bhāvya*); for [according to the Sautrāntikas], formless states lack mind, and those lacking mind do not abide stably. If one asks, "Is the consciousness of a Buddha also stable, and therefore susceptible to perfuming?"—it is not so;
for perfuming occurs only when there is equality [of stability]. It is like agarwood (*candana*), which does not receive the scent of *tāla* or *kāṣṭha*. It is not...

It is well said that mugwort does not receive the fragrance of moss. Only indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas do not contradict the three natures; therefore, the Buddha’s eighth consciousness maintains the perfuming of the causal stage.

Are the mental associates (*caitta*), which are like the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)—which are firm and indeterminate like solid rock—also objects of perfuming?
No. This is because mental associates are like a provisional basis, while unconditioned phenomena are as firm and dense as solid stone. Thus says Master Ji.

The dependent nature (*paratantra*) includes both [the associated and] the dissociated (*viprayukta*), such as the categories of the provisional (*prajñapti*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). If it is like a jar holding water, what fault is there in provisionally maintaining [the dependent nature]?

Because a jar is conventionally designated as "holding" based on its being maintained by real dharmas (*dravyadharma*), just as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) maintains the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Is the subsequent consciousness, possessing the aforementioned three [conditions], that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*) by the other [prior] consciousness? No; this can be understood.
"What is it that is called 'capable of perfuming'? [The commentary] states:

Within the second category of "capable of perfuming," the phrase "excluding the resultant (*vipāka*) mind and mental factors" refers—as Ji explains—to citing the eighth consciousness along with its associated mental factors, as well as their objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), and the resultant indeterminate (*avyākṛta-vipāka*) states within the six consciousnesses.
This does not mean that all mind-states arising from maturation (*vipākaja*), such as those involving grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), are incapable of perfuming.

If they function as objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*), then because the eighth consciousness is the object of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, it is perfumed by its objective image (relying on the power of the seeing-part).

It perfumes the seeds of the essential nature (as in the case of the maturation-aspect within the *manas*). Cè states that the three types of concentration—such as those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and so forth—are capable of being perfumers. Regarding the two explanations for "maturation" (*vipāka*):
first, it is said that all karma-induced [states] are definitely incapable of perfuming; they arise solely through natural law (*dharmatā*), and because they are inferior, they are assisted by karma.
One explanation states that there are two types of karmic retribution: that which is powerful can perfuse (*vāsanā*), while that which is inferior cannot.

The Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang] maintains the latter view (meaning that it is the mental factors manifesting as images that perfuse, because they manifest the power of names and phrases regarding objects; whereas the wholesome and unwholesome [images] manifest within the resultant *manovijñāna* cannot perfuse, because their basis is inferior—just as when the fundamental consciousness transforms the seeds of the three natures, or in the case of the eye and ear faculties nourished by material form).
Regarding the presence of increase and decrease, Master Ji states that even when the *manas* reaches the stage of outflow-free purity (*anāsrava*), there is still increase and decrease.
Regarding sentient beings who lack the nature [of liberation], this seventh consciousness never has a time when it moves or shifts;
being devoid of increase or decrease, it should not be a perfuming agent. There are two explanations for this: first, it is said that from beginningless time, its mode of activity has been obscure.
In each and every moment, the seeds and manifestations increase. This is like the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) entering the noble state and gradually increasing in clarity;

yet, it is extremely difficult [to comprehend]. (Regarding that which is difficult to understand: as noble wisdom gradually increases until reaching the perfection of Buddhahood, what category will the *manas* of no-nature (*niḥsvabhāva-manas*) belong to throughout the limits of the future? Second, it is said:

when arising in the higher or lower realms, because there is an increase or decrease in the coarseness or subtlety of the bonds of the stages (*bhūmi*), although there are nine grades, they nonetheless consist of the objects of experience and sensation according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Because the continuity of the elements (*dhātu*) is not easily severed, it is called "a single category" (*ekajātīya*). Although [the afflictions] are abandoned all at once, this is like the path of immediate departure (*sadyoniryāṇamārga*) in the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
It is not that the Bodhisattva’s vajra-like concentration lacks nine grades; the intention of [Vasubandhu’s] measurement is the same as this. (This is also difficult to understand:

if the Buddha’s equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna*), just as in the stage of a bodhisattva, enters various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) through ascending and descending, coarse and subtle states, then since there is increase and decrease, it should be capable of being perfumed (*vāsya*). If the Buddha’s wisdom were to rely on only a single stage, then the bodhisattva’s untainted [wisdom] would not be the Buddha-nature; this would be a fault. As for other stages...)

Furthermore, it is said: "Because the manas that lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) belongs to the same category as that which possesses intrinsic nature (sasvabhāva), there would be [the fault of] increase and decrease."

The argument that [the Buddha] destroys [defilements] himself is not tenable. Otherwise, the seven consciousnesses of a Buddha—which are of the same category as those that serve as causes—would also be able to act as perfumers (*vāsanā*). As the *Guān* states:

"The seventh consciousness of one with inherent nature (*gotra*) is initially without increase or decrease; later, through increase and decrease, it becomes capable of acting as a perfumer for the wholesome dharmas of the Buddha-fruit."

If there were no increase or decrease later, but there was increase or decrease previously, it would follow that [the former] must be the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*). The commentary explains: "If the object to be perfumed (*bhāvyatva*) is lacking, the perfuming agent cannot be established.

[I now say: This is not so. If the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) does not exist, then because it is not the object to be perfumed, the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses) of the Tathāgata could not themselves function as perfumers. Furthermore, establishing a third meaning would be useless; moreover, the aforementioned fault remains.

[These views] are not to be relied upon, as they do not fully accord with reason. I shall now provide a distinct explanation: namely, that the seventh consciousness serves as the support for the six [consciousnesses].

To the extent that the defiled dharmas of the six consciousnesses increase, to that same extent the force of the defiled manas increases; to the extent that the wholesome dharmas of the six consciousnesses grow, to that same extent the force of the defiled manas diminishes.
Thus, it is affected by the superior power of factors that are either adverse or favorable, resulting in either harm or benefit.

Therefore, since sentient beings have no inherent nature, how could there be any divergent paths? Regarding the concluding statement that "only the seven evolving consciousnesses and their mental factors [are熏]" (are perfumed), Ji says:
"This cites the subjective perceivers (*ālambaka*). If they were the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*), what dharma would act as an obstacle?

This is because the eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*) for the sixth and seventh consciousnesses; [if it were the image], it would be perfumed by them. Furthermore, how could [the eighth] serve as the perfumer (*vāsaka*)? Only its own..."

Regarding the "substantial parts" (*tǐfēn*): for instance, the self-part (*zītǐfēn*) is so called because it only receives perfuming (*vāsanā*). It is the substance of the seeing-part (*jiànfēn*). [The Preceptor says: For now, we speak of the perceiving capacity. It perfumes its own kind of part.

Because the image-part (*xiàngfēn*) has a distinct arising function, perfuming is a secondary function; it is subsumed solely under the substance, because it does not perceive the seeds that are being perfumed. If one were to say that the function of perfuming is identical to the function of perceiving, then wherever there is perceiving, there must necessarily be perfuming.]

The image-part (nimittabhāga) has no object; therefore, it should lack the capacity for perfuming (vāsanā). However, the statement that the seventh [consciousness] perfumes the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) means that the essence of the seeing-part perfumes its own kind; this is the intended meaning here.

"Thus [the perfuming agent] is able to perfume... up to all types of characteristics. The commentary states: This third section establishes the conclusion. The old seeds produce the present; the present perfumes new seeds. Thus, the one present phenomenon and the two types of seeds—these three factors exist simultaneously.
This differs from the Sautrāntika school’s view that cause and effect occur at different times. Question: When the old seeds produce the new present, the new present...
It immediately perfumes a new seed. Since the new seed arises from the present [state], it should also produce a new present [state].

Answer: The manifest activity functions in the present; since one [instance] is sufficient, another does not arise. The seed serves as the cause for what follows, and thus there is no fault in its being perfumed.

Regarding the statement "like the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and so forth," Ji says that this cites the Sarvāstivāda school, using the simultaneous cause and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) as analogies. Cei says: "First, one [says]..."
The same as before. One interpretation says this refers to specific instances (*vastu*). Since the Mahāyāna also possesses the meaning of the six causes (the first explanation is superior;

the *Asvabhāva-śāstra* states that "arising from seeds to manifest" constitutes the homogeneous cause, for in the Mahāyāna [causality] is not necessarily restricted to temporal sequence). Regarding these two: first, they are identical in that the seed and the manifest arise one from the other.

Regarding the statement that "the preceding moment's seed produces its own subsequent category" is a figurative designation: this is because the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle 4, states that all six causes are subsumed under the condition of cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), and because the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* refutes [any other interpretation].
"Because this consciousness arises from the seeds of its activity (*ākāra*). [Commentary:
This is the second major section, which provides a combined explanation of the objects (*ālambana*) and mental aspects (*ākāra*). It contains two parts:

a brief indication and a detailed explanation. This is the former. Regarding the phrase "the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of marks (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), and discrimination (*vikalpa*"): these are the five categories (*pañcavastu*).

In the middle [of the three natures], True Suchness (*tathatā*) has no seeds; Correct Cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is untainted (*anāsrava*). Although these depend upon this consciousness, this consciousness does not take them as its objects;

therefore, they are not retributive sensations (*vipākavedanīya*). The objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are signified by the tainted phenomenal parts (*nimittabhāga*), are collectively termed "phenomena" (*nimitta*).

The substance of sound that signifies them is termed "name" (*nāman*). The self-substance of the transforming mind and mental factors is termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). The Tripiṭaka Master says: "Name..."

Regarding the term "basis" (*āśraya*): here it refers to the name, because there is no substantial seed (*bīja*). As for "sharing the same security and peril," there are two types of appropriation (*upādāna*):

first, the locus of sensation and awareness; second, that which is grasped as its own substance. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The five material elements (*dhātu*) in their entirety and one portion of the four [non-material] elements [are the basis], according to the first gate.
Master Ji says: "If one relies on the ultimate principle, that which generates sensation and awareness is exclusively the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*)."

The other four faculties—form, odor, taste, and touch—are also called "perception" (*vijñapti*) because they do not exist apart from the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and are gathered together in one place;

however, their substance is actually not so. The *Pañcāśatikā* (Treatise on the Fifty) states: "Five are appropriated (*upātta*), five are non-appropriated, and the remainder are exclusively non-appropriated.

Yuan Ce comments: "Based on this, although sound is hollow and sparse, it does not produce perception because it is subsumed as a substance within the location of the faculty [from which it does not depart]," as in the *Pañcāśatikā*.

Third: it means that the object upon which consciousness relies shares the same state of security or peril [as the consciousness itself]. Furthermore, this serves as the basis for the arising of various sensations (*vedanā*).

Thus, two aspects are explained together; here, in this *Vijñaptimātra*, we rely on the latter aspect. That which is transformed is taken as the object-condition (*ālambana*) because the seeds, the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and the physical vessel (*bhājana-loka*) constitute its substance.
Nevertheless, it is said that this object-condition comprises immeasurable forms of appropriation (*upādāna*), as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya*.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in ten fascicles states: "The ālayavijñāna takes names and forms as its objects, like [the illusion of] hair-tufts. Jì explains: "The substance of 'name' is sound;
alternatively, it refers to the seeds of the four aggregates, or to the object-aspect (ālambanabhāga) perceived by the self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga).

Therefore, there is no contradiction. As for that [sūtra] stating that it knows all objects simultaneously, this is because it does not apprehend its own stated objects gradually; it is not the same [as other systems]."
The *Satyasiddhi* [school] holds that the eighteen spheres (*dhātu*) are the objects of cognition. Within this, the "knower" (the subject) proceeds spontaneously for each.
The commentary states: In the second part, the detailed explanation, there are two sections: by way of the aspect (*ākāra*) and by way of the object (*ālambana*). The first also has four parts.
There are two parts, three parts, four parts, and one part; this refers to the two-part [system]. Cè (Cé) says:
"The Buddha primarily taught the One-Part [system], as the sūtras state: 'The triple world is mind-only.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the ninth century, Asaṅga and Vasubandhu expanded it into two parts, namely the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) and the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect). Subsequently, Dignāga and others added the *svasaṃvittibhāga* (self-verifying aspect)."

One thousand one hundred years later, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, relying on the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* (now called the *Guhyasamāja*), composed a provisional treatise establishing four divisions (*catur-bhāga*).

Although the expansions and contractions differ, the underlying principle does not contradict [the original]. (Now it is said that Asaṅga and Vasubandhu established only two divisions; this tradition is erroneous, for the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of three divisions.

Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "All conditioned phenomena are like stars, cataracts, lamps, and illusions. Both treatises explain this together; herein, "stars and cataracts" metaphorically represent the perceived and perceiving divisions (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*), while the "lamp" represents the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*). Since these dharmas and metaphors are manifest...)

Regarding the statement that there are three [aspects] and thus they are "similar to" the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the subjective aspect (*nimitta*): as previously stated, these are not real, for they are merely conceptualized by the mind.

Having thus set forth our own school’s position, we shall next refute the positions of others. The Saṃmitīya school asserts that while there is seeing within the mind, there is no objective aspect (*ālambana-nimitta*).

Bhāviveka maintains that, conventionally, there is only the aspect of the object (*viṣaya-nimitta*), but no subjective aspect (*ālambaka-nimitta*). Sthiramati holds that there is only the substance (*svabhāva*) itself, lacking both the seeing and the objective aspects.
Because both [subject and object] are equally imagined, the refutation of the absence of an objective support (*ālambana*) entails two logical consequences:

First, your own mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) would be unable to take their respective objects as supports, because you admit they lack the characteristic of an objective support, just like other objects (i.e., as stated below, the word "only" implies they are like other things).
Second, each individual mind would have to take all other objects as its support, because it lacks the characteristic of an objective support, just like its own object.

(He then provides an analogy, the rest of which is as in the original text). Although non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) lacks an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), it possesses an aspectual form (*ākāra*) that resembles an object; thus, it is like the consciousness that resembles an object according to the Sarvāstivādins. Therefore, there is no fallacy of uncertainty.

Refuting the claim that there can be no cognizing subject (*ālambaka*) also involves two types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). First: Your mind must be incapable of cognizing [objects], because it lacks the characteristic of being a cognizing subject, just like space and so forth.
Conversely, your space and so forth must possess the characteristic of being a cognizing subject, just like the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*). The first...

It refutes the Saṃmitīya school; subsequently, it refutes Bhāviveka; and together they refute Sthiramati. This is the traditional account. (Since this is an inference, there are no faults such as contradicting worldly direct perception or one’s own scriptures.

Furthermore, one should not raise the charge of inconclusiveness by claiming that correct cognition takes suchness or the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its object, as stated in the ninth chapter: "Correct cognition bears the image of suchness," and in the fourth part below: "It possesses both the perceived object and the perceiving subject, and thus there is no fault of infinite regress.
It cites verses from the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*: first, internal consciousness is maintained; next, external objects are negated; and the second half [of the verse] opens [the discussion].
Internally, one establishes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). [The opponent] maintains that these three entities are distinct from one another.

[The author] states: This is an explanation based on the two-fold and three-fold divisions. Within the object-part, there are two [sections]. First, it distinguishes the differences between the three matters in contrast to other schools.

Later, the three divisions were established. Excluding the Saṃmitīya school, nineteen schools state: "Upon the mind there is an appearance resembling the object of cognition, which is called the 'aspect' (ākāra).
It is not the object itself, nor is it the cognitive act [of perceiving the object] (for the object is external and the cognitive act pertains to the entity).
Although that school does not establish the designation 'aspect of seeing,' one may interpret their teaching by applying the terminology of the Mahāyāna. Thus, the object and the aspect are one.
The bases and objects each carry the aspects of their respective domains; their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are similar, and the number of kings [the subjects] is one for each.

It is said that the number of things is equal because their essential natures and characteristics are distinct, and thus they differ in appearance. In the Mahāyāna, the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) is called the mode of activity (*ākāra*), which understands the characteristics of the mode of activity or the mode of activity itself.
Regarding the self-substance that is the basis of both the seeing and the perceived parts: if these two did not share a single general substance, [they could not exist].
They appear as distinct because these two are separate dharmas. Just as the mind and its object are not different in essence but possess two distinct functions, there is an objection:
"A sword cannot cut itself; how can the mind take itself as its own object? The explanation is: because they are distinct functions, it is not the same as [the case of] self-cutting.

For this reason, the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying portion) is established separately. If the self-verifying portion did not exist, the previously perceived *darśana-bhāga* (seeing portion) would be lost.
Regarding the power of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*): one does not recollect a preceding mind, because it is like seeing a form that has never been experienced before.

As for the statement that the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are similar, this is because each transforms its own reflection; nevertheless, they are extremely similar. The first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that they share the same object of focus.
Furthermore, the *Yogācāra* intention explains that the essential substance (*svabhāva*) is established as three parts based on two reasons.

First, just as in the world there are objects of cognition, means of cognition, and the cognizing mind, which are all real entities according to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Kī (基) asks: "What is the meaning of 'result' (*phala*)? It is the sense of the cause being fulfilled.

If there were no result of cognition, what benefit would there be in having a cognitive object? Second, the two parts must necessarily have a common substratum (*āśraya*), lest [the relationship between them] be untenable.

Because each distinct entity is an external object of the mind. The *Pramāṇasamuccaya* (Compendium of Valid Cognition), which extensively compiles the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), was composed by Dignāga.
Furthermore, because the mind and mental factors [are such that] they constitute the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
The commentary states: This is the third section, the analysis of the four parts. Regarding the statement, "Since the mental part is the same, it should likewise be realized," Woncheuk says:
"The third, the mental part, should possess a mind capable of illumination, because it is subsumed under the mental part, just like the seeing part."

The *viṣayāṃśa* (objective aspect) turns back toward this [subjective aspect]. Alternatively, there is no proof [of its existence] (*asiddha*). [The opponent refutes this, saying: "The thesis (*pakṣa*) is redundant (*pratijñā-samāna*), because the *manovijñāna* is admitted by rival schools to be universally pervasive (*sarvālambana*).

The reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the mind are themselves aspects of that mind. Now, I say this is not so. To take "directly illuminating" as the thesis is not redundant. Furthermore, it is logically incorrect to claim that the four characteristics are aspects of the mind, for they are commonly accepted by all parties as being neither matter (*rūpa*) nor mental factors (*citta-dharma*). *Cai* says: [Note: The bracketed sections represent the opponent's objection and the author's rebuttal.]

Third, self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) necessarily exists as that which cognizes [itself], because it is a constituent part of the mind, just like the aspect of seeing (*darśanabhāga*). [The opponent] objects: "This has the same fault as before. [The proponent] replies: "There is no such fault; it is the same as before.

To establish this through inference (*anumāna*), one who maintains four aspects (*caturbhāga*) sets forth this formal argument in order to refute those who maintain three aspects: [Thesis: Self-cognition exists. [Reason: Because it is a constituent part of the mind. [Example: Just like the aspect of seeing. [The opponent] says: "There is a fault identical to the previous one. Now, [the proponent] says: "There is no fault; it is the same as before. He states the formal inference (*prayoga*) to determine this: "For the sake of refuting those who maintain three aspects, one who maintains four aspects establishes this inference."

The self-cognizing [aspect] must necessarily possess an intrinsic capacity for cognition, because it is subsumed under the category of mind, just like the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and so forth.

Otherwise, the self-cognizing [aspect] would not be subsumed under the category of mind, because it would lack an intrinsic capacity for cognition, just like a rabbit’s horn and the like. The judgment states:
Both of these [arguments] are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Although the arising-phase of visual consciousness is subsumed under the category of mind, it lacks an intrinsic capacity for cognition.

[Objection: Although the three aspects (*ākāra*) of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) do not exist, it is the very substance [of consciousness] that can realize [them]; however, because they are subsumed under the category of the mind’s own parts (*cittabhāga*), [this is not so]. [Response: This is incorrect.

When the Master [Dharmakīrti] speaks of the "parts of the mind," he refers to the aspect that takes objects as its cognitive focus (*ālambana*). Why, then, would he say that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are called "parts of the mind"? For those [aspects] belong to the category of form (*rūpa*) and the category of that which is neither form nor mind (*naiva-rūpa-na-citta*). To establish this proof, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated:

The third part (the subjective aspect) must necessarily exist as something distinct from the seeing [aspect], for it is the very substance that can realize [the object], and it is subsumed under the category of the mind’s own parts as that which possesses the capacity to cognize (*ālambaka*).

Because of this consideration. It is like the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing aspect). [The opponent] objects, saying: "If one excludes the correspondence [of the *darśana-bhāga* with the object], there is a fault here as well—namely, that it is not the essence itself (as explained in the *Mātṛkā*). Furthermore, there is a difficulty:

whether the *darśana-bhāga* takes the *nimitta-bhāga* (the appearing aspect) as its object, and whether it is a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or an invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*), it is invariably direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is its fruit. How could it be a hindrance for self-cognition to be invariably direct perception? Or, if it were inference or invalid cognition, the *darśana-bhāga* would be its fruit. Therefore, the treatise explains: "That which realizes its own essence must..."

Because it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). That is to say, seeing external conditions, or inference (*anumāna*) which is not valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), all internal conditions realize their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the single moment [of consciousness] do not coexist as direct perception and inference, because the mind is not [so divided]. It is just like self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*). Question:
If the Buddhas and the causal five or eight consciousnesses, etc., are exclusively direct perception, they should have only three parts; how can the seeing-part constitute the second?

[The opponent claims: "Because it is the third fruit. Baso (基) replies: "Not so. Because the internal and external are fixed. The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the external as its object; it does not serve as an internal fruit.
A single function cannot take both the internal and external as objects. [The opponent] cites a proof to challenge this, saying:

"The uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeing-part should not take the third [fruit] as its object, because the internal and external are fixed. One must say that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) necessarily possesses four parts, because it is a consciousness that cognizes objects. As for...
Regarding the objection that this is not a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not so. The *Ki* commentary states below:

"Even if the Buddha’s seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes its own self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) as an object by acting as an image-object (*pratibimba-ālambana*), it is not the case that the meaning of the four parts would thereby be lost.

Therefore, in the eighth [chapter] below, with the sole exception of the seeing-part, it is accepted that the seeing-part also takes the self-cognition-part and so forth as its objects; however, it does not directly realize them. The preceding...

Second, regarding "external": this refers to seeing external objects as conditions; it does not mean that their essence is external. Even if one were to say that [the seeing-part] pervades both [internal and external], there would be an objection:

seeing and so forth would be unable to take [external objects] as conditions, because they would be direct objects of cognition (*sākṣātālambana*), just like the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) of the mind.

Master Ji says this is not so, because the meaning is distinguished within the single cognizing subject (*ālambaka*). If it were the image-part of the mind, it would not be the essence of the cognizing subject (for the function of the seeing-part and so forth [is distinct]).

Based on the nature of the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*), the nature of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is without such consideration; thus, it cannot be treated as an analogy. Question: Since self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is established, and self-cognition is the result (*phala*), there should be no distinction between the object of cognition (*prameya*) and the result.
Response: This is not so, because the two meanings of "nature" (*tattva*) and "object" (*artha*) are not confused.

As for the statement that it is "useless," since the third [cognition] has already cognized [the second], what need is there to cognize it again? It is just as the third [cognition] does not cognize the first.

Regarding the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the proof states: "The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) does not become manifold in accordance with its objects, as the seeing-part itself lacks diverse characteristics;

nor is the self-cognizing-part (*svasaṃvitti*) manifold. One interpretation says: "The third and fourth parts would successively become manifold," yet the fourth part only takes the third as its object.

Because the function of seeing does not take itself as its object, and because there would otherwise be an infinite regress; therefore, the former explanation is superior. (The intention of that [opponent] is this:

if the function of taking three or four objects were not admitted, the Master’s original formal inference (*prayoga*) would suffer from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This too is because no mental factor (*caitta*) has the capacity to prove it. [I have] collected and extensively cited the formal inferences (*anumāna*) of various schools; those that are unnecessary have not been included.

Regarding the phrase "the objects and the subject of grasping" (*grāhya-grāhaka-paryavasthāna*), Sthiramati says: These refer only to the four parts of sentient beings; therefore, they are called "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*). They consist of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and coarseness (*audārika*).
Because they possess two types of fetters (*bandhana*), the untainted (*anāsrava*) [cognitions] possess four [aspects], yet they are not bound by them. The meaning of this verse is as follows:

the first two are called "external" because their objects of perception (*ālambana*) are external; the latter three are called "internal" because they realize their own essence. However, there are only various distinctions within the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*). Cè (測) says:
"The four aspects are mutually related as the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), and thus they are called [bound]."
They are *paryavasthāna* (obsessions). They also extend to the untainted (*anāsrava*). This does not mean they are called *paryavasthāna* simply because they are obsessions of affliction (*kleśa*).

(This is from the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra-śloka*. According to the *Dharmaguptaka* school, "all parts" refers to both internal and external; thus we know that the internal parts also have two kinds. According to the *Mahīśāsaka* school, "all parts" refers to the internal and external collectively.)
"Thus, from the four parts [up to] the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness.
Commentary states: This is the explanation of the fourth part. Master Ji says: "Asaṅga [held it to be] one part; Nanda, two parts; Dignāga, three parts; and Dharmapāla, four parts.
However, in this current text, Dharmapāla’s system is presented through both expansion and condensation; the rest of the text is easily understood.
Regarding the phrase "as for the locus" (up to) "each appearing as one":

the commentary states that this second section extensively explains the objects of cognition (*ālambana*). Within this, there are three parts: external objects, internal objects, and [objects] distinguished by their cessation.
The first of these also has three parts: the direct explanation, the question-and-answer, and the analogical explanation. This is the first [of those]. It is distinct.
That which is familiar [to all] is the transformation through the fruit; that which is the seed of common characteristics is the transformation through the cause.

By the power of these two transformations, the receptacle world arises. However, there are four permutations regarding the common and the uncommon: first, that which is common among the common, such as the great earth, mountains, and so forth.

2. Common among the common, yet uncommon [to others], such as the perception of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and others. 3. Uncommon among the uncommon, such as the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*). 4.
Uncommon among the common, such as the physical bases (*āśraya*) of the faculties; this refers to their "common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Regarding this, Zé (側) says:

"This is because the first two phrases exhaustively encompass the objects. Jī (基) says: "The first phrase [is primary]; the latter [phrases] are explained according to this principle, as they are distinguished based on it. Although one knows the person...
The distinct transformations undergone by individuals are termed "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). Nevertheless, there exists a sense of shared commonality that is experienced collectively;

this is designated as the "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Jiqi (基) states: "It is not the case [that the common] is non-common within the common, like one's own fields or houses; for it is common within the common.

This means that while there is a distinction between transformation and karmic retribution (*vipāka*), although the scope of what is retributed differs according to poverty or wealth, the transformative function within the same realm of existence (*gati*) is identical.
Because they are mutually similar. Regarding the phrase "form and so forth" (*rūpādi*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and real dharmas (*dravyadharma*).

Jī mentions that this is not like the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which can separately apprehend conventional designations (*prajñapti*); since these [conventionalities] lack a separate essence, they cannot be apprehended [by the senses]. Regarding the phrase "that is to say, external":
Because they belong to the category of non-sentient things. Regarding the statement that "each is pervasive and appears as one," the *Shuyao* says:

"The *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter Three, uses the analogy of a single visual consciousness arising in dependence upon two faculties, like two lamps together emitting a single light. How should this be reconciled? This [passage] follows the Hīnayāna, while that [analogy] is based on the Mahāyāna;
it is like the term "concordant sound" (*sahabhū-śabda*), which is produced through both common and individual causes. If that were so, [what of] many lamps?

How is it that shadows differ? To explain this point directly: when many wicks and their causes are situated together, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) in close proximity collectively produce a single form;
because two separate lamps with distinct wicks do not produce [a single form] together, their shadows exhibit similarity or difference.

Thus, the two treatises do not contradict one another. The proof states: each lamp emits its own light, which exists through mutual support. One is the "great" provisional light, while the other refers to the two treatises [respectively].
It is said: "Just as when many people raise a single, solid sound, they assist one another so that it becomes great;

by means of this provisional sound, it is heard from afar. Because the individual lights are distinct, the shadows have differences. Because there is a provisional light, the light itself becomes even brighter. (I now fear this is not so.

If there were a single great light outside of the individual lights, there should likewise be a single great shadow produced outside of the individual shadows. Since the resultant shadows do not exist, the causal lights are the same. It is simply that they assist one another, and each is individually increased in brightness—just as many threads assist one another to suspend a heavy weight). Ce says:
There are four propositions regarding that which appears as one: 1. Different substance, same perception: as when the various Buddhas manifest emanations in the same location that appear as one.
2. Same substance, different perceptions: as when each person perceives a Buddha standing before them individually. 3. Same substance, same perception:
as when a single Buddha manifests an emanation that all perceive as a single body. 4. Different substance, different perceptions: as when the various people of the world perceive things differently.

Regarding these objects: now, these [objects] are of different substances yet perceived as the same; they accord with one another and do not mutually obstruct each other, just like forms that occupy the same location without being separated. Why?
Because they are all produced by the same maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
The commentary states: Regarding the second question and answer, Master Ji says that Bodhisattva Dharmapāla provisionally presents three interpretations.

The first is identical to that of Candragarbha; the second, "without a teacher," is provisionally established as a distinct meaning. Master Ce says: the first is from Candragarbha, the next is the interpretation of Nanda, and the last is the interpretation of Dharmapāla.
As for Candragarbha, it was not included among the ten previous interpretations; Dharmapāla cites it here in order to clarify and contrast the underlying principles.
Guān Yún stated: "The *Candragarbha-sūtra* appears after the *Nanda-śāstra* and before the *Dharmapāla-śāstra*. For this reason, the *Dharmapāla-śāstra* relies upon the *Nanda-śāstra* to refute it;
the former [the *Nanda-śāstra*] states that all three realms, nine stages, ordinary beings, sages, and the five destinies undergo mutual transformation."

The Tripiṭaka Master says: "Even the refutation does not allow that the Buddha transforms a defiled land" (Commentary: All commentaries exclude the Buddha’s initial question regarding who the *vipākavijñāna* transforms).

"According to one interpretation (up to the point where it says) 'because they all transform together,' the commentary states: this is the second interpretation. The phrase 'should truly transform' excludes transformation that is merely provisional.

This is because the Buddha temporarily transforms impure lands in accordance with sentient beings, while ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles transform them into pure lands by following the Buddha’s footsteps. [Regarding] "pure lands of other directions..."
Regarding "wondrous lands," these are such as Sukhāvatī and others. Regarding "pure and wondrous lands within this realm," these are such as Gṛdhrakūṭa.

As for the statement that those born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) will certainly not descend again, Jì (基) says: "This is stated with reference to the manifest locations [of rebirth], namely the form realm (rūpadhātu);

other cases of different levels are likewise so. Cè (測) says: "It is not said that noble ones (ārya) are born in the form realm; rather, they possess a physical body (rūpakāya) and go to the desire realm (kāmadhātu)."

Therefore, Jì says: "The claim that a Sage who has suppressed [defilements] to be born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) would instead be reborn in the form realm (rūpadhātu), or that one who has severed the afflictions (kleśa) to be suppressed could be said to be born in a higher realm based on the severance of lower ones, is incorrect.
As the seventh [chapter] states, there is no principle of being born in a higher stage by suppressing [afflictions] of a lower stage;

this is because, according to the second [chapter] of the Abhidharma (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya), the eye-faculty does not exist [therein]. What are the boundaries regarding the present abiding and future birth?"
The Tripiṭaka Master says: "That which manifests as the body's dwelling within a single Sumeru world-system is the second place of birth immediately upon rebirth.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it should not be said to be only one birth; rather, it transforms according to those who may be reborn, whether ordinary beings or sages.

The former explanation is superior because the latter is limitless. (Ji and Ce agree with this record. Ji says: "Although those in the formless realm who are about to be reborn below also transform into lower forms," [the manifestation occurs] there.

However, the *Fifty-one [Questions]* states: "That consciousness does not take the external vessel-world of lower realms as its object" because noble ones (*ārya*) do not take such things as objects nor are they born there.
Although noble ones are not born in the hells or among the long-lived gods (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*), they are currently categorized as residing within those realms;

thus, it can be said that [the consciousness] transforms them. (Here, "long-lived" refers to the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); this differs from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which identifies the eighty thousand great kalpas of the Heaven of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception as the "long-lived gods").
There is an interpretation [that it exists] and yet appears as present.
The commentary states: Regarding the statement of the orthodox school of Dharmapāla that there is a material body (*rūpakāya*) and so forth, Woncheuk says:

"Even granting your own school’s position—such as that of the Mahāsāṃghikas who hold that there is a material body even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or that a body is born in the higher realms which possesses both coarse and subtle matter, or that there is a suspension [of matter]..."
Separated by distance, they do not support one another. For example, when the Brahmā King transforms a separate ground below himself, because it is distinct from his own body, he cannot utilize it;

therefore, such a transformation would be useless. This interpretation is the same as that of Cè (Paramārtha). Regarding the Dharmapāla school, it maintains that only within the Desire and Form Realms does each realm transform its own respective vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
This distinction across the nine stages is likewise applicable according to the circumstances, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the gods of the Pure Abodes (*Śuddhāvāsa*).
Residing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one transforms the lands of the higher realms;

this is because the lands of the desire realm cannot sustain the bodies of those in the higher realms (Master Ji says "upper stages," while Master Ce says "nine stages"; it is clear that their explanations refer to different levels within the same realm). Regarding the statement that there can be such sustaining function, Master Ce says:

Regarding the place where the body manifests and resides, one travels back and forth through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). The Tripiṭaka Master says: "If by means of one's own power, it is near and not far;

if by means of another's power, that which is transformed is limitless, for the supernormal powers of Buddhas and others have no boundaries. [This passage is not clear regarding the place where the body manifests and resides.

Within a single *Sumeru* world-system, ordinary practitioners of the Two Vehicles cannot traverse beyond a great trichiliocosm, as this would contradict the principle that [the environment] is transformed by the consciousness of oneself and others. However, the intention of the Tripiṭaka Master is that whether by one's own power or another's power, they may merely be sustained or used, yet everything is indeed transformed; therefore, he summarizes [the point].

To speak of it: the transformations are limitless, excluding only that which cannot be sustained (unlike the case of the Moon Treasury). Ji says: "The Sage [perceives] from his own level in the Brahma Palace down to the hells."

Whether it be one's own realm or the various realms of others, such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) within a thousandfold world-system, there is no utility for one's own realm [therein], and thus one cannot maintain the body [there].
What benefit would there be in transforming it? The meaning of this statement is that although there is currently no utility, if the body were to go there...
It can be maintained by the body; therefore, it must be transformed. This does not mean that the manifested body itself is made capable of being maintained and used;
rather, it is said to be "usable" because it can be so employed. For instance, even if a noble one were to go to hell, would they not likewise be able to dwell there in reliance upon it?

Even if an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) were to travel to another region of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they would still be able to maintain their body, because their karma is identical and because there is no vast disparity between the coarse and subtle [states].

Although the form and so forth of the higher realms possess power through the influence of others, they can only be utilized when empowered; they cannot be used autonomously. This is not the case for one's own realm; there, the body simply travels to that place and is used immediately without further empowerment.

Because of this, although the *dharmadhātu* is without limit, it is like that which is seen in a dream; it does not depart from one’s own mind. Therefore, it transforms its own stage to pervade the entirety of the *daśadig-loka-dhātu*. As stated in the thirty-ninth verse of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "The Bodhisattva contemplates the world as arising from the karma of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Because false conceptualization is boundless, the world is likewise immeasurable. All lands appear through the subtle power of ideation; by means of subtle skillful means (*upāya*), one can enter them all in a single thought-moment. The commentary explains: The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* states, "It is like [the light passing through] a fine pore.

The Bodhisattva attains mastery in the skillful means of the emptiness of illusion (*māyā-śūnyatā*), such that in a single thought-moment and within a single atom (*paramāṇu*), they suddenly enter all lands. Regarding the phrase "even if born in another direction," *Ce* (Master Ce) says: "Another direction..."

In the desire realm, that consciousness is also able to transform itself into the various pure and impure lands of this Sahā world (this statement provides a general explanation of the meaning of transforming according to the species born in pure or impure lands;
it does not mean that the pure and impure are transformed as being intermingled, for that and other levels are refuted in the treatise).
This explains that [the objects] differ according to what is perceived by each.

The commentary states: Regarding the third category of explanation, as for what was previously described as "common within the common," if it is individually experienced, it is "uncommon within the common.
This should be understood accordingly: they undergo transformation together according to their respective types, but do not transform into other types, because what is perceived differs.
Regarding that heterogeneous [realm] as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): sometimes when the water is exhausted, the hungry ghosts' fire is extinguished accordingly;

however, this is not necessarily the case, for the ghosts perceive it as dried up even while the ocean remains overflowing. Question: When a person draws water to drink, four things come together. If they are used separately, why do all of them enter the "yesterday" [of the past]?
Answer: The vessel from which the person draws is of yesterday; the four consciousnesses transform them together. As the four vessels draw from the four [sources], they are all included.

Each enters into four types of transformations. Question: If they transform separately, how do the gods know of the water? Answer: Because their karmic destinies are superior, they also know of the lower transformations.
For example, Śāriputra saw only the defiled land, whereas the Brahmā King Śaṅkhapāla could perceive both the pure and the defiled.
Question: In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and other texts, the Buddha refutes the attachment to permanence by manifesting the burning of heaven and earth.

Why, then, do these treatises maintain that the world is formed and destroyed by karma? Answer: This is because at times, in accordance with the suitability of the occasion, he manifests such transformations.
"Regarding the various seeds... (up to) not contradicting Vijñaptimātra. Commentary:
This is the second [section], concerning internal objects. Within this, there are two parts: because of the seeds and because of the faculties. This is the first.

Regarding the statement that this consciousness is subsumed under a specific nature (*svabhāva*), although there are many interpretations, it is well-explained that its nature is identical to that of the *sāsrava* (contaminated).

This is because this consciousness must directly apprehend [its objects] and does not take the *anāsrava* (uncontaminated) as its object. Since the seeds of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) are neutral (*avyākṛta*) by nature, the three realms (*dhātu*) should likewise be considered a single realm from the perspective of their essential nature.
Jì (基) states: "Nature" (*svabhāva*) has the meaning of "essential category. From the perspective of their essential nature, they are neutral; thus, the realms are one.

This is the meaning of bondage. The three realms are vastly different. Question: Since objects are transformations of the mind and are bound according to the mind, when one is born in a higher realm, one generates craving for the moisture of that higher state;
while depending on and taking as an object a body of a lower realm, the reflection [of that body] is bound to the higher realm.

Why, then, does the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) take the seeds of all three realms as its objects, and also take bodies and the receptacle world (bhājanaloka) of different planes as its objects? For instance, when one in a lower realm gives rise to the divine eye (divyacakṣus).
[The text] says: "Furthermore, when taking formless realms (*ārūpya*) as objects, tears fall like rain; the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) are distinct.

The seven consciousnesses are not like this. He himself explains: "The fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) must necessarily have practical utility; therefore, it transforms the bodies and environments (*deha-bhājana*) of other realms, and its perceived and seeing aspects are distinct.

The seven consciousnesses are not like this; therefore, their bondage follows [the realm] they share. (This contradicts what precedes and follows. Next, he himself admits that from the second dhyāna upward, when the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna arise, they take the forms of higher stages as objects, and their perceived and seeing aspects are distinct.)
This should be understood as the Master’s two interpretations regarding the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*).
Regarding the phrase "the body endowed with faculties" (*sendriya-kāya*) up to "is still seen as a continuum":

the commentary states that the second part concerning the seeds of the specific characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa-bīja*) of the sense-faculties refers to the latter two lines [of the verse], because they are contrasted with non-sentient things (*aprāṇin*).

Collectively, these are termed "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). However, because they serve as the objective bases (*ālambana*) for the sense organs and their respective objects, which are utilized by others, the fourfold classification states that they are "shared within the unshared.

Regarding the statement that there are seeds of shared characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa-bīja*) that reach maturation, both Ji and Ce state that these are "shared within the unshared" (meaning that whether they are one's own transformations or the transformations of others—both fall under the fourth category—because they are similar, occupy the same location, and are experienced in common). The proof [for this] states: "The transformations of others are exclusively shared, such as mountains, rivers, and so forth; know that this is not logical. Among these, the first interpretation [is as follows].
It also transforms to resemble the sense organs (*indriya*). Cè (Cè) says: "The *Candragarbha*, the *Nanda*, and others explain it thus. [Objection:

If that is so, how does the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* state that one "simultaneously discriminates and knows one's own body, the objects of enjoyment, and the vessel-world," yet speaks of the sense organs of other bodies? The Tripiṭaka Master says:

"In his explanation of that sūtra, he considers the sense organs of others to be 'vessel-places' (*bhājana-sthāna*) in relation to oneself. Jī (Jī) says: "If one grants that there is such a transformation..."

The sense organs (indriya) have no practical utility whatsoever, because they do not serve as a basis for anything else. As for the claim that they must undergo transformation for some purpose, this is also incorrect;
for they transform precisely because they serve as the locus for utility. Since the sense organs are absent, their locus would likewise be absent.

This is just as in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), where the loci of the nose and tongue exist only when those organs are present, serving to adorn the body, rather than for the purpose of generating consciousness.

Regarding the capacity for transformation: because the physical bases of the nose and tongue consciousnesses transform based on the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), this is the interpretation of the great masters such as Sthiramati and others;
the latter meaning is the interpretation of Dharmapāla Bodhisattva and others. Cè states: "The sense organs of others have no function of producing consciousness within oneself."
Regarding those homogeneous faculties (*sabhāga-indriya*), it is possible for the nose and tongue faculties of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to have the capacity to project [consciousness];

thus, one should not raise an objection based on parity. Baso (基) says: "If they transform even when lacking a function, why do the seven consciousnesses not likewise transform? Since they lack the function of objective apprehension (*ālambana*), yet they obtain objects, [the claim] is untenable. If they did not obtain [objects], their essential function would be impossible.

What transforms is the support of the sense-faculties (*indriyādhiṣṭhāna*), which is not of the nature of a faculty itself; its essential function is merely to project its own respective consciousness. Other faculties have no inherent function with respect to oneself, and thus, like the seven consciousnesses themselves, they do not transform."

Regarding the statement "therefore it arises in another realm" and so forth: although those two [types of] self-consciousness do not transform the corpse, there is still a residual body present, from which one knows that there is transformation by another.
However, since death lacks the sense faculties (*indriya*) and relies solely on the physical basis (*āśraya*), we know that the place of transformation prior to death is not the sense faculty itself.
Since it is produced from seeds that are mutually shared with others, why was it previously stated that it arises by the power of the projecting cause (*ākṣepahetu*)? The explanation is as follows:

prior to birth, it transforms and arises in accordance with its own producing causes; after death, however, it is transformed by others and cannot abide independently, for it must depend on the power of the deceased’s projecting cause.
Thus, even though the substance of the cause ceases upon entering *nirvāṇa* and so forth, it continues like an arrow that, once released from a drawn bow, persists by the force of its momentum.
[The] Practice.
Thus far, it has been explained up to the point of the "Initiation of Bonds.
The commentary states: The third section, the "Discrimination," contains three parts, because it is the gate of the distinctions in the functional power of karma. Transformation...
Because it cannot be altered by the gate of variation; this is the first point. First, the power of karma (*karmabala*) is cited to contrast it with the power of meditative mastery (*vaśitābala*).

That is to say, what is transformed by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth is not fixed. *Ce* (Cen Zhuan) says: "The word 'and so forth' includes the power of supernormal abilities (*abhijñābala*). Regarding the power of concentration:

as in the *antarābhava-sūtra*, the intermediate state of the formless realm (*ārūpya-antarābhava*) is produced. Regarding the power of supernormal abilities: as in the arising of the divine eye and ear faculties through the four dhyānas. Furthermore...
By means of the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*), the eighth [mind] of the desire realm transforms both the body and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) of the desire and form realms.

If one is born in the form realm and transforms the desire realm, it should be understood accordingly. The Tripiṭaka Master says that the word "etc. also includes transformations produced by the power of vows (*praṇidhāna-bala*).

(This commentary permits that what is transformed by supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is seen as belonging to the desire realm by those in the desire realm; this is identical to the *Śūyao*). There is a superior seed of the meditative matter (*dhyāna-rūpa*) bound to the desire realm. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If one relies on this [desire realm] bond, there is no capacity to induce or transform [matter]; however, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers..."

The fruit is bound by the same fetters as its cause (because it is produced from the primary elements [mahābhūta] created by those very fetters). Jì (基) says there are five: first, the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

second, the power of supernormal abilities (*ṛddhi*); third, the power of the Dharma; fourth, the power of borrowed consciousness; and fifth, the power of great vows. These apply to all consciousnesses. If the eighth consciousness undergoes transformation, there are only the first two.

Regarding bodies transformed by the power of supernormal abilities belonging to a different level: they produce the form and tangible objects of the sense organs (*indriya*)—namely, the eyes and ears—belonging to a higher level. Or...

There may be sound, but there is no separate textual explanation. However, one does not give rise to the eyes or ears of a lower stage while on a higher stage, because they would be inferior and useless.

As for the transformation of the environment (*bhājana*) of another stage through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), it is like when the Bhikṣu Aśvajit ascended to the Brahmā realm of the Form Realm by means of supernormal power;

the eighth [consciousness] perceives the *indriyādhiṣṭhāna* (the physical basis supporting the sense organs) within his body, which also consists of various forms and characteristics produced by supernormal power.

The deity was listening to the Dharma before the Buddha and caused this person to see [him]. (The meaning of this commentary is as follows: the body of the Brahmā-king manifested by Aśvajit is subsumed within the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), for it is not grasped or maintained by the consciousnesses of oneself or others.

Furthermore, it is accepted that the physical body manifested by a deity of the Form Realm is bound to the Desire Realm; thus, it is called a "receptacle of a different level. This does not accord with the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya*.
