[The commentary] states: This is the second refutation. First, regarding the Sautrāntika school: they posit a single category upon the substance of those consciousnesses;

this functional capacity perfumes the category of consciousness within the same moment. This category persists through preceding and succeeding moments, receiving perfuming and maintaining the seeds. Jizang and Fazang both state this.
He [the opponent] admits that "category" (*jāti*) is conventional (*prajñapti*), yet he refutes it. To specifically refute the [opponent's] valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says:

A category cannot sustain the seeds of internal phenomena, because it is admitted to be conventional, just like a jar and so forth. (The *Tattvaviniścaya* states: "It is admitted that there are two kinds of categories: first, the 'stream' of consciousness; second, the 'momentary category,' which is the stream of impermanence.
As in the latter case, we now refute the category of consciousness. It must be said: just as [the term] "pond" and so forth conventionally excludes real water, why is this not the same here?

[The opponent] says: "To explain: 'obstructing' (*vighāta*) has the meaning of 'ceasing. One may metaphorically apply this to the real. 'Sustaining' (*dhṛti*) has the meaning of 'maintaining,' and thus one metaphorically applies it to non-sustaining.

(This explanation is incorrect; since you admit that [the power of obstruction] is pervasive, it should likewise be maintained. For example, it is said that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) sustains the six bases. However, following the Sarvāstivāda, although the actual subtle entities are unimpeded, they metaphorically take up the designation of "sustaining" as an analogy for the mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*).

In the Mahāyāna’s actual doctrine, [this power] belongs exclusively to real dharmas; that is to say, among the real dharmas that are capable of sustaining, one speaks of depending upon them metaphorically for the capacity to obstruct and sustain). Regarding the statement, "different categories must necessarily share the same nature as their respective distinct entities":

This is not the same as [the case of] *nikāya-sabhāga*, because it is not a general category (*sāmānya-jāti*); rather, its nature is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and, being a specific category, it does not extend to other [factors].
(Ji and Ce agree on this). Ce states: "The ancient Sautrāntikas maintained that there is only the *sattva-sabhāga*; Vasubandhu, in the *Abhidharmakośa*, added the *dharma-sabhāga*.
Both are exclusively indeterminate according to the two Mahāyāna explanations. However, since there is no scriptural authority (*āgama*) for establishing a *dharma-sabhāga*, [it is not accepted]."

Only sentient beings share the same category as "superior," because the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa) classifies its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). [The author] now says this is not so, as in the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*.
The Sautrāntika school establishes two types: first, the general, and second, the specific. The general is indeterminate, while the specific pertains to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).

Now, our matured school refutes the nature of these general and specific entities. Jñānagarbha says: "Even if one were to grant their statement that it is of the class of the indeterminate, [the opponent's] refutation is still a refutation."

Regarding the claim that "in the absence of mind, there is certainly no such [perfuming] (even if one were to grant the possibility of a counter-argument based on the presence of examples)," concerning the point that "Arhats and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should mutually perfume one another," there are two explanations by Ji and Ce:

First, it is said that this is explained with reference to a single body. That is to say, within the body of an ordinary being, there exists the category of noble consciousness (*ārya-vijñāna*), which is the category of an Arhat;

thus, it should receive the perfuming of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). Conversely, the category of consciousness belonging to an Arhat that has not yet become an ordinary being may be said to receive the [perfuming] of the ordinary category.

Regarding the permeation by outflows (*āsrava-vāsana*): if one grants this, there would be the confusion and loss of the distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones (for if an ordinary being were to manifest as an Arhat in their present body, how could that *vipākavijñāna* not possess such a variation?).
One view states: it is explained with reference to different bodies; for those who are merely similar in type should mutually permeate one another.

This should be known through inference, just as in the case of one's own body (the interpretation of Yuance [Mei] takes this as the first explanation, while Jiji [Jizang] does not permit the inclusion of "taking" [upādāna]). Furthermore, there is the objection regarding the six sense-faculties and form.

Although the mental faculty (*manas*) differs [from the sense faculties], because its category as a faculty is the same, it would mutually perfume the faculties and consciousnesses; or, in the case of visible forms, sounds, and so forth, because their categories as objects are the same as those of visual consciousness, they would mutually perfume it—both of which contradict your own tenets.
Furthermore, [it is because] the six groups of consciousness (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya) necessarily coexist simultaneously.
The commentary states: This third section refutes the final remaining position. Master Ji says: "The preceding categories of phenomena and their simultaneity have already been refuted.

To save these phenomena and categories, [the opponent argues that] the former perfumes the latter. Therefore, [the author] provides a general refutation, stating: 'Consciousness perfumes the categories; the categories perfume consciousness; the categories perfume [consciousness]...'"* *(Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the refutation regarding the mutual perfuming of consciousness and its categories.)*
In all such cases, [the熏習, or perfuming,] is not established. That school admits only that the subsequent moment is perfumed by the preceding one;

[we] refute this because they do not allow for simultaneous existence, which would be like [a gap] of many moments. Cè says: "Although there are four permutations, we briefly do not refute [perfuming] within its own category; therefore he says 'it is not' (it is not so).
This is because [if we were to] separately refute it, his own position would be indeterminate; thus, he speaks of them collectively."
[The opponent] maintains that only the six consciousnesses (up to the point of) can possess the capacity to sustain seeds.
[The author] states: This second section refutes the Mahāsāṃghika school. Cè says: They assert that the six consciousnesses functioning simultaneously can sustain seeds without being perfumed.
Now, this is refuted by reasoning, as was done in the refutation of the Sautrāntika school. Since they are not what is perfumed, [the seeds] likewise do not exist [therein].

Regarding "maintaining seeds" (*dhāraṇa-bīja*): Jizang says that since this specifically refutes the simultaneous transformation of the six consciousnesses, we know that the initial refutation targets only the Sautrāntika school.

Even if [the Sautrāntikas] were to establish simultaneous transformation—though it is not what receives perfuming—since they actually do maintain simultaneous transformation, the objection regarding the lack of perfuming cannot be sustained.

They do not posit a provisional category; they assert only the six consciousnesses, claiming there is no prior perfuming of the subsequent, and that they only transform simultaneously. (The two commentaries differ in their intent; Jizang describes their position as allowing for perfuming.)
[This is] due to habituation).
There are those who maintain that [this refers to] form and mind (up to this point), because it was already explained previously.
The commentary states: The third [section] refutes the Sthavira school. However, Wuxing says: "The Sautrāntika" refers to the Sthavira school.
There is a school that takes certain sūtras as its authority; thus it is called the Sautrāntika, not because it is the original Sūtra-piṭaka.

They assert that form (*rūpa*) and the mind (*citta*), etc., each produce subsequent instances of their own kind through prior perfuming (*vāsanā*). This is as refuted by Asvabhāva: because two moments do not coexist, they cannot undergo perfuming. The *Jīliàng* (基量) states:
"Prior moments of mind and so forth do not serve as seeds for subsequent moments of mind and so forth, because there is no perfuming," just as [in the case of] a lamp.

Regarding "tiles and rubble" (and so forth): because this is an inference from another case (*parārthānumāna*), one cannot claim that the seeds of the Mahāyāna arise in an indeterminate manner; for do not tiles and rubble themselves arise from their own kind? This is cited as an analogy to show that [the opponent's] position cannot give rise to the mind.

As for "interruption," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "In the formless realm, when descending [to a lower level], there is no cause for birth. This is because they assert that the past has no substance and the present lacks an entity.

The same applies to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). If it were as they say, there would be no subsequent aggregates (*skandha*). This is just as Vasubandhu refuted [the existence of] matter (*rūpa*).

The mind has two causes, which are eternally inexhaustible (the meaning of "inexhaustible" is as explained in the *Mātṛkā*). They [the opponents] argue that matter and mind arise from each other as seeds;

therefore, when there is an interruption, it is not a case of arising without a cause. To refute this further, it is said: one should also not maintain that they serve as seeds for one another in turn.
Some say that [the existence of] the three time periods cannot be established.
The commentary states: This fourth point refutes the Sarvāstivāda, who assert that the substantial entities of cause and effect exist throughout all three time periods.

[They claim that] when the causal activity functions, the cause is able to cease the effect, and once the effect has arisen, the cause no longer exists; thus, [their position] is not entirely tenable. The Master of the Treatise refutes those who deny the existence of functional activity.

Master Jiāngliáng says: "The two periods of past and future lack the nature of being causal conditions because they lack the activity of grasping a fruit, just like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth.
The remainder is easy to understand and need not be explained.
There are those who maintain that the Mahāyāna [teaches] this eighth consciousness.

The commentary states: "The fifth [section] refutes the position of Bhāviveka, who rejects the characteristics of what is grasped, asserting that the Mahāyāna is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and negates all phenomena.
Cè says: "In his *Madhyamakahṛdaya-śāstra*, in the chapter 'Entering the Nectar of Truth,' he says: 'The ālaya...'"
The *ālayavijñāna* has no separate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it is not subsumed within the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, and is like a flower in the sky.

(In reality, since the teaching of the *ālayavijñāna* had not yet been established at that time, one knows that the evolving consciousnesses arise from the ocean of the storehouse consciousness; apart from this inseparable [basis], there is no other distinct consciousness. Although this is so, the critique is made based on the conventional traces. Ceci (Ce) states:

"Because there are two fallacies, this is called a pseudo-inference (*tarka-pramāṇa*). First is the fallacy of the thesis (*pakṣa-doṣa*). If [the argument is] from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it commits the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*)."
I also grant that for them there is no distinct nature. If this is from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), it contradicts the *Abhidharmasūtra* and other such texts.

Second, there is a fault in the reason (*hetu-doṣa*): namely, that [your reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for others. For the *manas* is not among the six [sense-bases], yet it possesses a nature.

Furthermore, it is jointly inconclusive (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), because form (*rūpa*) and so forth are commonly accepted as existing conventionally. (This interpretation is unacceptable; since it is already known that their position is restricted to the ultimate (*paramārtha*), one should refute it based on the conventional. It is a laborious exercise to set it forth [otherwise].)

These are empty words. Since you claim to negate all things, yet your words themselves accord with those very things, you would thereby cause your own school to fall back into false views; therefore, we do not rely on this. Furthermore, as for the statement that one negates all phenomena:

As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śloka*: "The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty, because they arise dependently like illusions; unconditioned phenomena have no reality, for their non-arising is like flowers in the sky. Cè (Cè-lùn) says:
"If this refers to ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), there is the fault of contradicting [the existence of] dharmas; if it refers to conventional emptiness (*saṃvṛti-śūnyatā*),"
This contradicts the sacred teachings; therefore, the treatise as a whole contradicts the sacred teachings.

To claim that [the treatise] upholds [the doctrine] while simultaneously subverting and harming the sūtras cited previously—since the teachings of the third period all contain the eighth consciousness, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and so forth—is subject to the same fault mentioned before. If you say they are in agreement, you likewise deny [their existence].

Since this is neither a case of total negation (*apavāda*) nor the establishment of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), Candrakīrti’s objection that the *Dharmapāla* [Śāntarakṣita] contradicts the entirety of the sacred teachings is based on the following: according to the sūtras, the causes and effects of defilement and purification exist not only conventionally but also truly;

they are not non-existent. If they were truly non-existent, they would necessarily be non-existent even conventionally, like the horns of a rabbit. Thus, he [Candrakīrti] contradicts the sūtras. Kuiji states:

"The verse from the *Tattvasaṃgraha* relies on a pseudo-inference (*tarka-anumāna*) to negate this consciousness and all phenomena (without citing the *Madhyamaka-aṣṭadaśa-śāstra*). A 'pseudo-inference' is one where a portion of the subject (*dharmin*) is not ultimately established."

This results in a logical fallacy (*prasanga*). Since [the proponents] do not mutually admit that emptiness possesses a true nature (these points are irrational, as explained in the *Mātṛkā*), and regarding the phrase "the non-Buddhists' slanders" and so forth, both Bu ston and Tsoṅ kha pa state:
"If one were to defend [this position] by saying, 'I do not say that the conventional self does not exist, because it is neither real nor unreal,' then this would be identical to the non-Buddhists.
(Looking at the flow of the text now, it appears that the preceding wrong views are being refuted as being even more extreme than those of the non-Buddhists.)
Furthermore, the Sūtra says (up to) "this eighth consciousness. [The commentary] states:
This is the second proof. Ji (Jizang) says: This refutation applies equally to both the Sautrāntika and Sarvāstivāda schools. Ce (Xuanzang) says:

That which is reckoned as being produced by the karma of the six consciousnesses is called true maturation (*vipāka*). However, since the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) are reckoned as general maturations, they are cited here as examples.
According to the *Vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra), fascicle 150 and elsewhere, this refers to the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
Although the four objects, such as visible form and so forth, are not the collective maturation [of karma], it is nonetheless not admitted that they can be severed and then resume.
Nevertheless, a sutra states that King Viśvāmitra plucked out both his eyes and gave them to a brahmin, and through his vow, they were restored.
In truth, their eyes have not yet been plucked out, for Śakra has restrained them. That person finally said:

"Other masters say that the hell-beings' bodies are severed into hundreds of pieces and so forth, yet the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) remains continuous, like a lotus fiber that has been cut. This is because a single sentient being cannot possess two bodies.

As for the observation that worms continue to move even when severed, this is due to the movement of the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*); they do not possess the body-faculty or the four [faculties] such as the eye."

Regarding the sense faculties (*indriya*), it is accepted that their object is not severed; for example, when the divine eye arises, the eye obtained at birth remains, even though the ripened matter (*vipāka-rūpa*) has been severed, as there is no principle of reconnection [for such matter].
As for the Sautrāntika school, they accept that once ripened matter is severed, it does not reconnect.

[However,] the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that sound possesses ripening, whereas the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that sound is not a true ripening result (*vipāka*). Thus, according to the Mahāyāna, it is accepted that [matter] is severed and then reconnects.
Because they arise intermittently. By this principle, the eyes and other faculties also have interruptions, for the eyes of all donors are born again.

However, the sense organs of those in the hells and other such realms necessarily have no interruption, because they constantly experience suffering through all their gates. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
Because the eight faculties are necessarily matured through both their manifest and seed states, the *Prajñapti-śāstra* states: "The faculties of those in the hells are subject to interruption.

This is because various schools hold differing views regarding the *Abhidharma*. Regarding this, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "The six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, which are produced by karma, are born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Master Cè offers two interpretations: first, he says they are not true maturation, because they do not continue in a constant stream. Master Jì [provides the following...].

The analogy is stated as follows: "It is like sound, which [the opponent] themselves accepts. Regarding the Mahāyāna acceptance of [sound] as being born of maturation (*vipākaja*), Master Ce has two explanations. One says it is the same as the previous case.

The other says that this formal argument (*pramāṇa*) takes "not being a true maturation" as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), and thus the analogy establishes what is commonly accepted [by both parties].

(The latter explanation is superior; for although the Mahāyāna accepts that sound is born of maturation, if this were the thesis, the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because virtuous and defiled minds, though not continuous, are not born of maturation. Thus it is said.
Regarding the phrase "acting as the support for sentient beings," Ji (Jizang) says: "Because this provisional person (*pudgala*) is established based upon this consciousness.
As for the *viprayukta-dharmas*, they specifically counter the Sarvāstivādins, because [the Sarvāstivādins] establish sentient beings based on the commonality of life-force (*jīvitendriya*).

Next, the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) specifically counter the Sautrāntikas, because they establish sentient beings based on the six consciousnesses. Therefore, the subsequent refutation states: "Furthermore, based upon what dharma are they eternally established?"

Regarding sentient beings, as for the term "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*): Jì (基) says it refers to the objects experienced by the body, not to the category of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Cè (測) says that the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya* states:

"In states such as meditative concentration, there is the eighth consciousness which experiences [objects] through contact that is either disagreeable or agreeable; therefore, it is called 'bodily sensation.

[This is because] the sensation associated with it is named 'bodily sensation,' just as the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) names the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) 'bodily sensation. Thus, he now refutes [the opponent's position]: since your consciousness does not coexist [with the object], and you claim that the mind and so forth do not perceive that contact, by what means could one subsequently experience the tranquility or irritation?"
Later, he establishes that the phrase "not the Buddha" serves to distinguish it from the stage of Buddhahood, for fear of contradicting the fundamental tenet.

This is like the position that when those [minds] arise, they are permitted to be the true maturation (vipāka) resulting from karma, as accepted by the Hīnayāna, where the six consciousnesses are held to be truly matured by karma.
Furthermore, a sūtra states [up to] "this eighth consciousness.
The commentary says: This is the third proof. The Sarvāstivādins admit only that the five aggregates of maturation (*vipāka*) within the destinies and births constitute its nature;

however, they do not admit the existence of an eighth [consciousness], which leads to logical fallacies. For a substantial entity is established only when it possesses four characteristics: first, it must be substantially existent (*dravyasat*).

Second, it must be constant and continuous, because it persists throughout the duration of a single lifetime (*ekakāla*). Third, it must be universally pervasive, because it extends through all nine stages (*navabhūmi*).

Fourth, it must be unmixed, because it arises only here and is designated as this specific destiny (*gati*). Regarding the term "actual" (*samyak-tattva*), this distinguishes it from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that arises from the afflictions and karma which initiate those destinies, for that too is called a "destiny.
Jizang says: "This is not found in other schools; they do not distinguish it from the *manas*, or [they do not use] the word 'constant'."
Briefly stated: because there is an easy explanation. To say "only the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*)" is the essential point.

Question: Is the substance of the destinies and births one or many? If it were one, then based on the six [bases], it would be a mere designation (*prajñapti*), like a jar. If it were many, then one [being] would have to be six [beings]. Answer: There are two senses. First, it is one, yet a designation; however, this is said in terms of the bases (*āśraya*). Regarding the essential point: [The text continues: ...because there is an easy explanation. To say "only the maturation-consciousness and its mental factors" is the essential point. Question: Is the substance of the destinies and births one or many? If it were one, then based on the six [bases], it would be a mere designation, like a jar. If it were many, then one [being] would have to be six [beings]. Answer: There are two senses. First, it is one, yet a designation; however, this is said in terms of the bases. Regarding the essential point:

They truly exist. Of these two, the real [entities] are only the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*). However, because they follow along with their characteristics (*nimitta*), one speaks of them as including the mental factors (*caitta*). The latter interpretation is superior.

(The *Zhèngshì shūyào* contains a third point stating that it is no fault for them to be in the same aggregate and both be real; this is incorrect. The *Shūyào* says: "Or, if there is no fault in saying they are in the same aggregate and both [exist], then [the text] explains the mental factors as following along toward rebirth and establishes the thesis that they are real and not provisional.
This is not so. It would mean that the six classes of beings are not in the same aggregate, which is absurd). The *Zhèng* says: "If they were not mental factors, they should be established as..."

Since the meaning [of "destination"] is restricted to only four categories, it is known that these also include the realms of rebirth (*gati*). Just as there are eight consciousnesses, yet based on the preeminent eighth consciousness, one is designated as a "sentient being" (*sattva*), so too is this case.

Since the destinies are real, those that are non-associated [with mind] are excluded (this shares the same fault as before; for it correctly takes the six real entities and the six types of persons as the destinies).

Since this conforms to the destinies of sentient beings, mental factors (*caitta*) should also be considered merely provisional designations. Thus, by restricting the meaning to only four categories, non-associated phenomena are excluded; however, the terms "afflictions" (*kleśa*) and "karma" refer to the actual, real destinies. Even if one were to grant [the inclusion of other factors],...

Regarding the phrase "the destinies (*gati*) and births (*upapatti*) encompass all contaminated (*sāsrava*) states," this directly refutes the Sautrāntika school, as they generally maintain that the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) constitute the essence of the destinies.

As for the "previous fault" mentioned: it refers to the fault previously held by the Vaibhāṣikas—that when one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) gives rise to wholesome or defiled states, those are not [considered] destinies or births.
And as for "this loss": it refers to the subsequent [fault] of the Sautrāntikas—that when one born in the formless realm gives rise to an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind, [it is not a destiny].

It refers to the loss of the destination (*gati*). That the Tathāgata is neither a destination nor a realm (*dhātu*) means that "destination" refers to that which is reached, having the sole meaning of karmic maturation (*vipāka*).

"Realm" refers to bondage, encompassing all that is tainted (*sāsrava*). Because the Buddha has abandoned suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), he has uprooted conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, the Sūtra says [up to] "this eighth consciousness. The commentary states:
This is the fourth proof. Regarding "only the present world," it is because past and future lack the arising of cognition and experience.

That [body] must certainly have a mind that can appropriate it. Jì (基) says: Although the sūtra speaks only of the body having appropriation (*upātta*), since the body itself lacks any dharma appropriated by its own [mind], it is clearly known that there is another [mind] capable of appropriating it.
The phrase "induced by prior karma" refers to the five reasons among the eight proofs in the *Yogācārabhūmi* for why the appropriation of the basis (*āśraya-upādāna*) cannot be found.

That is to say, in sequence: (1) being drawn by prior karma (wherein the preceding actions share a common fruition); (2) being non-virtuous or defiled karma (whereby both good and evil are obtainable in the six evolving consciousnesses);
(3) being of a single type (whereby a single type of neutral [avyākṛta] is not obtainable); (4) being pervasive (whereby they evolve separately according to their respective bases);

and (5) being continuous (whereby they maintain a constant grasp of the physical body through perpetual appropriation, rather than sometimes grasping and sometimes not). Regarding the statement that the evolving consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness lack these "single types," it refers to the first five meanings.
The first two [of the three categories] both belong to the third category; therefore, there is no category that lacks the first three.

Regarding the statement, "Because all evolving consciousnesses manifest as dependent origination," etc., the first five are inferences (*anumāna*), which serve as the causes for the five causes of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* respectively.
As for the phrase "all minds and all mental factors (*caitta*) also include the mental concomitants," one interpretation by Cè states: "The evolving consciousnesses that are to be refuted..."

Regarding the inclusion of mental factors (*caitta*): one interpretation states that the term "maturation-consciousness" (*vipākacitta*) also includes mental factors, because both are capable of grasping (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, the term "evolving consciousnesses" (*pravṛttivijñāna*) also includes mental factors, because neither are they themselves the grasping subject (*grāhaka*). Regarding the phrase "not the material sense organs (*rūpindriya*) and so forth," *Cai* says:

this refutes the Sautrāntika position that the body-sense organ (*kāyendriya*) is the locus of appropriation (*upādāna*), because the four [faculties] such as the eye all depend upon it. It also refutes the... [Sāṃkhya].

The *pudgala* [is associated with] the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), which can be grasped by the body; or it may be understood as a general negation. Jizang says:
"Although a general name is mentioned, one must certainly take the life-faculty and the homogeneous character, because others do not accept the rest; or else, it excludes the rest."
Furthermore, the Sūtra states [up to] "this eighth consciousness.

The commentary says: This is the fifth proof. The first logical reason (*hetu*) states that there is "intermittence" and "transformation," which refers to the specific [characteristics]. "Lacking constant sustaining function" refers to the general [characteristic].

Taken together, there are three reasons, forming three syllogisms (*anumāna*). These collectively refute the various schools' claims that the six consciousnesses are capable of acting as the sustaining [consciousness].

Next, the thesis is established as follows: "Consciousness alone sustains vitality and warmth. Regarding the statement that vitality and warmth are like [the sustainer], this analogy is not fully established, because vitality and warmth do not each sustain one another.
Cè (Cèlún) says: "The words are general, but the meaning is specific;

when consciousness sustains vitality, warmth serves as the analogy, and when consciousness sustains warmth, vitality serves as the analogy. The summary refutation concludes: "Among these three, it is consciousness alone [that sustains them]."
It is not the case that [the three] are of one kind; rather, it accords only with correct reasoning. The *Ceshi lun* (Treatise on Measurement) states:

"Life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) must necessarily continue in succession, because each is subsumed under one of the three supports (*dhāraka*). This is just like life-force and warmth. Next, the *Waizhi lun* (External Commentary) states:
"That supporting consciousness does not exist at all times, because it is subsumed under one of the two supports, excluding life-force. This is just like its...
"Warmth" [is absent] because one who is born in the formless realm lacks warmth. The Master’s explanation resolves this; it is easily understood.
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of this eighth consciousness... [up to] ...this eighth consciousness.
The commentary states: This is the sixth proof. Regarding the phrase "not the mindless absorption" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it means neither the state of being without mind nor meditative absorption.

Therefore, your explanation is unreasonable. Furthermore, the Sautrāntika says: "In the case of one who has entered the attainment of cessation, although feeling and perception have ceased, the subtle *prajñā* (wisdom) persists; therefore, the mind should also persist. The Master objects: "That is not correct, for *prajñā* is not the cause of the mind. Rather, the mind is the cause of *prajñā*. This is because *prajñā* arises from the maturation of karma, whereas the mind arises from the maturation of karma and from the outflow of the mind itself. Therefore, when the mind ceases, *prajñā* also ceases. It says: "The Mahāyāna states that the Buddha is without vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). Although this is not universally accepted, it is a point established after having thoroughly studied the treatises of other schools;
thus, one should know how to enter into the doctrines of others. Cè (測) says: "That school asserts that even the Buddha’s speech arises from vitarka and vicāra.

They claim that just as [the Buddha] produces conventional selfhood through bodily action accompanied by mental action, you likewise produce it through verbal action accompanied by mental action. Since these two difficulties are equal, [your objection does not hold]."
"This is only incorrect. The commentary explains: "Regarding phenomena, there are those that are pervasive and those that are not.

As for the statement 'admitting it to be like volition (*cetanā*) and other universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*),' this is because the *Saṃyuktāgama* on Contact (*sparśa-sūtra*) takes only volition as representative of the three universal factors, whereas the *Jātaka-sparśa-sūtra* school takes volition as representative of the four universal factors.
Since this is so, [the objection that] 'faith (*śraddhā*) and the others are likewise absent at this stage'—Master Ji and Master Ce state: 'The Sūtra...'"

[The opponent] says: "Because 'faith' and so forth are designated as states of volition (*cetanā*), one may take volition as an example to establish that [contact, feeling, and perception] do not exist within it;
thus, all instances where the mind is present serve as the corroborating analogy (*sapakṣa*) for this inference. The rest of the text is easily understood.
If there is nothing [to which it] corresponds, it should be understood in this way.
The commentary states: Second, the refutation of the absence of mental factors (*caitta*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

"The meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) must lack mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it lacks mental factors, and because the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) have ceased, just as in cases such as fainting" (the views of Kuiji and Fabao are the same). Fabao says: "Alternatively, it may be illustrated by the remainderless nirvāṇa (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*)."
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Junchengye lun) admits the existence of a subtle mind (*sūkṣmacitta*), as it also maintains that even during sleep or fainting there is still a mind present.

Alternatively, in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) ought to cease, because its universal concomitants (*sarvatraga*) have ceased; just as speech ceases when its corresponding [mental factors] cease.

Furthermore, according to your position, the sensations (*vedanā*) and other [mental factors] would not be "universal ground" (*mahābhūmika*) factors, because they do not pervade all states of mind, just like greed (*lobha*) and so forth. If you attempt to defend this by claiming that the term "universal" refers only to those states where a mind is actually present, [the same fault remains].

By establishing a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) to refute the existence of mental factors (*caitta*), it follows that they would not be associated (*saṃprayukta*) dharmas, just like matter (*rūpa*). Furthermore, as a defense, one might ask: "What prevents them from being non-associated at that time? Just as unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is non-obstructive among forms, one refutes [the opponent] by stating that [mental factors] lack a basis (*āśraya*), etc., just like matter. I, however, accept that the realm of the unmanifest is not matter. This constitutes a genuine refutation. As for the opponent’s defense—claiming that when one is weary of greed and so forth, the mind perishes along with them, and subsequently a distinct mind arises—it must follow that at the time of such weariness, the mind perishes along with sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), and that thereafter a distinct mind arises which is devoid of these.
Therefore, he further refutes this by stating that the mind does not perish; it is only at that time that it is termed "mindless" (*acittaka*).
Jizang says: "In this context, the mind should also be extinguished, because its name does not exist [as a distinct entity], just as feeling and perception are extinguished.

Even if one were to grant that there is a mind, which of the three natures (trisvabhāva) would it belong to? That school only grants that bodily and vocal karma, etc., are 'concomitant wholesome' (*samutthāna-kuśala*);

they do not grant that the substance of the mind itself is also [wholesome]. [Cai] says: 'That school holds that bodily and vocal [karma], the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and the four types of perception, etc., are concomitant wholesome; they do not grant that the substance of the mind is also the originator. Immediately following a wholesome mind..."
The three natures that are produced should all be equally arisen as wholesome, because they are induced by a wholesome mind. The mind in such a state [is explained] thus;
the rest of the text is easy to understand.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says (up to): "because it maintains those seeds."
The commentary states: This is the tenth proof. It consists of two parts: the thesis and the explanation. This is the first [the thesis].
Master Ji notes that this passage exists in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Āgamas*, and other texts. The meaning here is as follows:

the present seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) constitute the defiled and pure mind, thereby giving rise to defilement and purity. "Taking the mind as the basis" is the general statement. "The manifesting [consciousnesses]" refers to...

It arises from the causal seed-mind and abides by depending on the manifest mind. As for the "seed," it refers to the mind’s reception of a heavy [karmic] burden, as well as the maintenance of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) [with many further iterations established according to one's preference].
"However, the defiled phenomena (up to the end) are also not established.
[The commentary] states: There are two distinct explanations: because of defilement and because of purification. This is the first. Master Ji says:

According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, this primarily refutes the Sautrāntika position that the past and future are not real, while incidentally refuting the Sarvāstivāda. "Subsequent phenomena of a different category" refers to the *Saṃgraha*.
The treatise, having first discussed mundane and supramundane minds, logically extends this principle to all [minds] when viewed across different stages (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "formative forces (*saṃskāra*) condition consciousness (*vijñāna*)," Cè states: "In terms of the links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this simultaneously refutes both the Sautrāntika and the Sarvāstivāda schools. The Sarvāstivādins maintain:
"Wholesome minds in active manifestation are called 'formative forces,' while the first arising of defiled consciousness is called 'consciousness. [This refers to] taking birth."

The first moment of thought is exclusively defiled because it is moistened [by craving]. According to the Sautrāntika school, the three types of manifest karma constitute the "formative action" (*saṃskāra*).

The seeds of karma, which are perfumed by those actions and are sustained by the defiled consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), constitute "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). Master Ji says: "The perfuming of consciousness by formative action is called 'conditioned by formative action, there is consciousness'.

(This refers to the consciousness that sustains the seeds of karma; the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the first moment of the intermediate state is called "linking rebirth"). Now, this treatise has already discussed the process of receiving perfuming prior to this point.

Regarding the phrase "because it is excluded," this directly refutes the Sautrāntika position. Regarding the phrase "the defiled consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking is not [produced] because formations have ceased," this directly refutes the Sarvāstivāda position.

If one were to argue as a counter-objection that "since formations induce [rebirth], formations are admitted to be the condition for consciousness, and thus the defiled consciousness at rebirth-linking is indeed turned by formations."

Even so, because the retributive consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) exists within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is said that "volitional formations are the condition for consciousness. [The opponent] refutes this, saying: "One should rather say that 'volitional formations are the condition for name-and-form'.

[Paramārtha] says: "Furthermore, this interpretation also refutes the Sautrāntika school. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: 'They too [admit] that the defiled consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) is [the retributive consciousness]'. Even if one were to concede that name-and-form has volitional formations as its condition, the meaning of "condition" as it pertains to the member of consciousness would not be established.
This also refutes the Sautrāntikas, for according to them, prior karma has long since ceased and no longer exists to be experienced.

The *Vibhāṣā* masters explain that it perfumes consciousness; regarding the consciousness at the moment of rebirth, they maintain that it functions without [karmic] objectivity (*anartha*). This is the intention of the *Viniscaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, and the *Śū-yao* (Essential Summary) is likewise. Master Ji says:

"That [opponent’s] defense is based on explaining dependent origination in terms of specific stages (*avasthā*). Although the defiled consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*) is not produced by formations (*saṃskāra*), at this time it possesses form and has maturation (*vipāka*) as its nature;

it is therefore also called the 'consciousness member' (*vijñāna-aṅga') and is termed 'consciousness conditioned by formations' (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*). This is the orthodox defense of the Sarvāstivāda school.
The Sautrāntika refutes this by stating: "Furthermore, the action exists in the present, while the resultant form exists in the future—perhaps separated by an eon or eighty thousand [kalpas].

Since they are remote and utterly disconnected, there is no possibility of a causal relationship; therefore, because this [causality] is not established, the subsequent [causality] is also not established.
As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* says: "Moreover, the condition of grasping for existence (*upādāna-pratyaya-bhava*) cannot be established either. Vasubandhu’s commentary states:

This refers to the consciousness that has been perfumed by the aforementioned formations (*saṃskāra*). By the power of grasping (*upādāna*), the perfuming increases and transforms into existence (*bhava*). (Cai [Mei] says:

"It is clearly understood that according to the Sautrāntika school, the seeds perfumed by karma are called the member of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*); when those very seeds are moistened and become functional, they are called existence. However, this is not necessarily the case here. It is the increase of the seeds within the perfumed consciousness that is called the member of existence.)

If the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that transform the seed-consciousness (*bījāvijñāna*) were not themselves branches of consciousness, then how could it be said—as explained in the *Vyākhyā*—that "conditioned by formations (*saṃskāra*), the evolving consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness, which arise simultaneously with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth, are accepted as the branch of consciousness"? One must understand that this branch of consciousness is the same as that held by the Sarvāstivādins).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that it is not merely that the subsequent branches, such as "appropriation conditions existence" (*upādāna-pratyaya-bhava*), would fail to establish the meaning of "conditioning. (Jikido Takasaki and Seizan Yanagida agree on this point).
"Because all pure dharmas (up to) never arise again. The commentary states: This is the second purification.
Mundane paths suppress [defilements]; supramundane paths sever them. It refers to the attainment of the unconditioned fruit (*asaṃskṛta-phala*) resulting from that severance.

There are two meanings regarding mundane paths: because they eliminate rebirth in higher realms, the former constitutes the defilement of karma, while one becomes free from the defilement of the lower realms.

Therefore, it is now established as the path of purification (*viśuddhi-mārga*). Regarding the fruit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-phala*), the seeds are held within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*); it is from that [consciousness] that abandonment is attained.
Consequently, this refutes the Sautrāntika position that there is nothing to be abandoned, and it refutes the Sarvāstivāda position regarding the "attainment of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-prāpti*).

This is because the Sautrāntikas claim that when the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises, neither the defilement nor its seed can arise; therefore, they describe it as abandonment at the moment the characteristics of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) occur within the realms (*dhātu*).

Therefore, one has not yet realized cessation (*nirodha*). The Sarvāstivādins say that at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), although there is no present possession (*prāpti*) of the afflictions, there is the acquisition of their possession;
it is by means of the acquisition of abandonment through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that one realizes cessation. What the Mahāyāna explains appears similar to the Sautrāntika view:

that in the moment prior to the path, the seeds of what is to be abandoned are established. As for the question "In dependence upon what, and by means of what?"—it refers to which affliction [is the basis], and by means of what...

The path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*). If, by the power of the path, [the defilement] subsequently does not arise, this refutes the Sautrāntika defense that there is no distinct fruit of abandonment;
rather, it is simply the non-arising or the non-existence of cessation (*nirodha*).
"It is permitted that this consciousness exists" (up to) "one should believe and accept it with deep conviction.

[The] Commentary says: This concludes the chapter. Regarding "the principles being boundless": among the eight proofs, the first—the fact that the cause for the arising of manifest activity cannot be found—is not yet discussed here. Therefore, [the principles] are boundless.
Thus, having already explained [up to] "the path does not exist," the commentary states:
The explanation of the second transformation has two parts: the presentation of the root text and the detailed exposition. This is the first.

The verse contains ten sections: first, the section on the designation of the name, because it is named *manas*; second, the section on the basis, because it functions in dependence upon that [ālayavijñāna];
third, the section on the object-condition, because it is said to take that as its object; fourth, the section on essential nature, because its nature is deliberation (*manana*);

fifth, the section on the mode of activity, because its characteristic is deliberation; sixth, the section on association with defilements, because the four [defilements] are either simultaneous or co-existent; seventh, the section on mental association...

1. The gate of association: because it occurs simultaneously with contact (*sparśa*) and other mental factors. 2. The gate of the three natures: because it is subsumed under the obscured (*nivṛta*). 3. The gate of realms and stages: because it is bound according to the realm of rebirth.
4. The gate of suppression and abandonment: because it does not exist during the three times [of past, present, and future].
The Treatise says: [up to] "therefore it is called *manas*.

The Commentary states: There are two parts to this explanation: first, the formal explanation of the ten gates; second, the establishment through scripture and reasoning. The first part consists of eight sections:

(1) the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and its modes of activity (*ākāra*) combined as one section; (2) its association with the defiled [factors] combined as one section; and the remaining [sections] individually.

Because it is singular; this is the first point. Regarding "constantly and thoroughly deliberating," the *Ṣaṣṭitantra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sixty-three) states: "The untainted (*anāsrava*) manas is free from inversion because it correctly deliberates.
This indicates that it extends to the untainted state. However, fearing that this seventh [consciousness] might be confused with the sixth, [the text clarifies].
Third, regarding the "proximate basis," Ji says: it accords with the same [type of] conceptualization; when the six [consciousnesses] take objects, the seventh provides them with power.
As in the fifty-first [verse], because the eighth exists, there is the manas; the manas serves as the basis.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) undergoes transformation. To distinguish it from the eighth [consciousness], which serves as its remote support (*dūrasaṃniśraya*), it is said that "that upon which it depends for its transformation" is because it grasps an object of perception (*ālambana*).

Commentary: This is the second section, the "Gate of the Support" (*āśrayamukha*). Within this gate, there are three parts: the primary explanation, the incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), and the conclusion.
Therefore, this is the first [point]. Regarding the explanation of the term "basis" (*āśraya*), as for the initial meaning: Master Ji says that Nanda and Vijñānakāya both state this.
If that were so, one could say that the eighth consciousness serves as the basis for the arising of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Their interpretation states:
Due to the guiding power of the seeds of the seven consciousnesses, the seeds of the sixth consciousness then give rise to their actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*). Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"With the manas as its support. This is as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says regarding the seed of visual consciousness, which depends upon the seed of the eye-faculty.

Regarding the second point, there is another interpretation according to the commentary of Dharmapāla and others, which holds that there is a transformation; this refers to the fact that [the seeds] undergo change through the wholesome and defiled states of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) and so forth, just as with other [seeds].
The evolving consciousnesses must necessarily have a present basis (āśraya). [This concludes] the extensive questions and answers; it need not be further elaborated.
All minds and mental factors—up to and including those that are not other phenomena—are [thus established].
The commentary states: This is the second ancillary discussion. Because this basis (*āśraya*) is common to all consciousnesses, it possesses a support.
Within this, there are two parts: the concise and the extensive; this is the former. Regarding "possessing a support," this applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. As the *Abhidharmakośa* says:
"Mind and mental factors are called 'possessing a support' and 'possessing an object,' etc. (*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter 50).

The five [reasons] explain the many names for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), namely: because they possess an object (*sālambana*), are associated (*samprayukta*), have mental formations (*sākāra*), have a support (*sāśraya*), and so forth.
Regarding the statement that there are "generally three kinds," as in the first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it refers to the support of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).

The simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) refers to the eye and so forth; the immediate support (*samanantara-āśraya*) refers to the mind (*manas*); and the seed support (*bīja-āśraya*) refers to the seed-ālayavijñāna.
Thus, the *Shuyao* (Essentials of the Pivot) asks: "For what reason are the four conditions [only] three supports? The explanation states: "Because they are proximate and predominant in their power.

The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is remote. Regarding the term "opening and guiding" (*kai-dao*), Master Ji says: "Opening means avoiding; it leaves the place of arrival and opens up that [space]."

Because it is the path, it guides; that is, it leads them to cause them to be born in this place. If one were to say "immediately" (*anantara*), it would mean that the seed which has just ceased serves as the support for the subsequent seed. To distinguish it from that, one says "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*).
"First, the basis of the seeds (up to) that which flows from the seeds. [Commentary:
This is the second, the extensive explanation, which is divided into three parts; this is the first. Within it, the first meaning refers to Nanda.

Or, the objective aspect is termed "form" and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is termed "consciousness"; since these two share the same seed, it is called the "seed of form-consciousness."

nevertheless, their status as a "basis" (*āśraya*) is identical, and this is cited here as an illustration (the words are general while the meaning is specific:

there are two types of bases—the causal basis, which refers to the manifest perfuming agent, and the co-existent basis, which refers to the manifest perfumed). This subsequently establishes the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) as the objective support (*ālambana*). This is transmitted from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
