Regarding "concentration and so forth," Ji Ce states that it must possess four meanings to constitute a support (*āśraya*). First is the meaning of "determination.
This excludes the five consciousnesses based on causal conditions as proposed by the former masters, as well as the material sense organs and sounds etc.

that serve as supports for the material *ālayavijñāna*. All other such factors are likewise excluded because they are not determinate supports; conversely, this establishes the position of the former masters.
1. It serves as the locus [of the consciousnesses]. This excludes the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), which do not rely upon the seventh or eighth consciousnesses.

2. It possesses the sense of being an objective domain (*viṣaya*). This excludes phenomena such as seeds (*bīja*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); although these definitely exist, they are not the support (*āśraya*). 3. It possesses the sense of being the dominant factor (*adhipati*).

This excludes the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga*), which, although they definitely possess an objective domain, are not the support. 4. It causes the mind and mental factors to apprehend their respective objects of cognition.
The third master [simplifies] the perfuming agent (*bhāvakatṛ*) and the perfumed object (*bhāvya*) as the basis for the seeds, because they cannot cause the seeds to apprehend an object.
Furthermore, he excludes the six sense faculties—apart from the mind and mental factors—from being the basis for other phenomena such as form (*rūpa*). What, then, is the foundational substance?
It is simply the six internal bases (*ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana*). All other phenomena are either not objects of cognition, or are not determinate.
Alternatively, it may not be the primary [basis], because it serves as a basis merely in the manner of a king.

Furthermore, since only the mind and its associates are said to possess a basis (*āśraya*), we know that this also fulfills the fourth sense. Regarding the "provisional designation according to suitability," it was stated previously that there are three kinds of bases in total;
therein, the seed-basis (*bījāśraya*) was described as the basis. In the first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, however, it speaks only of the "basis" (*āśraya*).
Regarding the eye: as for their statement that the "basis" (*āśraya*) is the "support" (*niśraya*), this should be explained according to the context of the text.
By means of this, the five consciousnesses [from the verse] accord perfectly with both reason and scripture.

The commentary states: This is the second establishment. Among the four kinds of bases for the five consciousnesses, it should be understood that they depend upon the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).

Regarding "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*): as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, when the five sensory consciousnesses arise, there must necessarily be a discerning mental consciousness.
The fourth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "The five consciousnesses take the mind (*manas*) as their support; for when the mind is distracted, the five do not arise.
As for [the claim that it] depends on the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], this is because of the verse cited below. Since one support is sufficient, why would four be necessary?

Because they differ in their functional capacity (*śakti*): the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) share the same objective domain; the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) performs discrimination; the *manas* is characterized by defilement and purity;

and the *ālayavijñāna* is the fundamental basis. Because they differ in their power (*bala*): the *Śūyao* (Essential Pivot) states, "When considering the body-faculty in relation to the four consciousnesses, what is lacking that prevents it from being a support (*āśraya*)?

One interpretation holds that there is no definitive meaning [to this objection], because a lower faculty can give rise to a higher one, such as visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Another explanation holds that it lacks the quality of having an object (*sālambanatva*).

Only those sense-faculties that possess the same objective domain (*sabhāga*) are termed "possessors of an object. Since the body and the four consciousnesses lack this quality, both [theories] are unreasonable;

furthermore, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses would then not be the supports for the five [sensory consciousnesses]. Now, I shall explain their specific meanings. First, among the determinate factors, they are not necessarily co-existent. There are four types of determination:

first, determination regarding the apprehension of the object (which refers to the sense-faculties sharing the same objective field, as they function in accordance with one another); second, clarity...

1. Determination regarding the object of perception (*ālambana-niścaya*)—this refers to the *viniścaya-kuśalamūla* (roots of discernment), as it pertains to both meditative concentration and the non-concentrated state. 2. Determination regarding the differentiation of the three supports (*tri-adhiṣṭhāna-viśeṣa-niścaya*)—this refers to the roots of defilement and purity.

When the seventh consciousness reaches its ultimate completion and becomes untainted (*anāsrava*), the other consciousnesses necessarily follow suit and become eternally untainted; however, this applies only to the causal stage when that completion has not yet been reached. 3. Determination regarding the support for what can arise (*utpādaka-adhiṣṭhāna-niścaya*)—this refers to the fundamental root (*mūla-kuśalamūla*).

Since seeds can serve as the support for the arising of manifest phenomena, this specifically takes the present Buddha as its basis. There are likewise four [determinations] regarding the subject (*grāhaka*) which functions as the dominant factor, such as the "conforming apprehension" (*anugraha-grahaṇa*) and so forth.

The four [faculties] each possess the quality of determination (*niyama*). Having an object (*viṣayin*) as their primary characteristic and being conjoined with the capacity to apprehend their respective objects of perception (*ālambana*), they are termed "bases" (*āśraya*).
In contrast, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) lacks all four of these meanings in relation to the four consciousnesses; therefore, there is no fault [in the definition].

(Regarding the visual and other consciousnesses, the body-faculty—comprising twenty-nine factors in total—is subsumed under the four fundamental meanings of "conformity," "apprehension," "defilement/purity," and "basis"; it possesses the meaning of being determined and having an object as its primary characteristic, thereby enabling the visual and other consciousnesses to apprehend their respective objects. The proof states: If that were so, then certainly...

The definitive selection of the factors is complete. This means that "having the same object" (*samāna-viṣaya*) already implies "having an object" (*saviṣaya*), and "being fundamental" (*mūla*) already implies "being primary" (*pradhāna*);

therefore, the other three [characteristics] are redundant. Now, to explain: with respect to the remaining four consciousnesses, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) lacks the status of being primary; thus, although the body-faculty exists, it is not included.

If any of the four faculties are lacking, the four consciousnesses do not arise; therefore, it is known that [the sense bases] are not dependent upon them. As for the claim that "the definitive selection of dharmas is exhaustive," since these four definitives reside solely within the six faculties and there is no overlap, what need is there for the remaining three?

However, this does not fully accord with reason. If one speaks only of "definitive" (*niyata*) without mentioning "having an object" (*saviṣaya*), then the seeds manifesting as their own [objects] should be considered the definitive basis for defilement and purity, as they possess the power to bring about defilement and purity and can serve as the root.

If one does not mention "predominance" (*adhipati*), then the mental factors (*caitta*) accompanying the five [consciousnesses] should be considered the "definitive concordant apprehension" (*anugrāhaka-niyata*) for the five consciousnesses, because they necessarily share the same object. Furthermore, the mental factors accompanying the sixth [consciousness] serve as the "basis of clarity" (*vyakta-āśraya*) for the five consciousnesses, because they possess discrimination (*vikalpa*). Thus, the meaning of the "field" (*kṣetra*) is omitted.

The fault [you have raised] is as previously refuted; the same applies to the failure to establish your thesis. Although the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) exists, if the other four faculties are lacking, the four consciousnesses do not arise; therefore, it is not the primary [agent]. Consequently, the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses should likewise not be the primary agents in that regard, for they too do not arise when those [four] are lacking.

Thus, your objection is invalid, and your own position is likewise unestablished. It is clear that the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot) is indeed a well-stated work. This is the specific interpretation of Guanfan, which contains only Chinese terminology.

Regarding what was said by the Tathāgata, the ninth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* discusses [the ālayavijñāna] being constantly associated with the manas. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 63, states:

Because it always functions simultaneously with the manas. Furthermore, it is stated that the ālayavijñāna always relies upon defilement (*saṃkleśa*), as in the third fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Regarding the statement that "the seeds of consciousness cannot presently grasp objects," Wonhyo says there are two meanings:
first, to show that the seeds have no basis; second, to show that the seeds are not themselves the basis.
"Subsequently, it serves as the basis for opening and guiding (up to:

serving as the basis for opening and guiding). Commentary: This explains the third basis. There are three masters' interpretations. This first one is Nanda. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter Three:
"The five groups of consciousness do not have two moments that follow one another and arise simultaneously; nor do they arise in immediate succession."
They arise alternately. Furthermore, it is said that once the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has shifted, the five [sensory] consciousnesses take only the sixth as their support.

Moreover, according to that treatise, because the mental consciousness necessarily arises immediately after the five [sensory] consciousnesses, the sixth also takes the five consciousnesses as its support.
There is an interpretation [up to] "because of what was stated previously.
The commentary states: Ce says this is the explanation of Viśeṣamitra (Jingyue). Ji says it is the explanation of Sthiramati and others. [The text] says:
"Abiding in the stage where mastery has not yet been attained," etc. Ce says: "Prior to the eighth bhūmi, one has not yet attained self-mastery..."
While it is present, its object is not superior; thus, they cannot be in a continuous succession. There are four permutations regarding this: First, the mind is superior while the object is not.
This refers to an *nisyanda* (outflow) mind arising toward an inferior object, which is termed "superior mind" because it is induced by the determined power of either defilement or purity.

Second, the object is superior while the mind is not. This refers to a sudden (*ābhoga*) mind arising toward the fires of hell. Third, both the object and the mind are superior. This refers to [a mind] directed toward a superior object.
It gives rise to a mind of natural outflow (*niṣyanda-citta*). Among these four types of minds, both the object and the mental state are not superior;

that is, when a sudden, impulsive mind (*ābhoga-citta*) arises toward an inferior object. Now, we rely on the fourth [category]. Even if one were to concede that [the mind] does not continue [in the second case], the meaning of the second line is that the seeking and determining [minds] necessarily arise in succession; it does not mean that a sudden mind persists for many moments.

If one is in a state of mastery—whether on the eighth ground or above, or from the first ground upward (the proof states: ordinary beings do not have mastery over the mutual use of [supernormal powers], whereas those from the first ground upward possess such mastery).

It is not that [the mind] becomes spontaneous (*anābhoga*) only from the eighth bhūmi upward; rather, it is spontaneous because there is no searching with distraction (as in the five stages of the *pañcavijñānakāya*).

Spontaneously following the object means that the initial moment possesses the sudden encounter (*ābhoga*), the fixed state (*niyata*), and the pure state (*viśuddha*). In the second moment, the sudden encounter is removed and the continuous flow (*pravāha*) is added.

The third [moment] generally refers to all the states of the "equal outflow" (*nisyanda*); the fourth specifically refers to the sudden encounter when the object is superior, which arises in immediate succession. Consciousness (*vijñāna*)...

Because it seeks [its object], it differs from inferior objects; having arisen as a *saṃtīraṇa* (investigative) cognition, it determines defilement or purity solely within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and only then induces the subsequent production of the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that flow from it.

(The actual meaning of the various schools is thus). Regarding the "playful delusions of the gods" (*krīḍā-pramada-deva*) and so forth—the term "and so forth" including the "malicious-minded" (*dauṣṭhulya-manas*)—Tse says:
these two apply to all six heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi-ṭīkā* states: "Since this is not the case, that..."

How is this so? Since it is not admitted that the five consciousnesses, having been interrupted, take their own preceding kind as an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), but rather take only the continuous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their condition; then how can the mental consciousness during those mindless states—which has itself been interrupted—take its own preceding kind as a condition?

Therefore, one knows that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses serve as the "opening and guiding" supports (*āśraya*). (This is the position of the masters of this treatise, as maintained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, fascicle 5.)

It is said that because the previously extinguished mind is without an object and entirely devoid of its own nature, there is no interval within the mind itself. Regarding the phrase "relying on compassion and vows," it means that the Bodhisattva is born in other realms in accordance with their vows.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly.
"There is an interpretation [that it is] not a mental factor (*caitasika*) and so forth.

The commentary states: This is the third section, the orthodox doctrine of Dharmapāla. Within this, there are three parts: the establishment of its essential nature, the refutation of attachments, and the formal proposition.
This is the first. Regarding the statement, "It is said that there are dharmas with objects," Cè says: It must necessarily possess four meanings. First...

1. It possesses an object of cognition (*ālambana*), which distinguishes it from matter (*rūpa*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). 2. It acts as a cause for arising (*janman*), which distinguishes it from all mental factors (*caitta*). 3.
It functions as an equal-and-immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for a consciousness of a different category. 4.

It opens the way and guides the subsequent arising within its own homogeneous class (*sva-jātīya*), thereby distinguishing it from the final mind of an Arhat. Master Ji states: "The first three meanings are the same as before; the fourth meaning distinguishes [this mind] from the subsequent [mind]."
The preceding basis (*pūrvāśraya*) and that which is simultaneous with the mind as its support for mental factors (*caittas*). Fan [Wenlan] says there are three meanings;

here, "opening the path" (*mārga*) is explained in reference to those arising subsequently and so forth, because it does not make distinctions. The third meaning excludes the final mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This is the proof.
The third [condition] is superior because the final mind and so forth are accepted by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna as not being this condition. (Now, we say:

although the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma acts as this condition for its own class of consciousness, since the final mind alone cannot do so, there is no fault in using a distinct definition to exclude it; thus, it is included in the "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) condition, and each is also [a condition]. Question: If that is so, the first existence (*bhava*) would have no function as a condition. Answer:
Not so, for other schools accept that matter (*rūpa*) has conditions for its arising, as the third definition excludes matter entirely.)
"If this [condition] and that [condition] are equal immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The commentary states: This is the second refutation of the attachment [to the notion of simultaneous arising]. It means that within a single body, it is impossible for dharmas to arise simultaneously; thus, the opening and yielding [of space] cannot be established.

Furthermore, as for the two moments—prior and subsequent—their quantity is not fixed, and therefore the meaning of "equality" is not established. Regarding the phrase "form and so forth," the term "so forth" includes the non-associated [conditioned factors] (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

It should be so, because the preceding and succeeding moments of the same category are indefinite in their quantity. Question: Since the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are always singular within a single body, why is it certain that matter (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates lack this condition?
Answer: Because the body-faculty co-exists with both maturation (*vipāka*) and nourishment (*aupacayika*), whereas the life-faculty is merely conventional (*prajñapti*).
This is because their seeds are dual. If one were to allow [the presence of] matter and the others, it would contradict the thirty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are stated solely with reference to all mental factors (*caitta*). Regarding the method of affirmation and negation:

the Sautrāntikas among the Mahīśāsakas state that although form (*rūpa*) possesses the immediately preceding and causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it lacks the foundational consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, let us set aside the Avīci hell for a moment. [The term] "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*) would be redundant if it did not specifically exclude the sequential causal conditions of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

This is because the word "equal" (*sama*) implies that each preceding and succeeding factor is singular; only then can they be called "equal. As for the statement that "simultaneity" expresses a category of causes, this is an attempt to salvage the argument by asserting that the individual self-natures (*svabhāva*) of the mind and so forth act as these conditions.
Therefore, [the theory of] the eight consciousnesses (up to) "profoundly accords with the scriptural principles.

The commentary states: The third section establishes the thesis (*siddhānta*). This consists of two parts: the formal exposition and the resolution of objections. Regarding the resolution of objections, there are five points.

First, the objection that since all consciousnesses arise simultaneously, it is not the case that the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) serve as mutual objects; if they arise simultaneously, by what means do they perceive one another? Thus [begins the objection].
The Commentary states: It is endowed with five meanings. First, because they are associated; this refers to the four meanings of "one" and so forth.

Second, because they are harmoniously combined and appear as one, as stated in [Treatise] 55: "The four formless aggregates should be said to be harmoniously combined and indivisible, such that their distinctions cannot be separated.
Third, they arise and cease simultaneously. Fourth, their activities are necessarily identical. Fifth, they provide guidance.
Because they are identical, each one leads to and conducts the subsequent group of dharmas. The various consciousnesses cannot be so; thus, they do not serve as an analogy.

Second, regarding the objection that if there is no distinction in their being conditions (*ālambana*), there should likewise be equality in their being supports (*āśraya*): the commentary explains that "support" has the sense of "that which sustains," whereas mental factors (*caitta*) are not supports.
"Condition" has the sense of "that which is reached," and mental factors are also such. Third, regarding the objection as to why [the mind] does not [arise] from its own kind:

Is it because of the principle of similarity that they are called "śramaṇa"? (Ji says: This refers to the characteristics of the meaning of "śramaṇa"; perception pertains only to perception, and feeling pertains only to feeling; they cannot be intermingled.)

Therefore, the commentary explains: regarding the newly arisen seventh and eighth consciousnesses upon the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there is an absence of conditions; the four difficulties are as previously stated.

When emerging from a state of mindlessness, it is accepted that the ever-present seventh and eighth consciousnesses serve as the basis. What hindrance is there in this? Both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses take the faith and other factors associated with the sixth consciousness as their conditions.
Thus, the commentary explains: "The meaning is that they are of their own kind, having resided in the past and being about to arise in the present."
At the time of cessation, it has already been able to serve as a basis; since this is not admitted [by you], why cite it as an example?

Fifth, if this were so, it would contradict the holy teachings. In the first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it states that by means of the arising of visual consciousness, three types of mind can be obtained;

and that the visual consciousness of outflow is induced by the defiled and the pure. This clearly shows that consciousnesses mutually induce one another’s arising. (*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, Chapter 7, Verse 8)

Regarding the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), how does one reconcile [this] with the *Abhidharma-kośa* and other treatises which speak of taking birth through the power of compassion and vows, as well as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* which states that from this consciousness, various consciousnesses arise without interval? Therefore, the treatise provides a reconciliation, which can be understood according to the text.
As for the statement that "the first two bases have superior function," it is because they possess immediate and direct efficacy within the same moment.
Thus it has been explained [up to this point]. What fault is there in this as well? The commentary states:

The explanation of the three types of objects (*ālambana*) through four meanings is provided. *Ce* says: "Although there are four explanations, the fourth is the correct one (as proof shows there is no other;
it is a calculation of a different master. Dharmapāla provisionally acted as host and guest to reveal [the truth]). *Ji* says: "The first refers to Nanda and others; the second refers to Mahāmati."

[The masters] such as Sthiramati, followed by Dharmapāla, and so forth. An objection is raised: "If [the ālayavijñāna] takes other dharmas as its object, it would contradict the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
The three masters reconcile this, respectively, as follows: "Because the inferior is concealed and the superior is revealed; because the characteristics are subsumed within consciousness;

and because the conventional follows the real. Thus, there is no contradiction with those teachings. Otherwise, one would contradict the sixty-third chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the first chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

Regarding "self" and "what belongs to self," both the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Categories) and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-bhāṣya* (Second Part of the Compendium) state that these are distinct entities.
How does the third master [Sthiramati] reconcile this? Jizang says: It means that they are said to exist in contrast to their non-existence as objects of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Within the system of Dharmapāla, there is no single mind that possesses both annihilationism and eternalism; he cites this as an example to show that different objects do not arise simultaneously.

Ji says: The two attachments to persons and phenomena do not have separate objects; because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) do not differ, they are co-existent. Cè says only that this is because their objects are the same.

[If there were a self and what belongs to the self, yet they were not co-existent as entities, then their functions would likewise have to be so. The subject and object stand in opposition; what belongs to the self must be a different entity from the self.

An entity is defined by its function, and apart from an entity, there is no further capacity. As for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), why must they necessarily possess a function? Like "non-characteristic" being a characteristic, or "non-object" being an object, it is simply the functioning of that very thing. Both [attachments] take the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as their objective support and its "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) as their basis.

Regarding the phrase "it does not [perceive] other parts": Zhiyi (Ji) states that because the coarse and subtle aspects belong to the same category and resemble what is permanent and unitary—whereby "resembling what is permanent" distinguishes it from form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as these are all severed by the gates [of the path];

and because the seeds are either temporarily suppressed or permanently eradicated; and because "resembling what is unitary" distinguishes it from mental factors (*caitta*), which consist of many dharmas occurring together;

and because it takes only the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, performing the function of experiencing the objective sphere (*ālambana*) in a manner resembling a self (*ātman*); it does not perceive other parts.

The functions of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) and so forth are subtle and difficult to know; therefore, they are not discussed separately in the *Cechu* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*). [However,] this [interpretation] seems incorrect, because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is not unitary.

Since it is stated that the seeds of the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and so forth are intermittent, the seeing-function that takes them as its objects must likewise be intermittent. If one were to argue that the seeing-function is called "constant" because there are other similar instances of it, then the same would have to apply to form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as to seeds. The *Shuyao* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*) states: [one passage].
Regarding the view that takes [the aggregates] as its object, it is said that the subject which perceives them—consisting of all three parts—is collectively termed "view.

Because it serves as the basis for all phenomena, it universally takes the three [aggregates] as its objects. [If one argues that] although the name "view" applies to all three parts, just as the three parts depend upon their own essence (*svabhāva*), the view likewise takes only that essence as its object;

this interpretation may be acceptable because there is no contradiction. However, an objection is raised: Why does [the self] not take only a single [aggregate], such as feeling (*vedanā*), as its object? Furthermore, why is it not both permanent and unitary?

Therefore, the *Śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Treatise) states: "Because it constantly serves as the basis for all phenomena. Regarding the self (*ātman*) of the ignorant, it takes sovereignty as its basis;

this is the doctrine of the "Lord of All Things" (*sarveśvara-vāda*). Thus, concerning this self: Jiteme (基測) states that the former self is the provisional entity (*prajñapti*) of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), which is the object of the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*);

the latter self is what is conceptualized by the seventh consciousness (*saptamavijñāna*). Alternatively, it is said that the former refers to the self [of] a preceding moment relative to a succeeding moment.

...and so forth, as explained at length (all of which do not accord with the treatise). Now, [we] say: first, there is the view of a self as one's own; second, there is the view directed toward others and toward that which is not-self.

There are ten kinds of equality, as found in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts. Furthermore, the "image of the Buddha" is like that described in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, the *Buddhabhūmi*, and other works.

Among these, awakening penetrates the sphere of non-self throughout all untainted stages (*anāsrava-bhūmi*). As for those who are deluded and restricted to the sphere of self—those who do not pervade [all stages]—they are included [within this category].
It is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The verse says "deliberation" (*manana*) up to "because it lacks the characteristic of a self" (*anātma-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states: This explains together the two sections on the fourth nature (*svabhāva*) and the fifth aspect (*ākāra*). Jikaya says: "Self-realization" (*svasaṃvedana*).
The seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) is the substance of the two dharmas. Its nature is difficult to know; it is manifested through its modes of activity (*ākāra*).

In reality, "cognition" (*manana*) refers only to these modes of activity (this explains that the subject who cognizes is the substance of consciousness, while cognition is the function of that substance). Regarding the distinct names established for it:

although the terms *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* apply generally to all eight consciousnesses, according to their predominant characteristics, they are specifically designated as the seven [consciousnesses] excluding the *ālaya*.
"This [refers to] the association with the manas (up to) 'fundamentally contrary'.
The commentary states: In the explanation of the sixth gate, the association of the seventh [consciousness] with the defiled, there are two parts:

association by way of cause and association by way of fruit. The first [part] also has three sub-sections: association with the defiled, association with the remainder, and association with feeling. This...
This is the first [section]. Regarding the analysis of how manifest pride (*māna*) and feeling (*vedanā*) coexist with views (*dṛṣṭi*), this explains the analysis of the tenets in the verse:
it shows that both manifest pride and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arise together with views, and also that manifest craving arises together with pride.

This refutes the Sarvāstivāda position that craving, pride, and views—these three—each arise through their own power, and that these three factors are strictly non-associated when compared to one another. "Turbid" (*yao-luan*) means murky; it means turbid. It means turbid. It means turbid.

The defiled manas, together with the six consciousnesses, constitutes defilement. "Defilement" refers to that which is *sāsrava* (with-outflows), encompassing all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).

Regarding the question of how the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) can arise simultaneously—given that this associated view does not arise independently of its objects, such as the notion of "mine" (*mamakāra*) following the notion of "self"—this is a question posed by various Hīnayāna masters based on their own tenets. To reconcile this with the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is done so through four points.
This means that because the coarse [aspect] of conceptualizing external objects is being discussed, it is said that greed causes one to be inferior toward those who are superior;

pride does not do so. Cè (測) says: "Among those [afflictions] arising from conceptualization, this [greed] may exist; for this very [greed] ceases all [such states], as it possesses an object within and is associated with both craving and pride.
Jì (基) says: "Furthermore, add the gate of its concomitant transformation (*anuvartana*)."
"Because this mental factor (the *manas*) [is associated with]... [up to] "...it is not simultaneous with those. The commentary states:
"The second [category] is 'simultaneous with the rest' (*śeṣa-sahabhū*). However, there are two masters' interpretations regarding the word "rest" (*śeṣa*).

The first is that it refers to the remainder of the four [mental factors] that are either [associated with the *manas*] or are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). The "rest" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), which is precisely the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), as stated in the *Pañcāśatikā-śāstra*.

Seeing them as conventionally existent is a portion of wisdom (*prajñā*). Jī says: "This is the Master’s [Asaṅga’s] teaching that each of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) because they are all derived from the root [afflictions].
There is an interpretation [extending to the point of] clarifying the secondary afflictions.

The commentary states: This is the general heading for the remainder of the second section on the nine dharmas. The verse mentions "obscured" (*nivṛta*), making the term "the rest" (*śeṣa*) redundant.
Regarding this, there is an interpretation [which continues] as previously explained.
The commentary states: Within the second explanation, there are four masters; this is the first. Regarding the phrase "among the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)," Master Ji says:
"Twenty" excludes wrong resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*) and the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* sometimes describes them as secondary afflictions.
"Secondary afflictions" excludes the ten root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). [This refers to] the *Abhidharma*...
The seventh [category] is also called a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*). To explain: it is distinguished from the ten [afflictions] such as anger (*krodha*) because those are exclusively coarse;
it is distinguished from lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) because, although they extend to both the coarse and the subtle, they are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*);

and it is distinguished from torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) because, while these two generally obstruct both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the former [the secondary afflictions] specifically obstruct concentration and the latter [the ten afflictions] specifically obstruct wisdom. Furthermore, regarding the "two doors" of the favorable and the opposite, they are difficult to distinguish in terms of their general obstruction versus specific obstruction.
Because they are manifest, do not distraction and faulty wisdom constitute separate obstacles? Although this is so, they are not like [the obstacles of] depression and elation.

Regarding the twenty-two secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, they are for the purpose of excelling in desire and resolve; the meaning of the distinction follows the previous principle.
There is an interpretation [up to] "as explained above" which should be understood accordingly.

The commentary states: This is the second explanation. Regarding the phrase "it must take as its object that which has been previously experienced, etc.": for instance, although the six consciousnesses have not previously experienced [a certain object], they take as their objects things belonging to the same class as what was previously experienced;
even when taking *nirvāṇa* or the *mārga* (Path) as objects, they take as their objects names, categories, defilement, purity, and so forth, which are the outflows of such classes.

Your kind [of beings], the *manas* is likewise so: its objects since beginningless time are of the nature of the *ālaya*. Therefore, there is forgetfulness (the Master’s intention is described thus by Ki and Ce).

That which opposes exclusively wholesome factors consists of: torpor (*styāna*), which is the opposite of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); restlessness (*auddhatya*), which is the opposite of equanimity (*upekṣā*);

lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), which is the opposite of faith (*śraddhā*); laziness (*kausīdya*), which is the opposite of diligence (*vīrya*); and negligence (*pramāda*), which is the opposite of non-negligence (*apramāda*). Since these oppose exclusively wholesome states, they are partial...

This explains "pervasive. Regarding the statement that the defiled ones are exclusively secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*): this distinguishes them from the root afflictions. Although greed and so forth are the opposites of non-greed and so forth, they are virtuous and are not exclusively secondary afflictions, as they are not said to be pervasive.

As for the preceding explanation regarding wisdom (*prajñā*), according to this master, the essence of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) is solely the mental factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*), and wrong view and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) are likewise solely wisdom. The remainder of the text is easy to understand.
There is an interpretation (up to this point) which should be understood as above.

[The] commentary states: Having established the debate, the differentiations are now determined. Within this, there are two [parts]; because it is abbreviated, this is the first.

"Continuity of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)": this refers to the state of being constant at all times. "A certain class of bodhisattvas": this excludes those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) through gradual awakening.

"The fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*)": Jì (基) says that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) is called "wisdom," while subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdhajñāna*) and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) are called "fruits," because they are induced by wisdom.
It is not the mind that clings to a self (*pudgalagrāhacitta*), for it does not take maturation (*vipāka*) as its object; [this is so] during the state of maturation.

"Long. [This refers to] the teaching that the object of the grasping for phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is not the mind that grasps at phenomena, nor does it take the *ālayavijñāna* as its object, because the *ālayavijñāna* is "short.
It is taught that the object of the grasping for a person (*pudgala-grāha*) corresponds to the aspect of the "seeing" (*darśana-bhāga*). For now, let us state this:

regarding the "Bodhisattva Path of Seeing" (*bodhisattva-darśanamārga*), Jiqi says that all Bodhisattvas must enter the Path of Seeing through the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-vipaśyanā*). This is not the true [view] of the three minds.

Regarding the meaning of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*): [The opponent’s school holds that] in the initial mind [of this path], there is still attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), as the *Zhèngyùn* states: "Dharmapāla [holds that] the three minds [of the Path of Seeing] do not give rise to attachment to phenomena, because they are all induced by the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Cè’s intention is likewise the same. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the term "also" (*yì*) in the middle [of the text] extends to the Path of Seeing;

for in the Path of Seeing with aspects (*sākāra-darśanamārga*), the wisdom that takes sentient beings as a conventional object contemplates only the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), and thus attachment to phenomena arises. The *Shūyào* agrees with this. (However, we now retain the first [interpretation]; the subsequent text refers exclusively to the sudden enlightenment of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), where only attachment to phenomena arises.)

This is because it does not refer to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Regarding the statement that "it takes as its object the stainless maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) and so forth":
if one considers the wisdom of a Bodhisattva, some say it follows the leading wisdom; since they lead together toward a single object, they follow what is led by others.

Therefore, in the first four stages (*bhūmi*), one contemplates the ultimate and conventional truths separately, whereas from the fifth stage upward, there is the possibility of contemplating them simultaneously. Others say that in the first stage, one contemplates both universally. (As stated in the *Renwang jing*.)

In the sūtras, it is stated that bodhisattvas of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) possess "double illumination" (*dvaya-prakāśa*). (Ji preserves the former interpretation, while Ce adopts the latter meaning; as for their respective merits and faults, they are discussed in the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-saṃgraha*. The *Śūyao* states:

"Is it possible that, by the power of the bodhisattva’s resolute intention (*āśaya*), one enters the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) in the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) directly from the non-conceptualization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)?
Or is it the reverse? It cannot be [the latter], because the former must necessarily serve as a precursor, as in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. This is a natural outflow (*niṣyanda*)."

This contemplation is identical to the fundamental contemplation (*mūla-vipaśyanā*). Regarding this, the *Ji* (Commentary) states: "If one considers the distant outflow (*nisyanda*), it is also easy to enter.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that [the outflow] is not obtained at all, except for that which already exists within oneself. However, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts maintain that for the most part, mastery has not yet been attained (according to the *Asvabhāva-ṭīkā*, this refers to the fact that one must transform through one's own power; this is recorded in the commentary on that treatise).
The same should also apply here regarding the *pudgala*. The commentary states:
The second part, the extensive explanation, has two sections. This extensively explains the *manas* as the grasping at a person (*pudgalagrāha*).

Regarding the point that the grasping at a self (*ātman*) necessarily arises based on the grasping at phenomena (*dharman*), it is as stated in a cited verse from scripture [numbered] sixty-five: "Because one grasps at phenomena as autonomous, one grasps at a self."

[The mind] transforms according to its nature. Ce (Ceshi) says: "Delusion regarding the stump is like the attachment to dharmas; calling it a 'person' is a metaphor for the attachment to self (*ātman-grāha*). (This briefly illustrates the relationship between the fundamental and the derivative: delusion represents the attachment to dharmas, while clinging represents the attachment to self.

The attachment to self actually possesses both delusion and clinging. The Tripiṭaka Master says: "Just as the arising of the attachment to self necessarily depends upon the attachment to dharmas, so too the realization of the emptiness of dharmas must be accompanied by the emptiness of persons.
Therefore, in the fifteenth chapter below, the "Chapter on the Contemplation of the Emptiness of Persons," [it states that] if it were not outflowing (*sāsrava*), [the following would not hold].

Alternatively, at times when one is without mind (*acittaka*), both [emptinesses] may manifest. Since the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) existing as a distinct entity (*kevala-dharma*) has not been excluded, the *Vipaśyanā* states:

"There is the emptiness of distinct phenomena; however, because it is possible for the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) to arise within this state, the treatise does not exclude it. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

The emptiness of phenomena arises separately at certain times, because it is subsumed under one or the other within the wisdom of the two emptinesses, just like the wisdom of the emptiness of persons. The proof (*sādhana*) states: Three...
The *Zang* [tradition] is correct, as it possesses both scriptural authority (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*). The *Xiāngwéi jué* states: "Phenomena must necessarily entail the emptiness of persons;

for that which is profound must necessarily realize that which is shallow. This refers to the stage of dual realization. (Now, I maintain that these reasons are individually unestablished (*asiddha*), because the remote school’s reason is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, in our current debate regarding the emptiness of phenomena, they certainly do not function in isolation; the most profound and the most shallow [realizations] are necessarily conjoined.)
This is because cognition grasps one or the other of the two [self and dharmas], just as birth grasps [one of the two]. Regarding the statement that they "rely upon the same wisdom," Ji says:

"The self and dharmas differ in their functions, but the essence of wisdom is one; they arise from the same seed, which is not contrary to reason, just as a single visual consciousness has multiple functions according to its objects."
However, these two types of grasping are not "not non-existent" because they do not exist within a single mind; rather, they arise as two modes of grasping toward two objects. Question:
Previously it was said that doubt concerns principle (*li*) while conviction concerns phenomena (*shi*). Is this not a case of a single mind operating upon two objects? Answer: That is not grasping.
Grasping consists of seeking out and adhering firmly [to an object]. (That incorrect interpretation has already been refuted previously; one should not employ it here.)

[Objection: Regarding this, it is difficult [to maintain]. Consider the question: (1) the two types of grasping (*grāha*) have the same substance and object; (2) the two types of grasping arise in a single mind; (3) *vitarka* and *vicāra* have the same substance and object;
and (4) the two [types of] acquisition (*prāpti*) arise in a single mind. [Response: The two types of grasping arise in a single mind because they are mutually compatible (*anuloma*).

Their coarseness and subtlety are contradictory, so they do not arise simultaneously. [Regarding "mutually compatible," their own commentary says: "because they function as obstacles to the Path" (*mārga-vibandha-kārin*), etc. This is incorrect. Let it not be that they coexist with the obstacle of discrimination (*vikalpa-vibandha*). Both *vitarka* and *vicāra* equally obstruct the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), for they exist together in a single mind. Furthermore, it is difficult [to claim] that within a single mind, one factor is subtle while the other is coarse.

[The opponent claims: "They are coarse; they are also contradictory because they should not coexist. [The author] now says: The two attachments, with respect to a single object, each grasp what appears as a self and what appears as dharmas. Because these appearing distinct characteristics are different, it is like the coexistence of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). However, vitarka and vicāra are not like this, because the objects of their activity—the meanings of names and so forth—are not distinct.

This is due to the principle that two sensations do not coexist in a single mind. Master Fan says: Two attachments of the same substance perfume [the storehouse consciousness] to form two kinds [of seeds].
Because they are severed sequentially, when the subsequent fruit arises, the two kinds arise together, just as a single visual consciousness perfumes many [seeds] through much usage. Subsequently...

At that time, many [mental factors] arise together to produce a single consciousness (this interpretation is attested; however, I now maintain it is not so. Although the functions [of the mental factors] are many, they rely upon and permeate (*vāsanā*) a single [consciousness]. Were it otherwise, it would contradict the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which states: [text follows].

Although their essence is non-dual, their functions are distinct. From this, a single type of seed-essence is produced through perfuming; for this reason, [the tradition] maintains that the basis and the seeds are of the same kind (as held by Master Ji). Jì (Ji) says:

"Some claim that within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses there are separate seeds of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that arise independently. When the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons arises, the seventh [consciousness] arises from those [seeds]. This interpretation is a great error.
Both the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* state that their essence is one, while their functions are divided into two, because they are abandoned sequentially. As for the...
Cognition (*jñāna*) is also explained in terms of various afflictions (*kleśa*), such as attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) and aversion (*dveṣa*).

If there were a cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that existed independently, apart from the afflictions, under which of the one hundred dharmas would it be subsumed? All the teachings state that all afflictions rely upon the cognizable (*jñeya*);

this is attested by the existence of such statements. If it were to arise separately, with which mental state (*citta*) would it be associated? It certainly cannot be associated with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), nor with an unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
It is indeterminate. If it were unwholesome or obscured, one would know that it must be of the same substance; therefore, this treatise states:

"That which is abandoned in the three stages is called the delusion of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-moha*), because in the past it frequently coexisted with sensual desire. Furthermore, within the seven consciousnesses, it may be present to a greater or lesser extent.

As with the afflictions (*kleśa*), [the question arises: "The Sāṃkhya’s *pradhāna* (primordial nature) and the Vaiśeṣika’s *guṇas* (qualities) are distinct entities and not the self; how do they reconcile [with this]? [Answer: Because they are conceived as "mine" (*mama-ātman*), they are likewise of the same substance.

Now, it is said that [the manas] is associated with the seventh consciousness; it should be as described. Because one portion [of the afflictions] is suppressed by the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*), there is no sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) that arises independently.
This would contradict both principle and scripture. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: "If one grasps at the marks of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*)."
This constitutes clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. The *Vivṛti* (Commentary) explains:

"When mere notions of phenomena (*dharma*) and non-phenomena (*adharma*) arise, the notion of 'self' (*ātman*) and its underlying basis do not cease; nevertheless, because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the notion of 'self' are not severed, this constitutes the grasping at a self.
The explanation states: "When one merely perceives phenomena, the notion of 'self' and its supporting afflictions [persist]."

Because affliction does not cease, it is clearly known that there is also a "solitary" (*mukhya*) attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Attachment to phenomena that involves exaggeration or depreciation is termed "dharma" or "non-dharma.
This is because it is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), though it is designated by the name of an affliction that resembles its activity (*carita*).

Consequently, while it is subsumed within the one hundred dharmas, although it is said that afflictions necessarily depend upon the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), it is not said that the objects of knowledge are necessarily always accompanied by afflictions.
Because the supported [the mind] must be separated from the support [the afflictions], this proof is also not valid.

Since the treatise specifically mentions a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*), if one considers the case of a Bodhisattva, it would be subsumed under the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Why then laboriously seek a mind associated with such [afflictions]? Furthermore, it says:
In the past, [the term] "many" was frequently associated with desire and greed (*rāga*), which served to exclude the possibility that shadow and manifestation might possess distinct entities.

Furthermore, when it is said that [certain factors] are "fewer" than the afflictions (*kleśa*), this indicates that the number of dharmas such as greed and anger is small; it does not necessarily imply identity of essence, and thus there is no fault of contradiction.
The learners (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles (up to and including those at the final stage) are all included within this [category].

The commentary states: Second, regarding the extensive [treatment of] the *manas* that clings to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-manas*): since sudden enlightenment arises solely during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmyajñāna*) is established as the clear wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Subsequently, within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the "equal application" (*samavihāra*) is established; however, this pertains only to the fruit of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyaphala*). It pervades...

Regarding the function of conditions: although that true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is subsumed under the wisdom of both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena, because it induces the subsequent path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is said to have "only the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as its basis.
Since it is called a "basis," it is clearly understood that the two types of grasping are originally of the same substance;

they are subsumed under the two obstacles according to their respective functions, as the entire substance follows those functions. It is merely by means of the Noble Path that the power of one portion is suppressed; this is explained in terms of the mental faculty.
It is associated with consciousness. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "From the eighth stage upward, there is no grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Regarding those called 'unstained' among the two vehicles and so forth, the term 'and so forth' includes the category of bodhisattvas’ wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), as well as the wholesome categories of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) among humans and devas."

However, because Great Bodhi is obstructed by everything, both obstacles are considered defiled from the perspective of a bodhisattva. Guān says: "The six consciousnesses are the basis for unwholesome afflictions;

if viewed from the perspective of a bodhisattva, they are generally categorized as either evil (*akuśala*) or obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), but if viewed from the perspective of the two vehicles, they are born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
[This is incorrect, for those [two vehicles] cannot produce the maturation of suffering]. The *Shuyao* says: "Even within an unwholesome mind, there is only non-existence..."

Commentary: The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* attests to this meaning. Question: It is accepted that both the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) are associated with hindrances; should it not be the same for the non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)? Answer: They are similar in that they both possess obstructions.

The unwholesome and the obscured-neutral share the same nature [as being afflictions]. The non-obscured-neutral is not abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), whereas the wholesome is of the same nature as that which is abandoned through cultivation.

Question: For those without lineage (*agotra*), there is no obstruction; both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are non-obscured. If you say they are ultimate obstructions, then what of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*)?

However, the *Zhengjie* (Commentary on Proof) states: "The presence of nature (*sattva*) is designated as an obstacle based on its being obtainable; the absence of nature (*asattva*) is designated as an obstacle because it is ultimately unobtainable. [Now, I say this is not so.

When a Bodhisattva’s attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is viewed in relation to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*), it is called non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*). Even when viewed in relation to the emptiness of self-arising (*svabhāvaśūnyatā*), it is still termed non-defiled.

Why, then, should the attachment to phenomena within the body of one who has entered tranquility (*śamatha*)—though termed non-defiled when viewed from the perspective of the category of the emptiness of self-arising—not be termed ultimately defiled when viewed from the perspective of the emptiness of phenomena itself? In the same way, these two obstacles of the absence of nature should be designated as ultimate obstacles according to their respective applications. Furthermore, the two types of wisdom belonging to one's own category are termed defiled and obscured (*kliṣṭa-nivṛta-avyākṛta*), while they are termed non-defiled when viewed in relation to others.

Regarding the statement that "this name is pervasive": those not subsumed under the three conditions are all included within the dominant (*adhipati*); those not subsumed under the three neutral (*avyākṛta*) states are all included within the born-of-maturation (*vipākaja*).
How this should be understood [is as follows]... [omitted] ...therefore, it is not described in detail.

The commentary states: Having already explained the ten gates, within the second major section—“Establishment through Scripture and Reasoning”—there are also two parts. This first part concerns scripture.

However, the former cites the unique (asādhāraṇa) teachings, while the latter cites the common (sādhāraṇa) teachings. Jñānagarbha says: "In the Hīnayāna, that which is future is called 'mind' (citta)."
The past is *manas* (mind); the present is *vijñāna* (consciousness). However, as they possess no distinct substance, they are now established as distinct [categories].

Regarding the *Vimokṣa-sūtra* (Liberation Sūtra), it is commonly accepted that "liberation" (*vimukti*) within the teaching carries the meaning of "falling away" (*vinaṣṭa*). This is because it does not enter into the four *Āgamas* or the separate recitations (*pṛthak-caryā*).
Fan [Wenlan] says: "By means of the Path, one severs hindrances and causes the mind (*manas*) to be liberated; this principle is called a 'Sūtra' (*sūtra*). Cheng [Shi] says: "Later, gradually..."
This is a recent text. If that which does not enter into the *Āgamas* were called "liberation," then scriptures such as the *Devaparipṛcchā-sūtra* should all be called "Liberation Sūtras.

Since it says "at all times," how can this be reconciled with the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*)? [Won]ji says: Because schools such as the Sthavira maintain that there is a distinct, subtle mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that functions constantly;
whereas for schools such as the Mahāsāṃghika and the Sautrāntika, it is like the constant offering of food—it is not present in all cases.

At that time, the Sarvāstivādins say: "It is not the case that [the past and future] exist simultaneously with the four [present dharmas], nor that they exist both before and after, as in the case of giving food regularly.
One attains liberation from them at the moment of the Arhat’s Path of Liberation; one attains it through the Diamond-like Samādhi which severs [the defilements].

According to the Sarvāstivāda tenet, although [defilements] may be severed in the present, their existence in the past and future lacks substantial reality (*dravya*). Therefore, they cite an example accepted by all parties to show that the past and future cannot be cited [as proof].
Having already cited the Sages [up to the point where] this fault does not arise.

The commentary states: This second logical proof establishes the principle by relying on the hidden sūtras and manifesting the underlying reason. It consists of two parts: the proof and the conclusion.
According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are briefly six proofs. Within the first [of these], there are two: the primary explanation and the ancillary [explanation].

This is the first [point] of the treatise. "True meaning" refers to the three minds of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). "Never having been awakened" means that untainted wisdom has not yet arisen.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) would necessarily exist during the states of the wholesome and the neutral, because these belong to the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), just as it does when other [mental states] arise.
As for the claim that this [ignorance] must be intermittent, ignorance itself would have to be intermittent; however, the six consciousnesses are constantly defiled.
"The defiled mind is always co-existent with [these] and with those.

Commentary: This is the second incidental discussion. According to the Hīnayāna school, something is designated as "unshared" (*āveṇika*) only when it is co-existent with secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Therefore, this question is posed. Regarding the first point, it states that these three are secondary afflictions. Jizang and Fachi state: "There are two meanings here. The first says..."

They are not subsumed within the twenty [secondary afflictions], because the *Vinayakṣudraka-vastu* states that they exist in many varieties; these are simply distinctions in the states (*avasthā*) of the various afflictions (*kleśa*).

Second, it is said that they are indeed subsumed within the twenty: lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) is identified as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), arrogance (*mada*) as the pride of self (*ātma-māna*), and agitation (*auddhatya*) as self-love (*ātma-tṛṣṇā*), because ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is the root. Regarding the second sense, those that are exclusively secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—
To simplify, these are also called "secondary" (*anubandha*) because they follow the root afflictions.
These three—the views and so forth—as well as the six [categories] such as the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and the ten [categories] such as the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, are subsumed under the root afflictions.

However, among the gates of delusion, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the primary factor; it is that upon which the others depend. The remaining three are not primary and may thus be termed "associated" (*saṃprayukta*). This is because...

Because of delusion. An external objection states: "When they alternate as the primary [subject], it should be called 'unshared' (*asādhāraṇa*). There are two interpretations of this objection. Jì (基) says:

"This is because within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there are times when it acts as the primary subject; it is not the case that among the three [consciousnesses] within the seventh [consciousness], there are such times. Cè (測) offers one interpretation, saying: [The mental consciousness acts as the primary subject when it is associated with afflictions].

The seven [defilements], such as *dṛṣṭi* (view), are metaphorically designated as "lords" (*adhipati*). To prove their existence, it is said later: "Because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of beginningless clinging to a self and attachment are subtle, and because these three are also lords.
When they function as lords, they should be called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*), for each has its own superior function. However, just as ignorance (*avidyā*) is designated as the lord of delusion...

The intent of this response is that [the Buddha] permitted [ignorance] to be the primary factor among grasping (*upādāna*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*). Although there are many interpretations, such is the meaning that accords with the text. Within the third sense, there are two further points:
First, although among the seven [factors] four exist and other consciousnesses are not absent, ignorance alone is designated by this name because it is the primary master;

the others are not the fundamental cause of delusion and are therefore not called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*). Second, or alternatively, one may permit that the other three are also unshared in their clarity; however, this is in contrast to other schools.

It is granted that other consciousnesses may function independently and not in common; however, this refers to ignorance (the second sense of the meaning). When four factors are compared with one another, the name "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) is established. This is the position of the third master.

Looking toward the *Ṣaḍvijñānakāya-nirdeśa*, [the term] "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) is established [for these afflictions]. That which is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi* is all associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Regarding those called "primary," this does not mean they are associated with greed (*rāga*) and so forth; rather, it means they arise specifically as primary while being deluded regarding the principles [of reality].

Regarding those called "non-primary," they do not correspond with the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*); although they are termed "unshared," they themselves are not primary, because they arise following a primary [affliction] such as anger (*krodha*). As it is said:
The *sūtra* refers to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the *sūtra* states that [it] is included within any one [of the categories].
The commentary says: "The *Ṣaḍdvaya-pratyaya-sūtra* is the second proof. Vasubandhu says: "Those of the same dharma" refers to the sixth, the mind (*manas*).
There is a similarity between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).

Those [five] possess the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), for which the *ālaya-vijñāna* serves as the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*). These five share this same characteristic: they are definitely devoid of the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*). Jñānaśrī says:

"That treatise seems to challenge a dissenting teacher of the Mahāyāna who accepts the eighth [consciousness] but does not accept the seventh. [Who is this dissenting teacher? Cheng says: "It is the Bodhisattva of the Single Consciousness (*eka-vijñāna*)."
As it is said in the world, "except for the eighth," which does not distinguish the seventh (because one has already believed in the eighth but has not yet believed in the seventh).

Cè says: "The two objects have two aspects: first, the sense organ and the object; second, the common and specific faculties. This treatise [of Asvabhāva] relies on the first [aspect] as a common object, while Vasubandhu relies on the latter.

[Dharmapāla] cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (vol. 51), which states: "By means of the ālayavijñāna, the material sense organs are sustained, and the five groups of consciousness function in dependence upon them. Vasubandhu establishes the seventh consciousness based on this, whereas Dharmapāla and Asvabhāva rely solely on the sūtras. First.
The establishment of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must necessarily have a dominant [condition] and a unique, simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

This refutes the Sarvāstivādins and others who maintain that only the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) serves as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). However, because the five sensory consciousnesses are used as a homologous example (*dṛṣṭānta*), this contradicts their own tenet that there are seven [consciousnesses] and six supports;

it violates their verbal assertion. The Abhidharma methods of the Hinayana differ: the six [sensory consciousnesses] do not take the seventh [mental consciousness] as their unique support, yet they follow it.

Because it is one, just like the five consciousnesses. This is the first [interpretation]. Regarding the general definition of "mental factors" (*caitta*) within the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa*, although there are many explanations, Master Ji’s sub-commentary states:

"The first meaning excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), because they do not arise in dependence upon the mind; the second meaning excludes matter (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), because they lack the four characteristics."
The third meaning distinguishes [this] from the eight consciousnesses as mind-kings (*citta-rāja*), because they act as their own sovereigns. Regarding the clarification of the aspects (*ākāra*):
the mind (*citta*) apprehends only the general aspect of the object, such as blue and so forth; the mental factors (*caitta*) apprehend both the general and the particular aspects. Ji says:

"The master refers to the *pāṭha-śāstrin* (the teacher), and the *vātsīya* (the student) refers to the disciple. Just as the master creates the mold and the disciple fills it with color—when the colors are applied to the mold, they do not depart from the mold."

Therefore, Ce says: "Briefly stated, [the mind] does not correspond to the specific objects grasped by the mental factors; the first interpretation is superior because it does not deviate from the model. Ce further states:

"Furthermore, regarding the four doctrines of the Sarvāstivāda in the Western regions, one school asserts that the mind grasps only the general [characteristics], while the mental factors grasp only the specific ones, because their functions are distinct."

One interpretation states: the mind (*citta*) apprehends both the general and the particular, whereas mental factors (*caitta*) apprehend only the particular; this is because the mind possesses sovereignty. Another interpretation states:

the mind apprehends only the general, while the mental factors apprehend both the general and the particular; this is because the superior [mind] does not follow the trivial. A third interpretation states: both the mind and the mental factors each apprehend both the general and the particular, as their activities are identical.
The Mahāyāna agrees with the third view. Furthermore, since mental factors necessarily follow the mind, their attention (*manasikāra*) is distinct. Regarding...

Zhongce says: "It also refers to that which has not yet been understood by the mind; that is, the distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) apprehended by the various mental factors (*caitta*). Jī says:
"That is, the distinct characteristics apprehended by the other mental factors should all be [objects] not yet understood by consciousness (*vijñāna*).

It is the single dharma of attention (*manasikāra*) alone that is able to apprehend those numerous characteristics. For this reason, attention is able to universally arouse [the mind]. (The meaning of this interpretation is that the distinct characteristics of the objects of apprehension each...)

There are two meanings: first, the arising of the mind from a substantial entity; second, the manifestation of the aspect (*nimitta*) within the mind. Among the other mental factors (*caitasika*), each takes only the second meaning, whereas attention (*manasikāra*) universally takes both the first and the second. How is this known? It is known through scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*). Regarding scripture: the *Gāthā* states that "attention, being able to give rise to the aspect of consciousness, apprehends it.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* mentions "consciousness," while this treatise mentions the "factors" (*dharma*); these mutually illuminate one another to show that attention universally apprehends the objects of the mental factors and gives rise to the aspects of the subjective cognizer. Regarding reasoning: each factor individually apprehends its own specific object-aspect. If attention did not separately apprehend them through its perfuming and grasping, there would be no purpose for its existence according to reason.

Furthermore, attention must possess functions such as reception and the apprehension of images, just like contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*). Perception (*saṃjñā*) is understood to function in accordance with the arising of speech.
Regarding the explanation of "conception" (*saṃjñā*): it refers to the characteristics of volition (*cetanā*) that arise in accordance with the three natures through thorough understanding.

Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it states: "This term expresses both the object and the subject. As for the phrase "in other places," Woncheuk says: "The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* states that the mind (*citta*) only performs general comprehension, whereas mental factors (*caitta*) also perform specific [comprehension].
He further notes: "Since the *Madhyāntavibhāga* does not provide a distinct explanation [regarding this], one should cite the final commentary from the Western regions (India)."

Regarding this teaching, the four "all-inclusives" (*sarva*) are explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* as: all places (*sthāna*), all stages (*bhūmi*), all times (*kāla*), and all [minds] (*sarva*).

I shall now explain them in order. "Place" refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). "Stage" refers to the three stages (*tribhūmi*). "Time" refers to the moment the mind arises; all these are fully manifest.

Although greed and other afflictions may extend to stages associated with discursive thought (*vitarka*), hatred and other afflictions do not pervade all such stages and thus lack certain stages depending on their specific category.
"These six evolving consciousnesses... [up to] are associated with the three feelings.

Commentary: Regarding the second point, the "three feelings," there are two [subsections], because they are the causes. Within the first [subsection], there are also two, for the purpose of explaining the verse.

Regarding the various categories (*dvāra*): it should be understood that the number [of categories] increases herein. As for the statement that "painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*) also arises from the untainted (*anāsrava*)," Jñānasena says:

"Because the five consciousnesses arise at the time of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Although sorrow (*daurmanasya*) can serve as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the untainted, [it does not arise from it directly].

Because they do not arise simultaneously, they are not subsumed under the untainted (*anāsrava*). As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is both tainted and untainted;
it is defined by being tainted. The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is tainted; it is defined by being both tainted and untainted.

For an Arhat, the faculty of suffering is not abandoned, because the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) accords with and tends toward the non-abandonment of dharmas. Grief is termed 'not abandoned,' yet it is not [untainted]."

Regarding the study [of this], the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*) pertain to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

As for the statement "dividing them into four in total," the Sarvāstivādins maintain that suffering (*duḥkha*) pertains to all three moral natures, with the exception of the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

According to their school, the obscured-unspecified in the desire realm exists only in the body and is pervasive across two views; because it is associated with the five consciousnesses during the seeing of suffering, [the text] initially follows that school’s position and thus says "dividing them into four in total. However, in the Mahāyāna...

The "obscured" (nivṛta) [afflictions] are established separately within the intermediate category because they are logically associated with the five [mental factors]. Regarding the spontaneous greed and delusion [associated with these], Master Ji says:
"Because hatred is unwholesome (*akuśala*), it is excluded from this category. Master Ce explains there are two reasons: first, greed causes delusion, and a portion of it coexists with hatred;

since delusion is unwholesome, it is excluded. Second, the greed and delusion associated with the five [mental factors] also pertain to the unwholesome, as they are induced by the volition that initiates karma.

Therefore, the former explanation is superior. Guan (觀) says that the latter explanation is superior because the statement regarding the non-arising of karma does not refer merely to the mental consciousness associated with pure suffering, but rather serves to exclude the arising of karma within the five sensory consciousnesses. The first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The five consciousnesses arise following the production of karma, and they are also able to grasp pleasant and unpleasant fruits" (this citation supports the rescue of Ce’s [測] position, which maintains the meaning rather than the literal text). Cheng (證) says:

As with the afflictions of the upper realms, they give rise to non-agitated karma (*āniñjya-karman*). Similarly, the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) states of the desire realm also give rise to meritorious karma (*puṇya-karman*).

However, with respect to non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya*), it is said that they do not give rise to such karma. The *Yogācārabhūmi* is cited as evidence that the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) may be found in relation to suffering.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* is cited as evidence that not giving rise to evil is of an indeterminate nature. Among the five categories of enumeration, the first two are merely sub-divisions of the [preceding] parts.
Regarding the term "joy" (*prīti*): Kuiji states that it does not apply to the pleasure of the five sense faculties.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Xianyang) itself states that it is not a pervasive or complete pleasure (differing from the Sarvāstivāda, which holds that all preparatory stages [sāmantaka] involve only equanimity, while the first two fundamental dhyānas involve only joy, and the third fundamental dhyāna involves only bliss).

Regarding the two meanings of "oppression within the mental faculty," Kuiji states that the former refers to the meaning of "growing from" (*āyūhana*), and the latter refers to the meaning of "protecting the Dharma" (*dharmarakṣā*).
