Since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* does not state that the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are neutral (*avyākṛta*), therefore now...

The introductory remarks should be understood in the same way. One *Shuyao* (Essential Summary) states: "From the perspective of principle, *daurmanasya* (sorrow) can be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), whereas *kaukṛtya* (remorse) must be associated with sorrow.

Since [remorse] can be indeterminate, [the former view holds]. However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Sorrow is not indeterminate; this is because it is taught from the perspective of its concomitant functions.

(This contradicts the intent of the present treatise and should not be cited as proof for that meaning, as it is stated that remorse is also associated with the sensation of equanimity [*upekṣā*]). The former master explains: "In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there are three other [positions], namely..."

Regarding joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*): because these six do not necessarily function within the consciousnesses [of the five sensory faculties], the latter master refutes this, stating that only sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and not equanimity [is absent].

This is because equanimity is necessarily present in the seventh and eighth consciousnesses. (Master Cè provides a fourfold analysis to explain the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; here, he incorporates his own [inference] into the records of that treatise. Is it not already clear from the subsequent discussion?
One should know that the "eight faculties" refer to the six faculties beginning with the eye, plus the life-faculty (*jīvita-indriya*) and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣā-indriya*). The remainder...
The Master [Vasubandhu] has three reckonings: first, that sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is the eighth; second, suffering (*duḥkha*); and third, the physical form (*rūpa*). An opponent raises an objection:

"Since those evil karmas may result in the absence of eyes and so forth, how can they be said to cause one to experience suffering? The treatise explains: "It causes one to be fully endowed with the experience of suffering. One experiences the suffering of touch through the body, while the physical form is rendered useless.

This differs from the Sarvāstivāda position, which holds that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) necessarily constitutes four faculties, whereas the others are not fixed. According to this master, it is possible to relinquish those [faculties].
Is it matured? Master Ji says: "Even if it exists, there is no hindrance. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises state that hatred is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) at its final stage.

Alternatively, even if it is said not to exist, there is no hindrance (because the first [stage] is predominant; as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: 'excluding coarse material food, it refers to other foods']"). Question:

Does a human being in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) experience mental suffering? As stated in the twelfth fascicle of the *Bandhumatī-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish): "Aṅgulimāla, among humans..."
Having attained the fruit of arhatship, because one is burned by fire, [the opponent] answers: "There is suffering, but there is no fault.
However, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that when it says, "The karmic fruits arising in the mind are unmixed," this refers for the time being to different realms (*dhātu*).

This is because the seventh chapter of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (the *Prakaraṇapāda*) allows for the experience of the full karmic fruits of rebirth (*ākṣepaka-karman*) in other destinies (*gati*). [The *Śūyao* raises an objection: "If so, why is there no mental suffering (*daurmanasya*) in hell? ... [it continues] until it concludes: 'This meaning is difficult to understand. Now, I say it is easy to understand, as explained in the *Mātṛkā*."

Therefore, as for other passages stating that those [mental states] possess "concordant pleasure" (*niṣyanda-sukha*), Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* follows the Sarvāstivāda school in making such a claim;

thus, this treatise reconciles the text [in a way that] does not contradict the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-ṭīkā*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The continuity of sorrow and suffering. Jizang says:

This follows the Mahāsāṃghika and other schools which assert that all consciousnesses arise simultaneously. Regarding the statement that "investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) are accompanied by sorrow," this follows the *Anuvartaka-sūtra*.

Section. Vitarka and vicāra exist only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Regarding the texts that fully elucidate this meaning, such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚論), the second chapter states:
"That is to say, this body is moistened by the joy and bliss born of seclusion; it is thoroughly gladdened and thoroughly pervaded.

This refers to the preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna, as stated in the Sūtra. Furthermore, it says that throughout the entire body there is not even the slightest part that is disturbed.

It gives rise to joy and bliss. As for that which is not pervasive: because it pertains to the fundamental stage (*maula*) of the first *dhyāna*, and because it includes the *yogācārabhūmi* (such as the fifty-seventh [chapter]) and so forth, it refers to the arising of agitation and the seeking of delight, as these are common to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*). Regarding the eleven faculties:

they consist of the mental faculty, the five beginning with faith, the fifty-three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), as well as joy and equanimity. As for the "many doors": the five feelings have various modes of maturation and so forth, which arise simultaneously.

Regarding the three types of sensation being simultaneously admitted within a single door, Ji says: For example, when one hears a sound while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the concentration itself is associated with joy (*saumanasya*), whereas the initial ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) is associated only with equanimity (*upekṣā*). Thus, they are distinct.
"Because one attains the state of one's own level [up to] the occurrence of sorrow and suffering.
The commentary states: Regarding the second fruit-level (*phala-sthāna*), the *Ji-shu* (Commentary on the Basis) offers three interpretations. First, it says:

Although the three contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses exist only in two stages, the five uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses pervade the four stages of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), because the five sense organs (*indriya*) are present there—just as there is uncontaminated [consciousness] in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

The eye sheds tears like rain. Regarding the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, they exist only in the fourth dhyāna; although they exist in other stages, they do not manifest there, just as in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

When cultivated alongside the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they exist as seeds but are not manifest; or rather, while seven or eight types [of consciousness] exist, only the fourth type [is manifest].

This is because the virtues of the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] depend upon that limit (*prāntakoṭika*). One opinion states that the five uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) sensory consciousnesses also exist only [in the fourth dhyāna].

The first dhyāna is like this because it possesses outflows (*sāsrava*), just as it possesses vitarka and vicāra; since these do not exist in the higher stages, the three consciousnesses [of sight, hearing, and touch] may be present there.

But how could the nose and tongue exist? Because the three consciousnesses are present, their corresponding objects must also exist; thus, by analogy with the two consciousnesses, there must be the two objects of smell and taste, just as there are the three types of sensory objects.

One view states: "The five uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses exist only in the fourth dhyāna, just as the seventh and eighth consciousnesses do; one may accept this according to one's inclination. Another proof states:

"The five consciousnesses do not exist in the third dhyāna or in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), as there is no textual evidence for them [there]. (Regarding the acceptance or rejection of these points, see the notes in the preceding fascicle and the commentary on the *Mātṛkā*.)
The meaning briefly indicated previously shall now be explained in full. The commentary states:
Within the second section, the detailed explanation, there are two parts: the specific manifestation of mental factors (*caitta*) and the general determination [of their nature].
Of these, the first reveals the first two stages. This explanation has two parts; the first concerns the omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) factors. Three scriptural citations are presented.
The beginning and the end refer to arising and ceasing. This refers to the *Hastipadopama-sūtra* (Elephant’s Footprint Simile Sūtra).

Since the initial transformative verse has already clarified the five natures (*pañca-dhātu*), the present verse provides an explanation that briefly reveals the meaning of pervasiveness. Regarding the statement "it must exist by virtue of contact" (*sparśa*), Master Ji says:

it exists by virtue of the harmony [of the three]. If contact were absent, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) would necessarily become disordered and scattered. Regarding the statement "if this were absent":
Regarding the statement "the mind should be non-existent," Ji says: "If it were non-existent, there would be no capacity for alarm, and thus no manifestation.

Regarding the statement "thought causes the mind to grasp the true cause and so forth," Guan says: "The mind-king also grasps specific characteristics; of this there is no doubt. Ce says: "Thought has two functions."

This means that [the mind] is able to grasp the characteristics of the primary cause and so forth for itself, and also causes the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) to grasp the characteristics of the cause and so forth.
Although the mind grasps them for itself, it cannot cause others to do so; therefore, one cannot say that the mind grasps distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the mind-king primarily grasps the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while incidentally including the distinct characteristics. The first interpretation is superior. The proof states: if it were as the latter says, it would result in [the mind] grasping [only the general characteristic].

[The opponent says: "They are distinct. If one causes another to grasp, that is a secondary function. [The author] now says: Volition (*cetanā*) is able to cause the mind to follow primary causes and so forth, such that each performs wholesome actions and the like;

therefore, each is a "grasping" (*upādāna*). This is not a grasping through discernment (*vijñapti*). In this passage, the Preceptor (*upādhyāya*) may speak of "volitional grasping" (*cetanopādāna*), which refers to the characteristics of primary causes and so forth that cause the mind to engage in activity. He speaks of grasping only in its general sense, just as a painter [is said to grasp the brush].
Next, the specific objects (viṣaya-viniyata): up to "such as faith, greed, and so forth. The commentary states:
Within the second category, the specific objects, there are two parts: the formal explanation and the various classifications. This is the first.

Regarding the three explanations of the "desired object" (*iṣṭa-viṣaya*), Woncheuk says: "The third [explanation], the 'most excellent object' (*parama-śreṣṭha-viṣaya*), is somewhat broader; at the end of each, it says 'some say,' and so forth."

This refutes the Sarvāstivāda position, for they maintain that the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) are omnipresent. Regarding the power of scriptural authority and reasoning, Master Ji states:
"The power of realization (*pramāṇa*) refers to consciousnesses such as direct perception. Other masters of the Vaibhāṣika school say: "Adherence (*adhimokṣa*) has the nature of being unimpeded.

If one were to defend [the existence of] the sense faculties and so forth, it would be solely through the predominant power of adherence that consciousness and other factors are produced; [they do not exist independently]."
Because it is obstructed, it destroys what is superior. Regarding the phrase "the infinite categories of objects that depend on others for their resolution," Jì (Jìzàng) says:

"When non-conceptual wisdom first arises for a single moment, each [moment] takes those categories as its object; although they have not been previously experienced, they are each previously experienced. Cè (Cèbǎo) says:

"The initial [moment] of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is also that which induces the categories of objects of the observing wisdoms; from the second moment onward, they are called 'previously experienced.'"
The substratum of sensation consists of preceding moments of mind and mental factors, or the force of perception (*saṃjñā*). The proof states: this is the cause of the object-cognition;

because the object and the mind mutually infuse one another with seeds through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), they can later be recollected. However, recollection does not necessarily arise solely from those seeds;
rather, those seeds assist other seeds capable of recollecting, such as those of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth, which possess the characteristic of recollection.

Therefore, Ce says: Because it is the object of the wisdom of prior preparatory application (*prayoga-prajñā*), the object traversed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is also called the "object of observation" (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, virtuous concentration is described as being the basis of wisdom (*jñāna-āśraya*). As for the statement that "the characteristics are merely subtle and hidden," this is the position of the masters of the *Nyāya* school.

The Master of the Treatise (the *śāstrakāra*) challenges [the opponent], saying: "One should speak the truth. Now, as for my knowing that what is fixed is precisely the mind (*citta*)," Paramārtha’s commentary (*Ji ce*) states:
The Sautrāntika masters maintain that all mental factors (*caitasika*) are essentially the mind itself;

thus, the analogies of mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth, as established [by the opponent], are unproven. As for the later Sautrāntikas, they establish three, four, or more [mental factors], while others [establish] the mind...

The dharma [of resolve] is conceptually established based upon volition (*cetanā*). If one were to argue against this that it is certainly not identical to the mind itself, there would be the fallacy of contradicting the scriptural authority.
The commentary states: "This refutes the final position; for although other mental factors (*caitta*) are established, the Sautrāntikas maintain that resolve is necessarily identical to the mind."
The Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) cites the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and other works composed by Kātyāyanīputra as evidence for the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

The Master of the Treatise (Śāstrin) refutes this, stating that the enumeration of ten is not based on the Sūtras. He provides proof by citing the seventeenth fascicle of the *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, which says:

"Each has its own intrinsic nature, such as the ten universal [mental factors]. What are the ten? Namely: feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), desire (*chanda*)," and so forth.

Liberation, mindfulness, samādhi, and wisdom. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 27, states: "The lower concentration refers to the concentration among the mental factors within the ten universal [mental] grounds (*mahābhūmika*).
Since both the *Mahāyāna* and *Hīnayāna* sūtras speak of the ten universal grounds, how can it be said that this is not a sūtra?

The explanation is as follows: Masters such as Saṃghabhadra did not recite the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*; they believed only in the *Abhidharma*. It was based on their calculations that [the opponent] refuted [this position].

However, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* is a scripture of the Saṃmitīya school; that the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* follows its lead is not the ultimate truth, and therefore it is not a valid basis [for our position].

(This interpretation is incorrect. That [text] should be taken as evidence for this being the ultimate truth. Furthermore, as it is a Buddha-sūtra—just as the third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states—it has already been reconciled [with other teachings].
Therefore, I shall not explain it again here.)
There is an interpretation [extending] to this point that such categories are not limited to these alone.
The commentary states: "The second section consists of various gates; for now, three gates will be discussed. This first is the gate of simultaneous arising within its own category. Jì (基) says:

Regarding the first interpretation, Master Sthiramati was collectively criticized by those in the West. Later, Dharmapāla and others, since they termed these "distinctive objects" (*viṣayaviśeṣa*), maintained that they do not necessarily arise together.

[The claim that] they are for the sake of stopping the distracted mind of the ignorant class—Master Ji says—merely refers to those who study the "abiding mind" (*sthiti-citta*) and so forth during the intervals of their practice.
As for the statement that there are twelve [mental factors], it means there are ten categories, with two arising together. From the beginning... the first... [and so on].

Once the first [set of] *kṣaṇas* has been combined with the latter [three], next the second [set of] *kṣaṇas* is combined with the latter three, continuing until the fourth is combined with the fifth;
this constitutes twelve combinations. The same applies to the three together. One then cultivates the desire, resolve, and mindfulness for the concentration of bliss (*sukha-samādhi*).
2. Regarding concentration on bliss, there is the desire, resolve, and concentration. 3. Regarding that very object, there is the desire, resolve, and wisdom. 4.
Regarding the cultivation of observation, there is the desire, mindfulness, and concentration. 5. Regarding that very object, there is the desire, mindfulness, and wisdom. 6.

Regarding the object of observation, there is the desire, concentration, and wisdom. 7. Regarding the cultivation of observation within concentration, there is the resolve, mindfulness, and concentration. 8. Regarding that very [object]...

1. Understanding, mindfulness, and wisdom regarding the arising of objects; 9. Understanding, concentration, and wisdom regarding that which is observed in meditative absorption; 10. Mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom regarding the cultivation of observation.
Regarding the "four [sets] of five phrases," this refers to the four objects—the five factors beginning with desire—and so forth, because one [factor] is mutually excluded from each set of five.
"From the seventh and eighth consciousnesses up to the wisdom of accomplishing activities.
The commentary states: This is the second section, the gate of the association of various consciousnesses. Master Ji says:

The first master interprets the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, stating that when the eye and ear [consciousnesses] function simultaneously, the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness constitutes the two types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*). However, this does not accord with the text. As for the intention of the latter master, it follows...
The mental consciousness induces subtle desire and so forth, attaining a state of mastery characterized by the absence of decline in aspiration and other qualities;
it takes the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) as its proof.
These five object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) are associated with all five types of sensation (*vedanā*).

The commentary states: Regarding the third section, the "Gate of Association with the Five Feelings," the first master maintains that these five [desires] do not coexist with the five consciousnesses;

rather, they are feelings belonging to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), asserting that craving alone is their primary nature. The latter master, however, cites the fifty-seventh [verse] and others to establish that desire and so forth are associated with sorrow and suffering.
The fifty-ninth [verse] states: "Greed is associated with sorrow and suffering. From this, it is known that when the mind desires an object, it is accompanied by these [feelings].
● In the sixth fascicle of the *Śāstra*, it has already been stated that [the mental factors] range from the universal (*sarvatraga*) to non-harming (*avihiṃsā*). The commentary states:

Among the wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-caitasika*), there are two [sections]: because of the general inquiry and response, and because of the detailed exposition. This is the first [of these]. It says:
Regarding "the cultivation of equanimity": this refers to the equanimity within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), as it is distinguished from the equanimity of feeling (*vedanā*).
The treatise says: "...there are definitely eleven.
The commentary states that there are two parts to this explanation: the direct explanation and the various categories. The first part also has two sub-sections: the names and the enumeration.
Because it is a fundamental (prakṛti) karma; this is the first point. It is associated exclusively with wholesome (*kuśala*) minds.

This explains its name, distinguishing it from the Sautrāntika masters, for whom faith (*śraddhā*) and diligence (*vīrya*) pertain to all three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*), as stated in the *Śraddhā-varga* of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

Furthermore, it excludes the Vaibhāṣika position that pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is omnipresent in all wholesome states; thus, it is said to be "exclusively wholesome. There are eleven factors in total; this explains their number. The *Abhidharmakośa* establishes ten, excluding [one].
Non-delusion is wholesome because it is identical to wisdom. According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, there are twelve [mental factors], because joy (*abhirati*) and aversion (*vidveṣa*) are added.

According to the *Saṃmitīyanikāyaśāstra*, there are thirteen, because joy and aversion are added to the eleven. To preclude such increases or decreases, it is stated that there are definitively eleven.
"What is faith? [From] "purity of mind is faith. The commentary states:

This is the second [category], the nature and function; this clarifies faith (*śraddhā*). Generally, among the mental factors (*caitasika*), the *Vyākhyā* says: its nature consists of the primary object-conditioning function (*ālambana-vṛtti*) and the secondary function (*parivāra-vṛtti*), which is not shared with others.
Its function is to be common to others. Regarding the statement "it can attain and can accomplish": it can attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It is able to accomplish the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The Abhidharma itself declares, "I possess power. This [power] extends to the virtues of others.

*Kṣa* means "certain" or "real"; *ma* means "just" or "merely. To explain the subtlety of the mind’s purification through these three interpretations, if one takes it as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound):

It should not be a mental factor (*caitasika*), because it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound based on proximity; it should therefore be associated with shame (*hrī*) and so forth. Answer: By taking it as a *tatpuruṣa*, it is distinguished from shame and the others;
it is merely revered and is wholesome. Regarding the statement "some say": this refers to the Sthavira school. Regarding the statement "some maintain": this refers to the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Alternatively, both may be teachers of different lineages within the Mahāyāna.
"What is *hrī* (moral shame)? ... [it] is so called because it pertains to oneself and others.

The commentary states: Next, *hrī* and *apatrāpya* (moral dread) are explained. The *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* says: "Based on the predominance of oneself (*ātma-adhipati*) and the predominance of the Dharma (*dharma-adhipati*)."
"Feeling shame for one's transgressions. This commentary explains: "By the phrase 'based on one's own nature' (*svadharma*), the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is revealed;
it is as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa* regarding 'veneration. By the phrase 'feeling shame for one's transgressions,' the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is revealed;

it is as in the *Abhidharma* [treatises]. The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* and other texts speak of three kinds of predominance (*ādhipatya*): first, predominance over oneself (*svādhipatya*), which refers to those of superior capacity who feel shame before themselves.
"Action" refers to evil. "The two factors increase and predominate" refers to those of middling capacity, who refrain from committing various evils in order to protect the holy teaching.
"The gate of the three periods of time increases and predominates" refers to those of inferior capacity, who refrain from committing evil in order to protect worldly fame and profit.

The intention of the protector of the Dharma (Dharmatrāta) is that the first two [roots] are the basis for *hrī* (moral shame), while the latter is the basis for *apatrāpya* (moral dread). Basiasp states:

"One who possesses virtue or non-virtue is called 'noble' or 'vicious'; the qualities they possess are called 'virtuous' or 'non-virtuous. Because one honors or rejects both the person and the qualities, these two [roots] are established."

Regarding the claim that [the self] should not be substantially existent: although its essence and characteristics are the same as others, it differs in its relative dependence, just like "long" and "short," and thus must be merely nominal.
This would contradict the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states that eight [factors] are substantially existent.

As for the argument that whatever object one encounters always possesses the sense of honoring the good and rejecting the evil, this is because it serves as a secondary function. The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that I, too, am the same as you in feeling shame regarding both myself and others?"

This is because it is used subsidiarily. The commentary explains that the characteristics are identical and thus not lost. There are four difficulties: first, the difficulty that there is no distinction within a single substance;
second, the difficulty of non-correspondence; third, the difficulty that it must be a provisional existence; and fourth, the difficulty that it is not universally virtuous.

However, regarding the two meanings of "regarding self and others" found in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, and other texts, the first meaning can be understood through their exegesis. As for the intent of the latter meaning, [Master] Ji...

It is said: "Promoting good is defined as 'self,' while rejecting evil is defined as 'other. That which benefits oneself is called 'self,' and that which harms oneself is called 'other' (*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*).
[The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: 'Present evil causes are called 'self,' and future evil effects are called 'other,' each being based on a different sense of the term].'"
Regarding "non-attachment and so forth" (up to) "must necessarily exist separately":

The commentary states that the texts concerning the subsequent three roots of goodness can likewise be understood. "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three realms of existence; their cause is called "possession of existence. "Suffering" refers to the three types of suffering;
its condition is called "possession of suffering. As for the distinction between "possession of existence" and "possession," [the Master] Cè says: "Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools admit this."

Greed does not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object. Only the Mahāyāna permits that hatred and delusion take the untainted as their objects. Baso (基) says: "The cause that acts as a conforming condition is exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*);
however, the cause that acts as an objective condition also includes the desire for *nirvāṇa*, because it can give rise to greed and the other afflictions.

What is the proof for this? It is stated in the treatise below: "To explain in detail: greed, hatred, pride, the three views, and doubt arise simultaneously; they correspond accordingly to those [afflictions]. Since it is permitted that wrong view takes cessation and the path as its objects, and that greed associated with delight takes them as its objects, it is because [greed] takes them as its causal condition."

Greed (*lobha*) pervades all three realms; it initiates karma and moistens rebirth. Generally speaking, it is said to possess both existence (*bhava*) and the instruments of existence (*bhavopakarana*). Hatred (*dvesa*) exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

because its power to initiate karma is superior, it is called the suffering (*duḥkha*) and the instruments of suffering (*duḥkhopakarana*). As for the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*), such as the severing of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and the severing of doubt (*vicikitsā*), they have superior functions.
Later, the Dharmapāla school maintains that these three dharmas are associated with all six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna-samprayukta*), thereby distinguishing them [from other afflictions].

Doubt and the like are subsumed under the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), distinguishing them from lack of faith and so forth. Because they possess these two characteristics and give rise to evil with particular intensity, they constitute the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
Since these roots are difficult to remedy, two types of antidotes are required.
"Movement" refers to diligence (*vīrya*), up to the distinction of "superior progress.
The commentary states: Next, diligence is explained. Jizang says: "The 'brave' ascend; the 'stout' are firm and steadfast.

Regarding the meaning of "insatiability," it is explained as the ultimate path of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and so forth. The two types of practitioners are those who are distant and those who are near.
"Peace" (*praśrabdhi*) refers to [the state] up to "transforming into peace and comfort.
The commentary states: freedom from heaviness is called "lightness," and being well-regulated and harmonious is called "peace.
Regarding "heedfulness" (*apramāda*), it is because there is no distinction [between it and] meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The commentary states: This heedfulness (*apramāda*) has four dharmas as its essential substance (*svabhāva*), while their distinct functional capacities (*vṛtti*) are metaphorically designated as "heedfulness. (Master Ji says: "The interpretation is thus. The meaning is that these four dharmas each have secondary functions;

according to how one [dharma] diminishes another, the four dharmas are divided into four parts, which are collectively established as the single substance of heedfulness. Is it not the case that these secondary practices constitute its characteristics and functions?

The masters of the *Nyāya* school and others maintain that it is difficult to establish a real entity based on a metaphor, lest there be an infinite regress. [However, in this system,] the four dharmas are capable of providing protection.

[The opponent] argues that cultivation must necessarily depend on something else, and thus non-laxity (*apramāda*) should also be so; [if it were], it would depend on another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). The rest of the text is understandable.
As for the question, "How is equanimity practiced? [it is because it is] identical with the mind and so forth.
The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "by means of heedfulness, one first eliminates the defilements," there are two explanations from the masters Ji and Ce.
One says that heedfulness is the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), while equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Another says that although they occur in the same moment, they are described as preceding and succeeding in terms of their meaning (the latter being superior because both are universally associated with the wholesome).
"What is non-harming? ... It is because it is non-hatred. [The author] explains:

This is to clarify the distinction between the two characteristics of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*). Among the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), loving-kindness is non-hatred, while compassion is non-harming.
Previously, it was stated that great compassion has non-hatred and non-delusion as its essence; why, then, is compassion here defined as non-harming?

[This] is the essence. Ji says: "That [refers to] the substantial reality; this is established as a phantom-like conventionality. Alternatively, that refers to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), while this is merely compassion (*karuṇā*).
Regarding the statement "some say," this refers to the Sarvāstivāda school.
"And it reveals the eleven [mental factors]... one should not hold them equally accountable. The commentary states:
"The word 'and' (ca) in the verse serves to subsume the remaining mental factors" (Master Ki says: "From here on, the various categories are analyzed;

however, I do not agree with this, as it is intended to explain the words of the verse"). In the Sanskrit language, the term *ca* has two meanings: first, "and," and second, "two. The meaning of "and" thus reveals the ten [mental factors].
"First, individually. This meaning of "etcetera" (*ādi*) indicates that other dharmas are also included. The present treatise explains it solely according to this sense of "etcetera.
According to the *Āgama-sūtra*, such as the *Saṃyukta-vastu* chapter, there are many names for defilement (*kleśa*); correspondingly, there are various names for their opposites within the wholesome.
However, because they do not differ from the eleven essential natures, they are not established separately. "Non-envy," etc.—the "etcetera" includes the eight [wholesome mental factors].

Nineteenth, "not being indignant," "not speaking with malice," and so forth; "not being stingy or arrogant," and so forth—these are to be understood according to [the *Śrāvakabhūmi*] 89, where "and so forth" includes "not seeking [faults]" and "not having great desire.
Herein, "non-concealment" (anivṛti) first protects the meaning of the Dharma, as explained below in accordance with the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding "non-pride" (amāna), there are three explanations. In the third section, the main body of the treatise, among the fundamental afflictions, pride and doubt [are discussed].

There is no equivalent term [in the Indic original], and therefore it is treated separately. It is not among the three types of doubt. Jizang’s *Shelun* commentary evaluates this last. The *Wushiaba* (Fifty-Eight) states:

"Hesitation and discernment are precisely the opposites of those [three]. The *Zhengyi* (Proof) says: "Because the mental aspect (*ākāra*) existing within the middle is the opposite. However, below the section on doubt, it says:

This causes wisdom (*prajñā*) to be indeterminate, because it is not identical to wisdom itself. Regarding the ten minor [afflictions] that correspond to the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), as previously explained regarding those corresponding to the intermediate [afflictions], since one already possesses shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*), among the universal secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-upakleśa*), only distraction (*vikṣepa*) and lack of mindfulness (*asmṛti*)—these three factors—are not inverted into the wholesome;
therefore, they are now explained separately. [Guṇabhadra] asked: "Does right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) invert forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*)? It applies to both the defiled and the pure."

This mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the opposite of distraction (*vikṣepa*) in the context of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). [Objection: If it were so, both the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and the pure (*viśuddha*) states would have to be "concentrated" (*samāhita*).

[Response: This is not a valid analogy. Both the defiled and the pure are called "mindfulness," as they both take mindfulness as their essential nature (*svabhāva*); however, within these names, there is a distinction between concentration and distraction, and thus their substance (*dravya*) is not one and the same.

Why are non-regret (*avipratisāra*), the eye-faculty (*cakṣus*), and so forth not established [as mental factors] in the same way as the universal (*sarvatraga*) factors and others? Because [the former] pervade all three moral natures (*tridhātu*). As for the statement that their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*vṛtti*) differ: [this refers to the specific distinctions among them].

Faith and the other seven [mental factors] possess both substantial essence (svabhāva) and function (vṛtti). Equanimity (upekṣā) and the others lack a distinct substantial essence, yet they possess a specific, superior function that distinguishes them from non-anger and so forth;

thus, they exist only as functional entities (artha) without a separate substance. Furthermore, greed, hatred, delusion, lack of shame (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), and lack of faith (āśraddhya) and so forth pervade all six consciousnesses.

Although harm (vihiṃsā) is less pervasive in its defilement, it is established separately among the wholesome because it encounters such heavy [obstacles]. As for forgetfulness (muṣitasmṛti) and distraction (vikṣepa) [among the unwholesome],...

Right awareness (*saṃprajanya*) has three aspects. Although it pervades all six consciousnesses, as the direct opposite of the "object-specific" (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) mental factors, it is not established among the wholesome factors.

Regarding the distinction between forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) and right awareness: if forgetfulness were a derivative of delusion (*moha*), then its opposite would simply be non-delusion (*amoha*). However, because the specific characteristics [of the factors] are emphasized, it is said to enter among the object-specific factors.

As for the statement that "the understanding of the principle is pervasive," *Ji* says: "Because wholesome dharmas accord with the principle and are harmoniously integrated, they are not [separately] described."
"These eleven dharmas... because their characteristics and functions differ.
[The commentary] states: There are ten gates from here on; this is the first, the gate of the provisional and the real.
According to one interpretation, all eleven exist throughout the three stages.

The commentary states: Regarding the second section, the Gate of Simultaneous Arising (*sahabhū-mukha*). As for the distinction between the bases (*āśraya*) of shame (*hrī*) and modesty (*apatrāpya*), although they are of the same category, they differ because shame takes both self and others as its object of cognition (*ālambana*), whereas modesty does not;

thus, they do not arise simultaneously, just as painful and pleasant sensations (*duḥkha-sukha-vedanā*) do not. This [distinction] is certain with respect to their objects. There is faith (*śraddhā*) and no lack of restraint (*apramāda*);

this is stated according to what is possible. These ten pervade all wholesome minds (*kuśala-citta*). It is not necessarily the case that they do not arise together, nor is it necessarily the case that they always arise together; however, it is accepted that shame and modesty are necessarily not simultaneous.

[The term] "all" (*sarva*) and so forth still contradicts the treatise’s statement that [the ten universal states] follow immediately after a wholesome mind. Since the ten are universal wholesome states, they are called the "preparatory stage for concentration" (*samādhi-prayoga*).

As for those who attain the name "ground of concentration," because there is a sense of composure during the preparatory stage proximate to the hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*) of the desire realm, the second [alternative] is preferable.
Because these eleven types [of consciousness] necessarily possess pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). The commentary states:

This is the third section on the concomitance with consciousness. Regarding the two meanings of the five sensory consciousnesses, it is traditionally said that according to the first master, the Buddha does not possess the five sensory consciousnesses.
Because fifteen of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*), the following section constitutes the main body of the treatise.

Although there are three interpretations, the correct one—as Mece says—is that the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna and the five consciousnesses of a Buddha are the first to possess pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); this is because the mention of "five consciousnesses" refers to the general category.
"These eleven are wholesome" (up to) "should be considered according to principle.

The commentary states: This refers to the latter seven categories. That is to say, the statement that "eleven are exclusively wholesome" pertains to the gate of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). As for the "remaining gates," they are as follows:

The tenth [section] is the "Comprehensive Summary Gate," which includes those with maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth. As for the six faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), because the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) also pertains to the out-flowing (*sāsrava*), they are said to be abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) based on their turning away from and abandoning [the defilements].

If they do not arise, as in the case of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the karma of the Northern Continent (*uttarakuru*), and so forth, these are also abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*), as will be explained later regarding the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Thus, having already explained [the afflictions] up to doubt and wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the commentary states:
"In the exposition of the afflictions, there are three questions and answers for the sake of explanation; these are the first two. As for the term "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*):
it is called "wrong" (*mithyā*) because it deviates from reason; it does not necessarily mean that it is unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The Treatise says: "...because they are defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*).

The Commentary states: There are two parts to this explanation: the direct explanation and the various categories. Within the first part, the general and specific aspects can be understood from the textual structure.

These are the first three unwholesome roots (*akuśala-mūla*). "Existence" refers to the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*), which possess the fruit of suffering as their maturation (*vipāka*). "Possessing" means that [these roots] are endowed with it.

It is capable of producing afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), and so forth. If one examines this by means of the Four Noble Truths: there is that which is exclusively the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);

there is that which fully encompasses both suffering and its origin (*samudaya*); and there is that which takes cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as objects but does not increase in accordance with them, and is therefore not "fully encompassing. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that craving (*rāga*) does not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.

Master Ji says: "The subsequent section explains that [craving] shares its objects with views (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth; it takes the untainted as an object and gives rise to craving through dependent origination."

These are all termed "possessing the instruments" (*sādhana*). The Sarvāstivādins claim that craving directed toward the untainted (*anāsrava*) is a desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*).

In the Mahāyāna, however, attachment to the Buddha and craving for cessation are both defiled (*kliṣṭa*). The *Zhènglùn* (Treatise on Proof) states: "Since [craving] does not accord with cessation and the path, and since it does not increase hatred and so forth, it is still called an 'instrument of suffering' (*duḥkha-sādhana*).
Even if it does not accord with craving, how could it not be an instrument? Nevertheless, there is a principle that craving associated with false views takes cessation and the path as its object."
It is not yet exhausted. If one slanders cessation or the path by repudiating what is wholesome, this is associated with hatred (*dveṣa*) and is certainly not accompanied by craving (*rāga*).

If it is a view of superimposition (*samāropa-dṛṣṭi*), it takes as its object that which is not cessation or the path, calculating it to be such; therefore, it does not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object. If it is associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), it takes only suffering (*duḥkha*) as its object.

(The repudiation of what is wholesome is said to be associated with hatred, while the basis for [such] repudiation is stated to be associated with both. Repudiating another’s good qualities does not necessarily involve hatred. Since calculating the path to be "not the path" is not a basis [for attachment], greed may arise there. As the Upādhyāya says: ...as if...

Upon hearing of the Buddha-nature, one reckons it as the object of self-love that is untainted (*anāsrava*). It is logically difficult to establish the claim that craving never takes untainted phenomena as its object, for it is certain that craving should necessarily encompass attachment to untainted phenomena.
As for "wrong concentration," this refers to the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*). The remainder of the text is clear.
"What is pride (*māna*)? [From "up to" ... "arising also involves no fault. The commentary states: "Virtue (*guṇa*)" refers to moral virtue;

"one who possesses virtue" refers to a person. Regarding the seven types of pride: according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises, these range from pride (*māna*) to false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
As for the nine types of pride (*mānavidha*), they are as described in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*: "I am superior," "I am equal," "I am inferior," "There is one superior to me," and so forth.

There is "equal," "inferior," "superior," "not superior," "not equal," and "not inferior. Among these seven, the first three, as well as "inferiority-pride" (*ūnamāna*), and the nine types of pride (*māna-vidhā*) arise with respect to the three categories of inferior, equal, and superior, each being assigned accordingly. "Self-pride" (*asmimāna*) arises with respect to the self;
"conceit" (*abhimāna*) arises with respect to qualities. Jī says: "Conceit causes one to claim what does not exist; conceit of superiority (*adhimāna*) [causes one to overestimate]."

Regarding "one who [thinks]": it refers to one who perceives their own small portion of virtue as being great or superior. Thus, there are two types of pride (*māna*). [The two explanations are as in the *Abhidharmakośa* 19.

According to the *Jñānaprasthāna*, among the seven types of pride, three are based on the sequence of views, forming three groups of three. The first three, in order, are pride (*māna*), pride beyond pride (*atimāna*), and pride greater than pride (*mānātimāna*). The middle three are the reverse of those. The last three are pride, pride beyond pride, and pride greater than pride. According to the *Prakaraṇapāda*, the first, the pride of self (*asmimāna*), arises from three types of pride—namely, pride, pride beyond pride, and pride greater than pride—because of the distinct reckonings of inferiority, equality, and superiority.

The pride of equality (*sadṛśamāna*) and the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*) arise from two types. The pride of inferiority arises from one type. The three reversals for "having a superior" and so forth follow the same order as those for "having no superior," etc.]

"Superior over the inferior. (The latter explanation fully elucidates the principle). *Abhidharmakośa* 19: Seven are common to both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: Nine are common to both what is abandoned by the path of seeing and what is abandoned by the path of cultivation.
The Mahāyāna is likewise the same.
"What is doubt? ... [up to] "...it does not have wisdom as its essence.
The commentary states: "Hesitant discernment" refers to what the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* calls "discriminative cognition" (*vikalpa*).

Since cognition (*buddhi*) is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), and furthermore, in the etymological analysis (*nirukti*), the term *vimati* is added before *prajñā*; thus, it is a synonym for the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
Therefore, the Mahāyāna masters do not hold that this is a distinct school (nikāya) doctrine. The later *Zhengyi* states:

"Whether through doubt at the same time or doubt at different times, it causes wisdom (*prajñā*) to be indecisive; it is not wisdom itself. If the south were *jñāna*, then by assisting it with *vī* [the prefix vi-], it would conversely be called consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The intent of this objection is clear. "Element" (*dhātu*) refers to the "syllable-element" (*akṣara-dhātu*). "Element" has the meaning of "cause. It is transformed through the assistance of conditions.
It is not necessarily the case that this refers to the original substance [of the view]. Why? Because it is said that "evil views lead to the experience of much suffering.

The commentary states: Among the six types of views, the first is general and the subsequent ones are specific; this is the first. "Evil" (akuśala) means to revile or censure; therefore, it applies universally.

Regarding the statement, "Those who engage in erroneous speculation concerning the principles of the Truths are [afflicted] by the obscured," Master Ji says: "This refers exclusively to delusion regarding the principles (*tattva*).

Although there are degrees of proximity in terms of the objects of cognition, they are equal in their sense of deluding the principles. (This does not fully capture the principle. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the ten afflictions of one's own level and so forth are mutually related as objects of cognition.

For instance, when the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) takes wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) as its object, how can it be said that there is any difference in proximity between this and the case of the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*)? Although one speaks of "deluding the principles," because these afflictions take only phenomena (*vastu*) as their objects, they can only delude the functional aspect; thus, there is merely a distinction of proximity.)
"This mode of viewing (extends) to being subsumed under that which arises from conceptual discrimination.
The commentary states: Within the second category [of specific views], there are five. This first one is the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

It involves conceptual discrimination regarding the objects of perception—the aggregates (*skandha*)—but does not involve conceptual discrimination regarding the locus where it arises; this consists of twenty propositions. It involves conceptual discrimination regarding the objects of perception—the aggregates—and involves conceptual discrimination regarding the locus where it arises.

This means that one [of the six elements] is taken as the self (*ātman*), while the remaining four are taken as objects; each is further endowed with ornaments, servants, and dwellings, thus forming sixty-five [categories].
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Vasubandhu’s commentary), chapter five, verse 80, states: "Twenty phrases arise through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
By extension, the same applies to the sixty-five. The word "etc. includes the *dhātus* and *āyatanas* as phrases. For a detailed explanation, see the *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā*.
The two extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) are included within those arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpaja*).

The commentary states: "Practicing the Middle Way" refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*); "renunciation" refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). "Tendency" (*nati*) means inclination.

Among the sixty-two views, thirty-seven are subsumed [within these categories]: thirty are views of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), and seven are views of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); all of these take the self as their object. There exists... [the view of existence].

Because they involve the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. The word "etcetera" includes the fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛta*), such as permanence and impermanence. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise 58) states that these all arise from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Regarding the four types of universal eternality (*sarvatraga-nityatā*): the first three rely on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the fourth arises from discursive investigation (*vitarka*), as recorded in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Jizang says that those arising based on concentration pertain to the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*). Regarding the four types of partial eternality (*ekadeśa-nityatā*), it is as in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

The *Śāstra-ṭīkā* records that Ji said: "The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) in the lower realms conceives of the Brahmā King as being partially eternal, though it cannot take dharmas of another stage as its object and designate them separately as 'self,' because it is a conception of another's self.

As for the 'partially impermanent' [view], although this is not annihilationism (*uccheda*), it defiles wisdom through such grasping and is not subsumed under the five views. Furthermore, regarding the alternative interpretation of wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), the former explanation is superior. It is not [the latter].

This is because it is taught that a portion [of these states] is associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Regarding the sixteen types of perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth, they are recorded as in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
However, the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* (the "Brahma-cutting" chapter) of the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "After my death here, I shall be born with form and perception," and so on.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this may be interpreted as: "Having been born after possessing form, one possesses perception. This is because [the sūtra] proclaims "possessing form" and so forth as the essential nature of the self (*ātman*). Thus, there is perception.
The term "etc. refers to the place of rebirth; thus, it is an error on the part of the translator. Jñānagarbha states:

"There are sixteen [theories] regarding perception, sixteen regarding non-perception, and eight theories concerning non-perception. Based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), both vitarka and vicāra are capable of arising.

Regarding the eight theories of 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' one observes that sentient beings have entered the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and their perception is not clear, thereby forming this attachment: that only vitarka and vicāra do not depend [on concentration]."

The meditative absorption [of the Peak of Existence] (bhavāgra) is necessarily not of the form realm (rūpadhātu). Regarding the seven types of annihilationists (ucchedavāda): humans, the gods of the desire and form realms, and those of the four formless realms (ārūpya)—each considers that annihilation is attained only after relying upon their respective bases.
This is also stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the "Chapter on Brahma’s Movement" (*Brahmavihāra-varga*).
The three types of wrong views (up to) are all subsumed under wrong view.

The commentary states: "Denying cause and effect," and so forth, as recorded in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*. The two [types of] "no-cause" and so forth constitute fifteen wrong views, as recorded in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Jì says: "Īśvara refers to Īśvaradeva; Maheśvara refers to Maheśvaradeva" (Cè says one).

The *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra* (so called because it concerns the Four World-Protecting Kings). "Śakra" refers to Śakra-devendra; "Brahmā" refers to Brahmā-deva. Regarding "other categories of things":

since they do not admit a self (*ātman*) but merely calculate [them] as being eternal, this is not the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). According to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it is categorized under the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) below the section on suffering, because it calculates specific distinctions;
thus, it is not included within the view of truth (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Jñānaprasthāna states: "It is the false view below the section on the accumulation of causes for all things."

However, it does not involve the estimation of superiority (*abhimāna*). While the conceptualization of being superior constitutes [the view of] superiority, this is not because it takes views or their attendants as its object;

rather, it is subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The conceptualization of false liberation (*mithyā-vimukti*), although it is not actually superior yet conceives of itself as superior, does not take views as its object.

It does not conceive that "this can attain purity," nor does it conceive of what is not the path as the path; thus, it is not a delusion of views (*dṛṣṭi-moha*). Because it does not conceive of itself as superior, it is not the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*). (Since it pertains to the Truth of the Path...)

"Why is this? Because it is for the sake of extinguishing the characteristics of superiority and inferiority. The term "etcetera" includes the fourteen indeterminate points, such as whether the world has an end or not.
The four types of view-grasping (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) are subsumed under [the category of] grasping at what is not the two [i.e., grasping at views and grasping at precepts and observances].

The commentary states: These are the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). However, there are places where it is taught—such as in the first fascicle of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and elsewhere—that each mode of appearance (*ākāra*) possesses two meanings.
First, because they are reflected and manifested such that each possesses both [aspects]. Second, because they follow the perspective of the Sarvāstivāda.
Furthermore, the fifty-eighth [fascicle] states that each possessing both is superior, as they both attain the purity of *nirvāṇa*. If...
Regarding those that do not involve misrepresentation (*aviparyāsa*) or conformity (*anuvartana*): how can there be fifty-eight?

Among the delusions concerning the Four Truths, to conceive of what is not cessation as cessation is called false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), but it is not the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). To conceive of what is not the path as the path is [false view], but it is not the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Therefore, we know that these two functions both rely on "view" to be named the grasping at views; they both rely on "precepts" to be named the grasping at precepts. Otherwise, [this would contradict] the *Śūyao*.
"Realization" refers to the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*), which is not [to be understood] according to the Abhidharma exegesis (as it has already been analyzed).
Thus, whether taken collectively or individually, [these views] arise either spontaneously or through discrimination.
The commentary states: Among the second set of various categories, there are ten gates. This first is the gate of co-nascent (*sahaja*) and discriminative (*vikalpita*) [views].

Regarding the terms "general" and "particular," it is because the six are also ten. Master Ji says: "There is no fault in taking both interpretations of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), for the textual principles of each are mutually strong.
Within this, regarding animals as evidence for the co-nascent [view], the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (58) states: "There are two types of self-view (*ātmadṛṣṭi*): the co-nascent..."
Regarding those who are born [as such]: all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), down to birds and beasts, manifest these [afflictions]. Regarding those that arise through conceptualization (*vikalpa*):

they arise from the speculative calculations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the like. Guān states: "For this reason, in the evil destinies (*durgati*), there are no afflictions that arise through conceptualization."
Fan says: It is not so; for the passage below speaks only of "pure suffering" (*kevala-duḥkha*) and does not mention "mixed sensations" (*miśra-vedanā*). Cheng says:
In the realms of pure suffering and among the dull-witted classes such as birds and beasts, no conceptual discrimination arises.

There are explicit texts in the treatises stating that even in places of mixed sensation—such as among the ghosts, *nāgas*, and other clever and sharp-witted beings—one is able to hear the Dharma and engage in various forms of analytical reflection.
There is discrimination, as stated in the sūtras: a ghost struck Śāriputra on the head, causing him to fall into the Avīci Hell.

The manifestation of karma driven by ignorance is necessarily similar to that of the world. If a person is dull-witted and acts solely for the sake of food and clothing, they will not necessarily go to an evil rebirth, as they are like birds and beasts.

(Now, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, various types of suffering can be produced; as that treatise says: "In a former life, a nāga harbored anger and poisonous resentment, releasing great lightning and rain, and with a torrent of water, he harmed people, thereby being born in hell.")
"These ten afflictions (up to) their association [with other factors] is without fault.
Commentary: This is the second section, the gate of simultaneous arising among their own class. This first [affliction] is greed (*rāga*). Question: The objects of hatred and love are distinct.
The aspects [of these two] are also contradictory; how could craving coexist with suffering? Furthermore, hatred is associated with pleasure. Baso (基) says:

Because craving can arise by pressing toward both objects, their aspects do not contradict one another; therefore, this fault does not apply. (According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, because craving constrains the mind, it is possible for it to focus on a single object.)

Greed is not invariably opposed to painful feeling; hatred and pleasure may coexist, which should be understood by analogy. Hatred and doubt oppose greed in the same way as they do in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts;

their distinction lies in being overcome by craving (*tṛṣṇā*). See the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 58. Greed does not coexist [with them]; its basis is defiled pride. See the same work, fascicle 55.

In the sixth chapter of the Abhidharma, it is stated that [the attainment] is associated with the five views; this is according to the reasoning of the Master (alternatively, "as explained by the Master's principles"). Regarding its presence in various locations and its magnitude, it is identical to others and possesses no distinct meaning.
"Hatred, pride, and doubt (up to) may be absent or present. The commentary states:
This refers to the second [root affliction], hatred (*dveṣa*). Because it relies upon internal objects, it does not take those [objects] as its object of hatred.

The *Abhidharmapāda* (Sixth Chapter, Section 58) states that hatred and pride do not coexist, because they increase toward similar external objects. The [same work, Chapter] 55 states: [They do not coexist].

Hatred (*dveṣa*) coexists with pride (*māna*). This is because, at the initial stage of doubt, one does not yet feel hatred; as stated in the *Pañcāśatikā*, it is only after a long time that hatred arises.

The *Abhidharma* (*Dharmaparyāya*) permits their coexistence. Regarding objects that are favorable or unfavorable: when doubting that one's own faults will bear no fruit, this is associated with hatred.

When doubting that one's own faults will bear no fruit while they are unfavorable [to oneself], this is dissociated [from hatred]. Its coexistence with the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*) may be understood according to the text.

It is known that there are fifty-five [types of afflictions]. Those associated with both hatred (*dveṣa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) are explained in terms of the general characteristics of the six afflictions, because they involve the conceptualization of the aggregates as pleasant.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that hatred is not associated with views, because it involves the conceptualization of the aggregates as suffering. Regarding the two passages from the *Yogācārabhūmi*, hatred is associated with views:
there is hatred when abandoning what is pleasant, and no hatred when abandoning what is painful. This and the citation regarding wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are as previously established.
"Arrogance (*māna*) is fixed upon its object; [the phrase] 'even a portion' is likewise.
The commentary states: This is the third type of pride (*māna*). All treatises agree that it is associated with this [view of self-existence].

However, the claim that it is not associated with the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) contradicts the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. As recorded in that treatise, "a portion of the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is likewise," so says [the master] Cè.
It says: "One who grasps an extremely painful aggregate as 'self' is without conceit; one who grasps a non-extremely-painful aggregate as 'self' possesses conceit. Later it says:
"Because of relying on an inferior aggregate of suffering through association with craving. From this, it is clearly known that conceit exists within that which is not extremely painful. Jizang says:

"This is based on coarse characteristics [whereas the interpretation of Xuecheng in the following section is incorrect]. In the subsequent discussion of [conceit] co-arising with feeling, it states that the mind co-arises with suffering because of conceit. Jizang also contradicts the treatise; this treatise exhaustively investigates the principles and reconciles all [points].

Regarding the "portion of wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), Cè states: "Denying the existence of the aggregate of pleasure (*sukha-skandha*) is also not associated with pride (*māna*), because it contradicts one's own sentiments.

Jì states: "Denying the existence of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) is not associated with pride; however, denying cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) can be associated with pride, because one relies upon one's own pleasure to disparage cessation and the path.

[Commentary: The first interpretation is incorrect. Holding that the aggregate of suffering is subject to cessation also accords with one's own sentiments; thus, it ought to be associated with pride. However, at the moment of the intention to negate [the aggregates], there is nothing to be disparaged or relied upon.

When one negates suffering (*duḥkha*), what could there be to rely upon or to be arrogant toward? Later, it is likewise not so. Just as when one negates the origin (*samudaya*) of suffering, there is nothing to rely upon; so too, when one negates cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), there should be nothing to be arrogant toward. To maintain reliance on one’s own pleasure is not due to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Jì says:

"The view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is concordant [with pride], while the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) arises in a mixed manner. As for wrong view that negates a future result, it does not coexist with pride; therefore, it is said to be 'one part' [of the view].

This master allows only the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) as the primary [concordant factor], and holds that the accretive wrong view (*samāropikā mithyādṛṣṭi*) may coexist with pride. Guān’s single interpretation is the same as this regarding the view of a self; Fǎn... [text fragment].
The Master [Xuanzang] provides one interpretation: this is the same as the aforementioned wrong view (retaining this explanation).

There is doubt regarding whether [doubt] is not definitively resolved; [it continues] until "certainty and [doubt] do not arise together. The commentary states: this is the fourth type of doubt. Ji says: although discernment and hesitation, though associated with wisdom (*prajñā*), the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*)— *Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a philological commentary on a section of Abhidharma or Yogācāra literature, likely from Xuanzang’s *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) or a related sub-commentary. The passage discusses the relationship between doubt (*vicikitsā*), discernment (*viniścaya*), and the five views.*
[They are] all [included], because they must be examined and determined; because, in relation to the others, they proceed gradually from the former toward the latter;
and because among the five views, there is a mutual progression leading to much wisdom.
The commentary states: Regarding the fifth [category], the various views, as stated in the *Fifty-Eight* [Treatise]: "Furthermore, the five views are of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*)."
They are mutually non-associated, because a self-nature is not associated with itself (as explained in the *Mātṛkā* regarding the difficulty of the characteristics of wisdom).
Delusion is associated with nine types [of mental factors], up to "necessarily by means of delusion."
The commentary states: The sixth [category] considers doubt in relation to the nine [afflictions]. The Abhidharma says: "Ignorance is twofold:
first, ignorance associated with afflictions; second, non-associated ignorance. This refers, for now, to the former.
"Because these ten afflictions [arise] up to the point of giving rise to pride (*māna*) and so forth.
The commentary states: "The third is the gate of association with the various consciousnesses. 'Measuring' (*tulanā*) and so forth include 'hesitation' (*vimarśa*) and 'investigation' (*vitarka*);
this is because it is the gate of the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of pride and the like, and is not the same as the delusions arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*)."
[The text] analyzes these ten afflictions [up to their association with] joy (*prīti*). The commentary states:

Within the fourth section on the arising of the five feelings (*vedanā*), there are two parts: from the perspective of the actual meaning (*tattvārtha*) and from the perspective of coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*). As follows...
Fifty-nine states: Previously, based on coarse characteristics, this was intended to enable the practitioner to understand non-distraction (as already explained in fascicle fifty-five).

Now, based on both gross and subtle [characteristics], it is intended to enable long-term practitioners to discern the distinctions. This treatise provides a complete explanation of the first four passages;
here, the first concerns greed, hatred, and delusion. As fifty-nine states: "If the spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*) were universal..."
"All consciousnesses" refers to those associated with all faculties. Furthermore, it is said that they do not involve spontaneous craving;
rather, at one time they may be associated with joy and delight, at another time with attachment and suffering, and at another time with equanimity.
The same applies to hatred and delusion. According to this passage, one knows that the five consciousnesses also give rise to afflictions through conceptual discrimination.
Because it is taught that [craving] is associated with suffering; because afflictions of discrimination do not arise in the miserable realms (*durgati*);

and regarding the statement that "craving meets with adverse conditions," this is explained according to the difficulties as in the fifty-ninth [treatise]. It does not meet with pleasure; craving is associated with grief and suffering; and regarding the suffering of the destruction of enemies.

[It] is associated with both aversion (*pratigha*) and delight (*prāmodya*). One interpretation holds that it arises simultaneously [with them], because it can give rise to them. The commentary states:

"This is the second type of pride (*māna*). Regarding "relying on the inferior aggregates of suffering," this is as explained in the fifty-ninth [chapter]. If it is the pride of being lowly (*ūnamāna*), [it is as follows]:

Because it is associated with the faculty of craving (*rāga-indriya*). Regarding the second meaning: "If they were also associated," the *Fifty-nine* [Treatise] states that all afflictions arising simultaneously are associated with every feeling on the mental plane (*manobhūmi*).
The phrase "conceit and so forth" includes all afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).

The phrase "false teachings and so forth" refers to false reflection (*mithyā-manasikāra*). As for the statement that "they do not create karma that leads to the miserable destinies (*apāya*)," [this refers to] the fifth [point].

19. [The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] states: "This is because one must distinguish the afflictions that give rise to karma leading to the miserable destinies (*durgati*). Master Ji says: "This is based on a general discussion regarding the majority of cases.

As for specific retributions, those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) can also give rise to them. (This does not fully capture the principle, as seen in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra*, etc.).

By inference, we know that according to the former master, there are distinguishing afflictions in those destinies; due to the force of power from previous lives, one creates karma leading to the miserable destinies.
The *Shuyao* (Essentials of the Commentary) asks: "Can karma that produces purely suffering results create the realms of happy destinies? The explanation says: "This is not excluded.

It states that while there is no "non-discriminative delusion" (*avikalpa-kleśa*), it does not say that there is no karma for human or celestial rebirth. (Since this refers only to purely suffering [karma], which pertains to the evil destinies, what prevents one from creating wholesome karma or karma for places of mixed reception?

This is as recorded in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*). Furthermore, another explanation holds that [if one possesses] non-arising [ignorance] or specific ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*), how could one create the projecting karma for human or celestial rebirth? If we discuss the specific [types of ignorance]:

Answer: Both good and evil are acquired [as seeds]. (Regarding ordinary beings within the internal dharma, although they do not collectively create meritorious or imperturbable karma and likewise lack its actual manifestation, the power of their seeds differs, as recorded in the *Mahā-śāstra*.)
Notes on the Study of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (from the middle of the sixth fascicle to the seventh).
This concludes the remainder of the notes on the sixth fascicle of the treatise.
"Because doubt and the latter three views (up to the view of grasping at precepts and observances) are associated with the feeling of mental grief (*daurmanasya*).
Commentary: This is the third section. The two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are called the "latter three views. The Sarvāstivādins say:

"In the desire realm, doubt does not coexist with joy (*saumanasya*), because joy is coarse while doubt is subtle; their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ. It is for the sake of distinguishing [doubt] from that [joy] that it is so stated.

Regarding "desire, doubt, and [the views] that there is no suffering, etc.": first, one performs unwholesome actions while doubting that there is no suffering; because [these views] also coexist with delight regarding the Truth of Origination and so forth, they are included.

Since there is no unwholesome karma in the higher realms, it specifies "desire" (kāmadhātu). Question: Are the views associated with sorrow, as well as the two types of grasping (dṛṣṭi- and śīla-vrata-parāmarśa) associated with sorrow, objects of conditions?

"Why is it not associated with hatred? Answer: "If that which is held dear were [associated] with sorrow, it would likewise be so. Even though he whom one honors may harbor hatred, it does not increase within that person.
According to another interpretation, they are co-nascent (until as previously stated). Other points are as explained before.

The commentary states: This is the fourth section. Regarding the phrase "not associated with the five consciousnesses and being exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)," this excludes suffering (*duḥkha*) and mental grief (*daurmanasya*), because these are the opposites of the attachment to pleasure that is here being severed.
However, this first master contradicts the *Mahāśāstra*, which states: "All that arises simultaneously are accompanied by the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).
The second master says, "The rest is as before," which refers to the view of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*).
This should be understood according to the actual meaning as appropriate. The commentary states:
Within the second [section on] coarse characteristics, there are two parts. First, it clarifies their association with feeling (*vedanā*); second, it clarifies their associated stages (*bhūmi*).

Greed (*lobha*) and so forth proceed with joy; hatred (*dveṣa*) proceeds only with sorrow. Delusion (*moha*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) pertain to both joy and sorrow. Therefore, following the order of difficulty, greed is explained first regarding its stage.

Because delusion (*moha*) is associated with pleasure and is common to all six consciousnesses, it exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). In the [first] three dhyānas, it is associated with seven [feeling-faculties] and exists only in those three dhyānas;

because it belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*). All forms of doubt (*vicikitsā*) are said to be associated with feeling (*vedanā*); delusion is associated with all five feelings. However, this applies to doubt and independent delusion (*āveṇika-moha*) in the desire realm.
It is associated exclusively with two types of feeling (*vedanā*). As the Abhidharma states: "Because it is indeterminate and has not yet ceased, and because there is no longing for non-arising;

and because it is sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the form realm. Regarding the knowledge that other feelings arise in association [with these], one should understand them according to reason: those associated with greed are associated with joy (*saumanasya*); those associated with pride and the four views are associated with the same;
