those associated with hatred are each associated with three [types of feeling]; as are those associated with the remaining ignorance (*moha*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). These feelings, when assigned to the nine stages (*bhūmi*), are easily understood.
Therefore, it should be known that this is not different from the wisdom associated with the specific objects (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*). [The commentary] states:

This is the fifth gate, concerning association with the specific objects (*pañcama-viśeṣa-viṣaya-samprayoga-mukha*). As for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and the indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), they shall be explained when we reach them. Therefore, for now—
The object-specific [afflictions].
These ten afflictions (up to... do not obstruct the wholesome. Commentary:

This is the sixth section, the gate of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). This is proven by the *Abhidharmapitaka* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Regarding the two views of self and extremes (*satkāya- and antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*):
Only those [defilements] that are indeterminate (avyākṛta) are consistently profound and subtle, because in each stage they reside solely in the lowest-of-the-low grade.
These ten afflictions constitute either the primary afflictions or the secondary derivative afflictions.

The commentary states: Within the seventh section on the gates of realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi-mukha*), there are three [topics]: by way of affiliation, by way of the arising of characteristics, and by way of the objects of characteristics.

These two [presently] are the first two. One who has attained the fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*) of that stage is capable of giving rise to those defiled states with a mind of deliberate ease.

Therefore, Ji says: "The *anāgamya* (preparatory stage) does not admit of defiled [states]. Ce says: "In the Mahāyāna, all *sāmantaka* (threshold) stages are devoid of distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*);

this differs from the Sarvāstivāda, for which the *anāgamya* admits of defilement. Ji says: "If that were so, one would not enter the fundamental [dhyāna]. What happens if one dies [while in the threshold]? Such a thing must not occur;

one necessarily attains the fundamental [dhyāna], or else one dies only after having fallen away [from it] (for the birth of the fetters serves as proof; if one has suppressed the lower [defilements] to their end..."

When the fundamental [dhyāna] has not yet been attained, there is no death at that time; rather, one either progresses upward to a higher birth or regresses downward to a lower birth. (The explanation of this meaning is as found in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*). Regarding "subtle co-arising," Ji says:

"The two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), along with those associated with them. Ce says: "The two views and the nine types of craving for rebirth (*upapattirāga*), etc."

Regarding the statement, "He is merely deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*) and so forth," *Ce* says: "Delusion regarding phenomena excludes the conceptualization that is deluded regarding principles (*tattva*).

"Co-emergent [afflictions] based on external objects" excludes those associated with the internal views and so forth that take the Truths as their object. "The remaining greed, hatred, and so forth, which are distracted and coarse" [are also excluded].

Jian Rensheng accepted [this view], arguing that these coarse afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*) because they involve improper mental observation (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).

Since it has been stated that all afflictions may manifest, it follows logically that when one is born in a lower realm, the nine afflictions of the higher realms should arise. (The *Shu* and *Shuyao* contain many interpretations regarding what is included or excluded; however, as there is no textual evidence to the contrary, [the inclusion of all nine] is accepted.)

One must not rely on [this] fixed rule). According to the Sarvāstivāda, one born in a higher realm does not give rise to afflictions of a lower realm, because the basis (*āśraya*) is superior. The Mahāyāna is not thus.

Regarding the wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), they are to be categorized as conceptual (*vikalpita*) like other [wrong views]. Regarding the craving for rebirth (*upapatti-tṛṣṇā*) that moistens it, it is to be categorized as innate (*sahaja*) like other [cravings].

The actual matter concerning that intermediate state is explained extensively in the sixty-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. However, according to the interpretation of that school, death does not necessarily depend on the power of karma; rather, it is birth...
When the signs appear before one, one then slanders [the teaching] by shifting the meaning. There is certainly no sense in which the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) transmigrates between realms.

According to the Sautrāntika and Mahāyāna schools, the transmigration of the intermediate state is as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa* (Chapter Six). This differs from the Vaibhāṣika view that the intermediate state does not perform karma that brings about a future body, because its basis is precarious.
As for those who mostly follow the "gate of conformity" (*anuvartana-mukha*), they harmonize this with the fifty-eighth [fascicle] and others.
Ce says: If [the afflictions] were to arise in their entirety, how could this statement be said to refer to the majority?

Furthermore, it is stated below that when one is born from the lower realms into the upper realms, there is no basis for the arising of the lower [afflictions], because they do not properly moisten rebirth nor do they involve the denial of cessation (*nirodha*). If, on the other hand, they do not arise in their entirety...
Regarding how the established tenets are all manifest, three interpretations are presented: First, it is said that three arise:

the false view that slanders cessation (*nirodha-saṃjñā-dṛṣṭi*) and the craving that moistens rebirth (*janma-pratisaṃdhi-tṛṣṇā*), along with their concomitant ignorance (*avidyā*). This refers to both the conceptual (*vikalpita*) and the innate (*sahaja*) types.

Second, it is said that all [afflictions] arise; therefore, there is no contradiction [between these views]. Third, it is said that five arise, or perhaps six arise: to the [previous] slander of cessation, anger (*dveṣa*) is added; to the moisture [of craving], [the other afflictions] are added.

I see [this]. Or, perhaps, pride increases further, because there is no other distinct principle that can manifest. The Sūtra states that hypocrisy (*śāṭhya*) and guile (*māyā*) arise together with greed (*lobha*);
since their activity is merely coarse, they do not serve as a precedent for pride (*māna*). One view holds that all ten [defilements] may arise;

however, when it is said that the lower afflictions arise at two specific times, this is merely citing two instances by way of illustration, and there is no contradiction in applying this to the others. As for the phrase "for the most part," it is based on...
This refers to the time [of rebirth], not the non-enumerated [time]. Regarding the text on secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), it cites the subtle to exclude the coarse.

Furthermore, the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) that deludes one regarding the process of rebirth does not coexist with [the view of self] regarding objects. (Ji states that six arise; others have no signs of arising. However, when they arise in the lower realms, how could there be only two times? Although the Form Realm possesses wrong views of its own level, it is admitted that one still gives rise to wrong views of the Desire Realm.

The four types—extreme views, the two graspings, and doubt—are like wrong views and so forth; they are not suppressed by the worldly path. It is admitted that at the time of grasping at permanence and annihilation, etc., due to the power of habitual practice, the lower [afflictions] may arise).
Regarding the statement that "lower levels (up to) or other objects are said [to be conditions]," the commentary states:

Within the third characteristic of being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), there are two types: those that take higher levels as their object and those that take lower levels as their object. As for the first, it is as stated in the *Fifty-Eight* [Treatise]:
"Defilements of a lower level can take defilements and phenomena (*vastu*) of a higher level as their objects. This is the proof for the general proposition.

In the *Vibhāṣā*, it is stated that these correspond respectively to the stages of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*). Regarding the statement that there is "craving for higher concentrations" (*dhyāna*) and so forth within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the sixty-second [fascicle] is also like this.

Jñānagupta says: "These are abandoned through both seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). The fifty-eighth [fascicle] states: "Hating and envying cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).

By inference, one should know that worldly antidotes (*laukika-pratipakṣa*) are also increased. Jñānagupta says: "This anger (*vyāpāda*) is abandoned through seeing. Cien says: "There is no contradiction in its being abandoned through cultivation; it is also [abandoned by] the worldly path (*loka-mārga*)."

Although one practices [the path], there may still be craving and seeking; by this standard, what prevents one from also craving the cessation of suffering (nirodha) and the path (mārga)? However, because these aspects are subtle and latent, their coarse manifestations are not mentioned (Master Ji permits that the mind which takes the untainted as its object is thus). As it says in the *Eighty-eight [Treatises]*:
By means of the mundane path, one may reach up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), yet one is not yet liberated from its afflictions.

Due to this view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one regards all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the higher and lower stages as being mixed with one's own self, and thus generally asserts them to be "I" or "mine.
Although that [text] does not explicitly mention the views of permanence and annihilation or pride (*māna*), it is understood by implication.

The view (*dṛṣṭi*) necessarily takes [its object] collectively (*saṃmugdha*). (Cai says: "If the view associated with greed (*rāga*) takes [its object] collectively, it necessarily takes it collectively; however, pride (*māna*) regarding superior meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) takes [its object] individually. Nevertheless, one should understand that this treatise implies this by way of indirect indication.")

Master Ji says: "The sixth consciousness is associated only with what is abandoned through cultivation (because it is universally accepted that [afflictions] abandoned through seeing have only distinct objects;

even if my view of self were conceptually arisen, there would be no logical contradiction in its taking all manifest phenomena across the upper and lower realms as a single self). Alternatively, there is another interpretation:

the view of self abandoned through seeing can take the 'entirety' and 'permanence' as objects, because it takes the three [realms] collectively as self and so forth. (This [interpretation] refers only to the sudden taking of various selves—both one's own and others—as objects, and not to taking all phenomena collectively as a single self; therefore, that...)

The *Śū* (Commentary) states there is an alternative interpretation. The *Zhèng* (Proof) says: "If, as the Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika schools distinguish, the self (*ātman*) is already omnipresent, why would it not take all phenomena as its object?

Therefore, [their] conceptualization (*vikalpa*) also takes everything collectively. This is incorrect; for they conceive of a single self apart from the aggregates (*skandha*), rather than regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as a whole. Regarding the phrase "the other five": [it refers to the remaining five types of clinging].

It is universally established in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna that ignorance (*moha*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) take the higher realms as their objects.

As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Among the afflictions of the desire realm, with the exception of ignorance, [false] views, and doubt, the others cannot take the higher realms as their objects. The commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* explains:

"'Views' here excludes the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because worldly beings grasp other phenomena as being a self. Yuan Ce further notes: "This also excludes the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Therefore...

Regarding the statement that [the afflictions] have objects despite not being explicitly mentioned, the term "and so forth" refers to the *Abhidharma-kośa*, which includes greed, hatred, pride, and so on;

"and so forth" here also encompasses the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). As for the phrase "not taking the higher [stages] as their object," this is said because they function according to coarse characteristics or because they are distinct.

Regarding the phrase "not seeing the worldly conventions or the dharmas of other stages," both Jñānagarbha and Puguang offer interpretations that do not exceed two paths. One interpretation states that it is intended to exclude [the afflictions] from being [viewed as] a self.

It does not exclude the self of others. Regarding those who hold that a portion of the permanent dharma is the Brahma-self: this is because they wish to distinguish it as having an object in a higher realm.

One opinion holds: "It does not take a lower realm as its object when directed toward a higher one; for it is a view of self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) bound to a higher realm, induced after the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).

[This] proves the latter position; however, the former is also acceptable. When taking a lower realm as an object within a higher one, it is like the case in the *Pañcāśat-sūtra* regarding objects belonging to another realm—namely, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) with respect to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding the afflictions of the realms and modes of conduct (*dhātu-gati-kleśa*): the statement concerning the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) in relation to the afflictions of the form mode of conduct (*rūpa-gati*) serves as a general proof.
Within the specific details, as stated in the *Pañcāśat* [Treatise] in sequence: "To rely on one's own superior virtues is pride (*māna*). Master Ce states:

"Because there is no textual distinction, it generally takes all as its object, since both the discriminated (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) types of pride have already been established. Furthermore, setting aside doubt, the latter three views should be considered according to reason.

Regarding this, there are two interpretations by Ji and Ce. The first says: all [defilements] can take the lower realms as their object. This includes doubt regarding the suffering and origin of the lower realms, as well as the false view of denial that arises when one has attained a higher meditative absorption;

these also include the two types of grasping (satkāyadṛṣṭi and antagrāhadṛṣṭi) arising in the higher realms, because they grasp at the previously cultivated mixed meditation on the desire realm during the stages of hearing and reflection as being the supreme cause.
The second says: none of them take the lower realms as their object, as there is no scriptural evidence to prove otherwise.
It is better to evaluate this before [the formal discussion], because the initial presentation of the thesis contains no specific qualification.

As for the statements in the *Pañcavastuka* (58) and the *Abhidharma* that [the mind] does not take lower levels as its object, those are based on the majority of cases; in the Sarvāstivāda school, [the mind] generally does not take lower levels as its object because it has already abandoned desire for them.
Alternatively, they may be based on specific conditions, as explained according to the preceding analysis.
"These ten afflictions... [omitted] ...because they are exclusively wholesome. Commentary:

The eighth section concerns the "door of being neither. These are not included among those [afflictions] associated with the trainee (śaikṣa) or the one beyond training (aśaikṣa), because their nature is exclusively wholesome.
"These ten [are abandoned] by cultivation" (up to this point). The commentary states:

Regarding the ninth section on the three modes of abandonment, it says that there are both general and specific ways in which the delusions regarding the characteristics of the truths (*satya-lakṣaṇa*) occur.

Master Cè provides two interpretations. The first says: All ten afflictions have both general and specific aspects. For instance, ignorance (*avidyā*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) all [function as] direct...

There are four types of delusion, each consisting of fifteen phrases. These consist of six phrases for specific delusions regarding the four truths taken two at a time, and four phrases for general delusions regarding the four truths taken three at a time.

The six phrases for specific delusions regarding pairs are: 1. Delusion regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*). 2. Delusion regarding cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga*). 3. Delusion regarding suffering and cessation (*duḥkha-nirodha*). 4. Delusion regarding the origin and the path (*samudaya-mārga*). 5. Delusion regarding the origin and cessation (*samudaya-nirodha*).

6. Delusion regarding suffering and the path (*duḥkha-mārga*). The four phrases for general delusions regarding triplets are: 1. The first three [truths] excluding the path (*mārga*). 2. The last three [truths] excluding [the first]. 3. The middle three [truths] excluding [the first and last]. 4. The first and last [truths] excluding the middle.

Regarding suffering: the first two and the fourth [of the three types of ignorance] constitute the first category; the first and the last two of the four [categories of ignorance] collectively constitute delusion regarding the Four Noble Truths, which is subsumed into a single phrase.

When there is direct delusion regarding suffering, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is added; the subsequent arising of the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*), craving (*rāga*), and so forth, is also termed "distinct delusion."

One should understand that this refers to general delusion (*samudāya-moha*). Although the essence of all delusions is one, their number is determined according to the specific truths (*satya*) they obscure.

Thus, there are one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*) across the five categories of the three realms. Why, then, are there two views (*dṛṣṭi*) regarding the truths of origination, cessation, and the path?
Ji says: [The opponent] takes the aggregates of afflictions and so forth under the three truths as being "self" and so on; taking this meaning as the standard, there is no third interpretation.

This should be understood by analogy with those who are deluded regarding the principle (*tattva*): they are directly deluded regarding the truths themselves. Ji [argues that] since the two views [of self and what belongs to self] are distantly related to the three truths, [the opponent's position] does not accord with the teachings or the principles. Secondly, it is said: This refers to a general delusion explained in terms of specific delusions;
there is no separate general delusion apart from specific delusions. All afflictions are such that they cannot comprehend [things] through causes and conditions.

The basis (*āśraya*) and the locus of fear (*bhaya-sthāna*) are termed "general delusion" (*sāmānya-moha*). Taken collectively and distributively, these constitute twenty-eight [delusions]. It is not that the specific delusions (*viśeṣa-moha*) alone number this many.
This is because the two views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*)—delude one only regarding suffering (*duḥkha*).

(The commentary states: "The first interpretation is logical; the latter follows the text. To say it is 'logical' means that there are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), etc., who generally harbor doubt and denial regarding the Four Truths. To say it 'follows the text' means that both are described as general delusions by way of their causal bases and loci of fear. Quiescence (*śama*).

It says: "Those who are deluded in general" are deluded regarding the non-established [truth]; "those who are deluded in particular" are deluded regarding the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*). (The commentary states this is incorrect, because the causes, bases, and so forth still belong to the fourfold gate of the established truths.
Regarding those who are "deluded in particular," Fan says: whereas the preceding general delusion is a delusion that does not take [an object] as its focal point, this particular delusion...

Regarding delusion (*moha*), it also takes [other phenomena] as its object (*ālambana*). [The Commentary states: "It is not so; for one does not take what is not cessation to be cessation, nor what is not the Path to be the Path, because both take other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena as their objects. Although the specific modes of delusion differ, they do not take those [specific objects] as their objects.

Of the three phrases concerning suffering (*duḥkha*), the first refers exclusively to direct delusion (*sākṣāt-moha*), namely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). The second refers exclusively to indirect delusion (*pāramparya-moha*), namely the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

The three types of penetration [of the truths] involve both direct and indirect delusion. As for the remaining afflictions, the two phrases beginning with "accumulation" (*samudaya*) do not refer exclusively to direct delusion (the commentary states that doubt and false view are considered indirectly delusive, excluding those that contradict the holy teachings).
Regarding the mention of "specific emptiness and non-self," this distinguishes them from "general emptiness and non-self. The names of the sixteen aspects are distinct; as Ji says:
"General emptiness and non-self take all four truths as their object collectively, because one must sever the afflictions by means of them. Thus, Ce says:
This means that all four [noble truths], such as suffering, are non-self. Regarding the statement that "doubt and the three views are directly deluded regarding the principle of suffering":

this is because doubt clings to a self and so forth, and because [the view of nihilism] negates [the truth]. Master Ji says: "The nature of the two types of grasping (satkāyadṛṣṭi and antagrāhadṛṣṭi) has a profound mode of activity;

because they are deeply deluded and cling [to objects], they can be said to be 'deluded regarding the principle. However, they do not directly delude one regarding the principle of non-self, etc., as they give rise separately to afflictions such as craving."

"Deluded regarding the objects [of the truths]" (this explanation is difficult to understand; why is it that one is deeply deluded regarding the principles of the truths [satya] yet only superficially deluded according to the various holy teachings? This is as explained in the *Mātṛkā*). Regarding the phrase "respectively and accordingly":
one gives rise to attachment toward one's own views and so forth, and gives rise to aversion toward the views of others and so forth;

hence, it says "respectively. One relies on oneself and disparages others, giving rise to pride; hence, it says "accordingly. Kīrti says: "This refers only to being deluded regarding the objects of the four truths; in principle..."

Regarding "distant" and "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇika-avidyā*): this refers to the primary delusion regarding the Truths. Just as one is personally deluded regarding Suffering, so too the unshared ignorance under each of the other three Truths is individually and personally deluded regarding those three.
It should be understood that the subsequent discussion of "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) and "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) applies by analogy to the [other] three Truths.

Hatred (*dveṣa*) is deluded regarding Cessation and the Path; this distinguishes it from the Sarvāstivāda position. Greed, hatred, pride, and so forth, have only the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object.
Because the coarse characteristics of the basis lack the principle of hatred (*dveṣa*) regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), this is not discussed here.

In the detailed section, as for the three—greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and pride (*māna*)—if they arise independently and take views (*dṛṣṭi*) as their object, they are remote, as previously described.

If this greed and pride arise together with the three views, or if hatred arises together with the three views and doubt (*vicikitsā*), they are, according to their respective associations, like that immediate delusion.

The category of innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*), although deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering, is not abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) because it is subtle and difficult to sever, unlike those [views] that arise discriminately (*vikalpa-utpanna*).
Although the latter involve delusion regarding specific objects, they are not abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) because they are coarse and easy to sever.

As for the statement that "delusion arises regarding distinct objects without contradicting the contemplation of the truths," this refers to delusion regarding distinct sentient beings or objective phenomena; it is not the same as discriminative [delusion], even though such delusion exists.
Matter (*vastu*). It takes only the views and so forth as its object, because it is an internal, profound gateway.
Although all afflictions [should be considered] according to principle, [the commentary] states:
"The tenth is the gateway of the differentiation of objects. Within this, regarding the gateway of 'having matter' and 'being without matter,' it is as follows: [as in the preceding section].

The *Dharmaskandha* (Treatise on the Aggregates of Dharma) in five fascicles, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in fifty-nine fascicles, and others have already explained these according to their respective texts. Regarding the objects of outflow (*sāsrava*) and so forth, Cè states:

"False view, doubt, delusion, anger, and those [afflictions] associated with them are termed 'having uncontaminated objects' (*anāsravālambana*); the remainder are 'having contaminated objects' (*sāsravālambana*). Kì’s intention is also the same.

Based on coarse characteristics, the other categories—whether they possess or lack maturation, and their specific distinctions regarding the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*)—are subsumed [here].
The remainder of the text is easily understood.
This concludes the explanation of the fundamental [factors] up to lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).
The commentary states: Among the fourth category, the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), this verse provides a general question and answer.
The treatise says (extending to the "great secondary afflictions").
The commentary states: There are two parts in the explanation: the direct explanation and the various classifications. The first also has three parts, beginning with the distinctions of their stages.

Therefore, because their natures and functions are distinct, and because they are associated with [the primary afflictions], this is the first category. There are two meanings for "secondary" (*anuvartin*): first, they are states of the afflictions, meaning anger and so forth are nominal;

second, they are outflows of the afflictions, meaning lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth are substantial. Regarding the first ten, they necessarily do not arise simultaneously when compared to one another;
although they coexist with the medium and great [afflictions], they are called "minor" (*parītta*) secondary afflictions. The middle two arise together. They coexist...

Birth (*jāti*) is exclusively pervasive within the unwholesome (*akuśala*). The latter eight are pervasive within the defiled (*kliṣṭa*); they are called "great" because they are great. The proof states:

fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), according to this, are of three types. Solitary ignorance (*avidyā*) is called "small," because it arises individually. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is exclusively unwholesome; when shared with others, it is called "middling.

The remainder are common to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); when shared with others, they are called "great. (This does not constitute a valid precedent, for shared ignorance is not a separate category, and hatred is not pervasive across all [unwholesome states]).
Because it arises from a wholesome mind, and because greed and other [afflictions] do not pervade all defiled minds.
What are the characteristics and functions of anger (*krodha*)? [This continues] up to the characteristics and functions of arrogance (*mada*).
The commentary states: Within the distinct natures and activities, there are three types—small, medium, and great. This is the first, the small. It does not provide benefit.

"Manifesting through activity" refers to [the manifestation] in opposition to an adverse object. Regarding the frequent production of bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*), this first explains the case of "wielding a staff"; in reality, it also applies to speech and mental intention.
However, as for the statement that restlessness (*auddhatya*) pervades all defiled states, it actually has a distinct substantial entity, as it is also a derivative of delusion (*moha*).

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (58) states that it is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of deceit (*śāṭhya*); this is said because it is categorized as being of the same class as the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). "To pursue" means to seek; it is also to slander.
"Risky" (*khaṭuṅka*) is a name for that which is unreal. Regarding the statement "or concealing what has already been lost," *Kuiji* says:
"Deceit (*śāṭhya*) gives rise to concealment (*mrakṣa*) subsequently; one performs prostrations as a result of it. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between concealment and deceit.

Regarding "one who harms sentient beings and lacks compassion in mind," *Kuiji*’s *Ce* (Commentary) states: "This also takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) [dharmas], such as the Path of Cessation, as its object."
Regarding the phrase "one's own prosperity," Zhi says: "Relying on the dharmas one knows also extends to the untainted (anāsrava).
How is it that shamelessness (āhrīkya) [and so forth] are not identical to those natures?"
The commentary states: This refers to the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) within the second category. Regarding the statement that they "should not be substantially existent," Cè says:
"Because they are distinguished based on a single entity, like the opposition between long and short. The *Fifty-five [Treatises]* states: "They are substantially existent. It says:

"If one grants that these two arise separately as real entities, then although painful and pleasant sensations differ in their nature of oppression and gratification, they are both equally experienced as feeling (*vedanā*)."

The same applies to shame (*hrī*): it is real and arises separately; while there is a difference between feeling shame for oneself and feeling shame for others, there is no difference in the absence of such shame.
Being real and arising separately, it contradicts the fifty-five [factors] that are said to be pervasive among the unwholesome (*akuśala*).
"What is restlessness (*auddhatya*)? ... because it universally defiles the mind. [The commentary] states:
This is the third of the great secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-kleśa*). Restlessness has its own distinct nature and pervades all defiled minds, just like lack of faith (*āśraddhya*).
Ji says: "This reason is not definitive, because it is not subsumed under [the category of] negligence (*pramāda*) and so forth. Restlessness obstructs equanimity (*upekṣā*). Next...

The hindrance to *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) is not found in other treatises; it was added by this author of the present treatise through reasoning. Because these two factors (*styāna* and *auddhatya*) have grave faults, each is said to have two hindrances.
*Laya* (sinking) and *auddhatya* (restlessness) are substantially real and are established as the correct meaning.

Since they specifically hinder *śamatha* (calm abiding) and so forth, while the various afflictions do not, it says "due to lack of faith" and so on; although one may have patience, delight, and desire for the wholesome, its essence is...
The desire for conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding reality and so forth is merely a lack of disbelief; it has no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) apart from non-disbelief and the like.
It is just as when, within the context of faith (*śraddhā*), there is no acceptance or delight regarding defiled phenomena and so forth—that is simply the absence of faith.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* that "this [ignorance] pervades all defiled minds": this is because the [five] object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*) do not pervade all defiled states.

As for the phrase "the former makes [the object] easy to understand, while the latter makes [the mind] easy to take as an object," Yuan Ce says: there are four permutations here. First: easy to understand, but not taking it as an object.
1. When one first conceives of form as permanent and subsequently conceives of it as annihilated; this is a change of object (*ālambana*) and not a change of understanding (*adhimokṣa*).

For example, after conceiving of form as permanent, one subsequently conceives of feeling (*vedanā*) as permanent. 2. When both the understanding and the object change; for example, after conceiving of form as permanent, one subsequently conceives of feeling as annihilated.

3. When both remain unchanged; the preceding and succeeding moments are identical. Regarding the phrase "by the power of mindfulness and so forth" (*smṛty-ādibalāt*), the Master Ki states that "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the like (here translated as "concentration and so forth," where "and so forth" includes...).

A certain type of *manas* associated with excitement (*auddhatya*) and distraction is restrained and sustained by another type of consciousness. Although there is no mindfulness or meditative concentration (because the two are not easily [established]), the first two among the states of non-awareness (*asaṃprajanya*) correspond to this textual description;
thus it is said that these are their outflow (*niṣyanda*). This is how the statement is made.
"Along with 'and also' (yāvat), it should be understood according to the principle.

Regarding the term "coarse" (*audārika*): it possesses three meanings. First, it is not an affliction (*kleśa*), which distinguishes it from greed and the like. Second, it is exclusively defiled (*kliṣṭa*), which distinguishes it from false resolve, wrong views, and the four indeterminate states.
As Master Ji says: "Although forgetfulness and so forth have mindfulness as their nature, they do not incur the fault of being indeterminate because they are categorized under delusion.
Third, it is exclusively coarse, which distinguishes it from the sixty-two views. This refers to those who proceed forward.

Because formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are not established as subtle [states]. Ce (Ceci) says: "The remaining defiled dharmas refer to the states (*avasthā*) of outbursts such as anger (*krodha*), and so on;

These twenty [categories] should be understood according to the above.

This is based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 58, which states that when torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) increase, they do not arise simultaneously. Question: Since vitarka and vicāra function as coarse and subtle respectively, it is not admitted that they coexist in a single moment of mind.

Likewise, since torpor and restlessness possess the characteristics of depression and elevation, they should likewise not coexist in a single moment of mind. Answer: When elevation increases, depression does not descend. (Conversely, when depression increases, elevation does not arise. Thus, they are not simultaneous.

Only *moha* (delusion) is not contradictory [to the others]. In the lower realms, *auddhatya* (restlessness) increases but does not arise intensely. Only *āghāta* (malice) arises simultaneously [with the primary afflictions]. This is not the case for *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), as their coarse and subtle natures are mutually exclusive;

however, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are identical. [The following concerns] four gates: 1) the gate of association with the various consciousnesses; 2) the gate of arising together with the five feelings (*vedanā*); 3) the three—*śāṭhya* (deceit), *māyā* (guile), and *mada* (pride)—pervade the higher realms;

and 4) regarding the statement that pleasure (*sukha*) on the mental level (*manobhūmi*) is associated [with these] just as with *daurmanasya* (mental distress), [this applies to] anger (*krodha*) and the others.
They are associated with joy (*prīti*). Avarice (*mātsarya*) and so forth are associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*). This should be understood by analogy with greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*).

According to the Hīnayāna, the five factors beginning with anger (*krodha*) are associated only with sorrow and equanimity (*upekṣā*), because they are subsumed under the predominant activity of a portion of hatred. Concealment (*mrakṣa*) and avarice are subsumed under the joyful activity of a portion of greed.

The three—deceit (*śāṭhya*), guile (*māyā*), and arrogance (*mada*)—are associated with the pleasure (*sukha*) of the higher realms and with the six object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-ka*).

[The section on] the gates: The seven afflictions arise together with stinginess (*mātsarya*); pride (*mada*) arises only with delusion (*moha*). Regarding the distinction between the mode of activity (*ākāra*) and the object of cognition (*ālambana*) [of pride and arrogance], Zé says:

"Arrogance takes oneself as its object and gives rise to stained attachment and intoxicated haughtiness; pride involves looking down upon others. Because their modes of activity and objects differ... (This does not fully capture the principle, for if one is proud by relying on oneself, the mode of activity is concordant).

Jī says: "Arrogance arises from taking oneself as the object and being uplifted; pride also takes another as its object" (This too is incomplete, because the pride associated with the *manas* does not take another as its object).

If one claims that when these six arise together, they must necessarily take other objects as their conditions, then one might say they "take distinct objects"; why then speak of them as "discerning distinct objects"? The Upādhyāya says: *māna* (pride) means being intoxicated and submerged; it differs from arrogance (*unnati*) because it involves a state of being submerged.

Regarding those [defilements] associated with concealment (*mrakṣa*), deception (*māyā*), and guile (*śāṭhya*), and with greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*): greed and delusion have two parts, for they arise in mutual association. The *Shuyao* says:

"These three are divisions of delusion and are not associated with hatred; this is stated according to coarse characteristics. In reality, however, they are also associated [with hatred]. This does not accord with the treatise; if it were according to the gate of coarse characteristics, they should have been specified separately. — *Ce*.
It is said that because vitarka and vicāra must coexist with greed and delusion, they cannot coexist with hatred, according to the Dharmapāla school.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that vitarka and vicāra must necessarily rely on two factors and be designated as three, if one follows the view of Siṃhabuddhi—that vitarka and vicāra are either wisdom (*prajñā*) or one or the other—this is not what is maintained here (this interpretation accords with the treatise).

In the first dhyāna, *śāṭhya* (deceit) and *māyā* (guile) may exist, but they arise only independently; in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they necessarily cause intense unwholesomeness (*akuśala*). They differ from the great universal [defilements] (*mahābhūmika*) because they are also distinct in their capacity for indulgence, and because they are based on different forms of greed and hatred (*lobha* and *dveṣa*).
