although volition is necessarily present, the superior essence [of wisdom] prevails (the meaning being that when wisdom arises, it eclipses the function of volition; therefore, right reflection is subsumed solely under the faculty of wisdom).

Furthermore, among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), right speech, right action, right livelihood, joy, tranquility, and equanimity—these six—are not faculties (*indriya*). Thus, at the time of the Noble Path, there is also a factor of volition, for right reflection must be understood as including those that are not faculties. (1)

It is said: "Both are established based on two [factors]. Within a single moment, they are shallow and deep respectively; because their two functions coexist, this meaning is measured and maintained. It is stated that they 'combine,' which serves as proof.
However, correct reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is subsumed under its predominant essence, and thus there is no contradiction.

(Regarding the initial statement that they "combine," this is intended to clarify the enumeration of the factors of enlightenment; it does not mean that at the time of arising they must necessarily combine in pairs. There may be solitary reflection, as it involves a shallow degree of deliberation. Seeds are substantial entities (*dravya*).
Regarding "and exist conventionally," this cites [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] 52.
Among the four [points], from "vitarka and vicāra" up to "the meaning of mutual association," the commentary states:
"The second is the gate of association among its own class. As for 'the substance and category are the same, while the functions differ as coarse and subtle,' Master Ji says:"

Their substance (*tattva*) consists of both vitarka and vicāra; their category (*jāti*) consists of both inference and deliberation. However, their substance and function, as well as their categories of coarseness and subtlety, are mutually contradictory, just like the sensations of higher and lower levels, because they do not arise simultaneously.
An objection is raised: "If, as in the Sarvāstivāda school, vitarka and vicāra can coexist, then it would be possible to establish three stages [of dhyāna].
But in the Mahāyāna, they do not coexist; how then can there be an 'initial stage with vitarka and vicāra'? Therefore, the treatise explains: "Based upon..."

Regarding vitarka and vicāra—whether they are associated with defilement or free from defilement—the three distinct stages are established. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are three masters’ interpretations, and Master Cè offers two explanations.
One states: "This treatise is identical to the second [position] therein. However, that [text] raises an objection: 'For one who has already abandoned desire...'"

The various dharmas of the lower stages are called "without vitarka" (*avitarkādi*). If one who has not yet abandoned desire were to claim that the various dharmas of the higher stages should be called "with vitarka" (*savitarka*), it would result in confusion.
Regarding this, some explain: "The lower [stages] are called 'without vitarka' and so forth because they follow from the superior [higher stages];

the higher [stages], however, turn away from the inferior [lower stages] and thus are not 'with vitarka'. This explanation is incorrect, because although the higher turn away from the lower, the lower still follow from the higher; thus, calling them "without vitarka" and so forth would result in confusion. Another says: "This refers to the abandonment of desire."

It is said that this differs from the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*). That is to say, while that *Śāstra* relies on the desire for afflictions (*kleśa*), this treatise relies on the nature of being free from desire for one's own level (*svabhūmi*).
As in [verse] 56: "Because those sentient beings are by nature free from desire regarding discursive thoughts (*vitarka-vicāra*) of their own level, they are called 'of their own level.

Not being mutually weary of them is called 'desire-nature' (*kāma-svabhāva*). [The opponent argues: "The higher levels are weary of the lower. [The author replies: This is also not the case; although they are not mutually weary of each other by nature, there is the power of defilement (*saṃkleśa-bala*).

Because the very nature of detachment is itself defiled. Apart from the desire for afflictions (*kleśa*), there is also the desire for existence (*bhava*). (There is no meaning in speaking of "non-confusion" where none exists). The *Śūyao* (Essential Summary) fully recounts the three explanations found in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary);
the interpretation of this treatise is identical to that [of the *Vyākhyā*]. Regarding its true meaning, two interpretations are presented:

first, it is said that those factors of the stages (*bhūmi*) which possess coarseness or subtlety must necessarily depend upon being defiled, because they are distinct bound phenomena (*bandhana-dharma*). Those of the untainted (*anāsrava*) class are likewise subsumed under their respective stages. Thus it is said.

There are those who possess defilement (*saraṇa*), and there is the active manifestation of defilement; therefore, while one established in a lower stage possesses the seeds of the three realms and thus possesses defilement, it is not designated as belonging to those [upper] stages.

As for the term "free from defilement" (*vītarāga*), this refers to the sense of being born in a higher stage. (This meaning is difficult to understand: regarding one born in a higher stage, what phenomenon is "free from defilement"?

If it refers only to the phenomena of the higher stage, then the same would apply to those in the lower stage; why then is it said that one is "free from defilement" only when born in a higher stage? Furthermore, if the three types of consciousness and so forth that arise in the lower stage were also called "without vitarka," it would result in confusion, just as in the *Pañcaṣaṣṭi-sūtra* regarding the consciousnesses with and without vitarka and vicāra.)
Because the seeds follow along and manifest [in these stages]. One interpretation states: that which is said to be "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) refers to active outflows (*samudācāra-sāsrava*);

that which is said to be "free from outflows" (*vītarāga*) refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth. Whether with outflows or free from outflows, they are subsumed accordingly; it is not said that being free from outflows means one is not included therein.

Therefore, it is stated that true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) also belongs to the three stages. (This does not accord with the text. If the phrase "with outflows" referred only to active outflows, this statement would only explain the first two stages. Outflows and freedom from outflows belong to the untainted.)
That [level] reveals the third level (as the basis-commentary states: "just as in the desire realm, one has not yet abandoned the desire realm, nor has one yet abandoned the defilements of desire").
By practicing the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one likewise subdues greed and other afflictions; this case is also like that.

Although they belong to the same *saṃyojana* (bond), it is only by first subduing discursive thought (*vitarka*) and defilement (*kleśa*) that one attains the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*). The *Ceshu* (Commentary on Difficult Points) poses the objection:

"If the three stages are established based on the departure from desire (*vairāgya*), then since the fundamental [attainments] of the intermediate state and the [lower] stages are equally free from desire, they should constitute a single stage, which would entail the fault of confusion. The explanation states: "Regarding the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) for departing from defilement, first..."

Regarding "separation from the defilement of vitarka": although the actual separation is the same, it does not pertain to a single level (the phrasing differs while the meaning is the same; we now retain this interpretation). This is as in the case of the separation [from defilements] in the *aśubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity), where the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*) are likewise.

Because the preparatory stage precedes the separation from the defilements of the first dhyāna, the factors of the desire realm and the first dhyāna possess both *vitarka* and *vicāra* defilements, whereas the intermediate dhyāna only suppresses the defilement of *vitarka*. Above this, they are separated in total according to the sequence of one, two, and three [levels].

As for the statement "not depending on whether those seeds or manifestations arise," if one depends on the existence of the seeds, then up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they are termed *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): if [the mind] relies on seeds that are absent, entering solely into the remainderless state (*anupadhiśeṣa*) is called the third stage.

If it relies on those currently present—namely, the desire realm and the four dhyānas—since consciousness accompanied by vitarka and vicāra arises there, or because only vitarka arises, one should establish four stages, as this is discussed in terms of both the momentary and the continuous states.
If it relies on those currently absent—the desire realm and the first dhyāna—[it is the fourth stage].
They are free from both vitarka and vicāra, or they are separated from them in the four stages, because at times one has vitarka and vicāra while the other does not.
Vitarka and vicāra are both associated with kaukṛtya (remorse) and middha (torpor); furthermore, kaukṛtya and middha are also mutually associated with one another.
"None of the four are associated with [vitarka and vicāra]... up to: they definitely lack vitarka and vicāra. Commentary:
This is the third section, the gate of association with the various consciousnesses. The Sarvāstivādins say: "The five consciousnesses are definitely associated with vitarka and vicāra;
the sixth is indefinite. In the desire realm and the first dhyāna, both are present; in the intermediate dhyāna, there is only vicāra; above that, both are absent. Thus says the treatise.
Regarding the statement that the five consciousnesses possess vitarka and vicāra, the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Five Categories), fascicle 56, asks:

"If one is born in the second dhyāna or in higher stages, and yet possesses vitarka and vicāra when visual and other consciousnesses manifest before them, how is it that these stages are said to be without vitarka and vicāra?

Furthermore, regarding the statement that vitarka and vicāra are themselves the seven types of discrimination, this is found in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 5; the first [of those] is as follows:
It says: "The unique characteristic of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is that it is associated with both sorrow and joy.

Regarding the statement "not separated from delight" (*abhirati*), Woncheuk says: "This is because the single feeling of delight is described as 'pleasure' (*sukha*). [Question: If the two feelings [of joy and pleasure] belong to the same category, yet 'pleasure' is used as a metaphorical designation, then the subsequent wisdom of the dual observation (*ubhayatobhāgavipaśyanā*) should also be metaphorically designated [as pleasure].

[Answer: In the mental consciousness, delight is metaphorically designated as the [fivefold] pleasure; its primary locus is the mental consciousness. Both types of wisdom are substantially real. However, in the third dhyāna, there is no function of delight at all; thus, the pleasure associated with the mind remains simply "pleasure" (*sukha*). This statement shows that [the designation of pleasure] primarily arises from that [delight].
Regarding "arising" (*utpāda*), Cè explains it in two senses: first, that one dwells for a short time in a concentrated mind and for a long time in a distracted mind;

second, that there is little *sater-er* (sudden) mind and much *deng-liu* (continuing) mind. Jī also provides two interpretations: first, that if one is within the meditative absorption of the desire realm...

When auditory consciousness arises suddenly (*saterī*), the mental consciousness (*manas*) shares the same object; it is not produced by being induced by the mental consciousness accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.

This is because the meditative absorptions from the second dhyāna upward also possess auditory consciousness belonging to lower realms. In other circumstances, the five consciousnesses are mostly produced by being induced by the mental consciousness accompanied by vitarka and so forth.
Just as there is sudden consciousness in the desire realm, [auditory consciousness] in the second dhyāna and above does not depend on the objects of vitarka and vicāra.

Qiangzhi (as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "The distinctions in the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of instruction from lower stages also include instances where mental states free from both vitarka and vicāra manifest at a single moment"). Second, it says:
[Mental factors] in the desire realm or the dhyānas do not necessarily arise induced by vitarka and vicāra, because they belong to their own stage (*svabhūmika*).

However, when arising in the second dhyāna or above, they must be guided by vitarka and vicāra to arise, because those [higher stages] do not possess such factors [as intrinsic]. [If it were otherwise,] since the five consciousnesses of a different stage must arise with vitarka and vicāra, and vitarka and vicāra would also be of a different stage, by what else could they be produced?

[It] induces [them]. Therefore, the previous interpretation remains [valid]: that [the mind] is indeterminate according to conditions (*pratyaya*). The proof states: "In both the *satera* (sudden) and *nisyanda* (continuous) stages, the mental consciousness takes the name-body (*nāmakāya*) and so forth as its object, and it is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra.
If this were not the case, it would not be induced by them; therefore, it is said 'mostly' (*prāyeṇa*).

Regarding the statement that "what is called 'spontaneous' (*svarasa*) is precisely the five consciousnesses," *Kī* says: "The 'intrinsic discrimination' (*svabhāvavikalpa*) is subsumed under the category of 'having signs' (*sanimitta*); it is not 'spontaneous'."

[The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*] subsumes [the nature of conceptualization] by stating that one knows the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) to be without intrinsic conceptualization (*svabhāva-vikalpa*). Furthermore, it is explained that there are two types of intrinsic conceptualization: first, the five consciousnesses themselves;

second, the applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The *Abhidharmapitaka* (or *Abhidharma*), based on the latter, states that there is mutual inclusion.

[However, this is] a proof [of the former] position, for the text does not mention both types of intrinsic conceptualization. Thus, [the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*] does not fully capture the principle; this should be understood as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*.
There is an interpretation [stating that] *kaukṛtya* (regret) [arises] together with mental suffering (*daurmanasya*).

The commentary states: This is the fourth section on the arising of the five feelings; as for the statement that it "proceeds exclusively in a dejected mode and is also associated with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)," Ki says:

Because it is of a dejected nature (*daurmanasya-gati*), it is associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya-samprayukta*); because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*). Since wholesome or unwholesome [remorse] involves strong volition, it must necessarily be associated with sorrow.
Equanimity, however, extends to both dejected and non-dejected states and thus can be associated with remorse. Cè (Ce) says: "This is stated to clarify its specific characteristic;

that it is indeterminate proves it is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-samprayukta*), not that it is exclusively indeterminate. In reality, both wholesome and unwholesome remorse are also associated with equanimity. Therefore, it is said that [remorse] extends to both joy (*prīti*) and dejection."
Regarding the transformation of the *madhyamā-pratipad* (the middle way), Ji states: "They correspond respectively to joy (*prīti*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Ce states:

"In reality, although dejection (*daurmanasya*) and torpor (*styāna*) also accompany equanimity, since [dejection] is associated with regret (*kaukṛtya*), it functions exclusively as dejection. The remainder of the text is easily understood.
All four [mental factors] are compatible [with one another], because they do not contradict each other.
The commentary states: This is the fifth section, the gate of association with specific objects.
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) are associated only with [the mental factor of] lightness-and-pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and so forth.
The commentary states: The sixth is the gate of association with the wholesome.
This is because remorse can coexist [with the wholesome] without contradiction. The commentary states:
The seventh is the gate of concomitance with afflictions. *Ce* says: Both the Sarvāstivāda and the Sautrāntika schools are identical to the Mahāyāna in this regard; however...

Within the Mahāyāna, there are two theories regarding the basis [of remorse]: one states that while the coarse aspect is the same as in the Hīnayāna, the actual remorse is associated with eight [mental factors].

Remorse is associated with greed when it concerns giving; it is associated with hatred when it concerns what is contrary to one's feelings; it is associated with pride and doubt at times of arrogance or hesitation; it is associated with the view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi) when one regrets something one has done;

and it is associated with the views of annihilationism or eternalism when one regrets the loss of objects through giving. Furthermore, as will be explained below, it is associated with the view of self when one regrets having practiced meditative concentration.

It coexists with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), but it does not coexist with the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*). This is because one clings to it as the supreme path and thus does not give rise to regret (*kaukṛtya*). Second, [the opponent] says:

"They certainly cannot coexist, for they arise alternately with regret and are not associated (*saṃprayukta*"). One should not raise the objection that regret is like anger (*krodha*) and the other [afflictions].
Because it arises independently, it should be associated with [mental factors] such as anger (*krodha*) and pride (*māna*), just as anger is associated with hatred (*dveṣa*).

[In this first interpretation,] the distinct entity of *kaukṛtya* (remorse) is not associated with subtlety (*sūkṣma*), because it does not coexist with subtlety. (The first interpretation contradicts the treatise, for within the treatise there is no further section on the gate of subtlety.)

For example, there is wrong view that regrets one’s cultivation of concentration. Wrong view first takes as its object the future non-existence of results, whereas regret takes as its object past actions regarding the cultivation of concentration; since their objects differ, they are not associated.
"Because remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and [the two types of] restlessness (*auddhatya*) all arise from that. The commentary states:
This is the eighth section on the concomitance with secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
These four are all pervasive because they share the same names and meanings.

The commentary states: Regarding the ninth section on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the phrase "also including remorse for neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma" distinguishes this from the Sarvāstivāda, which maintains that [remorse] is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome.
The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (First Chapter) omits the neutral category; this is because it is a presentation according to the perspective of the "conforming transformation" (*anuvartana*).

As for "remorse that is not defiled," since what is defiled is necessarily unwholesome and not neutral—because its nature is coarse and intense—the initial [mental factors of] investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) are excluded.

As stated in the first [chapter] of the *Mahā-śāstra*, within the seven types of discrimination (*vikalpa*), non-afflicted discrimination (*akliṣṭa-vikalpa*) takes only wholesome natures and the three types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) states;

it does not mention the maturation (*vipāka*). This is because the mind born of maturation produced by karma is weak and subtle in its understanding. However, this does not exclude the mind born of maturation that arises from the grasping of dharmas (*dharma-grāha*).
"Because [remorse] and sleep [arise] from objects already experienced. The commentary states:
Regarding the tenth section, the "Gates of Realm and Level," concerning the fact that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and sleep (*middha*) necessarily do not manifest in the higher levels, *Kai* says:

"The statement that there is 'remorse for having practiced meditative concentration while holding wrong views' refers to the stage of the fundamental level (*maula-bhūmi*). This is because at the intermediate level, one does not give rise to remorse for slandering cessation (*nirodha*)."

Furthermore, there is an interpretation that [vitarka and vicāra] give rise to remorse (*kaukṛtya*). According to the majority view, it is said that they do not manifest [in the higher stages]. Cè (Ce) maintains the first interpretation because there is no textual authority for the other.

Regarding the statement that "vitarka and vicāra also arise from below and above," Jì (Ji) says: when one enters the first dhyāna and so forth from the desire realm, this is called "arising from below to above.
From the second dhyāna upwards, up to the fourth dhyāna, one gives rise to the vitarka and vicāra of the first dhyāna as well as the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) of the desire realm.

This also includes the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The arising of minds such as those that moisten rebirth in the desire and form realms from [the formless realm] is called "arising above and descending below.

As for the mutual conditioning between the lower and upper realms, because their objects (*ālambana*) are broad, the wholesome, defiled, and neutral states of the desire and form realms all take as their objects those belonging to the three realms as well as those unconditioned by them.
"Regret is not of the Aśaikṣa (because it extends) to all that is Aśaikṣa.
The commentary states: Regarding the eleventh section on the gates of training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth, concerning "those who abandon through detachment from desire," Jizang says:

Just as sorrow (*daurmanasya*) must necessarily be abandoned at the time of detachment from desire, those in the third fruit and above do not necessarily pursue regret regarding indeterminate matters (*avyākṛta*), because they have already examined them thoroughly.

Because it is definitive. To feel regret for evil is *nirveda* (weariness). Ce says: The Vinaya states that there is an unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) transgression; sometimes one gives rise to regret and weariness, which is metaphorically termed "regret.
Regarding this neutral regret, it is actually wisdom (*prajñā*) and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Śāriputra hears what he has never heard before.

It severs all doubts and regrets. The *Shuyao* states: "The Dharma is what is doubted and regretted. (Question: If one abandons desire through wholesome regret, why would it not be the same for the Dharma? Answer: The nature of karma follows the secondary afflictions;
one abandons the grasping at dharmas because that grasping is neither an affliction nor karma.)
"Regret and torpor pertain only to [the path of] cultivation; this should be considered according to reason. The commentary states:

This is the twelfth section, the "Gate of Abandonment and Non-abandonment," which distinguishes [this view] from that of the Sarvāstivādins. Since for them regret is abandoned only by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the word "also" (*api*) is used.

Regret, like torpor, pertains to both the paths of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation; thus, the *Pañcavastuka* (Treatise on the Five Categories), verse 57, states: "The faculties of grief and suffering pertain to both [paths]; they are not... [The sentence is incomplete in the source].

Because it is that which is to be abandoned. To distinguish it, one says it is not the path; it arises simultaneously with its proximate cause and is not as deep as the preceding or succeeding moments of sorrow.
The *Ṣaṭṣaṣṭi-sāhasrikā* states: "The various contaminated phenomena within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called 'not to be abandoned' because their bonds have already been severed."
If one follows this approach, sleep (*middha*) is categorized as belonging to all three types [of consciousness].

Although vitarka and vicāra are not the truly untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), according to the first master, although they are neither the fundamental nor the subsequently attained paths, they are like sorrow (*daurmanasya*), which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

According to the second master, although they are not the fundamental path, subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and so forth are not included among those things to be abandoned. The proof for the second master’s position is found in the second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
[This is] because it is taught that right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is untainted (*anāsrava*). How, then, do we know that the essence of thought is precisely vitarka?
The second fascicle of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* both state: "That right thought causes the mind to seek."

The *vitarka* (applied thought) takes the investigation of textual evidence as its essence. Cè (測) states: "Since *vitarka* is untainted (*anāsrava*), by analogy, *vicāra* (sustained thought) is likewise so.
It is not that the essence of right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is also *vicāra*. As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 96, says:

'For what reason, when both *vitarka* and *vicāra* are present in the untainted path, is only *vitarka* established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*)? Because the aspect of the factors of enlightenment is sharp and intense, whereas the function of *vicāra* [is otherwise]...'"
They are weak and inferior; therefore, they are not established [as such]. Now, regarding the Mahāyāna, it is said that *vicāra* (sustained thought) is also a factor of the Path (*mārgāṅga*).

This is because even for one who is able to exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*) by relying on the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there is likewise the factor of *samyak-saṃkalpa* (right intention). As for the statement regarding the cause, see the first fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Higher Dharma), Chapter Ten, states that right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is the cause of speech.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle fifty-six, says: "Applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the formations of speech" (Cai [Kuiji] notes: *Daśabhūmika-vyākhyā*, fascicle one, states that Vajragarbha’s *vitarka* and *vicāra* are the verbal formations; it is clearly known that *vitarka* and *vicāra* are untainted wisdom [*anāsrava-jñāna*] on the Path. Ji [Xuanzang’s disciple] says:

having consulted the Sanskrit original, it only says "thought" [*saṃkalpa*] and does not mention *vitarka* and *vicāra*; the translator added this, for "awakening" [*bodha*] refers to *vitarka* and *vicāra*). Regarding the phrase "the stage when speech is not yet perfected," Ji’s first commentary states: "The eighth ground."

As stated above, although there is no further effort (*anābhoga*), because the fruit is not yet complete, there is spontaneous activity (just as there is spontaneous progress within one's own benefit, there is likewise spontaneous seeking for the benefit of others).
One interpretation states that there are two kinds of effort: first, self-benefit; second, benefiting others. From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards...
In the beginning there is none, and in the end there is none; for the Buddha, both are absent. However, the essence of correct reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is precisely volition (*cetanā*).

As for the previous statement that vitarka and vicāra are universal mental factors associated with speech, this was said from the perspective of their functional concomitance (*anuvartana-dvāra*). This is not the case in the Mahāyāna (because the *bodhisattva*'s vitarka and vicāra constitute the essence of the Buddha-nature;

even the fruit of Buddhahood still depends on the seeds of wisdom born of reflection. It is merely that the functional capacity is relinquished, like the use of a cause). Although there are many other explanations, none are superior or essential. That one must rely on vitarka and vicāra to preach the Dharma to others is as follows:

Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Chapter 24) states: "When a bodhisattva abides in this Vajra-samādhi, whatever they proclaim with a single voice is understood by all sentient beings according to their respective categories.
[Objection: Since the preaching of the Dharma necessarily presupposes vitarka and vicāra, it cannot necessarily occur simultaneously [with the realization of samādhi].
Therefore, there is no contradiction in preaching the Dharma while relying on the fourth dhyāna. Question: [As stated in] the *Benye jing*...
Question: In the realms of form and formlessness, beings each cultivate supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and proclaim the *bodhisattva-kaṇṭhābharaṇa-dharmaparyāya*.
How can they preach the Dharma without vitarka and vicāra? Answer: Because they preach spontaneously through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha;

this is not like the extensive activity of discernment performed by one’s own power. However, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states that there are no four types of speech within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). That statement refers to sound (*śabda*).

[This pertains to] the locus. Because it is not a locus of the non-Dharma. Question: What is the difference between *vitarka* (applied thought) and the mind that seeks? Answer: Seeking refers to searching back over objects already experienced;

*vitarka* and *vicāra* (sustained thought) refer to progressing toward and seeking objects not yet understood. Therefore, regarding *vitarka* and *vicāra*, one determines the preceding meaning through *vitarka*.
Thus, the two minds of "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*) and "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) are established based on this meaning.
Thus, [the text covers] the six stages up to the subtle principles of the ultimate and conventional truths.
The commentary states: This is the third major section, the analysis through questions and answers. First, the five teachings are challenged: 1. the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*; 2. the *Dharmapada-sūtra*; 3.
the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*; 4. the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; and 5. the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*. If one grants that the mind...

Regarding the statement that "it manifests as the aspect and the seer," one should likewise admit that it arises as something resembling greed and so forth. The subsequent refutation involves three proofs: first, the *Abhidharmakośa*; second, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*;

and third, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (which contains an interpretation of four teachings—namely, those associated with the mind and those distinct from others—but this does not accord with the literal text).

The intended meaning of the verse in that treatise is as explained in the fifty-sixth [chapter]. Regarding the "wondrous principle of the ultimate and conventional truths," Cè states: "The fourfold Four Noble Truths."

All [of these] rely on the second [consciousness]. According to the principle that conventional and ultimate truth are the natural law (*dharmatā*) of cause and effect, they are neither identical nor separate.
Because the second [consciousness] is ultimate, it has already been explained [that the six consciousnesses] [continue] up to the state of fainting.
The commentary states: Regarding the third transformation, the third section on the "Gate of the Arising State" contains two parts:
the statement and the explanation. This is the first.
The treatise says (up to): "As explained at length in the sūtra."

The commentary states: There are two parts to this explanation, because it provides both a detailed analysis and a summary. The first part also has two sections; this is the explanation of the initial verse.

That is to say, the first phrase of the verse generally indicates the six bases (*āśraya*). These six take the manifest *mūlavijñāna* (root consciousness) as their common basis and their seeds as their immediate basis.
Regarding the "conditions" (*pratyaya*), such as attention (*manasikāra*) and the objects of the sense faculties: for instance, when visual consciousness arises, there are nine simultaneous factors.

Conditions: the attention-seed and the four co-existent faculties. Because they clarify the object of emptiness, these are combined with the ten [faculties] of other time-periods, plus the immediate mental faculty (*anantara-manas*).
As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "When there is light and there is emptiness, only then is visual consciousness produced.

If this is so, why is darkness considered an object of the eye? It is because that which is subtle and faint is what the eye perceives. The celestial eye has eight conditions, like those of the nose, tongue, and body.

Because it excludes both clarity and emptiness; the ear excludes only clarity because it does not grasp through reaching [the object]. Regarding the statement "explained at length as in the sūtra," this refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
From the five evolving consciousnesses up to this point, they manifest according to conditions.

The commentary states: Within the explanation of the subsequent verses, there are two parts. First, the explanation that [the manas] arises constantly in contrast to other consciousnesses; second, the enumeration of the five states to clarify the occasions when it does not arise. This is the first part.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has six conditions, while the seventh and eighth consciousnesses each have five. They arise only when these conditions are complete, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Since the conditions required by the latter are few, it is easy to discern that they are constantly present. However, this is merely to exclude the coarse [states]; in subtle states, they are not absent.
It can be abandoned. What are the five stages? [This refers to] up until the point of the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*).

The commentary states: "The subsequent explanation clarifies the first of the five stages where [the afflictions] do not arise. Regarding "contrary to that which does not function constantly," *Ce* (Cen) says: "Due to the former..."

Regarding the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): because it opposes the ten mental factors—the six universal and five object-specific factors—within the substance of the six consciousnesses throughout a hundred eons, it is metaphorically designated as "non-associated" (*viprayukta*) to supplement the state of the mind.
As for the claim that the essence of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñika*) is primarily the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-nirodha*), Ji states:
"Non-Buddhists regard perception as the cause of birth and death; therefore, they specifically loathe it. Among the three interpretations, Ji says that this refers to the first master’s view.

[The first teacher] says: It is not necessarily the case for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) that [the intermediate state] arises through the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of the fetters (*saṃyojana*); rather, it is said to be fifty-nine [types of beings] based on what is most common.

This is because, as in the case of noble ones (*ārya*), there are also those who possess both latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and active outbursts; furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that for them, there are only the material factors (*rūpa-aṅga*) and so forth. The third teacher says:

That intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) must necessarily give rise to the afflictions that moisten rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*). [This is said] fearing that the previous two teachers might be aligned with the Sthavira.

Within this section, there is the position that there is no mind [at the moment of death]. This is because it is taught that at the time of passing away, the mind is always defiled, just as in other cases of "original existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*).

Cè states: "This is an inference (*anumāna*). The term 'initial' here refers to the beginning of a single lifetime (*ekajīvitakāla*), not the very first moment [of consciousness], for it is possible for the state of fainting at birth to be without mind.
Jì states: "The initial moments of non-arising and so forth do not necessarily possess mind; therefore, [the state of] having [mind] exists [only in certain cases]."

Regarding "the transformational consciousnesses born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and so forth," these must necessarily be states induced by the manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), such as the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) induced by manifest wholesome states.

If there were no separate mention of the term "born of birth" (*upapattilābhika*) regarding the present life, then other [states] would not be "born of birth," and thus they likewise would not function.
This is recorded in the first fascicle. Regarding the establishment of the "mindless states" (*acittaka-avasthā*) based upon the eighth consciousness, Ji (基) says: "This is merely..."
It is established upon the seeds of the cessation of the sixth consciousness; this is the interpretation shared by [Yuan] Ce.

One explanation states that it is established upon the seeds of the cessation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its associated mental factors (such as the intermediate state, the existence at birth, and the minds of death and rebirth, as explained in detail in the fifth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*).

Regarding how many consciousnesses manifest when one is first born in that heaven, [Dao] Ji says that four arise as the primary case, because it is like the time of the Sarvāstivāda school (namely, the mental consciousness of one’s own level and the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna, which together constitute the four).

This is because there is no logical contradiction. As for the statement that "the lower [realms] have coarse and agitated perception," this is because they possess variable feelings (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*).

Regarding the statement that "there is no place of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) as a maturation (*vipāka*) in the higher [realms]," this is because the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) are inhabited solely by noble ones (*ārya*). Furthermore, in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), there is no body; thus, one fears [the state would be] total annihilation.

As for the statement that "volition (*cetanā*) capable of inducing the attainment of non-perception" is as explained in the first fascicle: although there are many interpretations, it is associated with the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*), and a single volition penetrates [all stages].

Regarding the distinction between general and specific maturation (*vipāka*), the former is superior in principle. As for where one is reborn after death when the maturation of karma belonging to a particular stage (*bhūmi*) is exhausted:

Master Ji states that there is no textual authority for this in the Mahāyāna. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says that such a person must be reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the force of their karma for the form realm has been exhausted and they no longer cultivate the higher realms;
thus, it can be said that they are only subject to rebirth in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*). However, the present [explanation] applies to subsequent rebirths as well.
They are reborn throughout the desire realm and the lower three dhyānas, but not in the higher realms, because they have never cultivated [the necessary meditations] there. Fan says:

"Furthermore, since those beings die in that heaven and are reborn again in that same heaven, it must be admitted that there is karma that produces retribution over many lifetimes" (in general, they are reborn throughout all four dhyānas).
"And the two meditative attainments of the mindless" (up to) "not produced by the noble ones. The commentary states:

The second [section] consists of three positions, which may be understood through their general and specific aspects; this is the first of those specifics. "Causing the body to be peaceful and harmonious" means:

This is to gauge the existence of the mind. Regarding the statement that one necessarily falls back from the present dharma (*dṛṣṭadharma*), Ji says: "There are those who lead to the state of non-returner (*anāgāmin*); this teaching applies generally to subsequent rebirths.

There are those who practice returning [to this world], because they are born in that heaven. However, this receiving of the fruit applies to all postures—standing, sitting, and lying down—with the sole exception of walking, because one practices it while in those states.
As for the four types of karma applying to all three [times], the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), fascicle 12, and the Sarvāstivāda school maintain this.
The [orthodox] school maintains that it is exclusively karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*).

A certain class of masters holds that it is indeterminate (*aniyata*) as to being experienced in the next life, because it is possible for one who has entered the noble state (*ārya*) not to experience it at all (Mei [Kuiji] says this refers to the Sautrāntika; Ji [Woncheuk] says that in the Mahāyāna, entering the noble state generally involves the severing of karma, as determinate karma is distinct).

In the Mahāyāna, it pertains to all three types of timing. Jiji says: "Since it arises later in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one receives this retribution later; therefore, it pertains to subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*). However, since there are those who attain various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) but are not reborn in the upper realms, it must also pertain to [all three]."

It is indeterminate. Within two meanings, the first master says: even if one is not reborn in the higher realms, it still constitutes a subsequent retribution (*paścāvedanīya*), because one may return to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and again cultivate the auxiliary conditions.

However, if one has fallen away and been reborn in the higher realms, one will certainly be unable to give rise to it, because one lacks the power of explanation and because one’s wisdom and understanding are inferior.
As stated in the *Pañcaṣaṣṭi-sūtra*, it does not say that what was first produced here will later receive its retribution in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding "because of arising from meditative absorption," the later master says: "That which first arises here" refers to the initial arising from absorption;

"the subsequent [arising] in the form realm" refers to the subsequent arising from absorption; "the fourth dhyāna" refers to when one is about to experience its fruit; and "exiting while experiencing the fruit" refers to emerging from that state.
As for "excluding the Heaven of Non-conception," this absorption is obtained only through preparatory effort (*prayoga*). Regarding whether the absorption is lost or not lost...

If one is subdued by the defilements of a lower level and is born into the fourth dhyāna, they arise three days later; how much more so for the lower three dhyānas? There is no logical contradiction in this.

Even if one does not completely regress from all the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), although one may regress from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it is called "arising later" because of that.

Master Ji’s commentary states: "If one regresses from this [attainment], one must necessarily give rise to the defilements of a lower level; therefore, there is no principle of 're-arising' within the fourth dhyāna. (The proof states: This is not...)

Because it is argued that rightness does not accord with [the nature of] discourse. It is not merely a state of aversion toward perception, as one also delights in its retribution. Its essence consists solely of outflows (*sāsrava*). It arises in ordinary persons, not in sages.
As for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is so called because it reaches the point where all perceptions and feelings have ceased.

The commentary states: This is the third stage. Regarding the phrase "those who have suppressed the afflictions and abandoned craving for the sphere of nothingness": "suppressed" means temporarily subdued; "abandoned" means permanently severed.

This does not necessarily apply to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), as one may not yet have abandoned it. This [attainment] is common to both *pratyekabuddhas* (solitary realizers). There are two types of *pratyekabuddhas*. As Jñānagarbha says:
those of the "group-dwelling" (*vargacārin*) type may not necessarily attain it, just like the *śrāvakas*; however, it is held that those who are "solitary" (*ekacārin*) must certainly attain it.
Because he is identical to the Buddha. As stated in a verse of the *Abhidharmakośa*: "One becomes a Buddha by attaining [this concentration] after thirty-four moments of thought, not before.

There is a tradition in the West (the Western Masters) which asserts that a Bodhisattva in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) first gives rise to this meditative absorption; however, the Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra maintain [that it is attained only upon Buddhahood].

It is not the case that one first gives rise to the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and then, having severed the eighteen [defilements] of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), has no further opportunity to give rise to other minds;

therefore, it is said that one attains it precisely at the time of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). Because one has attained mastery over the arising and cessation of meditative absorption, the phrase "perception of cessation" (*nirodhasaṃjñā*) is used to distinguish this from the cultivation of the non-percipient state (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), which involves clinging to it as a permanent liberation and seeking the ultimate *nirvāṇa* in the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*). This refers to the mind...

Regarding the "extinction of mental factors" (*cittasamprayukta-nirodha*), Ce says: "Based on the 'subtle-subtle mind' (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*) stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), this is a provisional designation established upon the twenty-two dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*).

These are: the extinction of the universal (*sarvatraga*), the particular-object (*viśeṣa*), the wholesome (*kuśala*), and the consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); they are established by encompassing both the new and the old, as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*). [The author] comments: "This is not so.

One state of non-consciousness (*acittaka-avasthā*) is established based on these twenty-two factors; it does not mean that the twenty-two [factors themselves] constitute the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This is because, like the conscious attainments (*sacittaka-samāpatti*), they would then entail associated mental factors (*samprayukta*). Furthermore, only in the first fascicle does it appear to rely [on this interpretation]."

It is a new type of seed, because it is a seed of an extremely intensified mind of revulsion. However, the intended meaning of the current explanation is that, by the power of this new seed, the innate (*dharmatā*) seeds are enabled to function as a defense for the mind (the same applies to the state of non-perception). Among the three grades of cultivation:

Baso says: It is not that three grades are taught based on the superior, middling, and inferior faculties; for it does not exclude the case where one with middling faculties practices at a superior level, nor where one with superior faculties practices at a middling level, and so forth.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that because there are three grades of faculties, there are likewise three grades of cultivation.

If the faculties have been refined, the cultivation becomes a superior grade. (The first interpretation is incorrect, as it would imply that one whose faculty-nature has shifted could undergo retrogression. We shall therefore adopt the latter interpretation: those of the "retrogressive" (*parihāṇadharman*) faculty are of inferior-grade cultivation, because they are bound to retrogress. Those of the "reflective" (*cetana-dharman*) faculty...)

They cultivate the middle grade within the Dharma; because even through reflection and so forth, they do not regress. They abide securely in the "capable-to-attain" (*sātatyābhyāsaka*) immovability as supreme, for they will certainly not regress. As for what is called "wandering and observing," it is because they do not sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

As with the sixty-two [views], the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is untainted (*anāsrava*). This excludes the Sarvāstivādins, because it is a flow [of conditioned phenomena]. Regarding the fact that it can also manifest after the minds of other stages:
this is because there is the arising from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*). As the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XVIII) states: "If one has previously practiced it habitually..."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (350) states that one can enter the mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (12) contains a passage that appears to contradict this, as recorded in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which provides a reconciliation. If one enters [the form realm] from another stage (*bhūmi*), to which stage does it belong?

The two commentaries on the Tripiṭaka state that because [the seeds] are established based on the mind of meditative absorption (*samāpatti-citta*), they belong to whichever stage (*bhūmi*) that [absorption] follows.

One commentary says: "Because the seeds of the extremely subtle mind of the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) are struck and activated by a mind from another stage, they possess the function of obstruction.

Master Ji says the latter is superior, as it accords with various teachings. Regarding the statement that [these seeds] clearly belong to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), this is intended to distinguish them from the Sarvāstivāda position.
However, regarding the two categories of those training and those beyond training within the Truth of the Path: Udāyin means "Appearance," as he was born at the time of sunrise.
This śrāmaṇera was a disciple of Ānanda, as is explained in detail in the *Vibhāṣā* (Treatise on the Great Exposition), fascicle 153, citing a sutra.
Śāriputra said: "The gods born of mind-entry frequently enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Regarding the śrāmaṇera’s speech, there is no [contradiction].

"There is such a possibility. The Buddha asked the śrāmaṇera, "Do you mean that the mind-made beings (manomaya) are born in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)? He replied, "It is so.

The Buddha said to this foolish person, "According to the Sarvāstivādins, one who is a non-returner (anāgāmin) may fall back or be born in the heavens of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), and subsequently enter the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Because the śrāmaṇera was mistaken in his position, the Buddha rebuked him. Now, in the Mahāyāna, birth in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and other realms is indeed [real].
Because they arise from and enter into the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the śrāmaṇera is questioned as in [the section on] the fifty-six [dharmas].

Since the teaching of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) has not yet been established, it is not stated that one enters the attainment of cessation within the formless realm (Cai states: this refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and other sūtras, as well as the various Hīnayāna texts, where it is said "not yet established").

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot suppress or extinguish the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); in reality, they do not suppress the views of the three realms.

Regarding delusion, let us speak for now based on the final position as commonly accepted by all schools. The Sarvāstivādins maintain that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot suppress the delusions of the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), yet they are able to permanently sever the afflictions of both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) within the lower eight stages.

As for the phrase "attained subsequently according to circumstances," this refers to the emptiness of persons for the followers of the Two Vehicles and the emptiness of both persons and phenomena for Bodhisattvas. Regarding the severance of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), Cè states that the first interpretation is difficult to establish.
Regarding the latter point, An-hui, Hu-fa, and others state that the term "only" refers specifically to the non-returners (anāgāmin) and so forth.

This is because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 53) states that those who enter as learners (śaikṣa) are non-returners; the third fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* is likewise. Ji and Ce say:
The latter interpretation is superior, as it accords with the fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the Abhidharma. That is to say, regarding the second proposition:

when a noble one attains the fourth dhyāna, becomes weary of rebirth in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), and does not sever the fourth [level], they abandon the path of abandoning the fetters (*saṃyojana*) by relying on the path of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*) and enter the formless absorption;

at that time, [the fetters] are abandoned, yet because they rely on the path of suppression (*vibhavamārga*) to enter the higher meditative concentration, [they remain suppressed]. However, according to the Udāyin-sūtra...
It says: "Transcending those who subsist on physical food, they are born among those who are mind-made. This indicates that [beings] of the six desire heavens certainly do not arise [therein];

it does not mean that all subsequent births transcend their respective levels. (The first master explains: "This follows the intention of Buddhasiṃha; he speaks of the proximate levels and does not include the three lower dhyānas. Regarding those who, having previously severed [defilements], later fall back and are born in a higher stage:
at the time of death, they do not sever them by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*) path, nor do they fall back from what has been suppressed. It should be...

Because they are born from the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*). The answer has two parts: first, an answer by means of a hypothetical illustration; second, an answer based on the actual correct principle (*yathābhūta-yukti*).
These may be understood from the text itself. That is to say, for a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), birth in the higher realms occurs only after the seeds have been moistened and then severed.

There are those that are inferior yet capable of moistening the seeds; because they obstruct birth in the higher realms. (Master Ji says: The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, fascicle 59, states: "The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) moisten birth; this refers to those who have seen the truths, specifically those in the third fruit.")

Ce says that the Non-returner (anāgāmin) possesses only the moisture of seeds; this is stated with reference to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). As for the claim that the mind at the moment of death (*cyuti-citta*) is always defiled, this refers to the moisture of rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*). Both [interpretations] fail to exhaust the principle, as is recorded in the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding the two explanations in the *Shuyao*:
one says that when a Non-returner is born in their own realm, it is because they moisten [the seeds] through active manifestation (*samudācāra*), as they have not yet abandoned desire.

The other says that even if they are born in their own realm, they possess only the moisture of seeds, because there is a complete path [to liberation]. In this regard, the acceptance and rejection [of these views] is as recorded in the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra*; the *Shuyao* also contains [this discussion].

Question and Answer. Fan states that there are eight questions and answers; since the preceding [section] has already exhausted the principles, there is no need to adopt them. Ji says: "There are seeds of the first two fruits that have been suppressed by the state of birth but still provide moisture for rebirth; these have not yet been suppressed and are thus the same as those of ordinary beings. Now, we likewise do not rely on this, as it contradicts both scripture and principle.
As for the *Śāstra* stating that one enters the stage of the distant bodhisattva, the sixty-second [chapter] says: "Except for those in the distant stage, others are unable to practice it.

Regarding the sūtra’s statement that one arises from the meditative absorption of cessation in the sixth stage, the seventh chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* records the Buddha telling Mahāmati: "Bodhi..."

Because the Bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) from the first stage through the sixth stage. Jī states: "In the former [stages], compassion is predominant; in the latter, wisdom is predominant;

or [alternatively], wisdom and compassion are equal, yet their modes of engagement differ. That is to say, by desiring [the object], one suppresses [afflictions]; by not desiring it, one does not suppress them."
How can it be known that [the cessation attainment] also arises from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward? The *Mahā-śāstra* states:

"Because non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). If this is so, why does the *Mahā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* not permit Bodhisattvas to enter the meditative absorption of cessation?

There are three traditional explanations by the Tripiṭaka masters: First, some say that they do not actually enter the absorption; rather, they are said to "enter" it figuratively based on their capacity and power. Second, some say that [they do indeed enter it]. ... [The text continues: "The absorption..."

Those of a fixed nature enter meditative absorption; this merely excludes those of unfixed nature, as they delight in quiescence (*śamatha*). One interpretation states: "Transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are not suitable to enter [absorption], because the bodies of true practice (*bhūta-pratipatti*) cultivate it fully.
Regarding "sleeping without a mind" up to "being without sleep or drowsiness": [it refers to] the absence of such states.

The commentary states: This is the fourth fivefold category. Regarding the statement in the *Mahā-śāstra* that "the function of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) during sleep and fainting" takes as its essence the association with the mental consciousness in general, this is because that [consciousness] is subtle.
Now, concerning these states of non-consciousness (*acittaka*), the treatise provides two explanations. The first states:
"Sleep and fainting refer to the bodily states when the six consciousnesses are obstructed; there is no separate enumerated dharma [called] 'non-consciousness'."

Regarding sleep (*middha*): although it lacks both mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta-saṃprayukta-dharma*), because it is induced by mental factors, or because one lacks mastery [over them], it is conventionally designated as "sleep" at such times.
It stupefies countless phenomena; this is not said merely because of resemblance. As for "extreme fatigue, wind, heat, etc.," the word "etc.

includes the many conditions for sleep mentioned in the *Mahā-śāstra*. Later, it further states: "Both are subsumed under the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). In the *Abhidharma*, these are termed "fatigue" and "stupefaction."
