It is because one is born there only after having explained the tenth stage (*daśamī bhūmi*). However, this is not [ordinary] birth, for transformation necessarily lacks the process of dying and being reborn again.

Regarding the fact that the "retrogressive movement" (*pratyudāvarta*) and the "retention of the body" (*kāyasthiti*) must belong to the desire realm, see the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 80, on the section concerning transformation.

They remain in this body, specifically in this continent (*jambudvīpa*). This refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Those in the higher realms do not turn their minds back [toward lower states], because they lack the conditions for such a turning of the mind;

thus, while they may resolve to arise in the lower realms, they are not reborn there. Later, when they go to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is solely through the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*). The Master [Hui]he says:

"Although the body belongs to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), it is subsumed under the Form Realm, as in the case of the Palace of Maheśvara. Master Fan says: [The same].

This palace is subsumed within Akaniṣṭha, a place of pure excellence. The *Zhèng* (證) states: "Although it belongs to the fourth dhyāna, its location is distinct [from the ordinary fourth dhyāna realms]," because, as the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (*Dàlùn*) says, it transcends the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (*Shí dì yún*) states: "The benefit of the present retribution is that one attains the rank of Buddha;
the benefit of the subsequent retribution is that one is born in the abode of wisdom of Maheśvara. From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, this is fixed.

Regarding the transformation of rebirth (*pariṇāmika-janman*): if there were no death and birth, the two types of retribution would be difficult to distinguish. Therefore, even on the eighth stage and above, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not severed, as they remain useful for taking birth.
For a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment, births in the various happy realms have not yet attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because afflictions (*kleśa*) still exist.

Thus, although they undergo transformation of rebirth, there is still death and birth. (This contradicts the [Abhidharma] Śāstra below, which states that they lack "segmented" (*prādeśika*) birth, where one life ends and the next begins; therefore, that [interpretation] cannot be relied upon). First.

The intention of the two masters [Śīlabhadra and Pūrṇavardhana] is that they allow for the existence of Śrāvakas who turn their minds toward enlightenment (*cittavipariṇāma*) in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), because there is no scriptural prohibition against it. Logically, even Buddhas go there;
since Bodhisattvas are born there and possess eyes and ears, they should be capable of receiving transformation [by a Buddha]. Ji (Kuiji) says:

"With the exception of those in the first two fruits and the Pratyekabuddhas, [others do not exist] in the higher realms, as they are absent there. (Ji says: This master’s intention is to allow that those in the first two fruits are born in the Form Realm and turn their minds; this is incorrect, as it contradicts both scripture and logic. However, the second...

Eighty. For now, this is discussed with reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it does not exclude the other realms. However, since it speaks only of this continent (*dvīpa*), one might ask: are there not other continents? [Paramārtha] says there are two interpretations;

one may take whichever one pleases. [Xuanzang] says: [This refers to the later] Dharmapāla school. As for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there can certainly be no turning of the mind [toward awakening], because there is no actual physical body (*mūlakāya*) that could be retained.
Nevertheless, according to the *Antarābhava-sūtra*, the Buddha remained in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for twenty years and also manifested births in the formless realm.

Regarding this, Ji says: "The Sūtras of the Mahāsāṃghika school do not have the meaning of the Mahāyāna. (Although they recite those [Mahāyāna] texts, how could they contradict the words? It is simply because it causes their minds to produce a distinct interpretation.

Although they lack eyes and ears, it is said that they are being transformed. In Ji’s Commentary, he asks: "Since there are the first two fruits [of the path], one undergoes births before undergoing transformation (*parivṛtti*). If a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) generates the aspiration for enlightenment while still in the lower realms, there should be cases where they are born into the higher realms.
There are two interpretations. The first says: 'It is the same as before; there is certainly no birth in the higher realms,' because they are weary [of existence]."
Because of the coarse body, one immediately undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*). One interpretation states:

"Since there is no scriptural prohibition, it is permitted that one may be born in a higher stage, or undergo one birth, or undergo many births, as the various stages correspondingly undergo transformation. (Tánghuì [Cè] preserves the first interpretation; Jì does not permit it.

However, regarding the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) and so forth, even within this world-system of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are those who do not turn back. This statement from the Sūtra refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Furthermore, as stated in the one hundred and twenty-ninth fascicle of the first assembly of the sutra:
"Moreover, Kauśika, if men or women were to transcribe this sutra, adorn it, place it in a pure location, and honor and praise it at that time, then within this great trichiliocosm..."

The gods of the Four Great Kings, up to those of the Vast Fruit Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*), who have already resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, constantly come to this place to observe, pay homage, read, and recite [the scriptures], and so forth, as extensively described, before departing with palms joined.

The gods of the Five Pure Abodes (*Śuddhāvāsa*) also constantly come here to observe and pay homage, and so forth, until they depart with palms joined. It is the same in the ten directions. The commentary explains: "In other places..."
It is said that all [beings] therein resolve their minds toward Bodhi; however, it is not stated that they resolve their minds while in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
This is because one knows the five Pure Abodes to be places where no such resolution occurs. Speaking according to principle, Cè says: "There are only sages and no ordinary beings.

Because it is a place of ultimate bliss, the mind gives rise to attachment and thus does not resolve toward Bodhi. Just as those born in the Pure Abodes will certainly not be reborn in higher realms, nor do they turn their minds back to take [rebirth elsewhere]."

Because they are close to extinction [the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*]—according to the opinion of the later masters—states that from the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*) downward, all are said to "arouse the mind" (*cittotpāda*). This clearly shows that there are those among them who turn back toward the Śrāvaka path. The former masters reconcile this by stating that it refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) therein who arouse the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).

It does not mention noble beings (*ārya*); therefore, it does not constitute proof. Question: If that is so, why does the *Candramati-putra-sūtra* state that the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, upon seeing the prince leap into the jaws of a starving tigress, gave rise to the bodhicitta? There are two explanations for this:

first, it is said that the assembly in the Palace of Sovereignty (*vaśitā-vimāna*) of the tenth stage manifested the arising of the mind in order to benefit the lower heavens; second, it is said that...

In reality, few among those in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens have generated the resolve [for awakening]. However, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* speak according to the majority; thus, they refer to the Śuddhāvāsas (the "Pure Abodes" being the opposite of "impure").
Furthermore, it is said that among the śrāvakas present in the assembly of the *Prajñā*, there were some who had not yet generated the mind of great bodhi.

Therefore, regarding the five Pure Abodes, it is not mentioned that they have generated such a resolve. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (77) states: "If one enters the correct path of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas..."

Regarding those whose nature is separated from birth: they are unable to again resolve upon the mind of great bodhi, because they have already established a barrier within the stream of birth and death. The record states "no," for it says further below:

"If there were anyone among them who could resolve their mind and aspire toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I would likewise rejoice; and so too would the immeasurable bhikṣus in that assembly."

Regarding the bodhicitta, the Buddha bestowed a prophecy upon such individuals. How could these people be anything other than ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)? Therefore, what that [other] person says is logically far too narrow.

However, the intent of that sūtra is to protect indeterminate ordinary beings by not permitting them to generate the resolve [for awakening], while allowing those who are already noble (*ārya*) to turn their minds [toward it].

Furthermore, as for the statement "according to their inclination" (*yathābhirati*), this does not constitute proof. [The term] "inclination" refers to wisdom; the commentary states that it is used as a hypothetical expression. Even though the Buddha bestowed a prophecy, he did not explicitly state they were noble ones. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "If one attains..."

There is no possibility of attaining Buddhahood through the fruits of the path (*mārgaphala*). Nāgārjuna also refutes this. It is clearly known that it has not been taught that noble beings (*ārya*) can turn back [from their attainment]; for it is only at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly that they first hear [the teaching]. The meaning of "reality" (*tattva*) is as explained in the *Mātṛkā*.

Even those of sudden enlightenment attain the body of Akaniṣṭha before receiving the life-force of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), because it is superior. Someone raises an objection: "If the *Prajñāpāramitā* does not teach that noble ones turn their minds [back], why does the *Suvikrāntavikrāmin* say:
'If there are classes of sentient beings who, though not yet entered into the state of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), nevertheless...'"?

Regarding those whose disposition for the three vehicles is indeterminate: having heard this Dharma, they all resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
To explain: this is not intended to reveal that those who have already entered [the path] can generate [this resolve];

rather, because it was previously stated that those who have already entered gain benefits by swiftly realizing the stage of untainted (*anāsrava*) nirvāṇa, it is further taught here that even those who have not yet entered likewise possess great merit—namely, the generation of the great mind (*mahācitta*). Thus it is said.
There is no contradiction.
This is because the seventh *pravṛtti-vijñāna* does not arise there [in the formless realm].

The commentary states: "The second point clarifies that the seventh consciousness does not exist in the formless realm. Master Ji says: "This refers only to the defiled consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*)."

Regarding the conditions: if the subsequently induced *samatājñāna* (wisdom of equality) follows the guidance of the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness), it also extends into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as in the case of entering the fruit of the meditative absorption on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatā*) or the cessation absorption (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Since the sixth [consciousness] does not exist in the non-percipient realm (*asaṃjñisattva*), the seventh [consciousness] cannot descend there; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
"Because of the difference between clarity and dullness of the sixth evolving consciousness...

[The commentary] states: This clarifies the five [sensory] consciousnesses. Jì (寂) says: "The first interpretation is the view of Master Nanda, because [the consciousnesses] arise based on their own uncontaminated seeds and faculties.
Some say this refers to Sthiramati; however, this is incorrect, for only the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) are admitted to be uncontaminated.

Later, Zhongce raised this objection: "If it is argued that the contaminated (*sāsrava*) seventh and eighth consciousnesses can serve as the bases (*indriya*) for the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), why do you not likewise allow this for the five physical sense organs? Therefore, the treatise explains:

[The bases] must be contaminated (to exclude the five organs of a Buddha), uncommon (to exclude the eighth consciousness), necessarily co-arising (to exclude the 'opening and guiding' roots), and share the same object (to exclude the seventh consciousness). It is logically inconsistent [to claim they can] give rise to an uncontaminated consciousness."

Therefore, another objection is raised: "If the untainted (*anāsrava*) [consciousness] also takes the five objects as its domain because they share the same objective field (*ālambana*), what fault would there be in its arising?
The treatise explains: "Because of the difference between clarity and dullness; it is logically untenable for a clear consciousness to depend upon something dull. Master Ji (Jizang) comments:

"The tainted (*sāsrava*) five sense organs do not give rise to untainted consciousness, because they are tainted material organs (*rūpīndriya*). This is like other causes and supports which belong to the eight stages (*bhūmi*)."

Regarding the question of whether the nose and tongue consciousnesses arise in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), Master Ji’s commentary (*Ji shu*) offers two interpretations. The first states that they do not arise because they belong to a different realm (*dhātu*).
This is unlike the case where consciousnesses of a lower stage arise in a higher stage, for those [lower-stage consciousnesses] belong to the same realm as that [higher stage].

However, it is argued that since the sense organs can function interchangeably, the three consciousnesses may apprehend odors and tastes, or the body organ might perceive odors and so forth. The second interpretation maintains that they do arise, just as [consciousnesses of other types] arise in a different [realm].
Regarding the "ground" (bhūmi): according to the ordinary person and the two vehicles, it is taught that from the seventh ground (*bhūmi*) onwards, consciousness does not arise.

The interpretation of the former master is superior (as recorded in the *Yogācārabhūmi-ṭīkā*, which preserves the latter master’s view). The *Shuyao* states: "Since uncontaminated seeds exist within consciousness but do not engage [their objects], the same would apply to the uncontaminated five sense-faculties (*indriya*);

what fault would there be? The explanation says: "The manifest five sense-faculties must necessarily undergo transformation to become real; the seeds do not need to do so. This refers to their suppression (*vibhava*)."
Because it is a phenomenon (dharma). Third, because that which is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) can also arise.

The commentary states: Within the third condition, there are two [aspects]: because it establishes the essential nature (svabhāva) and because it distinguishes the characteristics (lakṣaṇa). This is the first [of these]. As for the word "if" (yadi):
Regarding "existent phenomena" (*dharmas*): these refer to conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena that possess only a substantial essence (*svabhāva*).

This is because even the shadow of what is non-existent must have an essence; it is like observing an object of cognition (*ālambana*), which possesses two meanings. This immediately excludes the Sautrāntika school, for whom direct conditions (*pratyakṣa-pratyaya*) are fundamentally non-existent.

Furthermore, the five types of direct conditions are merely provisional; if they were non-existent as phenomena (*dharma*), they could not function as conditions. As for the term "already-rooted," this refers to the characteristics of the object (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*), whether provisional or...
From the ultimate reality (*tattva*) up to suchness (*tathatā*), taking non-characteristics as their characteristic, each manifests its own mind; this is termed "carrying along" (*sahagata*).

Based on carrying along the characteristics of the object, it means that the mind and mental factors are themselves the results of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Because these characteristics manifest within the mind, they are called "that which is reflected upon" (*cintya*).

Because their substantial existence gives rise to the mind, they are called "that which is pondered" (*cintita*). As for the "proximate," these are the respective image-aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by each [consciousness].

This includes the suchness realized by fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Master Ji states: "That is to say, the self-substance, the object-aspect (*ālambana-bhāga*), the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), and so forth, all belong to this category.

As for the objective substance that is the goal of cognition, it is called the "remote object-condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*); it is not a constituent part of one's own essence, because it is separated by the mental image (*pratibimba*).

Regarding the statement that these are "the objects internally apprehended by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and so forth," Cè states: "The word 'and so forth' includes the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti*) which takes the seeing-part as its object, and the self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvittisvasaṃvitti*).
The self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing part is able to take the self-cognizing part as its object. The intent of the two commentaries is the same; however, this is what the treatise explains.

The object possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is capable of producing the nature of the mind; this is termed the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). That which is "contemplated" (*so-lü*) refers to the meaning of the manifest aspect (*darśana-bhāga*); that which is "relied upon" (*su-tuo*) refers to the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvitti*) relying [upon it] for its arising. Therefore, it is said that the "contemplated" and "relied upon" within the internal [aspects], such as the seeing-aspect, are the three parts (*trikalpa*) sharing a single substance.

This is not what is being clarified here. However, since the substance follows from its functions, they are conventionally designated as "this" and "that" in relation to one another as object-conditions. The phrase "may be the apprehending subject" (*neng-yuan...huo-you*) is an indeterminate expression.
Chapter Eight: The Mind-King (up to) "Because there is no external substance.
Commentary: This second section clarifies the characteristics. There are four points as in the text. Regarding the three masters on the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*):

the intention of the first master is that the Buddha’s other bodies and lands merely appear [to others] and do not rely [on external objects], because they arise solely through his own power. The second is the master who holds that these are transformational faculties (*nirmāṇendriya*). The third...
Regarding the third point, "Protecting the True Lineage of the Dharma," [the text] refutes the first master by stating that one’s own and another’s bodies and lands may be used interchangeably.
It refutes the second master by stating that one’s own seeds have no utility for another. It states that it is not the case that the seeds of all sentient beings are identical;

for the transformation of the contaminated fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) must necessarily have utility. If it were to transform according to another, its seeds would likewise be so; consequently, there would be no distinction between ordinary beings and sages.
Because there would otherwise be no distinct fault [in that regard]. Furthermore, within the causal stage, it does not transform other seeds or the five sense organs (*indriya*). Master Ji says:
"The fivefold number of cause and effect all rely upon what is transformed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as their substantial basis, for they themselves lack power.

Although the *Śāstra* speaks generally, this is not the case for the mental factors (*caitta*), which [the commentary] clarifies must have a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*) for their fivefold number. As for the coarseness of the five consciousnesses, it is because their characteristics are easily known; as for their dullness...

Because their practice and understanding are shallow, those of inferior capacity are led by others. Regarding the necessity of remote conditions (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*), the *Shuyao* states: "For now, we speak of the power of karma;

however, in the case of meditative or supernormal powers, there is not necessarily a substantial object. For example, when one born in a higher realm takes as an object the form of a lower realm, or when the body is in a lower state yet one gives rise to the divine eye or ear to take as an object the forms and so forth of a higher realm. Furthermore, it is explained that the five consciousnesses possess portions [of such objects].

Because they are distinct, they must rely on a fundamental substance (*vastu*). When perceiving objects in a different stage (*bhūmi*), although there is no fundamental substance for one's own foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), there is the substance transformed by another [consciousness], which serves as the fundamental substance.
If that were so, the six consciousnesses would never be without a substance, as they are constantly engaged in discrimination. Therefore, the former interpretation is superior.

Regarding this, the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot) on the second fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: "The divine eye and ear perceive forms and sounds of lower stages; they do not depend on a fundamental [substance]."

As for the objective basis (*ālambana*): as explained in the seventh fascicle, although that [position] was not accepted there, it is now accepted that taking an object from another realm as a basis is without fault.

(If one were to insist on a conceptual distinction, there must always be a primary objective basis; this would contradict the fact that the mental consciousness is sometimes without an objective basis. Therefore, this fascicle adopts the former explanation provisionally. Furthermore, if there were no objective basis of its own, it would have to rely on another’s;

yet what could the divine eyes and ears of others see or hear? Thus, the second explanation accepts another's [basis] as the objective basis). Ji and Ce both state that what is transformed by the mental consciousness also serves as the fivefold objective basis, as in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
The remaining [objections] regarding the record have already been refuted.
Regarding the four predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*)—up to the point where it says "because of the distinction between the four matters"—the commentary states:
Within the fourth condition, there are two [aspects]: by way of essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*vṛtti*), and by way of differentiation. This is the first [of these]. If there is...

"Dharma" refers to dharmas that possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This means they are distinguished from the non-existent, which is merely grasped through conceptual attachment; therefore, they are not mere designations (*prajñapti*). Regarding the two explanations concerning "conditions" (*pratyaya*), one says:

this term is broad enough to encompass both the real and the conventional. For example, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "That which exercises the predominance of maintenance (*dhṛti-adhipati*) is the power of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), by which the commonality of existence (*nikāyasabhāga*) persists.
Another says: this [term] is also not merely conventional, because it is subsumed under conditions, such as causes (*hetu*) and so forth. As for the object...

Regarding the statement that "life-force (*jīvitendriya*) sustains [the body] based on its seeds" (as noted by Master Guan in his initial commentary), the Master of Proof adopts the latter [position]. Here, the former is superior.

Since the *prātimokṣa* vows and the bodily and vocal manifest actions (*vijñapti*) are both causes of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), their cause cannot reside solely in substantial dharmas (*dravya-dharma*).

This is because the bases of body and speech are exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is understood as merely non-obstructive; it is a provisional designation.

There are also phenomena that do not obstruct arising and so forth, such as other real dharmas included within the category of the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)—because there exists a "capable agent" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) outside of the [other] four conditions.
Regarding the phrase "whether conducive or contrary," *Cè* says: "Dharmas that are conducive or contrary serve as the sovereign condition. *Jī* says:

"Because they can act as conditions for both conducive and contrary [dharmas]. (The first interpretation is superior; it means that with respect to the fruit, they can be either conducive or contrary. Contrary causes and effects are as recorded in the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*). The word "excluding" (*vinirmukta*) is used.

Regarding the statement that "it takes others," Master Ki says: although there is not a single dharma that is not an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), there is nothing further beyond the object-condition that constitutes a sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Nevertheless, when it is being perceived as an object, it is an object-condition; when it is not being perceived, it is a sovereign condition.

Thus, the four factors such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth—as explained in the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*—are such that those which are concordant can produce [an effect], while those which are discordant do not allow it to arise; this applies to the other three [factors] as well.
Thus it is. Furthermore, among the ten causes, the first nine are concordant causes (*anuloma-hetu*), while the tenth is the discordant cause (*virodha-hetu*) [the two commentaries agree on this].

*Ce* (Cen) formulates three propositions: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) in relation to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); second, the conditioned in relation to the unconditioned; third, the unconditioned in relation to the conditioned.

There is no fourth proposition for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), because when the permanent is opposed by the permanent, there is no superior efficacy (*viśiṣṭa-kāritra*). [Now, a fourth is added, explaining the svabhāva-kāya.]

It exists according to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Just as the three parts of the mind, though lacking separate entities, function as predominant factors—yet the manner in which they exercise this predominant influence should be understood as explained in the treatise.
The commentary states: "Regarding the second meaning, it says that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and so forth take on the transformation of the eye and other [senses].

Cè (測) says: "The 'and so forth' includes the fivefold group associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); although the images thus transformed do not themselves produce cognition, they are called 'roots' because they resemble them. Guǎn (觀) says: [as above].
It includes the seeds of the five faculties because they possess superior power. Regarding the statement that it is "not a true wholesome root," the fifty-seventh [treatise] says:
"First, it pertains to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and is non-bonded; its meaning is that it encompasses all that is both bonded and non-bonded. This refers to these faculties.

Furthermore, it is said that there are nine faculties (*indriya*) in their respective states. However, the *Abhidharma-śāstra* includes the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), because it relies on the stage of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-bhūmi*) to cultivate the preparatory provisions for the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*). Since this is the case, how can the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth be explained?
Eleven faculties can be acquired, because the non-percipient [attainment] possesses only eight. This treatise reconciles the previous statement regarding the three formless realms and so forth.
That is to say, there are two types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): first, cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), which refers to actual manifestation;

this is as previously explained, with distinctions based on the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) and the fundamental states (*maula*) of the form realm and the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*). Second, cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), which relies upon the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) for entry.

At the time of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates both the higher and lower stages universally. By the power of the manifest path of seeing currently active, the seeds of the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are made to increase and become clear.
One cultivates each of the three stages; the various seeds thus cultivated are designated as "the path of seeing" and so forth according to the stage in which they reside.

It is not necessarily the case that they arise as manifest [only] upon falling into the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), for they arise as manifest [earlier]. This differs from the Vaibhāṣika system regarding the four dhyānas.

In the interim, regardless of which level one relies upon, when entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one attains the cultivation of the path of seeing belonging to one’s own level and the lower levels, but does not cultivate those of higher levels because they have never previously been practiced. Jñānagarbha says: "It is not the case that all paths of seeing are thus;

it is only for Bodhisattvas, or those of the two vehicles, who have already cultivated the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) while in the prior stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), and subsequently enter [the path]."

Regarding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*): because what was previously attained is cultivated [on the path of meditation], the tenth chapter of the *Abhidharma* states that in the higher stages one cultivates only the lower; this is said according to a definitive rule, as those [defilements] are gradually abandoned.

Thus, there is no fault in the arising of present [cultivation] during the subsequent stage of the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Furthermore, it is explained that for a Bodhisattva, this occurs in the three formless stages (*ārūpyabhūmi*).

There is also an untainted path of vision (*anāsrava-darśanamārga*), yet because its seeds have been cultivated to such an extent that they never arise again, it does not manifest, just as the path of vision does not arise in the lower three dhyānas.
This point should be reflected upon: what would be the purpose of cultivation [if it were as you suggest]? (It would not be the Buddha-nature, for it would then be useless.

Furthermore, all factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are termed this "faculty" (*indriya*). Because one cultivates the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), this statement was made; this is found in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

One explanation is as follows: However, the untainted (*anāsrava*) formless states do not accord with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and are not subsumed under these faculties; therefore, they are not discussed here.
Consequently, this incidental cultivation (*pārśvabhāvanā*) is also exclusively untainted, as it pertains only to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and the unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).

As the *Pañcāśatikā* (Treatise on the Fifty) states: "The first faculty is established in the stage of practice through conviction (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*); the second faculty is established in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); [the third] is established in the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*)."
Third, it is for this reason that [Yaśomitra] does not mention them at the time of seeing the path (*darśanamārga*). Bas (基) states:

"Including the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) indicates that the first two faculties also pertain to the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*), which is consistent with the *Abhidharma*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, fascicle 45, states:

"The faculty of full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*) belongs to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and the Tathāgatas. The five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth..."

"Why is this? Yoga is known only by a Buddha. This is explained as follows: because those who have attained equal enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*) resemble a Buddha, it is said that the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are comprised within the faculty of one who has already fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Another explanation holds that those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) who have turned their minds [toward awakening] are called "possessors" (*āśrayin*) by virtue of their original name;

however, this is not like the first explanation, for if it were, those prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*) would also have to be called "possessors. Regarding the fact that the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is not clarified as being among these three faculties, Master Ji says: "However, it is said of them..."
These are "already known" and "fully known. Because they do not conform to the three faculties (*indriya*), they are not mentioned [in that context].

It is not that they are not included therein; otherwise, the three faculties would not exhaustively encompass the untainted (*anāsrava*). (Who says that the three faculties exhaustively encompass all untainted phenomena? For the untainted states of desire and so forth are not included among the faculties. The treatise states that in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, there are no three faculties.)

Thus, regarding the four conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*) [up to] "this is the basis for speech" (*vāk-samniśraya*).

The commentary states: This second section is a collateral discussion; it should be understood as consisting of a heading and an explanation. Within the explanation, there are four parts: first, establishing the causes based on their bases;

second, the mutual inclusion of the two types of causes; third, the sequential connection of conditions and causes; and fourth, the distinctions in the attainment of results. The first section contains ten points.

This is the first cause. "Speech" (*vāc*) is the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and "that which follows speech" (*anuvāda*) is the cause; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. The same applies to all subsequent instances.

The intent of the two commentaries is identical: they establish the meaning based on the substance (*tattva*). As recorded in the *Mahā-śāstra*, the proof states: "The *Mahā-śāstra* relies on speech as the cause and basis (*hetvadhiṣṭhāna*);
it understands that the cause serves as the basis for the fruit. It does not mean that the fifteen substances themselves are the basis of the cause."
However, according to the intent of the *Mahā-śāstra*, there is no contradiction regarding the locus of speech. Both the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* state:

"Because it precedes all phenomena, it is called 'conceptualization' (*saṃjñā*); because conceptualization precedes it, it is expressed. Thus, it is the cause for the expression of those various phenomena. Jñānagarbha says:

In this context, all phenomena (*dharmas*) constitute the fruit; "name" (*nāman*) is the basis for verbal expression; and "speech" (*vāk*) constitutes the causal substance, meaning it serves as the instrumental cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*) for that which is expressed.
Speech permeates all three moral natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*); names and so forth are neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Alternatively, according to the Mahāyāna, speech has no substance apart from sound, yet names permeate the three natures (the criteria for inclusion and exclusion are as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*). Paramārtha states: "The substance of the provisional basis upon which vocal speech relies permeates the three [natures]."
Regarding "nature" and so forth, as well as the expressions "view" and so forth, they are as explained in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.

If one relies on the *Abhidharma* [definition] where name (*nāman*), conception (*saṃjñā*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*) are the basis for speech, with speech being the result—this treatise explains the cause, encompassing both the causal and resultant states, whereas the *Abhidharma* refers only to the causal state.
Although seeing is not fixed, it is unlike vitarka and vicāra, nor does it pervade all levels; therefore, together with what is seen, vitarka and vicāra are eliminated.
These two are the bases for experience (upabhoga-sthāna), up to and including the condition of relative dependence (apekṣā-hetu).

The commentary states: This is the second reason. Regarding "the nature of the subject and object of sensation": "subject" refers to the five sensations (*vedanā*), and "object" refers to all phenomena (*dharma*). Master Ji says:

Among the mental factors (*caitta*), sensation is the only one that is both constant and universal across all minds; the others, such as the specific-object factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*), are neither constant nor universal.

Furthermore, among the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*), sensation alone possesses the five distinct states (*avasthā-bheda*). Therefore, sensation is singled out to establish the name "basis" (*āśraya*). Although it is singular...

All causes are dependent upon their effects. That which is "proximate" (*pratyāsanna*) is subsumed under other categories; this [cause] is only "remote" dependence (*viprakṛṣṭa-apekṣā*), as all schools agree. Master Ji’s commentary states:
"If that which is proximately dependent were also this cause, then based on remote dependence, it would not be said to obtain an effect of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

This interpretation is superior (the previous explanation follows the literal text). This cause consists of four permutations: first, the capacity that depends upon the object; second, the object that is depended upon by the capacity; third, the capacity...

3. The capacity for being depended upon (*pratīkṣaṇa-śakti*); 4. The object that is depended upon (*pratīkṣya-vastu*). For example, walking depends upon feet; because both are that which is depended upon, the others may be understood by analogy.
3. Latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) [persist] until they reach their own distant results.

The commentary states: "Internal seeds" refers to all seeds, both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). "External seeds" refers to the stage prior to ripening, such as wheat and so forth. Master Ji says:
"One must not see that because this attainment of *nirvāṇa* is a pure cause, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is therefore the fruit.
The unconditioned is remote; it is not produced by causes, and thus the treatise does not state that it is the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). Master Ce says: [as follows].

This treatise refers to the immediate [cause]. In reality, it cites the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "Being endowed with the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), one realizes the two types of nirvāṇa, because it serves as the cause of attraction."
"Fourth, 'possessing moisture' (yāvadrūpaṇa), because it is proximate to its own fruit.
The commentary states: This refers to the stage where the aforementioned seeds of maturation (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*) have already matured.

Although uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) seeds are not moistened by craving and the like, they are said to be "moistened" in a figurative sense because they mature when conditions are complete. Furthermore, this arising and projecting [of birth] consists briefly of five gates.

1. The gate of near and far (*āsanna-dūra-mukha*). As in the fourth chapter of the *Saṃgrahābhidharma*. 2. The gate of the primary and the residual (*mūla-śeṣa-mukha*). As in the second [chapter] mentioned previously. 3.
The gate of the arising of verbal expression (*nāma-kāya-vyavahāra-mukha*). As in the *Vitarkavicāra-bhūmi*: "The karma named 'attraction' (*ākṣepaka*) brings about the arising of its own seeds.

4. The gate of different and similar types (*vijātīya-sajātīya-mukha*). As in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*: among the causes of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to birth (*jāti*) and so forth acts as the attraction.
Regarding causes: the distinct individual seeds are called the "causes of origination. The gate of the five constant and impermanent fruits is as described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Within the cause of purification, the possession of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) serves as the "attracting cause" for the realization of the two types of nirvana;
the production of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) serves as the "cause of origination. However, these two causes here are based on the first gate.
"Five [moments] immediately cease (until) the discernment of the untainted. The commentary states:

"The three minds, such as the immediate [mind], etc., serve as the fruit. Ji says: "Although the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is future while the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is present, it is not the case that a present fruit has a future cause.
Functional activity (*kāritra*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*) constitute the fruit of action. Nevertheless..."

There is a distinction between the "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*) and the "immediate" (*anantara*) conditions, as well as between the "dominant" (*adhipati*) and the "objective" (*ālambana*). When consciousness arises, the sense organ (*indriya*) is the dominant condition and the object (*viṣaya*) is the objective condition;

the former acts as the instrument (*karaṇa*), while the latter acts as the agent (*kartṛ*). Both assist the seeds of consciousness to cause the arising of consciousness. Excluding the seed itself, the meaning of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is immediate; the other conditions are so called because they provide a connection.
Regarding the "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*), Kuiji and Fabao take it to refer only to the provisional entity (*prajñapti-sat*). As stated below, it is said that "only the human effort is obtained."

Because it is a fruit. Fan says: "This generally includes both substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*) and functional efficacy (*puruṣakāra*). However, this remote cause excludes the seeds of causal conditions (*pratyaya*).

The proof states that what is subsequent is superior; since other immediate causes are said to possess functional efficacy, how could the possession of functional efficacy indicate that [the dharma] is not a substantial dharma?

Regarding the phrase "true vision excludes that which induces its own seeds," Kuiji states: because the perfumed seed is the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition), it is able to assist in inducing and realizing [the fruit].

This means that untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) assists its co-existent dharmas in inducing subsequent moments and realizing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), thereby causing them to share in the function of being grasped as the meaning of the cause.
As for "properly inducing and realizing," it refers to the eliciting of acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth; such is Kuiji’s intention here.

The *Cheshu* (Commentary on the Compendium) states in one place: "That which assists assists what is associated; that which induces induces the subsequent moment; that which realizes realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

[This interpretation is not good, for if 'assistance' were taken separately, the other two would have to be considered direct [causes], resulting in confusion with other types of causes]. Regarding the statement "in general, based on these six," there are three meanings:
first, a cause that can connect to a fruit is called a "supporting cause" (*parigraha-hetu*), as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "that which has ceased without interval," and so forth.
Because it is that which is accepted, *Tse* (Me-tshe) explains it thus. Second, because it assists as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is called "appropriation" (*parigraha*).

As the *Abhidharma* states: "Although [a dharma] arises from its own seed, [the sense bases] augment its power. *Ki* (Gyi-jo) explains it thus. Third, because they assist one another, it is called "appropriation.
As this treatise says: "The five and six bases are appropriated so as to form a cause. *Tse* alone explains it in this way.
The fourth explanation is that [the four conditions] are combined and taken as three; since there is no contradiction in either case, this is acceptable.
However, it is not the case that all phenomena possess all five or six [conditions], for while mind and its concomitants possess them, matter and the like possess few.
"Eleventh, because it conforms to (up to) unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

The commentary states: According to the two commentaries by Jì and Cè, the arising of seeds from present [phenomena], the arising of present [phenomena] from seeds, the arising of seeds from seeds, the arising of present [phenomena] from present [phenomena], and the realization of unconditioned phenomena—all of these are this cause.
However, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* does not mention the arising of present [phenomena] from seeds, nor does the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

Regarding the statement that "seeds produce seeds" and so forth, concerning the coarse aspect of the differentiation of homogeneous categories (*sabhāga*), Master Ji says: the term "homogeneous" excludes those of a different category from acting as causes;

the term "superior category" excludes those of an inferior category from acting as causes. This is narrow when discussed in terms of nature (*dhātu*) and broad when discussed in terms of realm (*bhūmi*).

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle five, cites only those of the same nature, because it allows for [seeds] of higher stages. However, within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the seeds that serve as causes for both the wholesome and the defiled: they are also of the same nature with respect to their own manifestation. There are three interpretations of this:
First, it is said that the term "superior grade" excludes those of equal or inferior grades; one must look to the superior grade because it is designated as the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*).

This differs from the Sarvāstivāda position, which holds that innate wholesome and defiled states form homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) when compared across the nine grades. However, if it concerns acquired wholesome states (*prāyogika-kuśala*), it forms a homogeneous cause with those of equal grade.

Regarding "the superior cause" (*viśiṣṭa-hetu*): one interpretation states that "similar" (*sabhāga*) refers to the "similar class" (*sapakṣa*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), relying on what is preeminent, speaks only of the superior class.

Another interpretation states that it contains both meanings of "nature" (*svabhāva*) and "class" (*pakṣa*), because vitarka, vicāra, and so forth are said to induce both similar and superior classes.

The latter [position] is taught as superior. Question: Among the four propositions—seed producing seed and manifest, manifest producing manifest, and manifest producing seed—excluding the case of manifest producing manifest, the others are all common causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
What is this cause? Answer: There are various traditions regarding this. Jì says: It is the manifest that perfumes the superior seeds;
thus the manifest produces the superior. The other two are not superior. At the time of the Vajra Path, although there are superior seeds, they do not [produce anything].

"Because the superior manifest [arises], it is not the fruit of Buddhahood. (This does not fully capture the principle. Since one already admits that the superior manifest arises in a subsequent life, why not admit that seeds produce one another?

This is because a preceding moment of superior seed induces a subsequent seed; the two non-superior [factors] cannot serve as its basis. The proof states: According to the oral tradition of the Tripiṭaka masters, the seed produces the superior manifest.

By the power of the superior manifest, the seed is subsumed and rendered superior. The seed is the functional capacity of the perfuming residue of the manifest; its characteristics are subtle and obscure, and thus it is not superior to the perfuming of the manifest.

This is merely words; it lacks any [dual] meaning whatsoever. Since it is a single moment, there is no sequence of prior and posterior time. At what point could a superior seed produce a superior manifestation? And by means of this superior manifestation, how could its own seed be made superior? [For seeds that produce only their own kind must produce only those of the same class.

Regarding these two points of debate, just as various transformations arise in the tenth [chapter], manifestations mutually induce one another; thus, it is logically established that the former may be inferior while the latter is superior.
As for the selection and rejection of the principle that a seed produces a superior manifestation and a manifestation perfumes a superior seed, it should be understood through careful deliberation.

The *Mūlamātṛkā-bhāṣya* explains: However, regarding the tradition that all four lines [of the verse] constitute this cause, there is one interpretation: it is because they act as causes for their own respective categories (*sabhāga-jāti*).
That is to say, they produce present states of the same category and perfume seeds of the same category; thus, they maintain the constant continuity of cause and effect without interruption.

Alternatively, it may be that seeds and manifest states serve as mutual dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for one another; while they induce subsequent superior states, they are not necessarily direct causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Twelve distinctions (up to) the fruit of one's own vehicle. Commentary states:
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) constitute the substance of this cause; they are able to give rise to the conditioned and are able to realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Cè (Cè Yùn) says: "One's own realm," etc.—the term "etc. includes those that are non-bound (*apratisaṃyukta*). For example, as in the stage of vitarka and vicāra, those belonging to the three realms and those that are non-bound each arise [from their respective causes].

Regarding their own kind: furthermore, they are equal across the five destinies (*gati*). As the *Abhidharma* states: "The causal conditions for the five [aggregates] are called 'birth' (*jāti*) within one's own destiny. Master Ji says:

"Furthermore, they are equal to their respective causes and conditions, because the seeds of form (*rūpa*) and so forth each produce their own specific results. This is as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The theory of *dhātu* (elements) is narrow in its scope regarding the various distinct causes and conditions, whereas the theory of *prakṛti* (nature) is broad.
This is because one’s own element produces the maturation (*vipāka*) of evil; furthermore, it is because thirteen [factors] combine to produce a single resultant effect.

The commentary states: Of the preceding six [causes], these are specific; this one [the non-obstructing cause] functions universally. With the exception of the first (the efficient cause), the others lack the power of integration regarding matters such as arising and so forth, as they cause things to remain distant and contrary.
This [non-obstructing cause] possesses a superior power that encompasses all six causes; it is broader than the "non-contradictory" (avirodha) category.
"Connecting with the eight [factors] to eliminate contradictions;
fourteen obstacles (up to) such matters. The commentary states:
*Ce* says there are two interpretations. One says: it takes only the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the cause of tranquility. One...
It is said: "Pervading both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); once the Tripiṭaka remains in the background, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) does not establish a dwelling.
Because these are contradictory, what serves as the fruit for this cause of contradiction? Cè says: "By the power of obstruction, it causes phenomena (*dharma*) not to arise and not to abide;
this is precisely its fruit. Jī says: "In the Mahāyāna, although the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) does not depend on a cause, this cause merely [contributes to it]."

A cause for the arising of a subsequent dharma that is contrary to a preceding dharma is called a "contradictory cause" (*virodha-hetu*). It is not a cause for the cessation of the preceding [dharma] (because the preceding is considered superior;
the deliberation regarding what to adopt and what to discard is as recorded in the *Mahā-śāstra*).
Fifteen (up to): "Because of [the factors] such as arising. The commentary states:
All conditioned and unconditioned phenomena constitute its essence, with the sole exception of those that are contradictory, because they share the same causal principle.
"Thus, because of these ten causes (up to) the existence of non-causal conditions.
[The commentary] states: Within the second section on the connection between the two pairs of causes, there are two parts.

Furthermore, this is the first part, which explains the mutual inclusion of meanings according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Great Treatise). The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* says: "If that which is a productive cause is the nature of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)."
If the inferior means have these three conditions as their nature, the Master of the Treatise explains:

"This refers to the drawing forth (*ākṣepa*), the arising (*abhinirvṛtti*), the inducing (*āvāhana*), the fixed differentiation (*pratiniyama*), the commonality of function (*ekārthakriyā*), and the non-contradiction (*avirodha*)," and so forth. Jñānakīrti states:

"In that *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, 'drawing forth' encompasses the entirety of the drawing-forth cause (*ākṣepahetu*) and a portion of the other four causes, excluding the cause of arising (*jananahetu*). This is because [the seeds] have not yet been moistened.

Because it is matured. "Arising" (*utpatti*) subsumes the entirety of the productive causes (*janaka-hetu*) and a portion of the other four causes, excluding the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*), because it is matured after having been moistened.
(This refers to the six causes; while the words are general, the meaning is specific, for in reality each of those two types subsumes five causes. Cai states:

"The projecting cause also includes that which has not yet matured among the six [causes], and the arising cause also includes the stage of maturity among the six, because they are distant and proximate fruits respectively. (The meaning here is that both stages are common to all six causes.)
"One type is the expectation of the fruit (because it applies to both the produced and the producing). The Commentary states that the latter is superior.

Although Master Ji’s explanation accords with the preceding text on the produced and the producing, it contradicts the following [passage], which states that all causal seeds among the six causes are subsumed within these two categories. [Response: This refutation is not correct.

The causal conditions for the produced and the producing are each fully subsumed within their respective two categories as appropriate; thus, there is no contradiction. It does not mean that each of the six causes must individually reside within both categories. This reconciles the previous [discussion] on the essential nature, namely, the seeds of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

That which arises simultaneously and manifests maturation is called "arising" (*utpāda*). That which, in relation to the subsequent production of its own fruit, is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
Within this principle, there is projection within arising, and arising within projection; therefore, this [latter] is superior. (This interpretation is not correct.

Although the substance of the seed is one, the two gates of arising and maturation are distinct in their respective referents and do not intermingle—just as a single color is not confused when perceived in relation to length or shortness). Now, taking the explanation based on the "basis" (*āśraya*) as superior in terms of logic, for it does not...

This would contradict the teachings, as it would deeply accord with the principle [that seeds are real]. If all conditions (*pratyaya*) were capable of producing and encompassing the four functions—such as *āvedha* (projecting) and so forth—and if the manifest [dharmas] possess the capacity to perfuse (*vāsana*), why could they not produce [seeds]? Furthermore, these [manifest dharmas] also encompass the four causes. There are two interpretations in the treatise:

first, that the manifest [dharmas] do not continue [into the future], which is omitted here for brevity; second, that the manifest are conventionally designated as "seeds. This is like the seeds of rice or wheat: when the manifest perfuses the seeds, they must necessarily ripen simultaneously. Therefore, [the Bodhisattva...]

[The phrase] "all stages of the bodhisattva arise and connect" [is used]. As for the remaining causes: they consist of the entirety of the first, second, fifth, and ninth causes, as well as a portion of the six causes such as the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and so forth.
These are the remainder of the productive and ripening conditions (*janma- and paripāka-pratyaya*).
They do not belong exclusively to those two types within this *Bodhisattvabhūmi*; rather, they are the remainder of the eight [causes] among those ten causes. Those ten...

Regarding the two [types of causes] within the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), because there are those that are not *pratyaya* (conditions), the *Vitarkavicāra-bhūmi* (Stage of Applied and Sustained Thought) is explained. One should understand this accordingly;
since that *Vitarkavicāra-bhūmi* does not mention "seeds" (*bīja*), Dharmapāla takes both seeds and manifest phenomena as the cause and condition.
Or, from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* onwards, it should be understood according to the above.

The commentary states: This is the second [section], the sequential explanation according to the names. It says that within the two causes there are those that are not productive, such as the seeds of karma.
It says that within the remaining causes there are those that are not expedient means, as in the case of the remaining [causes] among the four causes; the others may be inferred accordingly.
Regarding the four conditions (pratyaya) that have been explained—[up to] their progression and regression—as before—the commentary states:
"The third section, the Gate of the Succession of Causes and Conditions, has two successive expositions; these should be understood according to the preceding [explanation].

As for the fact that other bases (*āśraya*) also possess the meaning of the two intermediate conditions, Baogui says: 'It is not only the fifth, the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), [that possesses this meaning]...'"
The six objects (*viṣaya*). As for the remaining [factors], such as experience (*anubhava*) and the lower conjunctions (*adhara-saṃprayoga*), they do not constitute obstacles.

Within each of the three bases (*āśraya*), there are two conditions; it is only through the dependence upon objects and so forth that the mind can arise. This is because the other two [conditions] are subsumed under the aforementioned [bases] to form their essence. Master Cè offers two interpretations:

the first says it is the same as before (this does not fully accord with reason, as recorded in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*); the second says that "immediate succession" (*anantara*) subsumes the ten [bases].

One location. Excluding the statement regarding the moistening of the *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies), there are three locations (namely, the sense-base of the mind, which also includes the "opening and guiding" [function], not merely the "coexistent" [function];

therefore, it is admitted that it extends [to all]). Question: Regarding the function of conforming to the distinctions of locations, the *Śrīlāta* school’s theory of nature (*dhātu*) is narrow; how can it include the "immediate" [condition]? Since the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) also induces other [factors], although there are cases where it induces only its own realm and stage, this condition is broad and thus contradicts that [narrow] location.

Answer: Although the conforming location may arise in another realm, there can still be causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); the immediate [condition] is likewise so. Regarding obstacles, there are two theories. One says they are admitted to extend [to all], as the characteristics of the defiled and the pure are mutually [opposed].

[Objection: Because they are mutually contradictory, [they cannot serve as conditions]. [Response: This is not so; for while they act as "contradictory" (virodha) by causing non-arising and the like, they act as "conducive causes" (anukūla-hetu) toward that which is being produced.

One view holds that [the condition of contradiction] does not apply, because they are contradictory. [This is correct,] for there is no fruit to be produced that is not the object of this condition. If it is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), it is invariably present. Regarding the remaining four, there are two interpretations:

namely, whether the linguistic habitual tendencies (abhilāpa-vāsanā) possess moisture or obstruction. One view holds that [this distinction] does not apply, because speech is contrasted with its meaning, and because of the cause.

Regarding the result and its contradictory [cause], they are not objects by way of the "object-gate" (*viṣaya-mukha*). [Speech and so forth are not like this; if one were to rely on the object-gate, only the sixth base would possess this condition, for it is the only one that has such an object.

However, a contradictory cause is not an object of the result, because since it prevents [the result] from arising, it lacks the capacity to be an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). One view holds that both are universal, because speech expresses the mind, and seeds give rise to the cognizing faculty.

Because the pure conditions the defiled, [the linguistic convention is logical; however, the reverse is not so, for the defiled does not induce the pure in a manner that constitutes a contradiction]. Other masters offer alternative explanations, which are prolix and unnecessary.

Since the preceding section clarifies how the two causes subsume the ten causes, and since these two causes subsume the conditions across all ten causes, yet the *parigraha-hetu* (appropriating cause) is separately extracted from within the *prayoga-hetu* (preparatory cause), it is because the two conditions are predominantly associated with those two respective locations.
In reality, this applies to other locations as well; one should understand this according to the preceding [explanation]. Regarding "advancing and retreating":

based on the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, six [factors] are designated as advancing and two as retreating; both seeds and manifestations are called advancing, while seeds alone are called retreating. Based on the *Vitarkavicārabhūmi*, six [factors] are designated as advancing and only one as retreating.
Regarding the statement "the causes and conditions [extend] to all that is possible," the commentary says:

This is the fourth section, the gate of the distinctions in attaining the fruits. As for "that which is born of maturation" (*vipākaja*), this is because "maturation" (*vipāka*) and "birth" (*jāti*) apply both generally and specifically.
If there are contaminated wholesome states that induce maturation, why does the *Mūlakarma-buddhamātṛkā-paṭala* state: "First..."?
All wholesome [states] receive the fruit of Buddhahood, whereas ignorance receives the fruit of conditioned arising and ceasing. The *Zheng lun* (Treatise on Proof) states:

"Liberation and its counterparts all tend toward the fruit of Buddhahood, because the fruits of the three realms are produced by ignorance. Wholesome habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) induce [results] across both similar and dissimilar times, as in the second [case] mentioned previously.
Habitual tendencies of equal outflow produce the eight consciousnesses and so forth, because the fruit resembles its cause. This is according to the *Abhidharma*.

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts state that because wholesome [karma] and so forth performed in a previous life increase in subsequent lives, [the result is called a "concordant fruit"]. Regarding the statement that killing leads to a short lifespan, Master Ji (Jizang) and Master Ce (Fazang) say:

"This is indeed a sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). By causing others to have a short lifespan, one’s own lifespan becomes short; this is the meaning of 'similarity,' which is conventionally designated as such for the sake of circulation.

Regarding the distinction between outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), those severed by the non-outflowing path are, for example, the thirty-eight [defilements]. As for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), [they are severed] by...

The mundane path (*laukikamārga*) does not result in the fruit of dissociation (*visamyogaphala*), because it does not bring about the ultimate cessation of all afflictions (*kleśa*). This is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts;
the term "and others" (*ādi*) includes the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the eighteen treatises. Regarding the phrase "all functional capacities that induce maturation results (*vipākaphala*)," etc.:
The number [of fruits] can be understood from the passage on how ten causes correspond to five fruits. As for the critique that [the definition] is too broad or too narrow:
if one were to take the locus of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) in its entirety, it would be too broad, because that locus also includes those who do not belong to a vehicle (*yāna*).

If one does not include the other bases (*āśraya*) in the comprehensive inclusion, then the scope would be too narrow, because there are also retributive results (*vipākaphala*) produced in those other places.
The rest may be understood by analogy. In explaining the bases, it is incidentally shown that the ten causes and four conditions (*pratyaya*) obtain their results;

therefore, it says, "Thus it is stated," meaning that the statement refers to how the five causes obtain the ripening result (*vipākaphala*), and so forth, according to the explanation of the "contingent condition" (*apekṣā-pratyaya*). Regarding...
Because the result is remote, it is not said to be "attained. Regarding the distinct results of the first three [causes], the second commentary states:

"Within the context of the appropriating cause (*parigraha-hetu*), from the perspective of human agency (*puruṣakāra*), no distinction is attained; however, according to the Dharma, it is also attained. Consciousness attains its result of outflow (*niṣyanda*) by means of seven causes."
Regarding the cause of acquisition (*prāpti-hetu*), Ji states: "Because true vision (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) also manifests in relation to its own kind, it is acquired in seven locations.

This explanation takes the person (*pudgala*) as the agent (*puruṣakāra*). Others say that since the dharma acts as the agent, it acquires the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) in nine locations.
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the person may act as a remote agent but cannot acquire [the result]. Among these three interpretations, Ce describes the first.

Regarding the statement that "later [the true seeing] only assists and induces the proof, thereby attaining it immediately; there is no reason why the immediate function would not attain it," this is based on the four conditions (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*). Since the two intermediate conditions are not said to obtain the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), it is clear that the remote function does not obtain this fruit.

Thus, the actual dharma's *puruṣakāra* (human effort) may be proximate. As for the statement that "the first and last conditions obtain [it]," Yuance says: Because the meaning of the seeds of names and words (*nāma-vikalpa-bīja*) is non-obstructive, they constitute a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Therefore, the other two conditions are not taken, as they are remote.
(Although the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) takes its own capacity to produce seeds as an object, it is only in the sense of a causal condition [*hetu-pratyaya*].)

It obtains the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*). Since the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is exclusively [the cause of] dominance (*adhipati*), it is so designated. Regarding the attainment of the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*) by means of five causes, Ji (基) says:

"Within the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*), only the true [cause] is taken; if real dharmas also function as the efficient cause (*puruṣakāra-hetu*) and so forth, they then act as the efficient cause.

However, this fruit is obtained through two meanings of 'efficient cause. The first is that it is obtained in the five locations of the person (*puruṣa*); only four causes possess those that are provisional (*prajñapti*)."
Because they function as such; other [factors] in relation to distinct phenomena are not "persons" (*puruṣa*). The latter applies to substantial phenomena (*dravyadharma*).

Regarding the eight causes and three conditions, within the context of the "appropriating cause" (*parigrahahetu*), two types—the remote and the immediate—act as the "person" (*puruṣakāra*) for true seeing. (Excluding the two remote factors of the sense organ and the object, which contradict the preceding explanation regarding the inclusion of the appropriating cause:

if the sense organ is admitted to be the agent in the production of consciousness, how can it not obtain this fruit at the locus of the organ? The same applies to the object. The treatise excludes the "object-condition" (*ālambanapratyaya*) because it is excluded from the three attainments (*prāpti*). Baso says: External phenomena are not like the activity of a person; therefore, the object-condition is excluded. There is no [other] condition.

The interval is not external (it is also called *puruṣakāra-phala*). Regarding the statement that "all [conditions] may obtain the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)," this refers to obtaining the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) from a contrary cause (*vipakṣa-hetu*), as recorded in the *Mahā-śāstra*.
Various schools have offered interpretations; the *Shuyao* states: "Regarding the ten causes of purification, the 'contrary cause' is so called because it is [the cause of] defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
Since it actually obtains the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) based on the cause of defilement, the treatise does not record it [as such]. This is incorrect.
Regarding those defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), if one considers them in relation to their maturation (*vipāka*), they are not contradictory causes [for that maturation].
This incidental discussion is concluded; it should be understood that the same applies [to other cases].

The commentary states: Regarding this incidental discussion, there are two interpretations. One says: from "the four conditions" (*catasraḥ pratyayāḥ*) onwards, the verse explains only the phenomena produced by conditions.
Therefore, one interpretation states that from the "ten causes" onwards, it clarifies that what is produced must necessarily be capable of producing. Master Ji adopts the second [interpretation].
The preceding section has concluded the explanation of the productive conditions (*janaka-pratyaya*). In the second major section, we now examine production (*utpāda*). This contains two parts:

first, the examination of the production of manifest phenomena (*vijñapti*); second, the examination of the production of seeds (*bīja*). The first part also has two sub-sections, as they concern the relationship between the seed and the manifest, and the manifest [and the seed], respectively.

Because it is manifest; this is the first [point]. Regarding the "manifestation of produced discrimination," this refers to the various minds and mental factors, such as the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing-part (*darśana*).

As for being the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for that which is capable of cognition: only the sixth and eighth consciousnesses can produce their own seeds from that which is capable of cognition.

If, in the untainted state (*anāsrava*), all eight consciousnesses are able to provide assistance, then the seeds of the faculties (*indriya*) are in relation to the consciousnesses, and the seeds of karma are in relation to the retribution.
"Purity" refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
From "manifesting discrimination" up to "excluding the equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
[Commentary: This explains the second perspective regarding manifestation. Having already explained all aspects of transformation in the root verse, we shall now explain what follows.

Due to the power of mutual transformation (*parivarta*), there are two types within this [category]: the defiled and the pure. At the beginning, there are five [stages], as they gradually become more abbreviated and reach a state of subtlety.
This is the first section, the gate of comparing self and other. The causes and conditions are not stated here, as they have already been excluded previously.

Regarding the predominant concentration (*adhipati-samādhi*) having an object (*sālambana*): why do seven [minds] not take others as objects? Six and eight can take the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) as objects.

There are two interpretations regarding this measurement. One says that it must rely on one's own eight [consciousnesses]; another says that it may also depend on the eight [consciousnesses] of others.
Otherwise, when one is born in a higher realm and perceives the forms of a lower realm, there would be no objective basis for such perception.
"From the collection of the eight consciousnesses up to the eighth characteristic. The commentary states:

This is the second section, the gate of mutual comparison among the self-consciousnesses. "The eighth exists in relation to the seven" means that the collection of the eighth consciousness possesses the sense of having an object (*ālambana*) with respect to the other seven consciousnesses.

However, the five [sensory] consciousnesses rely upon the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image-part), the seventh relies upon the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-part), and the sixth universally takes all as its objects.
The rest of the text may be understood. Regarding the statement that "the five consciousnesses rely solely upon the *nimitta* (objective aspect) of the eighth [consciousness]," the *Guān* states:

"According to tradition, the Tripiṭaka Master says that the five consciousnesses take the reflected forms (*pratibimba*) transformed by the sixth consciousness as their objective basis (*ālambana*). This contradicts this explicit scriptural passage. To provide a defense for this [tradition], it is argued:
The treatise has two sections. In the first, where the powerful project an image, only eight [consciousnesses] serve as the substantial basis (*pratibimba*).

If, however, they are like those gathered together such that each can mutually serve as the basis for what it resembles, then six are admitted as the substantial basis (this is merely a different formulation, as will be explained below in due order).
"Because they are of the same category, from prior to subsequent, up to the seeds of mutual perception.

The commentary states: This is the third gate, regarding the relationship between prior and subsequent. It is asserted that the latter five views take the former characteristics as their objects. The commentary states: [End of commentary].
Dignāga, in his *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, intends to maintain that the five subsequent consciousnesses take the preceding aspect (*pūrvākāra*) as their substantial object (*ālambana*).

He holds that the preceding aspect perfumes a seed, which gives rise to the subsequent objective part (*nimittabhāga*); thus, because the subsequent consciousness carries that preceding aspect, by analogy, one should likewise accept this for the seventh [consciousness].
Regarding this term "accepts" (*abhyupagamyate*), the Tripiṭaka Master offers three interpretations. The first says: Dignāga accepts the Sautrāntika doctrine; for they state:

It is difficult to believe that the five consciousnesses take past objects as their conditions, because a cause must necessarily precede its effect, and [if they were simultaneous], they would be like two horns.
This was Dharmapāla’s distinct intention, which he provisionally accepted in accordance with Dignāga (Jizang records only this). One version states: Dharmapāla provisionally accepted Dignāga’s view.

One interpretation states: "The actual admission constitutes the thesis" (*pakṣa*). Since Dignāga’s verse contains two approaches—one being the approach of provisional admission (*prajñapti*) and the other being the approach of actual admission (*tattva*), as the reasoning is non-erroneous—one may adopt either.

If one follows this approach, then among the eight [types of objects], the first seven serve as remote objects of cognition (*viprakṛṣṭālambana*) for the eighth; regarding the seeds of their respective images and perceptions, there are two interpretations by the Tripiṭaka Master.
