One interpretation states: the subject and object aspects (*nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*) of the seven consciousnesses mutually perfume their own seeds; here, the seeds serve as the direct condition (*pratyaya*), while the perfuming agents serve as the indirect condition. Another interpretation states:

the subject and object aspects of the eighth consciousness perfume the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, such as form and so forth; therefore, the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) serves as the indirect object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, because the seventh consciousness perfumes the seeds of that seeing aspect, the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvitti*) and others serve as indirect object-conditions. The eighth... [text ends].

The six pairs of perfumings should be understood according to principle. [These] subsume the characteristics [of the objects] into consciousness; thus it is said that they take the seven consciousnesses as their conditions (Master Ji only discusses the latter).

However, regarding the preceding statement, Cè says: "The preceding thought may be the first three among the eight [consciousnesses]. Among the two interpretations of the Tripiṭaka Master, the former possesses both meanings; if one follows the latter interpretation, it refers only to the first three among the eight, for if not perfumed by the preceding thought and moistened, they cannot produce the eighth [consciousness], namely, the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-part).
"Because they are of the same aggregate yet different entities (up to) not being of the same substance.

The commentary states: This is the fourth gate, the mutual comparison of those within the same aggregate. Cei says there are two successive expositions; the meaning of the latter exposition is as follows.

In the section on the eighth consciousness, the mind-king (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) take each other as their objective essence (*ālambana-pratibimba*), because they are similar to one another.

The same principle applies by analogy to the seven consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth; Master Ji says they are likewise the same. All [consciousnesses] arise only when they mutually serve as each other's objective essence.

However, according to the intention of the former masters, each [consciousness] transforms its own [representation]. Nevertheless, because they are similar, they are said to have the "same object of perception" (*ekālambana*); it is not necessarily the case that there must be an external objective essence.

As with the case of taking a non-existent thing as an object, some say that all minds must rely upon a substantial basis (*bhāva*). For example, when taking space as an object, one relies on its name as the basis.
[They argue that] the eighth mind-king arises with the fivefold transformation by relying on the power of the mutual dependence of the mental factors (*caitta*) as its substantial basis;

however, this [argument] turns against them. If associated factors were to mutually serve as each other's bases, then because their bases would differ, it would be inconsistent. Furthermore, since each [mental factor] transforms individually, why must they necessarily share the same basis? Therefore, the former master [holds this view].

This is truly worthy of contemplation. Cheng says: This subsequent explanation by the Master [Xuanzang] also conforms to Dignāga’s position that the subsequent cognition takes the preceding aspect as its object.

However, the manifestation exists substantially; it does not depend on the power of perfuming (for although it does not directly apprehend it, it acquires a semblance of it through the power of perfuming, since it is said to apprehend that object based on the power of perfuming).
"Because the identical substance and its objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) mutually serve as conditions.
The commentary states: This is the fifth section, the gate of mutual observation among the four parts. Here, we do not rely on the seeds of the objective aspect;

rather, if the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna) takes its own seeds as its object, it constitutes the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), which is to say, the three conditions. However, this now explains the second half of the verse.
Therefore, it is excluded.
[This applies] up to the point where the pure collection of the eight consciousnesses functions as the capacity for objective perception (*ālambana-vṛtti*).

The commentary states: Within the second section on purity, there are likewise five stages of gradual abbreviation. However, while the terms "self" and "other" here are general, their underlying meanings are distinct. Five.
Because they all function according to the respective self and other [aspects], it should be understood that the first three [moments of consciousness] all have objects of cognition (*ālambana*).

This is because they thoroughly know everything and penetrate the three periods of time. Regarding the fourth [moment], Lce states: "All [of these] take the three parts as their own and the four parts as the other, for this allows the internal part to take the external object as its domain.

Ki states: "The sovereign and the mental factors are both able to take one another as objects, because they universally manifest reflections. However, regarding the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of consciousness:

However, it is only with the "seeing" that perceives the same object as the "numerical" [aspects] that the internal [aspect] does not manifest as an image, because it is not an object of universal cognition (*parijñā*). There is an interpretation which states:

since the aforementioned "self-seeing" aspect has an object that is not identical to the material form (*dravya*), consciousness and the two "sees" (the objective and the self-verifying) share the same object;

why then would only the self-verifying seeing not take itself as its own object? If it were to take itself as its object, it should be identical to the self-verifying [aspect]; if it does not take it as its object, then...

This contradicts the preceding text. Here, there are two interpretations. The first says: while it was previously stated based on the causal stage that the seeing-consciousness and the perceived object share the same substance, it is not necessarily the case that the objects of the seeing-consciousness at the resultant stage must also be identical.

The second interpretation says: the seeing-consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and its object both take the self-witnessing consciousness (*svasaṃvedana*) as their common object and both transform into images;

this differs from the self-witnessing consciousness itself, which takes only the internal as its object. Furthermore, because [the seeing-consciousness] takes external objects in common with the associated mental factors (*caitta*), this principle [applies].

Although this is superior, it is somewhat difficult to understand (it clarifies that the self-perception is perceived as it is, according to the explanation in the *Mātṛkā*). Regarding the fifth [position], if it is abbreviated, Kīrti says:
"The third [moment] and its fourth part are also not mutually perceived, because both are subsumed under the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*). This means that the aspect of seeing is excluded;

subsequently, the aspect of seeing of the wisdom [moment] reflects back upon the self-perception (*svasaṃvitti*) to act as an image, yet this remains the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). Otherwise, how would it differ from self-perception? Only a Buddha...

The three parts mutually take all phenomena as their objects; this is called "universal object-taking. If that is so, what is the distinction between the three parts? That which was previously attained is obtained directly (*pratyakṣa-labdha*);
that which is obtained by what was previously attained is obtained as a reflection (*pratibimba-labdha*). Thus, a distinction is established. Furthermore, another interpretation holds:

here we merely negate that the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) can act as the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*), and we negate that the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) perceives the *svasaṃvitti* (self-cognition). This does not mean that the other two parts cannot take it as an object.

All of them. This does not reach the previous interpretation (however, the *Mātṛkā* commentary adopts this as its tenet because its reasoning is superior. That is to say, if your internal part—the new image—were to possess functional activity, it would necessarily be perceived by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as an object-image, just as the seeing-part itself is;
thus, all instances of subtle grasping and discarding are as explained in the *Mātṛkā*). In the *Ceshu*, there are four interpretations. The first says: "The three parts are equally defiled;

the seeing-part perceives the three parts, excluding itself, because otherwise there would be confusion between subject and object. The second says: "The seeing-part can perceive all four [parts], though the text excludes [itself]."

Therefore, the *Mūlamātṛkā* (Basic Treatise) adopts this principle as superior to the former. Third, it says: the three parts take the three [objects] as their conditions, each excluding its own category, because of the confusion between subject and object.

The fourth [section] on "Clouds" states: All three [mental factors] take the four [objects] as their conditions, as there is no textual passage prohibiting this. Regarding the phrase "excluding the seeing," this excludes the three [mental factors] that are capable of seeing; this is because the meaning applies universally.

As for whether the various parts mutually condition one another by transforming into reflections, there are fifteen interpretations. Specifically, within the first interpretation, there are two views:

first, some say that when the seeing [faculty] conditions the object, it transforms, whereas when it conditions the others, it does not transform; second, some say that when it conditions all three, it transforms in each case. Second...

Regarding the explanation [of the *pañcavastuka*], there are three positions. First, it is said that while the aspect (*ākāra*) of the object of seeing (*darśana*) undergoes transformation, the objects of the other [mental factors] do not.

Second, it is said that the objects of the three [other mental factors] transform separately, whereas the object of seeing does not (because it is its own immediate cause). Third, it is said that the objects of all four [mental factors] transform (this fifth position is superior, as explained in the *Mātṛkā*).

Regarding the third [position], there are four sub-positions. First, it is said that while the aspect of the object of seeing transforms, the others all remain unchanged. Second, it is said that the aspects of the objects of seeing and the three [others] transform, while the others...

All are unchanging. One interpretation states: the three conditions (*pratyaya*) change their characteristics, while the remaining conditions do not change. Another interpretation states: the three conditions undergo three types of change; the fourth [condition] has six [aspects]. One interpretation states:

the condition of seeing (*darśana-pratyaya*) changes its characteristic, while the others all remain unchanged (because they are external to the essence of the characteristic). One interpretation states:

the condition of seeing undergoes three types of change, while the others all remain unchanged (because they are external to the function of seeing). One interpretation states: the condition of seeing undergoes four types of change, while the others all remain unchanged.

One interpretation states that the object-condition transforms while the remaining conditions do not. Another interpretation states that the three conditions transform in three ways, while the self-condition does not transform.

Yet another interpretation states that the three conditions transform in four ways; there is a distinction between the primary and the secondary, as they are categorized without confusion. The primary refers to the grasping of its own specific object, whereas the secondary includes the remainder.
Regarding the mutual conditioning of the four aspects of a single aggregate’s substantial entity, there are also two explanations. One states that it is only the "seeing" [aspect]...
Regarding the four [objects], one school says: all three take the four as objects; this is explained through the three theories of "transformation of images" (*pratibimba-pariṇāma*). One says:

the visual consciousness takes the four as objects by transforming them into images, while the other two do not take them as objects (this belongs to the first interpretation; this occurs frequently in the original text). One says: the visual consciousness takes the four as objects by transforming them into images, while the others take them as objects without transformation (this division adopts the external [critique] of the Yogācāra school).

One says: all three take the four as objects by transforming them (these latter two explanations belong to the second meaning). Among these various interpretations, Dharmapāla’s [position is the correct one].

Thesis: According to the treatises above and below, the wise should reflect [on this]. (Since the Commentary does not permit it, the Proponent asserts: "Among the four original explanations, the fourth is correct, because the portion of the untainted mind is all-pervasive.

Among the fifteen explanations, the thirteenth, which takes 'that which realizes its own essence' as the subject, is correct because it is unchanging; furthermore, seeing and the object-condition realize self-cognition, and since this is also internal realization, it is like the refutation in the *Mātṛkā*: essence and function are designated as distinct names, yet there is no duality or redundancy.")
"Manifest discrimination (up to) also functions merely as a dominant condition. Commentary:
This refers to the second type of causal condition for the arising of seeds, namely, the condition that relies upon words to manifest with respect to the immediate seeds.
That which perfumes its own immediate seeds acts as the cause; that which acts as the dominant condition with respect to the immediate seeds refers to the mutual production of seeds.
"Based on this internal consciousness... up to "...possessing extensive discrimination. [The] commentary states:

This explains the three sections of the verse; the third is the conclusion. As in the fifth fascicle of the *Mahā-śāstra*, the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the three realms are all discrimination (*vikalpa*);
the false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) of the *Madhyānta-vibhāga* is likewise so. Second, as in the fourth fascicle of the *Saṃgrahaṇī*.
There are two types of parikalpita (imagined nature): first, essential nature (*svabhāva*); second, differentiation (*viśeṣa*).
Third, there is the conceptualization that follows after essential nature; fourth, as in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there is essential nature and differentiation, with both cognition and non-cognition.

Fifth, as in the *Saṃgraha*, there is conceptualizing meaning based on names, conceptualizing names based on meaning, conceptualizing names based on names, conceptualizing meaning based on meaning, and conceptualizing both based on both.
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes what is taught in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XIII), the six [categories] in the fifth chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*,
the ten kinds of discrimination (*vibhāga*), and other treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (chapters 38, 9, and 4), the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
"Although there is internal consciousness... [up to] other maturations. The commentary states:
Within the second section, the refutation of the objection that the continuity [of karma] is not established, there are two parts: the thesis and the explanation. This is the first.
The *Śāstra* says: "...because they have that as their nature.

The commentary states: There are four successive expositions; this is the first. Regarding "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karman*), the two commentaries state: "Wholesome [karma] of the upper realms that is non-concentrated is subsumed under this [immovable category].

(An explanation of these three types of karma is provided in the record of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*). Regarding "the retinue of karma," it refers to the mental factors associated with volition (*cetanā*) and...

Regarding the body, speech, and so forth: because they are established by volition (*cetanā*). To exclude those that are past or present results, it excludes the Sarvāstivāda position that past and present karma currently exists.
Regarding "those that appear as retribution": (1) the two divisions of the eight consciousnesses;
(2) name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), where the four aggregates are "name" and the aggregate of form is "form"; (3) mind and mental factors.
Because all five aggregates do not depart from this. Fourth is the primary and the derivative: the *ālayavijñāna* is the primary, while the other seven are the derivatives.
The fourfold twofold grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) is also that which is grasped (*grāhya*). As for "that which grasps," it refers to the fourfold grasper (*grāhaka*).

Within the grasper, the manifested objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the cause for perfuming the seeds of names and phrases within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). According to the principle of excluding the inferior and non-existent...

Regarding the phrase "the images appearing within the mind" (the *Śāstra* provides three explanations; here the first is retained), the expression "receiving fruits without end," etc., refers to the third section of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, concerning the characteristic of the non-exhaustion of experience (*anupabhoga-niḥśeṣatā-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of the exhaustion of experience (*upabhoga-niḥśeṣatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Within this, the principles of selection and rejection regarding newly perfumed seeds (*navavāsanā*) are as recorded in that treatise.
Furthermore, regarding the [passage] from "birth and death" to "meaning," it is explained as before.
The commentary states: In the second instance, Jī says that "cause" is named *qǐzhǒng* (arising-seed), and "name" is named *míngyánzhǒng* (linguistic-expression-seed).
Cè says that the Sanskrit term is *nāma*, which here means "name. "Name" carries the sense of "that toward which one turns" and the sense of "tending toward"; all phenomena are turned toward [it].
This refers to "naming" (*nāman*). As in the fifty-six [factors], the four aggregates (*skandha*) proceed in accordance with various objects of perception (*ālambana*).

Based on conventional designations (*vyavahāra-nāman*), one discriminates the meanings of those various objects of perception; this is taught as "naming. Regarding the phrase "following the two types of names":

if naming were non-existent, it would not possess the nature of a causal condition (*pratyaya*); likewise, form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates would not be the substance of the two types of names. Nevertheless, they follow the two names.

Regarding the characteristics of the manifested [objects] and so forth, each perfumes its own seeds of verbal designation (nāma-vikalpa-bīja) [this is the intended meaning of the *Ji-shu*]. A question is raised:
since these two types of verbal designations encompass only nine elements (*dhātu*), how can they be reconciled with the seeds of all eighteen elements? The Tripiṭaka Master explains:

for instance, the seed of the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of visual consciousness acts as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the seeds of the visible form and its acquisition (*prāpti*); depending on conditions, it can give rise to the eye-consciousness, the mental consciousness, and the fundamental storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Because they are divided into three aspects (*trilakṣaṇa*), and because they are equally within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and of the same nature, the seeds of the aspect-division (*nimittabhāga*) of such mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), in relation to the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), are all *hetupratyaya* (causal conditions).

This demonstrates that [the seeds] are produced by the power of two types of designation (*nāmakalpanā*): the designation of the manifesting object (*viṣayapradarśana*) which follows the meaning of the expressed term, and the designation of the reflection (*pratibimba*) of the eighteen realms, because of the perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Question: What is the designation for the "seeing aspect" (*darśanabhāga*) of visual consciousness? Tse says: There are two meanings for the seeing aspect. First, it is manifest...

The names of objects are of two kinds. Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes names as its object, it is produced by being led by names; thus, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is also twofold.

[This is distinguished] from the manifesting aspect (*darśanabhāga*) based on the distinction of the objects revealed. It is indirectly due to names. (This interpretation is incorrect. It is because the seeds perfumed by the power of names are called "name-words" (*nāma-vāk-bīja*). Not all seeds are themselves names.)

The *Commentary on the Basis* (*Cheng weishi lun shuji*) is superior. Since it is already granted that the manas is designated by the term "manifesting," why must form and the other [objects] possess both types of designation? Question: Are the seeds of the eye and so forth designated by a single name?

They are distinguished by name because they collectively give rise to the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). The Tripiṭaka-master says: "The designations for the five destinies do not overlap or confuse one another.
The Abhidharma-śāstra states: "Because there are specific, determinate causes, the five destinies are distinct; likewise, the various heavens and the four continents are also not confused."

It arises through the assistance of those karmas for its manifestation; if it is of the same category, it arises by constantly employing a single *dharmatā* seed of verbal designation (*nāma-vāsanā*), because there is no dual function.
The same applies to the untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding this, the disciples of Dharmapāla offer two interpretations:

that [the fruit] arises from *dharmatā*, or that it is produced by new perfuming (*navābhyāsa*). Tiaofu previously stated that there are two kinds, new and old: one is at the very moment of arising, while the other...
It is solely through the power of assistance that not even a single sprout is produced. The Son of the Most Victorious One (Jinaputra) says:

"When their powers are equal, they together produce a single fruit, such as a single grain of barley, because it is composed of many subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). Regarding the statement that "the grasping at self has two [aspects]," the *Ji* and *Ce* commentaries state:

"This applies to both the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses]; it is not like the *Saṃgrahaṇī*, which explains only the seventh. The *Guān* commentary states: "The *Saṃgrahaṇī* also applies to the sixth [consciousness]. Worldly...

The third [section] on "intimacy" (pratyaya) states: that which is oneself is taken as "self," and that which is other than oneself is taken as "other. The fourth [section] on "lack of intrinsic nature" (niḥsvabhāva) concerns the grasping at "self" and "what belongs to self" (ātman-ātmīya), and "other" and "what belongs to other.

[Question: How does this fruit differ from the fruit of the seeds of conventional designation (nāma-vyavahāra)? [Answer: The former is real and the latter is provisional; it is like the distinction between two separate entities. If it were not so, then even among the Buddhas there would still be a distinction between self and other, and one would have to discuss such a fruit.

However, their characteristics do not differ. As for the term "limbs" (*aṅga*), "limb" has the meaning of "cause," because the three existences have causes; or it has the meaning of "constituent part," because they are the causes for the differentiation of destinies.
Ji says: "Only the first [of the two types] universally applies to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as it also relies on the manifestation of meaning to reveal the object and its perfuming."

Ce says: "If the two types of perfuming are definitively *nāma-vikalpa* (name-and-conceptualization), there are also instances of *nāma-vikalpa* that are not these two types of perfuming—namely, the remaining indeterminate seeds, excluding those of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
As for the unwholesome view of self, it is perfumed by all three [types of] seeds within its own substance; this can be understood from the text."
Furthermore, regarding the meaning from "birth and death" up to [the end], it is as previously recorded.

The commentary states: Within the third section, there are two parts—the brief and the detailed. This is the first. Regarding the afflictions that initiate karma and moisten rebirth, the *Fifty-nine [Treatises]* states:
"All afflictions are capable of initiating and moistening; however, only those that arise through discrimination [do so]."
"Setting forth toward a bad result. *Ce* says: "Setting forth toward the results of the happy realms; it may arise simultaneously [with the intention]. *Ji* says:

The first volume of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "If one performs various meritorious formations (*puṇya-saṃskāra*) through sensual craving, one performs these formations based on that faith as a support."

Because one gives rise to firm conviction regarding birth and death, this craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are subdued by that conviction; I designate them as obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
This textual passage serves as proof that, apart from the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, there also exist independent unspecified cravings and other factors.

That is to say, craving arises taking future existence as its object and moistens rebirth (this clarifies that while these innate factors lack the power to incite evil, they nevertheless assist in the arousal of the wholesome, let alone their ability to moisten rebirth). However, they do exist.

There are two meanings (as recorded in the *Mahā-śāstra*). Afflictions (*kleśa*) are that which adhere, and suffering (*duḥkha*) is that to which they adhere. Sentient beings in the world do not frequently give rise to attachment toward the fruit [of suffering] (Master Ji says:
"This shows that, according to reality, it is also that to which one adheres; however, because it is not frequent [as a locus of attachment], it is not so categorized").
"These afflictions, karma, and suffering (up to the point mentioned) are all not the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

The commentary states: In the second [section], the broad exposition, the headings and explanations can be understood. The explanation consists of five parts: first, the brief enumeration of the factors;

second, the resolution of difficulties; third, the realms and stages; fourth, cause and effect; and fifth, the various categories (Master Ji’s *Shu* has ten categories; Master Ce’s *Shu* has seven categories). These explain the twelve links. However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts all establish them as such.

[This is] the text (as it is not narrated here). The first section also has four parts; this is the initial summary. Because of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), they cause the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth to possess the function of producing their respective fruits;

this is called "that which can induce" (*ākṣepaka*). In the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, fascicle 7, it states that if the karma produced and the fruit obtained are both cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), then in the second stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the karma of errant transgressions. This clearly shows that cognitive obstructions also have the capacity to produce [karmic results].

Although karma is what initiates [the process], it does not necessarily result in that specific lifetime; therefore, the text here specifies "that which directly results in that lifetime. Furthermore, there are three categories:
(1) those that initiate both the general and the particular, (2) those that initiate only the general, and (3) those that initiate only the particular.

Only the first two are taken here, as they serve as the primary causes for projecting the retribution. The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "External phenomena and ordinary beings are initiated by the four types of ignorance."

Regarding meritorious and other types of formations (*saṃskāra*): among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal dharma, if they are heedless (*pramatta*), with the exception of the single unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), the remaining types of ignorance give rise to non-meritorious and other formations; therefore, it is said that ignorance is the condition for the arising of formations.

If they are not heedless, or if they are noble learners (*śaikṣa*), the three types of ignorance serve as conditions for non-merit; however, non-merit cannot [in turn] act as a condition for [ignorance].
Because they invite the three evil destinies, these are not meritorious. I do not say that these are formations conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, through non-negligence, one performs meritorious and immovable karma; although this results in a superior rebirth, it is not said to be formations conditioned by ignorance.
For noble learners (*śaikṣa*), who have already abandoned the unique [unwholesome roots], no new karma is created. Kīrti says: "If one is negligent, there are three types..."

That which is incited by ignorance is distinguished from this [state of] non-negligence; thus, it is said that conduct is not incited by ignorance, because the ignorance associated with active manifestation does not arise.
It is not the case that the seeds of that ignorance fail to incite afflictions or produce the retributive result.

It is not said that internal factors cause ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to create new karma; for although those who are heedful may perform non-meritorious actions in the present, these do not constitute projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) that leads to rebirth in the three miserable realms.

Therefore, they are not described as "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance. Furthermore, although meritorious and immovable karma are indeed projecting karma that brings about superior births, because they do not arise with present actions as their condition, they are likewise not described as "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance.
It should be understood that even the wholesome qualities of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and skillful means still possess a general projecting power at that stage.

Because it is a wholesome state acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*). This is included within the member of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*), as it is accepted that this path-factor still brings about a general retribution (*vipāka-phala*). However, this contradicts various teachings because the members of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) are not [states of] those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth.

As Vasubandhu states in his *Vyākhyā*: "It is actually a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Alternatively, it is said that those two types of preparatory wholesome dharmas (*prayoga-kuśala-dharma*) do not bring about a general retribution, but are merely causes for specific retributions (*pratyeka-vipāka-hetu*).

It is not a factor of right practice (*samyak-pratipatti-aṅga*), nor is it subsumed under non-practice. This is not so; for otherwise, distinct karma would not be called "karma," and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth—which are induced by karma—would not be subsumed under "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
However, the intention of this treatise is to take only the primary [factors]. Thus, for now, those associated with practice and what is induced by them are excluded.

(In this context, "distinct" karma is metaphorically termed "formations" because it arises intermittently during the stages of meritorious and discerning karma; by association, it is also called meritorious or immovable formations, as they do not entirely lack projecting power like the state of an Arya. As in the case of the six [consciousnesses].

Seventeenth, it says: "Those who follow liberation," etc. Although their nature involves aversion [to suffering], they assist other merits; thus they are also called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). Ce (Cesheng) explains this in three ways: first, he says they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) regarding external phenomena.

Due to ignorance, merit, and so forth, all are termed "formations conditioned by ignorance. Internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*) are not like this, because they do not possess these four [conditions].

(This contradicts [the view that] although it is said that the various fetters and karmas are "formations conditioned by ignorance" based on only three [conditions], [they actually lack one]). One explanation states: although the four are not complete, they nonetheless manifest.

It also produces collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*). Regarding "ignorance conditions formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*): [formations] such as those resulting from non-negligence and merit do not project a [new] birth (*ākṣepaka-phala*).

Or, even if they do project one, because they are projected by a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*), they are likewise not said to be "conditioned by ignorance. (The phrase "projected by a wholesome mind" clarifies that it is not projected by manifest (*samudācāra*) ignorance. One interpretation states:
those who practice non-negligence up to the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) also project a [new] birth; thus, formations conditioned by ignorance [apply to them].
The Sūtra merely negates that noble ones (*ārya*) create new karma. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:

"Even though those who have not yet seen the truths give rise to wholesome thoughts, because they are deluded regarding the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), they produce the cause for future existence (*punarbhava*). Thus, although [such thoughts] are produced from the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā*)," [they do not constitute new karma for the noble ones].

Because they do not manifest [in the present life]. First, with respect to negligence (*pramāda*), the Sūtra does not state that "ignorance conditions formations" (as stated by [Kui]ji in his initial explanation;

this has already been refuted above. Here we retain Ji’s later view, which is superior among the interpretations of [Dao]ce). Regarding those [karmic results] such as the favorable-in-this-life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) that are not members of the "formations" (*saṃskāra*) link, Ce states two interpretations. The first says:

Those that accord with the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) induce only the retribution of consciousness; however, those that accord with both future and present lives induce [retribution] in both future and present births, because the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) receive retribution in the present life.

Nevertheless, they are called "immediate" (*ānantarya*) karmas from the perspective of their primary nature. As for the statement in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* that karma which accords with the present may induce retribution over many lifetimes, this reflects the intention of the commentator.

It is not established as a definitive rule [that this karma ripens in the present life and draws forth multiple births—just as the *ānantarya* [karma] is included within the *saṃskāra-aṅga* (the link of volitional formations) yet, in this treatise, it is categorized under "subsequent birth" and only induces retribution in the present life, being termed "karma conducive to the present" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*)].
One might say: "Karma conducive to the present also induces multiple births; however, what is excluded here is only that which induces the present. This is also incorrect.

If it were to induce multiple births, it would likewise be a *saṃskāra-aṅga*, which would contradict the treatise’s statement that "all karma conducive to the present is not a *saṃskāra-aṅga*. Alternatively, it may be that although it is conducive to the present, even if it were to induce...

It is produced over many lifetimes; it is only a completing karma (*pūraka-karman*) and not an attracting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*). Therefore, there is no contradiction. (This is excellent. Furthermore, regarding the five immediate offenses (*pañcānantarya*), in terms of both their essence and their meaning, if categorized according to the category of karma ripening in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), they are exclusively karma of distinct retribution (*pratiniyata-vipāka-karman*).)

If it follows the gate of successive rebirth (*upapatti-dvāra*), it encompasses both the general and the specific; that is to say, because the preparatory application of karma (*karma-prayoga*) brings about results in the present life. Question: Since the moisture [of defilements] in ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) must manifest, how can there be the arousal [of seeds] by seeds alone?

Answer: At the stage of the inferior mind at the moment of death, even noble ones (*ārya*) cannot suppress it. Question: Regarding the statement "internal and external phenomena," what is their status? Answer:
They belong to the sons of the Buddha (*jinaputra*) or to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), or to those who have not yet planted the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
"Second, because the drawn-out branches [of existence] (*ākṣiptāṅga*) necessarily do not coexist.
The commentary states: This is the second abbreviated text, referring to the seeds of the five fruits and their causes and conditions. There are two successive expositions.

First, the seeds of the *ālayavijñāna* in its unmixed essence are established as the branch of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*), excluding the seeds of the subsequent six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).

The remaining *vipāka* (maturation) phenomena are termed the "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) limb. This consists of fourteen factors as its substance: namely, the five sense objects, perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manasikāra*), the five specific-object mental factors, and the indeterminate factor of sleep (*middha*).

When combined with the subsequent intermingled factors—excluding the manas consciousness—the seven remaining consciousnesses each have five universal and five specific factors, plus the indeterminate sleep;
together with the five sense faculties and the five sense objects, these total twenty-eight, all of which are termed [the name-and-form limb].

It is subsumed under form (*rūpa*). Among the various types of maturation, the four remaining [aggregates] are distinguished as the primary causes of retribution according to their predominance. They experience objects through contact (*sparśa*), as each is predominant in its respective order.
However, although there are ninety-three [factors], the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are provisionally designated as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) because they are the most prominent.
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the general category, while the consciousness (*vijñāna*) and mind (*manas*) bases are specific instances. Cè (測) states:

"If one relies on this gate, consciousness is said to have causes and conditions, such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth. However, in the subsequent text, according to the first sequence, it is said to be without causes and conditions.

Since it is stated that [the teaching] relies on the non-confused explanation, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) encompasses both the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the projected (*ākṣipta*). This refers to the upper fascicle of that [sūtra]."
It is said: "One portion—namely, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—is also called 'that which is produced' (*janyamāna*). Master Ji says:

This is spoken in reference to their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), not to the seeds (*bīja*), which are thus termed "produced. Although consciousness is also like this—functioning as both that which induces and that which is induced—it is omitted here for brevity.

There is one portion of feeling called "that which produces" (*janaka*), because it refers to feeling that grasps objects (*viṣaya-vedanā*) and excludes feeling that is a result of maturation (*vipāka-vedanā*). This is due to two reasons.

There is a sequential order in their explanation. First, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the primary recipient of retribution (*vipākādhipati*), while the other four are its companions. Among the companions, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the aggregate, while the other three are specific.

Among the specific factors, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are predominant, while the other two are subordinate. Among the subordinate factors, contact (*sparśa*) is the cause and feeling (*vedanā*) is the result.
Second, there is a distinction based on the stages of arising in the future and the present, as stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*: they simultaneously perfume and trigger one another.

According to the sequence to be explained hereafter, it is exactly the same. Because this relies on the perspective of what will arise in the future, treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Abhidharma*, and the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* all state that the five factors—consciousness and so forth—are "active" (*samudācāra*). This is because, while in the state of a cause, they certainly do not exist as manifest phenomena;
thus, we know that [the term] refers to the future fruit when applied to the present cause. Furthermore, by means of this perspective, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "If..."

If [the projecting cause] were to project [the result] at the same time as it arises, then because the state of being moistened and the state of not yet being moistened would not actually coexist, we know that the present cause is metaphorically designated by the name of the future result (this is the intended meaning of the treatise).

However, Cè’s Commentary (*Shūki*) states: "Regarding the stages of arising and aging, one speaks of consciousness and so forth in a figurative sense, because at the time of the cause, there is definitely no sense of actual manifestation.
Furthermore, by this principle, the projecting [cause] and the arising [result] are simultaneous; at the moment the produced [result] arises..."

It possesses both the projectors (*ākṣepaka*) and the projected (*ākṣipta*). Among these four, three are of the same moment. First is that which is produced (*janyamāna*); second is the projector; third is the projected.

If one speaks of the four as being simultaneous in terms of a long duration—that is, within a single lifetime—it is because it possesses both the projectors and the projected, as well as both the producers (*janaka*) and the produced.
This is the intended meaning of the *Ki* commentary. After that [moment of] moistening, at the stage of what is about to arise...
Regarding the explanation of "projecting birth" (*janmākṣepa*): it is accepted that there are six distinct factors—such as the formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth—that exist simultaneously;

these are termed the "projecting members" (*ākṣepakāṅga*), and taken collectively they are called "existence" (*bhava*). This is established as the member of birth (*jātyaṅga*). [Objection: Although this may seem logical, it contradicts the intent of the treatise (*śāstra*). To metaphorically designate the future fruit within the present causal stage in order to manifest the distinctions of the cause is precisely the tenet of this treatise. However, the two commentaries explain this by metaphorically designating the prior projecting [factors] within the subsequent stage of birth.

How could this conform to the meaning of the treatise? Furthermore, Master Cè states: "If one considers a long duration, a single body possesses all four [members of existence]; this is also not logically sound. This is because once the fruit has been moistened, its production constitutes a separate body. If, however, one relies on the perspective of the seeds (*bīja*), the meaning is complete.
[The third category is] the "producing factors" (janaka-aṅga), because they possess four [factors] within a single moment.
[This refers to] the "producing factors" (tṛtīya-janaka-aṅga), because they serve as the seeds for consciousness and so forth.

The commentary states: The third [category] is the abbreviated factors, namely the three beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The phrase "conditioned by... and below restates the projecting and projected [factors]. Furthermore...

The section beginning with "Based on [the aforementioned]" correctly explains that which gives rise to delusion regarding internal results and so forth; as it is explained extensively in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra-vyākhyā*, there is no need for further elaboration here.

Regarding the phrase "giving rise to craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), this refers to the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*). In the lower fascicle of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, four types of craving are mentioned:

namely, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), craving for renewed existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), craving accompanied by greed (*rāga-sahagata-tṛṣṇā*), and delighting in this and that (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī*). The commentary states that these correspond respectively to: 1. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) 2. Craving for renewed existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) 3. Craving accompanied by greed (*rāga-sahagata-tṛṣṇā*) 4. Delighting in this and that (*tatra-tatrābhinandinī*)

Since it is thus that [ignorance] arises within the present and future self-entities and their constituents, and since the first two [types of ignorance] are deluded regarding internal maturation (*vipāka*), why is it said here that they are "deluded regarding the dominant fruit" (*adhipatiphala*)?

Although they take the internal body as their object, the objective field (*viṣaya*) comes first; this is because, like craving for one's own self-identity (*ātmabhāvatanhā*), they are solely deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*).

This delusion regarding the characteristics of phenomena is recorded in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. Regarding the four graspings, such as desire and so forth, these are the limb of grasping (*upādāna*). [End of excerpt from] the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Treatise, Chapter Ten. It takes up only the category of *rāga* (greed). As stated in [the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*,] fascicle 89: "It encompasses both the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), as well as that for which one grasps (*yad-artham-upādānam*);

these are collectively termed 'clinging' (*upādāna*). Greed is the grasper; desire and so forth are the grasped. One grasps them in order to obtain desire and so forth, and for the sake of the function of craving. As for that for which one grasps—such as the actual five sense objects—they are not themselves the moistening essence;

however, because they are conducive [to clinging], they are also included in 'clinging,' just as in the case of the mindfulness of objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*). This treatise, following the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, explains all afflictions by encompassing both the primary and auxiliary causes of moistening. [This is the view of] Bas.

It is said: "In this context, the two delusions (*moha*) are explained according to the sense of being predominant (*anuśaya*). In reality, however, delusion regarding the internal also moistens rebirth (*upapatti*), and delusion regarding external objects is also capable of initiating karma (*karma-samutthāna*), because it is taught that all afflictions (*kleśa*) both initiate and moisten [rebirth]. Only 'karmic existence' (*karma-bhava*) is mentioned, as in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other treatises.
Only five types are mentioned. Cè (Cè-lùn) says: 'The first chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that it is called 'existence' (*bhava*) because it is like the five kinds of seeds.'"

This refers to the appropriation of consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*). It means that because the seed-consciousness is moistened by appropriation, it [functions as such]. Master Ji says: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle five, explains the cause of arising (*utpatti-hetu*);
it is subsumed under the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*). Since that [appropriation] serves as the cause of arising for the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is so designated."
"The fourth, from the 'limb produced' (*jāta*) up to what is called death.

The commentary states: "The fourth [section] summarizes the limbs. *Cè* says: Because it explains the combination of the fundamental [limbs] and the production of the preparatory stages (*prayoga*), it is said that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is also subsumed under the category of the 'produced limb.
*Jī* says: That which is about to enter the phase of cessation is called the 'death limb. The essence of the phase of cessation is non-existent."

They are not factors of dependent origination; they are merely designated by the names of the three characteristics for the purpose of engendering revulsion. Their substance is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), not merely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Old age is not necessarily present [in all cases]... (up to)... this is said to be an increase of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

The commentary states: This is the second section, the explanation of objections. First, there is a preliminary objection: "Since aging and death have distinct characteristics, why are they established as a single category?

The intent of the explanation follows the text (Master Ji provides many questions and answers outside of the main text; these are found generally in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Mātṛkā*). Regarding the lack of pervasiveness and necessity of illness:
even if one enters a birth that includes places where illness occurs, it is not necessarily present, as was the case with the Venerable Bakula, who lived past the age of eighty.
For one lifetime, there is no affliction. Regarding "one part of all": ignorance, craving, and grasping are exclusively obscured [neutral], because they are only obscuring;

volitional formations and existence are exclusively wholesome, because their fruit is exclusively celestial. If the mind of the formless realm is what is meant by "name," why does the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* say:
If, in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there were only its name and it did not abide in form (*rūpa*) while arising in continuity, this would be unreasonable.

One interpretation states: that sutra speaks based on the realms possessing form. Another interpretation states: that sutra speaks generally of the seeds (*bīja*). As stated in the *Nin-jū-san* (Ninety-three [Sūtras]):
"In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the name serves as the support for consciousness (*vijñāna*) by means of the seeds of form. If that is so, then consciousness—
The branches (*aṅga*) also depend on other stages (*bhūmi*). Why, then, does the text below state that "only the formations (*saṃskāra*) depend on the lower [stages]"?

Cè (Cè) says: That treatise speaks figuratively according to the general trend, or it refers only to a partial aspect; therefore, there is no contradiction. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not depend on others because it is the entirety of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Jī (Jī) says: There is no fault in its depending on the seeds of form belonging to its own stage (*svabhūmi*). Fàn (Fàn) says: This is not so, for they are not maturation (*vipāka*). Regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*) not being universal (*sarvatraga*): it is as when one takes [something] as an object...
The first volume begins by asking: "If it were said that craving alone acts as a condition for existence (*bhava*) without being a condition for grasping (*upādāna*), what fault would there be?
The Blessed One replied: "Craving is defined as seeking. One does not seek the miserable realms (*apāya*); yet, through non-meritorious action (*apuṇya*), a contrary result arises.
How could this be conditioned by craving? For one who lacks craving seeks non-existence (*vibhava*). Through meritorious and immovable action..."

This contradicts the arising of the fruit. How could it be that all craving (*tṛṣṇā*) takes grasping (*upādāna*) as its condition? We know that craving is not universal, whereas the aggregate-factors (*skandha*) alone are universal.

Having understood this, the objection is resolved. Is it not the case that a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) does not seek? Without seeking, there is no existence (*bhava*). Regarding the intent of the treatise’s explanation:

for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), moisture is manifest; thus, it is determined based on the manifest. For noble ones (*ārya*), moisture exists as seeds; thus, it is determined based on the seeds. A non-returner is like one who possesses grasping and craving.

This is also the certainty of the planting [of seeds]. Furthermore, as for the subsequent statement that "craving is also pervasive," it means that there is craving both for the present self and for present objects.

Alternatively, when the self is taken as the object, it is called the "present self-object. While this may apply to those dying in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as described, what present craving exists for one passing away from the higher realms?
If it were craving for the desire realm, it would not be an object of the present; if it were [craving] for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)...

Regarding craving for one’s own realm (*dhātu-tṛṣṇā*), it should be understood as depending on other stages (*bhūmi*). Master Ce offers two interpretations. The first says: "For now, based on the explanation of death in a lower stage, craving is also universal;

however, when one dies in a higher stage and is reborn in an evil destiny (*apāya*), the remaining links [of dependent origination]—excluding volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)—depend upon their own stage. The second says: [omitted].
Once one has been born into the miserable realms (*durgati*), there is a craving for a truly existent self; this is not, however, the very craving that moistens birth.

Although there are these two interpretations, the latter accords with the intent of the sūtras. That is to say, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* refers to those already born, stating that they do not give rise to craving toward their wretched bodies.
The *Buddhadhyāna-samādhi-sūtra*, on the other hand, refers to the time when one is about to be born, asserting that one gives rise to perverted craving toward pleasant appearances. (From the *Shu*)
It is said: If one dies and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the evil is extremely heavy; having seen the signs of evil, one does not give rise to longing.

Since the offenses of the desire realm are light, if one dies and is reborn in the two higher realms and falls into an evil destiny (*apāya*), one does not see the signs of evil, but sees only inverted signs.
Regarding the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*): it is not so. If it were otherwise, there would be no craving or grasping (*upādāna*) for those who have died in the higher realms.

This is because, although they exist in the present and future, [beings there] simply do not crave [those realms]. (The *Shuyao* is superior [in its analysis]. If, as in Cè’s commentary, one must necessarily give rise to craving toward inverted characteristics, then the treatise should have used this to prove that craving is also universal. Why labor to cite "self-love after birth" as proof? There is no basis for excluding "moistening," yet it says "not moistening.

It is clearly known that there may be cases where longing-craving does not arise; rather, one merely takes up the moisture of the present existence in the evil destinies). As for the statement that at the time of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*), the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is manifested: from...

Among these, there is the first [existence], up to the existence of birth (*upapatti-bhava*). Regarding the statement "if one reaches the present," *Cè* says: "As in [the section on] the fifty-six [links].
Furthermore, the five members subsumed under the present fruit, as well as the two members subsumed under the future fruit, are called 'fruition-dependent origination' (*phala-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Moreover, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that the five members in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) serve to make known the stages [of existence]. (In some places, the fruit of the prior limit is divided into five types.)

Regarding the "thirteen bodhisattvas who observe in reverse," there are instances where the results of the future limit (*aparānta*) are divided into five types, as stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*. As for the statement that "craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is like water and so forth," the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* says:
"Because it is moistened by water, it must be irrigated repeatedly. This is a metaphor for how rain moistens the seeds of worldly crops to produce sprouts.

Regarding the phrase "although [it is] taken within the [twelve] links": in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Daśabhūmika*, craving is called "grasping" (*upādāna*) because the power of its moistening is predominant.
It is not that there are no remaining afflictions, nor is it merely their category; rather, it must be the superior branch of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Thus, the various branches of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) do not contradict reason.
The commentary states: regarding the third realm and stage, Kuiji says, "All rely on their own stage," which likewise takes the fifty-six [branches] as the basis.

Regarding that "one who possesses ignorance," it is the same as in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*. However, this applies only to the lower realms; in the initial arising of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), all cases are like this.

(This master previously maintained that non-heedlessness (*apramāda*) consists only of the seeds that trigger karma; however, the present text provisionally discusses external factors and internal heedlessness. Ce says: The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states:

"Bound by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of delusion regarding the true meaning. This is explained as follows: although [the production of phenomena] necessarily depends upon seeds, it must also rely upon their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).

Therefore, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* states: "External phenomena arise from four [conditions]; internal [phenomena] arise from three. Thus, one knows that [arising] cannot occur through seeds alone. (The Master preserves this point:

if it were produced by seeds alone, then since [the result] would not be improperly induced, he would not have stated that "ignorance conditions formations"; therefore, this is incorrect. If that were so, since [the case of seeds] would be identical to that of the Noble Ones, there should be no separate explanation. Whether manifest or...

Regarding the "seed" (*bīja*): according to the moisture provided by the arising of doubt, it is clarified that it must necessarily arise from its own level (*svabhūmi*). Therefore, the word "also" (*api*) is used. The two commentaries state:

"The 'present' refers to that which is associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*), while the 'seed' is that which is moistened. Cè (Cèlún) says: "Alternatively, it is not necessary for them to be simultaneous;
because [the seed] relies on distant factors such as concentration (*samādhi*) and so forth, they are associated through indirect dependence."
These twelve links [would] lead to infinity. The commentary states:
Regarding the fourth cause and effect, "this world" refers to the world of birth. Among these, the first seven and the [last] three—if they follow in the same lifetime—are of the same world;

if they follow in a subsequent lifetime, they are of different worlds. These constitute the two aspects of birth and death. Ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the three [links of the future].
These seven [factors] are each fixed as being of the same time period (*adhvan*). This differs from the Sarvāstivāda position, which allows for the projection of karma across different time periods;

that is, the *anāgamya-samādhi* (preparatory concentration) is said to have "ignorance as a condition for formations" (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskārāḥ*) by virtue of past ignorance belonging to its own level (*svabhūmi*).

The Sarvāstivādins (*Sabbatthavādino*) maintain that two causes in the past produce five fruits in the present, and three causes in the present obtain two fruits in the future. Regarding past ignorance...

In the present, these are designated as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*). As for the five effects in the present, if they occur in the future, they are designated as birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This establishes two layers of cause and effect, which are not different from a single layer; a second layer would be redundant, as a single layer is sufficient to manifest the process of saṃsāra.
The mention of causes refutes eternalism (*śāśvata*), while the mention of effects refutes nihilism (*uccheda*). The causes reside in the past, and the effects...
The cause is in the present, while the fruit is in the future; since they fully possess the functions of producing and nourishing, they truly span two time periods.
However, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, chapter eight, states: "Ignorance and formations are seen as matters of the past;

consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are seen as matters of the present; craving, grasping, becoming, birth, old age, and death are seen [as matters of the future]."

Regarding the phrase "matters of future lives," the Tripitaka Master examined the Sanskrit original and found that it simply mentions the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), the middle limit (*madhyānta*), and the subsequent limit (*aparānta*), but does not mention the "three periods" (*tryadhvan*).
That [text] clarifies the ten causes based on these three stages; furthermore, the Sanskrit original does not mention birth, old age, and death.
Although one layer is sufficient, you insist on explaining two layers; one should then explain a third, which would lead to an infinite regress. Ji says:

"In order to address those who are ignorant regarding the prior limit [of existence], two causes are explained beyond [the first]. Yet, there may be others even more ignorant regarding the limit prior to that; for them, two causes would still be too few."
Furthermore, one should explain that because causes exist in the past and future, there are two fruits;

yet for those who are still deluded regarding the subsequent limits [of time], these two fruits are insufficient, and thus one must further explain the fruits. Therefore, the treatise states: "Or it should exceed this.

However, by explaining a single layer, the refutation of eternalism and nihilism is completed, which simultaneously reveals the preceding and succeeding [stages]. The same applies to the preceding and succeeding [stages].
Because these twelve links [from ignorance] up to birth and so forth are so designated.
The commentary states: The fifth section on various categories contains seventeen doors. This first is the door of the provisional and the real.

That which grasps others as its own is called "provisional" (*prajñapti*); if it does not grasp others, it is called "real. For example, among the formations (*saṃskāra*), there are both the provisional and the non-manifest (*avijñapti*). However...
"Accompanied by real entities. This is because it does not grasp the preceding [factors].
"Five are one matter; the rest are not one matter. The commentary states:

The second [section] is the gate of "one is not a single entity. Ce says: "Consciousness" refers exclusively to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). Ji says: [The five are one matter because they share a common basis.]

Because it is solely the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) [that is intended here]—the latter being superior—if one were to follow the treatise’s exposition of the six consciousnesses as the members, then all mind-kings (*cittarāja*) taken together would be called "one thing. Likewise, one should also take the members that are mental concomitants (*caitta*) as being "one thing.
Since formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth pertain to both the nature of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), they are not called "one thing."
"Three are exclusively defiled; the remainder are common to both [defiled and non-defiled]. The commentary states:
This is the third section, the gate of the defiled and non-defiled. As the *Mahā-śāstra*, fascicle ten, says: "Three are defiled; the remainder are common to both."
The commentary explains: Because they can give rise to defilement; because other formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) can be either wholesome or defiled;
and because ignorance, craving, and grasping—up to the rest—are of a mixed character.

The commentary states: Regarding the fourth section on the characteristics of the distinct and the mixed, *Ce* says: "Although it is taught that the increase of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called 'clinging' (*upādāna*), because there is a distinction between what increases and what does not increase, they are not mixed [in this sense].

This is not the intended meaning of this treatise. Although all afflictions are subsumed within the limb of clinging, it is specifically called the 'increase of craving' because craving moistens and causes them to increase;

it does not mean that the inferior limb of craving itself transforms and increases into clinging. The meaning according to reality is as explained in the *Mātṛkā*. *Ji* says: "Although craving is predominant within clinging, it is not the case that craving itself transforms into an increase."

Because [the text] speaks of "greed" (upādāna) at the beginning, this accords with the intent of the treatise. Furthermore, the phrase "there is another dharma" indicates that there are other afflictions besides greed; therefore, it is not a case of "mixed characteristics. This is incorrect, lest one conclude that consciousness and name-and-form do not possess mixed characteristics.

The five factors—volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth—and the two factors—existence (*bhava*) and birth (*jāti*)—are called "mixed characteristics" because their essential natures are not distinct.
That their essential natures are not distinct accords with the fundamental tenets of the *Mātṛkā*.
Six are exclusively non-form (up to: ...), while the remainder pertain to both types.
The commentary states: This is the fifth gate, concerning form and non-form;
all are contaminated (up to: ...), because they are not factors of existence.

The commentary states: The sixth [category] is the outflow-free (anāsrava), and the seventh serves as the door to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). This distinguishes [the present system] from the Mahāsāṃghika, Mahīśāsaka, and other schools, which regard dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as unconditioned.
"Ignorance, craving, and grasping (up to [becoming]) also arise as wholesome and deep.

Commentary: This is the eighth section, the gate of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). Master Ji states: "The primary factor of the ignorance link is unwholesome in the desire realm; the auxiliary factors are generally obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). Craving and its auxiliaries are the opposite of this.
As for the ninth, the mind at the moment of death, it is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*); therefore, the four types of grasping in the desire realm are so described."

This is unwholesome, because the treatises are not uniform. The *Mahā-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states: "Four [links] are exclusively defiled; the others pertain to both the defiled and the pure. That [text] refers to the defilement of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*);

this treatise, however, defines it according to its intrinsic nature. As for the five resultant links, they are explained as being both defiled and pure in terms of their stages (*avasthā*) as they occur in the place of rebirth.
This is because the two meanings of old age and death arise within a single stage as defilement, just as stated in this treatise.

It is so. Because the two [types of compassion] frequently give rise to attachment and sorrow, as intended in the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*; the *Ji-shu* interprets it thus, though the intent of the *Mahā-śāstra* is as explained in that commentary).
Although both are common to all three realms, they are distinguished as being partial or complete.

The commentary states: This is the ninth section, the "Three Realms" gate. It refers to the entirety of the desire realm and a portion of the realms above. For instance, ignorance in the higher realms is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
furthermore, up to old age and death, the five aggregates are not fully present. These points should be understood as appropriate.
"Because one arises from the factors of the higher stages (up to that point). The commentary states:

This is the tenth gate, concerning the relationship between the remedial and the remediated. There is only one factor of practice (*pratipad-aṅga*) that remedies all the lower factors. As the *Mahā-śāstra* says:
"Is there a case where one relies on a factor [of a higher stage] yet abandons a factor [of a lower stage]? The answer is: Yes."
"All are exclusively [so], up to and including no contradiction with principle.

The commentary states: Regarding the eleventh section on the "Gates of Training" (*śikṣā-mukha*), some say that based on this text, one knows that the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) and so forth all produce a collective retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*).
Others say that this text merely speaks of those who definitely do not create [new karma], as explained extensively before; such is not the case for the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the creation of karma: how does one give birth to the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) realms? Jizang states: When a noble one practices the mixed meditations (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*), they take the karma that serves as the support for the three lower heavens—Anabhraka (Cloudless) and so forth—and thereby give birth to the Śuddhāvāsa realms.
The term "and so forth" includes the palaces of the Bodhisattvas and Maheśvara. This is the karma of total retribution (*vipāka-karma*) and is designated as the seeds of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*).

While still an ordinary being, one has already created the karma for the three lower heavens; because it is bound to a single level of existence (*bhūmi*), it arises through this supportive cultivation.

[Regarding this,] Ki’s commentary states thus (and Ce’s intention is likewise). Since [the fruit] is experienced in a different location, how can it be called "immovable" (*āniñjya*)? Ki says: "Because it remains fixed upon its object."
It is called "immovable karma. However, the Abhidharma states that it is "that which cannot be diverted to be experienced in another location.

This [interpretation] is incorrect, because it is spoken from the perspective of the majority; for the superior path and its heavy provisions are not indeterminate. That [karma] lacks the influence of such provisions and is by nature indeterminate, as it is experienced in a different location.
There is an interpretation [extending from] "ignorance" (avidyā) [up to] "as appropriate," which should be understood accordingly.

The commentary states: This twelfth section, the "Gate of the Two Abandonments," contains the interpretations of two masters. The textual characteristics are easy to understand. Regarding the statement that the "assistants" are not fixed:

according to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* and other texts, those abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) initiate karma; according to the *Abhidharma-kośa* and other treatises, those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) moisten rebirth.

However, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* maintains that both types of abandonment apply here, as they fully moisten the seeds throughout the realms; thus, it provides a comprehensive reconciliation. Regarding "that which is to be abandoned by its own nature":

this refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and their associated states that are unwholesome (*akuśala*) or obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). This is because when untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) arises, the seeds of darkness are immediately extinguished.

As for the statement "abandoning those [afflictions] that take them as objects and are associated with them," Cè (Cèlún) says: "The afflictions that take them as objects are identical [to those being abandoned]."

The Sarvāstivādins [assert that] one speaks of "severing the eye-faculty" because the afflictions that take the eye-faculty as their object are severed, and thus the faculty itself is freed from its bonds.
Jñānagarbha says: "When the afflicted states that take the seven consciousnesses as their objects—such as contaminated wholesome states and so forth—are severed, one speaks of 'severing the objects.

(While this accords with the Hīnayāna, it contradicts the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. For according to that, only present direct perception or the objects within its range possess the sense of being bound by objects, namely the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). How then could the five faculties and pure matter, which are wholesome or non-obscured-neutral, be considered contaminated merely by association [with the eye]?)

The *Jiyao* (Essential Points) contains five examples regarding the sense that the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the object of the seventh consciousness (*manas*), is bound; all of these refute this error. Regarding what is called "intermingling with that": at times it is also termed "attaining abandonment.
Second, there is the intermingling of various contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas before and after [the pure state], arising interspersed with the afflictions (*kleśa*) of their own stage.
This is said to be of two kinds: first, simultaneous intermingling, because all contaminated dharmas are established by the power of the afflictions of the *manas*.

The preceding and succeeding potencies of those black and white karmas are severed, rendering them incapable of functioning, just as the potencies of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna are attained through their preceding and succeeding stages.
However, this excludes the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) manas and the defiled or pure manas of other levels;

although the six consciousnesses may arise intermittently on other levels, they do not conform to the process of intensification. Question: If that which is associated with the seventh [consciousness] is called "mixed," then...

If one does not yet return to desire and possesses wholesome states, it should not be called "abandonment. Master Ji explains: "It is said to be 'abandoned' simply because the objects of cognition have been exhausted. Although there are still mixed afflictions, the sense-object (ālambana) is predominant;

thus, even as with what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), where the bonds of the objects are not yet exhausted, the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are also termed 'abandoned.

(The claim that all are termed 'bonds of the object' has already been refuted above). Now, taking the perspective of contemplation: the craving and so forth of the six consciousnesses are also mixed simultaneously; yet, because the six consciousnesses are exhausted, they are also termed 'freed from bonds.'"
(As explained in the *Mātṛkā*). Regarding the phrase "severing that basis" (*tad-āśraya-ccheda*): Cè (Cè) says that the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are called "that basis";

because when that basis is severed, the remainder is also extinguished. Jī (Jī) says that there are also cases where the cause is extinguished following the fruit, such as the wholesome karma that results in a separate retribution in the evil destinies (*durgati*).
This is not like the previous interpretation, for those [karmas] are also all extinguished following the afflictions of seeing. Regarding the phrase "the basis is freed from bondage":

Regarding the statement that [these afflictions] are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), Baso (基) says: Although the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) also take mixed objects as their conditions, because they have not yet been exhausted, they are not said to be "separated from bondage.

What is being discussed here, however, concerns those that have been fully exhausted; therefore, they are abandoned only through cultivation. This accords with the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (66), which states that abandonment occurs based on non-arising.

In the Mahāyāna, both types of cessation are attained through the path: analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which consists in the non-arising of the basis [of defilements]. This is stated in the *Pañcāśatikā-śāstra*:
"Because at the time of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one attains non-analytical cessation."

birth manifests the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); old age manifests the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); and death manifests the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are termed the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).

The remainder—namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are termed the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Master Ji states: "At the time when the agent and the object are being projected, the meaning of 'conditioned activity' (*saṃskāra*) predominates;
