Excluding the weak grade and so forth, there are fifty-five [moments].

*Ce* says: First, one abandons the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); next, one abandons the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*); finally, one abandons both simultaneously. The two preceding [stages] are uninterrupted (*ānantarya*).
The latter liberation is merely a designation for consciousness, as it does not constitute actual abandonment; this may be explained by Xian. Regarding the fifty-ninth [verse] and others:

the first two are *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena), and the latter is called *anvayajñāna* (subsequent knowledge). Ce says: "Because the former two take true suchness (*tathatā*) as their object, while the latter takes the categories of phenomena as its object.
Thus, the first two are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compounds), and the third is *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). Fan says: "Regarding the object of the third, the former two are like..."
Regarding the category [of *dharmanvaya-jñāna*], the commentary states that it is "initially superior" because it cannot be categorized as being non-different from its essence (*tattva*).

However, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, all three are *dharmajñāna*; they are named after their respective objects. Regarding the "True Path of Seeing" (*darśanamārga*) of phenomena, Cè (Cien) states: "The state of true seeing is called the 'Path of Seeing by Characteristics' (*lakṣaṇadarśanamārga*).

Within the True Path of Seeing, one always possesses both types of seeing. The specific uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) regarding phenomena constitutes the first two moments of mind; the general [uninterrupted path] constitutes the third.

The liberation through dharma (*dharmavimukti*) and [the liberation through concentration] are combined as the latter one; therefore, it is said that they are established both individually and collectively. Regarding "the obstacles abandoned by oneself," *Ce* (Cen) says:
"The wisdom of the two types of emptiness each abandons its own respective obstacle. *Ji* (Woncheuk) says: "Within the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), there are the uninterrupted and liberated paths;
according to the obstacles abandoned by each [path], [it is so called]. The Upādhyāya says: "'Self' here refers to the category of the two types of emptiness; according to..."

The two types of insight into selflessness (*dharma-nairātmya* and *pudgala-nairātmya*) possess the function of severing obstacles as a secondary aspect of their own nature; it is not that the function of insight itself severs them, for insight does not take obstacles as its object.

Alternatively, there may be further realization at a time when [the obstacle] is not being severed. This text may refer to the insights into the two types of selflessness regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and the obstacles to be severed by them.

Others say it may refer to the obstacles to be severed by the insights into the two types of selflessness regarding phenomena (the former being superior, as explained in the *Mātṛkā*). These are the two meanings.

The first yoga of the middle [section] serves as the proof; it is the fifty-fifth [chapter]. It contains three repetitions, clarifying the distinction between the three minds and the sixteen [aspects].

First, because the former is non-conceptual while the latter is conceptual. Second, because the former severs latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) while the latter contemplates the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Third, because the former is able to advance toward the supramundane path of abandonment within the path of cultivation, whereas the latter advances toward the mundane [path].

The mundane path is incapable of severing the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), whereas the supramundane path is capable of doing so. Paramārtha states: "The latter interpretation represents the orthodox school of Dharmapāla.

The *Pañcāśatikā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Fifty Verses) says: "Because one establishes the existence of a single mind through the principle of internally realized ultimate truth, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
However, regarding the three successive distinctions made in the first [section], there is a difference between the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the non-provisional (*apratiṣṭhita*).
"Second, the path of insight (*darśanamārga*) consisting of the establishment of the objects [of cognition] up to names and signs.
Commentary: Following the sixteen moments of mind, there are again two types, based on the distinction between the grasper and the grasped, and the eight truths of the upper and lower realms.

This is the first [of these]. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (IX) clarifies the preceding sixteen [moments], while the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (XVII) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (V) [treat them similarly].

15. Regarding the statement that the latter sixteen [moments] are relied upon: the *Ceshu* (Measuring Commentary) records that the Tripiṭaka Master said, "The three types of Bodhisattvas rely on the former;

one type relies on the latter; and one type relies on both. Therefore, they are now described in full. [Commentary: The first two [types] may be so, as they would follow the former time because of their extensive prior cultivation.

But how is it with the third? It has not been seen stated that there are thirty-two moments for entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). If it were only in those subsequent moments that the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) arises, then the first two types would lack this faculty, since there would still be something to be known that has not yet been known. Thus he explains.

Regarding the names "patience" (*kṣānti*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*): as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the terms "Dharma-patience" (*dharma-kṣānti*) and "Dharma-knowledge" (*dharma-jñāna*) refer to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Specifically, the four types of Dharma-patience constitute the uninterrupted seeing-portion (*anantarya-darśana-bhāga*) of the true Path of Seeing; the four types of Dharma-knowledge constitute the liberated seeing-portion (*vimukti-darśana-bhāga*) of the true Path of Seeing;

the four types of Subsequent Patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) constitute the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the uninterrupted [seeing]; and the four types of Subsequent Knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) constitute the liberated [seeing].

Excluding the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). Question: Since each of the two self-witnessing portions takes its own seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, how can the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) take both seeing portions as its objects?
[The text states that] subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) can take the immediately preceding self-witnessing portion as its object.

Cè (Cè) says: "Dharma" has two meanings: first, because it is the definitive determination (*pariccheda*) of dharmas; second, because it is the object of the object (*ālambanālambana*). (Regarding the first meaning, the eight truths are definitively determined. This does not serve to answer the preceding question. Although the objects of the two self-witnessing portions differ, [the subsequent patience can take them as objects].)
Furthermore, the objects and the cognitions are identical (this is the conventional designation of phenomena).
Second, regarding the "path of insight based on contemplation" (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-darśana-mārga*).

The commentary states: this refers to the subsequent sixteen moments of mind. Regarding the phrase "the realm appearing before one," Master Ji says: it means the lower realm appearing within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because one has entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the [truths] of the two higher realms do not manifest. *Ce* (Cen) says:

"Because those of the lower realm can be directly perceived" (the latter interpretation is superior, as they are coarse and manifest; otherwise, if one followed *Ki* [Baoshou], when explaining the turning of the mind toward the form realm, one would first have to contemplate the truths of the form realm).

However, regarding these sixteen [aspects], the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (55) establishes them based on the path of seeing, while the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (17) establishes them based on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). It is clear that, in reality, both are [correct].

All stages possess them. Contemplating the latter two minds is termed *dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding phenomena) and *dharma-jñāna* (knowledge regarding phenomena). Contemplating the former two minds is termed *anvaya-kṣānti* (subsequent patience), as they are subsequent to the former.
Following the *dharma-kṣānti*, there is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*); following the *dharma-jñāna*, there is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
"If one relies on the 'Extensive Exposition' (vistara-prasara) up to the 'Path of Vision of Names and Characteristics' (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*).
The commentary states: "The third [stage] consists of nine moments of mind. As for the term 'extensive exposition,' it refers merely to the provisional designation (*prajñapti*) of the teaching;

Next, following the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, it subsequently cites the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: by transforming the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one attains the four wisdoms.

Regarding those phenomena that lack a substantial self-nature—such as the faculties of others and their minds—they are not identical to the direct realization of one's own true nature. If there were no semblance-aspect, [this would be untenable]. I grant [the existence of such a semblance].

When taking form and so forth as an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya), one may say that it takes sound as its object; yet, both the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (prajñapti) lack substantial reality.
