The treatise says: "...therefore it is called 'abandoning'.

The commentary states: Within the second explanation, there are two parts: first, because it provides a brief explanation of the verses; second, because it provides an extensive explanation of the meaning of the verses. First...

There are two [aspects] herein: because of the cultivation of its characteristics, and because of the attainment of its fruit. This is the former. Master Ji says: "To be far removed from the grasped object (*grāhya*) is called 'non-attainment' (*anupalabdhi*);

to be far removed from the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) is called 'inconceivable' (*acintya*). Master Ce or Master Jie explains: "Being free from both the grasped and the grasper is termed 'non-attainment';
it is by virtue of this very meaning that it is also inconceivable. Regarding the term "proliferation" (*prapañca*), Master Ji says: "[It refers to] the outflows (*āsrava*)."

[This refers to] conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Because the clinging to outflows (*āsrava*) increases [through it], or because it is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). However, the intended meaning of the present verse is to generally exclude both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conceptualizations;

that wisdom which possesses these two characteristics is made clear by the treatise itself. As for the phrase "only this can sever," it is because it exhausts delusion regarding the principle (*tattva*).
"This is the fruit of the two types of transformation resulting from that relinquishment. [Commentary:

This refers to the first of the two successive expositions regarding the attainment of the fruit. It serves as a general basis for the specific [analysis], being consistent with the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

For ordinary beings, they conceive of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); whereas for the noble ones (*ārya*), they realize the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) within the dependent nature. Thus, it is "transformed."

At that time, the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) occurs by virtue of this name. Just as one transforms and abandons defilement (saṃkleśa) in accordance with what is grasped [as imagined], one likewise transforms and attains pure gnosis (viśuddha-jñāna) in accordance with the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Alternatively, the basis itself is called the Dharma-body (dharma-kāya).

The commentary states: Second, the basis for delusion and awakening. Although that which is transformed and attained, as well as that which is abandoned, are also called "bases," here we take the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the basis for those two. Regarding the proof for this, as the treatise says below:

"This is capable of being realized, yet it is not already realized, because one reaches the stage of fruition through the power of cultivating the path. There is an anticipated objection: "As in the first [case]..."
Next, one should attain two fruits; why, then, is nirvāṇa alone mentioned here? Therefore, the treatise explains:

"For now, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is mentioned in order to distinguish it from the liberation-body (vimukti-kāya) which shares the same essence, because the conditioned [body] and the essential body are distinct. *Muni* means "silent" or "tranquil";
it refers to the body that is the locus for the quality of tranquility resulting from the abandonment of hindrances.
"How is realization attained... by means of this realization? [The commentary] states:
Within the second section, the extensive explanation of the meaning, there are two parts: a general indication and a detailed exposition. This is the first. Regarding the "four kinds of ten":

these are the practice of the stages (*caryā-bhūmi*), the essence of the practice (*caryā-svabhāva*), the relinquishing of the practice (*caryā-tyāga*), and the grasping of the practice (*caryā-upādāna*); they should be understood in their respective order.
Regarding the statement "the ten stages" (up to) "therefore they are called stages":

The commentary states that within the subsequent detailed explanation there are two [parts]: because they are the causes that can realize [the goal], and because they are the fruits that are realized.

Within the first [of these two], there are four; this refers to the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). Regarding the term "noble nature" (*ārya-dharma*): Cè says it is that which can produce the first stage, being inherently uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) by its very nature.
The essence consists of the new seeds perfumed by the initial moment of thought, and not those of subsequent moments;

for at this time, one is able to abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), and thus even the manifest state is not [the essence], as it is subject to interruption. Jì (基) says: "It is that which gives rise to the initial untainted seeds of the three vehicles."

That which has already arisen through correct cultivation is called the "noble nature" (*āryatva*). Although it exists during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is not so called because it has not yet manifested;

furthermore, because its untainted nature (*anāsrava-dhātu*) subsequently functions to sever [defilements] and because it belongs to that same category, it is also termed the "noble nature. Regarding the three meanings of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), both serve to distinguish it from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Having attained the noble nature of the Great Sage, one alone receives the designation "virtuous" (*kuśala*). (The initial position is not tenable. If it were merely the initial mind, the noble nature would not be pervasive, as it is absent in the pure states of the formless realm. Nor is the latter [position]...)

Not so. If one were to definitively sever the category [of acquisition], then even manifest activity would have to be [considered] its substantial entity. However, as in the case of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is established as a real entity based solely on its seeds (as explained in the *Mātṛkā*). Cè states: "The nature of the noble ones (*āryatva*) is also subsumed under 'acquisition' (*prāpti*); this differs from the Sarvāstivāda position where non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) exists only as contaminated (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, because the power of understanding is superior, it does not establish it as a separate category of dharma (*dharmasaṃkhyā*);

observing it as a single instance, it is called 'acquisition' because it is first obtained. Regarding the three [types of acquisition], the Master Zhèng maintains that it is not established [as a separate category]. "Noble" [refers to the state of being a noble one].
The Dharma is supreme. That which can obstruct this supremacy has the most powerful function; thus, it is established as a dissociated [dharma].

The noble nature (*āryatva*) is not like this, and therefore it is not established separately. [This argument] does not fully accord with reason. Since that which is the most powerful antidote ought to be even more supreme, [the objection] is invalid. *Cai* says: "Because its power is supreme, it is not established as the noble nature. This is also incorrect, because other dissociated dharmas are established according to their predominance.

It is established as supreme by virtue of being "attainment" (*prāpti*), as explained in the *Mātṛkā*: when it is said that one "obtains the noble nature," there must be a "small attainment. This difficulty is not valid, because the noble nature is established as attainment through the increase of uncontaminated seeds; therefore, the noble nature is itself attainment.

Because it is not a dependent compound (*tatpuruṣa*), one should not abandon the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding the phrase "one who possesses pure ethical discipline" (*viśuddha-śīla-samanvāgata*), Vasubandhu’s commentary states:
The nature [of the precepts] is accomplished; it is not like the guarding of the precepts through deliberation on the first bhūmi. Regarding the term "Great Dharma," it refers to the vast teaching.
As for "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*), Vasubandhu’s commentary states that it is so called because it brings about the correspondence with non-conceptualization.

Jì (基) says that within the first four bhūmis, this has not yet been achieved. Cè (測) says that, according to the actual fact, in the first bhūmi, the two types of wisdom shine forth simultaneously. However...

Regarding the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), it is said to be "spontaneous" (*anābhoga*)—this is the interpretation of the Tripiṭaka masters; however, we shall retain the former view. This is because if the fifth stage were spontaneous, it would contradict the fact that the seventh stage still involves effort (*sābhisamskāra*).

Furthermore, since the characteristics of the preceding six stages involve the accumulation of [conceptual] distinctions, true contemplation (*tattva-darśana*) is difficult to sustain continuously; thus, one knows that the fifth stage is not yet spontaneous. As for the sixth stage, the "Manifest" (*abhimukhī*), one specifically cultivates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to induce non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and realize the absence of defilement or purity.
As Vasubandhu explains, this stage transcends the worldly path and that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). These are the first two [stages].

The first three stages are so called because their practices of giving, morality, and cultivation are identical to those of worldly beings. The fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are so called because their awakening factors (*bodhipakṣa*), the four truths, and the threefold contemplation of dependent origination are identical to those of the two vehicles.
However, according to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, it is said that one attains the fruit of an arhat in the seventh stage.

At the conclusion of the stage of segmented [birth], one is conventionally designated as an Arhat. Regarding the term "immovable," there are three types, including those with signs (*sanimitta*), because they cannot be moved.
As Vasubandhu explains, although in the seventh stage one is immovable regarding signs, one is still subject to movement through effort (*prayoga*). Now, however, one is immovable in both respects;
the same applies to afflictions (*kleśa*). Master Ji says: "The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that when the faculties and practices are fully matured, one is signless and uninterrupted."

Therefore, it is named "Immovable. Having transcended this stage, one clearly understands the signless (*animitta*), for there is no longer any interval [between wisdom and its object]. (This refers to the emptiness of persons;

the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is not so, because the manas that clings to phenomena (*dharmanirmāṇa-manas*) occasionally still functions. Regarding the term "virtuous water" (*guṇodaka*), Asvabhāva’s commentary states:

"The realm and wisdom of *tathatā* are like a great cloud, and the gates of *dhāraṇī* and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are like pure water. Asvabhāva’s commentary further states: "It is a portion of the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*)."

The term "stage" (*bhūmi*) refers to a position. This treatise takes the *tathatā* (suchness) realized therein as its general referent. Ji states: "It is the real dharma that serves as the basis for the provisional.

Ce states: "It serves collectively as the basis for the individual [stages]. Because the ten practices grow and flourish, it is the superior support and sustenance [for them] (the latter follows the sequence of the textual structure).
"Ten Superior Practices" (up to "Sentient-Being Wisdom").

Commentary states: The second [section on] the essence of the practices consists of a heading, an explanation, and a conclusion. The explanation contains twelve gates; this is the gate of categories (*prakāra*).

This should be understood as explained in detail in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith), specifically in chapters seventy-eight and eighty.

Among the three types of *prajñā*, works such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* establish three based on the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*): preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*), fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

In this treatise, the ten perfections consist solely of fundamental wisdom. Regarding the two types of skillful means (*upāya*), as Vasubandhu stated: "That which is directed toward enlightenment is..."
Prajñā (wisdom) is the transformation of sentient beings; this is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Wuxing says: it is the power of nirvāṇa without abandoning saṃsāra.
Regarding the two types [of power]: they are the power of manifest discernment (*cintā-vicaya*) and the power of the cultivation of habitual perfuming (*bhāvanā-vāsanā*).
"These ten natures... [down to] ...have merit as their nature. The commentary states:

This is the second section, the "Gate of Essential Nature. *Cai* says: "The seeds perfumed by a single moment of volition (*cetanā*), together with the innate seeds (*dharmatā-bīja*), establish the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*).

If it were the case that there were no unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) upon the innate [seeds], then these seeds would, from time to time, produce maturation (*vipāka*). Consequently, since maturation has the characteristic of being exhausted through experience, [the three restraints] would be as previously explained."

This is not logical. Although mental karma lacks unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), it is based upon the seeds thereof that one metaphorically designates as "unmanifest" (or, as recorded in the *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya* 53, this unmanifest is not a separate category of phenomena).
The three [roots], non-hatred and so forth, are respectively the essence of patience toward harm and so on. Regarding the view that the eighth [consciousness] and others [exist]:
the seventh chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the four latter perfections are the wisdoms attained subsequent to meditative equipoise (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which rely solely upon...
It excels. Regarding those two passages in that treatise: first, aspiration is defined as the resolve of desire; second, aspiration is defined as the resolve of faith.
Now, taken together, these three dharmas constitute its essence.
Regarding these ten characteristics (up to the fourfold analysis):

the commentary states that the third section on the "gate of characteristics" contains six points in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which correspond to the latter six [of the ten] here, excluding the first, the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Because it pertains to the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), within the *Abhidharma-lakṣaṇa*, the establishment begins with abiding in the bodhisattva lineage;

thus, [the categories] are increased to seven (established according to different meanings in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, *Saṃdhinirmocana*, *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and *Prakaraṇāryavāca*). Regarding "knowledge of signlessness" (*animitta-jñāna*), the *Saṃdhinirmocana* states:

"That which precedes the stages is called a *pāramitā*; it is clearly known that the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) are also termed 'non-ignorance' (*avidyā*). Its...

Regarding the second point, the distinction between the six [types of] existence, Master Ji states: "The initial mind directed toward the Path does not necessarily involve dedication (toward the goal).

[This is because] what was originally sought was bodhi, yet it was not necessarily what was being cultivated; rather, through distinct modes of practice, one dedicates [the merit] toward bodhi. The fourfold logical analysis (*catuskoṭi*) is as explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*.
However, this has ten [points] (up to) the detailed explanation, which should be understood.
The commentary states: The fourth is the gate of non-increase and non-decrease. This is as in other treatises; the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* [explains] the three causes as they are there.
The superior births and so forth are as in the *Abhidharmakośa*. The first three benefit sentient beings, while the latter three remedy the afflictions.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. Non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*) is as in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*.
Regarding the ten successive stages, the sequence is as follows.
[The author] states: This fifth section on the sequential gates has already been explained according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and the *Abhidharma*.
The explanation of the general and specific names is as stated elsewhere.

[The commentary] says: This is the sixth section, the Gate of Explaining Names. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and other treatises explain these ten cultivations (up to the point where) their characteristics are explained in detail.
The commentary states: Regarding the seventh, the gate of cultivation, the mention of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and so forth includes the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
However, it is an error to refer to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* as the *Samuccayavyākhyā*, for the former was never intended to be so called.
Regarding these ten inclusions (up to "because they take the conventional as their object"):

The commentary states that this is the eighth section on the inclusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*). As explained extensively in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts, it should be understood accordingly.
Regarding these ten fruits (up to) "or explained as two combined":
the commentary states that within the ninth section on the attainment of fruits, there are instances where it is said that five fruits are complete. As the Abhidharma (*Abhidharmakośa*) says:
Because each of the six perfections attains five fruits.
The ten [perfections] and the training (śikṣā) encompass the latter five up to wisdom (*prajñā*).
The commentary states: "The thirteenth is the gate of training (*śikṣā-mukha*). Regarding the various gates herein that are explained as in other places, they all subsume the Great [Vehicle].

Regarding the vehicles (*yāna*), the nature of offenses, prohibitions, and so forth, as explained in their respective commentaries (by Asvabhāva in the seventh [chapter] and Vasubandhu in the eighth), Ce states: "The four stages refer to the levels of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)."

No formal textual source has been seen [for this]. The ancient masters say: the first four stages are called the "Light of the Mahāyāna"; the fifth, sixth, and seventh are called the "King Who Accumulates Merit";
the eighth, ninth, and tenth are called "Worthy Protector" (Bhadrapāla); and the Vajra and Buddha stages are called the "Dhyāna of Steadfast Progress" (Vajragati).
As for their specific assignments, there is no distinction; they are subsumed according to their function in the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and subsumed according to what is manifested in the *Ga*.
Forty-nine. Regarding these ten stages (up to) which are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*):
the commentary states that in the eleventh stage, the door of the grounds, all five stages are complete; for instance, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is non-attachment (*alobha*).
[The first five] are for the sake of giving (*dāna*), up to wisdom (*prajñā*) as the last of the [six] perfections (*pāramitā*).
Because these ten exist during the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*), they are not yet ultimate.
The commentary states: "The twelfth position is the gate of names."
"These ten categories of meaning [extend] to the ten *pāramitās*. Commentary states:
This is the third conclusion. The nine gates of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and so forth—these various gates are as described therein.
Regarding the "ten layers of hindrances" (up to "...because they are severed all at once"):

The commentary states that within the third [stage], Equanimity (*upekṣā*), there are two sections concerning the gates of hindrances. The first consists of ten segments, as stated in the verse of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*:
"Within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there are ten types of non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭa-avidyā*). This is established in order to counteract these corresponding hindrances.
The establishment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) constitutes this first obstacle. This raises the obstacle that serves as the basis for the provisional grasping [of the self]. The *Shuyao* states:

"If all three realms possess it, by what name is one called an 'ordinary being' (*pṛthagjana*)? According to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) upon which one relies, one is named an ordinary being of this particular stage. The two commentaries state: [as follows].

The Lesser Sage (hīnayāna-ārya) who has turned the mind [toward the Mahāyāna] has not yet entered the first bhūmi; he is both ordinary and noble because his aspirations differ. (The meaning of severing the ten obstacles is explained at length in the *Mātṛkā*).
Regarding the difference in the mental application (*citta-prayoga*) for the period of severing afflictions and realizing cessation: why does the mental application not function simultaneously?

Even if one aspires to them at the same time, since one desires both severance and realization, the two intentional applications must necessarily arise sequentially. Paramārtha says: "It is still [in this state]."

That which is abandoned, or the characteristic of the extinction of seeds, does not exit beyond the realm; therefore, it is not liberation (*na vimuktiḥ*). [This interpretation] does not accord with the treatises and also contradicts reason, because the characteristic of extinction is non-existent and belongs to the preceding dharma;

furthermore, at the time of the characteristic of the extinction of birth and death, one is already a Buddha. The second interpretation is for the sake of abandoning the *dauṣṭhulya* (coarse heaviness). Regarding each stage (*bhūmi*), there are two delusions and one *dauṣṭhulya*;
this is all cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. There are two further expositions: the first is universal.

It encompasses the karmic fruits of all hindrances. Because [afflictions] such as attachment and aversion, as well as the miserable realms (*durgati*) and so forth, are collectively termed "delusion" (*moha*) even though they are not of the category of delusion itself, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the karmic fruits of the inhabitants of the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*), those in the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), women, and others.

Subsequently, for the sake of clarity, ignorance (*avidyā*) is specifically mentioned; "sharp" refers to the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*), while "dull" refers to craving (*rāga*) and the like. Ignorance that accompanies the sharp [views] is established as...

The first [type of] delusion and the dullness that are both ignorance serve as the cause for subsequent delusions; therefore, the term "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) is explained. Furthermore, in the second sequence:
the former is the seed, while the latter is the lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*). An objection may arise: "If ignorance is non-defiled, how can it open up the ten hindrances?

For the hindrances and the delusions are distinct. Therefore, the treatise reconciles this by stating: "Ignorance is precisely the delusion belonging to the category of the ten hindrances. This is the second sequence.

Although it is said that [these] are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the section from "the Bodhisattva" downwards is a composite citation from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Second, the obstacle of wrong practice (*mithyā-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*) [extends] to the delusion regarding the lack of understanding of karma.
The commentary states: This is the second hindrance. Regarding the phrase "or merely the ignorance that initiates karma and fails to comprehend karma," this refers to the second sequential stage.
It takes up only ignorance (*avidyā*), meaning that according to the sūtra, there are two types of ignorance which, respectively, initiate karma and fail to comprehend it. Master Ji says:

"This explains the hindrance to the wisdom that initiates [karma]. However, in terms of the production of rebirth, although the previously mentioned non-initiation lacks maturation (*vipāka*), [it still functions as a hindrance].

Because there are results of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and dominant results (*adhipati-phala*), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The karmic fruits produced [by such actions] are all [merely] cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The *Shuyao* says: "Just as when walking, although one is on one's own path, one does not accidentally injure [anything] by natural spontaneity; therefore, there is no transgression."
"It still exists in the first stage" refers to the three types of dullness-obstructions (up to those affecting the wisdoms of hearing and reflection).

The commentary states: "This is the third obstruction. Cè says: "In general terms, this refers to a portion of the innate [obstructions]; specifically, it refers to sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and..."

Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) share the same essential nature. Ji says: "Concentration (*samādhi*) directly gives rise to cultivation (*bhāvanā*);

wisdom (*prajñā*) directly gives rise to hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*). Therefore, they are combined into a single textual unit. As for the five types of sensual desire and so forth, they are presented here to manifest their specific obstructions;

it is not that they do not mutually obstruct one another, as they also function as general obstructions. The *Shuyao* states: "The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* says that in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*),..."

What has been done, contemplated, or spoken over a long period may sometimes be forgotten; however, this is not the case upon entering the stages (*bhūmi*). How then can it be said now that there is forgetfulness? The explanation is as follows:
that which is attained while established in the stages is free from loss, whereas much is lost prior to the stages; it is not so on the stages themselves, for its name and essence do not regress.

Nevertheless, that which is attained through hearing and reflection may still involve some slight forgetfulness. Furthermore, although there is no forgetfulness regarding that which is attained through the untainted (*anāsrava*), [the aforementioned distinction applies].
There is also the loss of the outflows (*āsrava*). In the third stage (*bhūmi*), these are absent;
in the fourth, even the subtle afflictions (*anuśaya*) never arise again.
[The commentary] states: this is the fourth obstacle. There are three meanings that explain "subtle," which accord with Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*. Jī says: "Supreme..."
Regarding the inferior grade: the sixth [category] also includes the conceptualized view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Because that is coarse and violent, it is called the superior grade.

Craving and so forth that arise independently are called the middle grade, because they are universally unwholesome (*akuśala*). In comparison to those two, this is called the inferior grade, because it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Cè (Cē) says: "The three meanings correspond respectively to the distinctions: because the conceptualized view of a self is abandoned first. Division.
Because it arises separately, it cannot reach as far as the fourth stage (the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages, though they possess afflictions, are here designated as "lowest grade" alone).

This refers to the [simultaneous] severance of the nine grades [of afflictions] by means of the ninth-grade path of the two vehicles (collectively termed "the most inferior"). Master Ji states: "Although there are separate births among those severed at this stage, they mostly arise as being of the same substance as the afflictions.
The term "etc. includes views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and so forth, as well as the "craving for fixed dharmas" (*niyatadharmatṛṣṇā*) mentioned below.
In the first bhūmi one practices giving; in the second, morality; in the third, cultivation—these are similar to those of the mundane [levels].

In this interval, [the practitioner] frequently cultivates the three types of merit. Regarding the statement "the two views of self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), Zhi Chè says there are three explanations. First, it is said that because the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are severed, the afflictions (*kleśa*) do not function;
thus, it is said to "harm the two views. Second, it is said that because of the notions of "self" and "what belongs to the self," they are called the two views of self-identity.

Third, regarding the statement that "both the conceptual and innate [afflictions] are exhausted," this is a general explanation (as described by Ki regarding the beginning and end). Are the obstacles to this stage and the delusions distinct? To answer this, the fourfold logical analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) is established:

there are obstacles that are not delusions; there are delusions that are not obstacles; [there are those that are both]; and there are those that are neither. Specifically, there are obstacles to this stage that are not delusions, and there are delusions that are not obstacles.
The afflictions of the miserable realms (*durgati-saṃkleśa*), the delusion regarding craving for meditative states (*niyata-dharma-tṛṣṇā-moha*),

and the delusion regarding obstacles (*āvaraṇa-moha*)— namely, the remaining nine obstacles and seventeen delusions— are included by the word "also" (*vā*) as being both obstacles and delusions (this interpretation accords with the treatise).
There are also those that are neither obstacles nor delusions, which are abandoned at the final stage within each respective ground.
"Fifth, regarding those who delight in nirvāṇa within the lower vehicles. The commentary states:

This is the fifth hindrance. Jī says: Previously, based on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), there was joy and aversion toward the present body and so forth due to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which affected the wholesome mind and other faculties.
Because the suchness (*tathatā*) of this stage is called "undifferentiated," one takes it as an object.

That path is called "undifferentiated," because there is no differentiation between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Cè (Cèyún) says: "On this stage, one contemplates the suchness (*tathatā*) of the Four Noble Truths;
one does not perceive any characteristics of defilement or purity that could be either craved or loathed."
The six coarse characteristics (up to) abiding in the contemplation of signlessness.

Commentary states: This is the sixth hindrance. According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, because it is viewed in relation to the preceding stage, it is called the "hindrance of the subtle habit-energies of affliction."

In relation to what follows, this treatise is called the "coarse aspect" (*sthūlanimitta*), because the Four Noble Truths are coarse in comparison to the gateway of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Although the five stages involve contemplating non-differentiated suchness (*tathatā*), they nonetheless rely upon the gateways of designation regarding defilement and purification within the framework of the Four Noble Truths.
"Seventh, the subtle characteristic (up to): 'the arising of superior activity. The commentary states:

This is the seventh hindrance. Cè says: "Dependent origination as arising and ceasing, and its reversal through cessation, are subtle when contrasted with the preceding Four Truths of defilement and purity.
Regarding the statement "clinging to the existence of arising and ceasing": "arising" refers to saṃsāra, because it is the primary factor.
It is not that one does not grasp the characteristics of the cessation of that cyclic flow—namely, cessation and further cessation.

Because in the sixth stage, while exclusively seeking the signless within the contemplation of true suchness (*tathatā*), one has not yet initiated superior practice; now, upon entering the seventh stage, because one no longer dwells solely in the mental state of seeking the signless, one initiates superior practice.
This is as explained at length in the ninth chapter of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
"Among the eight signless [states], because one does not contradict them.

Commentary states: This is the eighth hindrance. Guān (Guṇabhadra) says: "Having signs" refers exclusively to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). Zhèng (Paramārtha) says: Because its essence is neither form (*rūpa*) nor earth (*pṛthivī*).
One may rely on the *Jī* (Jinagupta) and *Cè* (Dharmaruci) for this; it is the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Among the nine [obstacles] to benefiting others, it is subsumed under the ninth obstacle. The commentary states: "This is the ninth obstacle.

In the preceding eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one attains the bliss of signlessness (*animitta-sukha*) and becomes attached to quiescence (*śānti*), being unwilling to benefit others. The *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot) asks: 'What is the intention behind combining three into one and making the fourth into one? **Note:** The term *shuyao* (樞要) refers to the *Dasheng qixin lun shuyao* (大乘起信論樞要), a commentary by Fazang on the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*. The passage reflects a structural analysis of the stages of practice.

The "three combined into one" likely refers to the integration of the seventh, eighth, and ninth obstacles into a single category, while the "fourth as one" refers to the grouping of the fourth through sixth obstacles. This arrangement emphasizes the transition from the cultivation of meditative absorption to the active engagement in altruistic practice. The question posed seeks to clarify the pedagogical or soteriological rationale for this specific categorization.

The first three are established because they are explained separately. Regarding the opening and closing [of the categories], which differ, the passage from "the tenth among the dharmas" to "that which is contained within" is explained as follows:
this refers to the tenth hindrance. The *Shuyao* states: "The two delusions correspond respectively to external karma and internal qualities; there is a distinction."
Because they are distinct. Regarding "the great wisdom of the Dharma," Master Ji’s commentary states: "The wisdom that takes True Suchness as its object;
because at this stage [one attains] the great roots of goodness regarding the Dharma.
My own commentary says: By means of the tenth hindrance, the hindrance to the Buddha-ground is clarified. Master Ce says: "The sublime contemplation of equality collectively eliminates this."
Regarding the obstacles: because that which is realized is the same, both the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms pertain to both the ultimate and conventional truths.

Fundamental wisdom doubly severs the obstacles of delusion regarding principle and phenomena, whereas subsequently attained wisdom severs only the obstacles of delusion regarding phenomena (the seventh [consciousness] has not yet been seen as a path capable of severing).
● Treatise, Chapter Ten:
These eleven hindrances (up to) "therefore they are specifically explained. Commentary:

Within the second section on the two hindrances, there are three parts: [the distinction between] the stages of suppression and abandonment; the distinction between sudden and gradual abandonment; and the path.

This is the first [point] regarding their differentiation. However, as for the initial explanation stating that these eleven hindrances are subsumed within the two hindrances (*dvayāvaraṇa*), this merely refers to their general categories;
it does not mean they are identical in scope. When a bodhisattva enters the stages (*bhūmi*), eleven hindrances are established, whereas the two hindrances are broader and more pervasive.

They abide fully within the three vehicles. Regarding the statement that [defilements] are already subdued prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), the *Fifty-eight [Treatises]* and others state that the mundane path subdues only the innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions], based on the six aspects of practice; thus, there is no contradiction.

As for why it is not considered an error, it is as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*: because it does not bring about suffering. Question: If it is not an error, why does the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*...

The second [point] says: If one is on the first stage (*bhūmi*), one’s power is not yet sufficient, one’s roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are not yet deep, and one has not long practiced the wholesome dharmas;
therefore, the faculties such as the eye still follow after various objects, the mind is not yet tamed, and thus the various afflictions (*kleśa*) can still cause harm.
It is like a person whose strength is insufficient who finds it difficult to go against the current. Furthermore, within this stage...
Māra and his followers create many obstacles; therefore, by the power of skillful means, one practices diligence with a diligent mind.

For this reason, it is called "difficult to cure. Answer: That which acts as an affliction hinders progress in cultivation. However, it does not bring about suffering nor does it contradict the profound and secret [teachings].
This refers to when, while in the first bhūmi for the benefit of sentient beings, one is led by the power of intentional effort (*saṃcetanīya*) toward afflictions.
"Affliction (nāman): although one may benefit others, it conversely obstructs one's own path. Thus, Nāgārjuna’s treatise does not contradict this. Cè says:

'The innate view of self (sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi) and the grasping at phenomena as having substantial reality (dharma-abhiniveśa) of the same nature are actually severed from the first bhūmi up to the vajra-like samādhi; yet, among the ten obstacles, they are severed in the fourth bhūmi.
This is discussed based on the single characteristic of the 'deer-mark' [of the second bhūmi], just as in the *Ratnaketu-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing), in the first and second [sections].'"

Regarding the three stages: because greed, hatred, and delusion are abandoned respectively [in the first, second, and third stages], this [interpretation] cannot be relied upon, as it specifically contradicts the treatises and lacks scriptural evidence.

Regarding the abandonment in three stages: these are the first, eighth, and tenth stages, as explained extensively in the *Forty-eight [Verses]*. Regarding the manifestation in three stages: because the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are completed;
because there is no partial contemplation of the mind; and because one first attains the distinction between the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
"Because there are many seeds of the two obstacles [to be severed]... [The commentary] states:
The second [point] concerns the sudden or gradual severance. Regarding "arising spontaneously within without coarse or subtle [distinctions]," there are many explanations as previously mentioned;
however, following the interpretation of Ji, it means that because they take only a single category of internal objects of their own stage as their object, they are called "one grade," and not three.

Within the realms (*dhātu*), there is generally no distinction between coarse and subtle. The manner in which the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) abandon afflictions has already been explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Ji* (Commentary), and other texts;

therefore, it will not be explained again here. However, regarding these two types [of practitioners], both commentaries (*śū*) state in common that this [text] omits the mention of those who have already abandoned desire to a greater degree (*bhūyovītarāga*).

Zhengyun says that this is included in the first [category]. Although they are abandoned all at once during the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) through the power of suppression, one abandons the remaining afflictions gradually upon emerging from that stage (this is correct).

Regarding "pervading both internal and external," Ceyun says: although the five consciousnesses only take coarse external objects as their domain, because they are induced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are not devoid of coarse and subtle aspects.
"The faculties of the two vehicles are dull... (up to)... all may possess [them]. The commentary states:

This is the second [section], the differentiation of the paths. Because the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) and "liberation" (*vimukti*) [paths] are difficult [to attain], they arise separately; this refers to their enumeration, inclusion, and exclusion.

As for "separately severing," it means that the preparatory (*prayoga*) and superior-progress (*viśeṣa*) [paths] arise individually. If, within a single contemplation, [defilements] are severed according to [the specific object], [then the paths arise accordingly].
How many categories? In total, there is one preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*), which is also the path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

In the stage where a bodhisattva exclusively severs the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), as they sever each subsequent moment, they realize the cessation of each preceding one; thus, the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arise collectively.

This is as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* among the five types of cultivation: because the various heavy residues (*dausthulya*) are dissolved moment by moment, the preparatory stage of the first moment is severed.
[The first] moment [is so called] because it leads to the subsequent category and because it eliminates its own specific hindrance. In the second moment, one possesses all four paths:

in relation to the preceding path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), and in relation to the subsequent path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*), which further adds the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*).

In the final moment, there is only the path of liberation and the path of excellence. Jì (基) says: "The second path of uninterrupted continuity is not the preceding path of excellence; it is merely the path of liberation. This is from Cè’s (測) *Śāstra Commentary* (*Shù*).
The intention [of this] is the same [as the previous point], because the fault of not exhausting the principle occurs at the initial stage of the journey.
Regarding the "ten suchnesses" (up to the point of) "successive establishment," the commentary states:

the fourth practice involves grasping, for it grasps the realization of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). This explains the name "suchness" (*tathatā*) in accordance with the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises.
Regarding the term "most excellent," it is because the virtue of its ethical discipline (*śīla*) is majestic; the other [aspects] may be inferred accordingly. Ce says:

Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) also does not separately realize the meaning of being "all-pervasive" (*sarvatraga*); rather, it is called "realizing the all-pervasive" because this is spoken of in terms of its designation. The same applies to the other nine [perfections].

Now, regarding this, what does "one who has not yet realized" mean? If it refers to the gateway of subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), then the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) would consist solely of the states of subsequent knowledge.

If it refers to the gateway of correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), then apart from the two types of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), what is meant by "universal activity"? The explanation says: it is the direct realization of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā-tattva*).

There are only two types of emptiness-practice. However, when the ten types of ignorance that obscure reality are severed, the correct wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) becomes preeminent and distinct;

the ten virtues induced by the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) then become clearly manifest. Although these ten gates are the domain of subsequent wisdom and pertain to both cause and fruit, the suchness (*tathatā*) of sentient and insentient beings is not identical to *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature).
It is only because it exists within sentient beings that it is designated as "principle" (*li*). It is not [otherwise].

They enter into the expression of emptiness; therefore, the conclusion below states that they are truly without distinction. Nevertheless, ten types of distinctions are established according to their superior virtues, for this is not a gate that eliminates all characteristics.
Question: Why are [the qualities such as] the exaltation of empty space and so forth not assigned to the various stages (*bhūmi*)? Answer:

Although these are also gates of principle that pervade all stages, they do not constitute a progressive superiority because they are not the basis for the [specific] virtues [of each stage]. Although one speaks of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), [they are not so categorized here].
This is because the ten dharma-realms are realized through the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Xiao says:

"Furthermore, there is the Buddha's realization as the eleventh, for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* contains the term 'solitary emptiness' (*ekākīśūnyatā*). Since the ten obstacles have been severed, one realizes the ten dharma-realms.
Regarding the statement that "the eleventh hindrance must have something to be hindered," this is not so, for there is no authentic evidence [for it].

If the principle to be expressed (the *lakṣya*) were to exist as an eleventh, then by analogy, the same would apply to the superior practices that serve as its proof (*lakṣaṇa*). However, the fruit merely fulfills the practices established by the cause.

There is no eleventh *pāramitā*. This case should be understood in the same way. However, because it is the principle realized through the cause of ultimate clarity and perfection, it is termed a "fruit.

There is nothing further to be added. If there were something newly added, it would have to be like the ten stages (*bhūmi*). That which is otherwise perfected and clear would not be subsumed under the "fruit" at that time;
rather, when the ten dharmas are gradually realized and suddenly become perfectly clear, there remains a subtle obstruction, which is then established [as the object of the final stage].

Eleventh: One should not, based on this, [conclude that] the increase in practice and its nature are identical. If everything has already been attained within the first stage (*bhūmi*), why are those obstacles specifically termed "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*)?
The explanation says: delusion regarding all ten is an obstacle, as their nature as non-saintly is the same.
The obstacles of the remaining nine stages should be understood by analogy with this.
In this way, the bodhisattva (up to) is able to realize it. [The commentary] states:
Having explained the capacity for realization, the second major section concerning the fruit realized contains two parts: first, to conclude the preceding and introduce the subsequent;

second, to provide an extensive explanation of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). This is the former. As for the two types of transformation of the basis, they are *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
The Distinctions in the Stages of the Transformation of the Basis (up to the point of) realization.

[Commentary: There are two broad explanations regarding the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); this is the first. Regarding "causing the real and the unreal to appear or not appear":

when the uncontaminated contemplative mind arises alternately with respect to the ultimate and the conventional, during the time of signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*), the ultimate appears and the conventional does not appear.

When one contemplates with signs (*sanimitta*), the conventional appears while the ultimate does not. Although from the fifth stage onward there are times when both are simultaneously illuminated, because the presence of signs supersedes them and the signless is severed [from them], this is not the case.
The commentary’s alternative interpretation—that the name "thoroughly imagined and grasped" (*parikalpita*) refers to that which is not a true characteristic—is incorrect.

That which is grasped by the object manifests as the mind; it cannot be called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), nor is it penetration (*prativedha*), because it is not the practice of the stages (*bhūmi*). For the most part...

This renders it non-genuine. Regarding "not manifesting": although the seventh stage possesses both independently arising wisdom and subsequently attained wisdom, because it is constantly signless (animitta) according to its functional expectation, it is described from the perspective of its predominant state as being purely cultivated in the signless.
The meaning here is that "vast transformation" encompasses the previously mentioned "complete transformation."
The Distinct Meanings of the Transformation of the Basis (up to) Gradual and Sudden Subduing.
The commentary states: Within the second meaning of the transformation of the basis, there are four [factors], namely, that which transforms and so forth.

The first of these also has two [aspects]: subduing and abandoning; this refers to the former. Cè says: There are two meanings of "subduing": first, subduing by means of the six aspects of meditation; second, observing emptiness.

I prostrate. However, since we are now discussing the obstacles of the latter ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) types, each of which has both sudden and gradual aspects.

"Gradual" refers to the preparatory application (*prayoga*) being distant for both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*). "Sudden" refers to the preparatory application being proximate for each respective stage.

This is like how the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) suddenly suppresses the conceptual [obstacles] of the higher stages; because it is a path of preparation proximate to those stages, the obstacles to be abandoned are rendered forever non-functional. (This does not...)

This is reasonable, because each stage involves gradual exhaustion rather than sudden suppression. Regarding the gradual [suppression] by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*) path, it is like the stage of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), which suppresses the grasping of the *manas*;

the sudden [suppression] is like the path of the moment immediately preceding the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*). [This too is not correct, for] the temporary suppression of the *manas* is not gradual suppression, and the moment preceding the diamond-like concentration is the final stage of the gradual process.

Master Ji says: "The severance of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) means that the afflictions of the same substance do not function; this is called 'suppression. It does not mean that a separate path arises to suppress the delusions of the four stages."
When entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one subdues the two obstacles by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Alternatively, preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) can only gradually subdue them, whereas fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom can subdue them both suddenly and gradually (the latter view is preferable). If preparatory wisdom were exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), why would there be a preparatory path at the stage of the "Vajra-like" [concentration]?
One should understand that this is explained in the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* (*Dapifa ji*). One must reconcile these points accordingly.
"Second, the path capable of severing [afflictions]... both are capable of correctly severing them. Commentary states:

This refers to the second [category of] severance. Regarding "that which is induced by the grasping at signs": Cè (Cèlún) says this refers to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, because they are induced by the two types of grasping (*grāha*).

Although all contaminated minds (*sāsrava-citta*) are not themselves forms of grasping, they are bound by the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and thus cannot be autonomous. As for "that which is... [the text continues].

Regarding "that which has been induced by realization but is not yet accomplished," Jī states: "Because the correct wisdom induced by the *tathatā* (suchness) that is to be realized has not yet been accomplished" (this refers to a bodhisattva who knows *tathatā*).

Cè states: "Although the cessation to be realized has not yet been attained during the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), it becomes 'induced' [by the subsequent path], whereby one is able to sever the obstructions" (this refers to the two vehicles who do not know *tathatā*).
Furthermore, regarding "also being able to permanently sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that delude regarding phenomena," this refers solely to cultivation.

This is the Path (*mārga*). Because delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*) is shallow, subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) also severs it. Jī (基) says: "In this [system], there are only two [types of obstacles]. Bodhisattvas practicing the path do not sever delusion regarding phenomena.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that one permits the severing of the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) concerning phenomena—such as the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) headed by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*)—which should be severed first because they are not obstacles of attachment.

[Paramārtha] (測) agrees with the first statement. The severing of the cognitive obstacle occurs only through fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*); subsequent wisdom is for the purpose of [expounding the teaching of] liberation. This is logically untenable.
[This is] because it would be obstructive). Question: The subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the two vehicles consists solely of established practice (*vyavasthāpana-caryā*).

Here, however, it is said that "the characteristics of establishment appear clearly before one," whereby the delusions regarding phenomena (*vastu-moha*) are severed. How is it that in the *Yogācārabhūmi* there is only a single clear observation (*abhisamaya*) that eternally destroys the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)?

Fan [Guangyi] says: "The universal principle severs phenomena; there is only a single clear observation. Now, we speak of the specific severance of delusions regarding phenomena. (The meaning of "as it truly is" is as explained in the *Mātṛkā*).
Regarding the second point, the basis of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): this is not mentioned here. The commentary states:

Within the second meaning, two aspects are observable. Although the other six consciousnesses and so forth also relinquish defilement and attain purity as their locus of support, they are omitted from mention.
The same applies to delusion and awakening; because they both universally depend upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature).
"Third, that which is abandoned through transformation, because it is not its basis. The commentary states:
Within the third meaning, there are two [points] visible. "The remaining contaminated [dharmas]" refers to the virtuous and indeterminate dharmas that remain from the two obstacles.
Regarding "inferior uncontaminated [dharmas]," Ji says: one abandons the seeds of the manifest [dharmas] within the ten stages and attains the superior.

The abandonment of the inferior is as explained in the Abhidharma: one abandons the stage of the candidate (pratipannaka) upon attaining the fruit. Cè states that the Tripiṭaka Master’s interpretation says:

"This refers exclusively to the abandonment of the untainted (anāsrava) [attainments] of the two vehicles" (this interpretation is superior; for if one were discussing the abandonment of the inferior within its own class, it would be confused with the causal stage).

Regarding the statement that the "extremely perfected and luminous fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) acts as a simultaneous inducer," does this mean it induces at the same time [as the cause], or at the time of the fruit? Therefore, the two masters provide explanations: the first says it is simultaneous; the second...

There are no obstacles whatsoever. Since all inferior, outflow-tainted, and non-existent dharmas are unable to persist, [the ālayavijñāna] exists; yet it is not yet called "Buddha," because extinction (nirvāṇa) has not been realized.
Later, it says "at another time," which refers to the Dharmapāla school. The four reasons refute the previous [position]: there would be nothing to be perfumed.
Because there is nothing to be perfumed, one should be called a Buddha; yet because one is called a Buddha, the subsequent path would be useless, which contradicts the sūtras.
One who practices the path of unimpeded realization is called a bodhisattva. As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom), fascicle 94, quotes from a sūtra:
"Subhūti, within the path of unimpeded realization, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called a 'bodhisattva'; within the path of liberation..."
Being devoid of all darkness and obscuration is what constitutes a Buddha.
This refers to the fourfold transformation that attains the purified *dharmadhātu*.
[Commentary: Within the fourth meaning, there are two parts: the manifestation and the arising. Within the first of these, there are two further divisions: the general and the specific.
This is the first [meaning]. In Sanskrit it is called *parinirvāṇa*. This translates as *pari* meaning "complete" and *nirvāṇa* meaning "quiescence";
thus, it signifies "perfect quiescence. By retaining the abbreviated form, it is termed *nirvāṇa*.
The Meaning of Nirvāṇa (up to): It is called nirvāṇa because it is distinct [from saṃsāra].

The commentary states: There are three distinct explanations: because of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), because of the three vehicles (*yāna*), and because of the summary. This is the first [explanation]. Regarding "the characteristics of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa*):

Cè says this refers to the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, which is *tathatā* (suchness). Furthermore, among the seven kinds of suchness, it is the "true" (*bhūta*) [suchness].

□ *Tathatā* (Suchness). Because the two realities are manifested. "Free from all marks" means being free from the marks of the apprehended (*grāhya*). "Free from all conceptualization" means being free from the marks of the apprehender (*grāhaka*).

The path of discursive thought is cut off, for it is realized only through internal realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*). Just as it is free from the two types of grasping, so too is it realized only through internal realization.

When it is said that the Path of Realization (*darśana-mārga*) abandons this [state], it refers to the remainder of the basis (*sopadhi-śeṣa*), specifically speaking of the Two Vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*). "Basis" (*āśraya*) refers to—
Regarding the basis of the body, it is said that [suffering] is subtle. Second, as for the essence of nirvāṇa, it is as recorded in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*. Master Ji says:
"Although it takes non-abiding as its object and gives rise to the functions of wisdom and compassion, its essence is eternally quiescent; therefore, it is named 'nirvāṇa'."
"All sentient beings (up to) may be said to possess all four. [The commentary] states:
Within the exposition of the three vehicles, there are two [sections]: the formal exposition and the question-and-answer section. This is the former. Master Ki says:
Regarding the phrase "all possess the first": the Sūtra states that all things are originally quiescent by nature and are parinirvāṇa.

Generally, there are two types of those who have not yet realized the latter three [natures] among the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha learners; and for those of fixed nature who are non-learners (aśaikṣas) entering extinction, there are two. In total, there are the first three.

Regarding the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there are two [stages] before the turning of the mind (*citta-vivarta*) and two at the beginning of the stages (*bhūmi*). On the stages themselves, there are three, including the addition of the "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*).

For those who enter the stages through sudden awakening (*tad-ekakṣaṇa-abhisambodhi*), there are only the first and the last. Cè states: Regarding the ten stages, there are two explanations. One says that [the non-abiding] is not attained [until the end], because non-abiding belongs exclusively to the Buddha.
However, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* defines the "non-abiding nirvāṇa" (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*) of bodhisattvas as belonging solely to the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

Because they differ [in their respective scopes]. One interpretation states that it also attains non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita*), as this is subsequently superior and accords with the teachings and principles.
However, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* (Fodi lun), fascicle five, states: "When a bodhisattva first realizes the stage of the Tathāgata, they suddenly realize two kinds of great nirvāṇa realms;
these are also called the non-abiding great nirvāṇa realm. Nirvāṇa is the essence of true suchness (*tathatā*), in which obstructions are eternally exhausted."

Regarding the meaning: for now, we shall speak from the perspective of the ultimate state; therefore, there is no contradiction. [The Bodhisattva’s] partial realization is not yet termed "Great" because they do not abide in the two extremes and attain it through causes and conditions.
The *Shuyao* states: "The essence of Mahāparinirvāṇa has two meanings: first, principle (*li*); second, phenomena (*shi*).

This is because within True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are the three meanings of Mahāprajñā, Liberation, and Dharmakāya. Second, the essence has three aspects, and these three aspects are each distinct."
Therefore, they are collectively termed *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. Cè (Cé) says: "By citing the wisdom that accomplishes [nirvāṇa], the intention is to take what is accomplished as the referent.

The True Suchness (*tathatā*) in which obstructions are extinguished does not have wisdom as its intrinsic nature. Nevertheless, among all forms of nirvāṇa, that which is expounded by the Tathāgata in contrast to the two vehicles is called *Mahāparinirvāṇa* (though there are cases where both the secondary and the primary are included, as recorded in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*)."
"How can it be said that the Sugata possesses all four [powers]? The commentary states:
Within the second question-and-answer section there are four parts; this is the first. There are three successive explanations.

First, there is transformation (nirmāṇa), because it resembles that which is with outflows (sāsrava). Later, it exists by virtue of the support of the body, because it is without outflows (anāsrava). The proof says: "By this..."

The *Mingzhi* (Jñānaprasthāna) and the *Guān* (Vibhāṣā) state: "When one proceeds toward tranquility and enters nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), both the first and second [types of nirvana] are present.

Since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of the meaning of cause and effect, it is taught as three distinct types. It is not logical that one would enter cessation without relinquishing [the causal basis], for this would contradict the meaning of 'cessation of causes.

Why? Because the Tathāgata, based on the meaning of the cessation of causes, can be said to possess a remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*); what need is there for two separate explanations? Or else, [the text] should be augmented."
Because this constitutes three explanations. [The text says:
"If the śrāvakas and others [differ] from the Buddha. The commentary states:
This is the second question and answer. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that they have no nirvāṇa without remainder; therefore, this question is posed. Furthermore...
That sutra states: "Only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa because he has accomplished immeasurable virtues; the two vehicles do not do so.
To say "nirvāṇa" is a skillful means of the Buddha (resembling the parable of the illusory city). The Master of the Treatise uses this to transform the nature of that objection.
However, within the formal explanation there are two successive sequences, as can be seen from the text.
Regarding the statement, "All cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)... are subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*)," the commentary states:
Within the third question-and-answer section there are four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the objection; and fourth, the resolution. This was previously explained.
The afflictive hindrances [obstruct] nirvāṇa, while the cognitive hindrances [obstruct] bodhi; therefore, this question is raised.

Although it was not previously stated that the attainment of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is impossible if the cognitive hindrances are not abandoned, this objection is formulated based on the meaning [of the text] and applies to both sequences: first the provisional and later the real.

Regarding the phrase "because it is temporarily free from verbal expression," the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (18) states: "Because suffering and pleasure are temporarily dissociated, and because the mind and mental factors are temporarily dissociated.
The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (53) states that there is analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), but this is not because it is a permanent cessation.
This differs from the Sarvāstivāda position that everything is determinate (*niyata*).
Since the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are said to be "attained through manifestation," the commentary states:
the fourth question and answer is easy to understand. From "Thus" onwards is the third summary.
"Second, that which is produced reaches the category of mind associated with attainment.
Commentary: In the second major section on "That Which Is Produced," there are three parts—thesis, explanation, and conclusion. This is the first.
"What are the four wisdoms (up to) the tasks to be performed? [The author] states:

This explanation consists of seven sections; this first section establishes their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the term "mental complex" (*cittapakṣa*), it is used because it encompasses all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Among the seven characteristics that manifest the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), the phrase "free from all conceptualization" (*sarvavikalpa-vivikta*) refers to what the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* describes as being free from the notions of self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).

The "objects" refer to the grasped and the grasper. Master Ji says that "not forgetting" means the sense of constant presence, and "not being deluded" means the sense of freedom from confusion and darkness.
The fourth characteristic is that its nature is pure and untainted, as it transcends all defilements. As for the sixth characteristic:

Ji said: "The actual body and land that arise manifest as reflections of wisdom. Furthermore, it is explained that [the mirror-like wisdom] can produce phenomena within its own continuum and can manifest other phenomena because it is solitary.
Although the wisdom of equality realizes equality, it manifests differentiated reflections; this is called 'establishment without abiding.
The rest of the text is easy to understand."
Thus, the merits of these four wisdoms (up to) are all exhausted. [The commentary] states:

This is the second section, "The Gate of Attaining the Name. Regarding the twenty-four dharmas of the causal stage of the fundamental observational wisdom (*āloka-jñāna*), they are sometimes untainted (*anāsrava*) because they are accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra.
However, as for the twenty-two dharmas here that are designated by the name "wisdom" from the perspective of the fruit, it is as follows:

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Wisdom is of two kinds. The first is real wisdom (*tattvajñāna*), which has discernment (*prajñā*) as its nature. The second is conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), which is sometimes discernment and sometimes not discernment."
"This transformation of the outflows (āsrava) [leads] to the attainment of these four wisdoms.

The commentary states: This is the third section on the gate of accomplishment. For details, refer to the *Buddhabhūmi-alaṃkāra-śāstra* and other works (the reconciliation of conflicting passages is as found in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra-ṭīkā*).
"Because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom arises from mental attention (*manasikāra*). Commentary:

This is the fourth section on the initial arising. Regarding the primary meaning of the Mirror Wisdom: once the matured fruit (*vipāka*) has been relinquished, if the Mirror Wisdom were non-existent, [it would follow that there is no basis for the subsequent wisdoms].
Regarding the question of who maintains the pure seeds—those who are destined to attain Buddhahood without increasing their untainted (anāsrava) seeds—there have long been two interpretations.

Master Ji maintained that it refers to those who increase the superior seeds through perfuming; Master Zheng maintained that it refers to those who perfume only the equal-grade seeds. The judgment of which of these is correct is as explained in the *Mātṛkā*.

As for the five consciousnesses arising at the stage of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), since they are already tainted (*sāsrava*), why would they be considered defiled roots? [This was] the view of Cè.
Yun states: "The equalizing manas serves as the basis for purity, just as the [cognition] based on the emptiness of persons is the basis for the defilement of attachment to phenomena.

Cheng states: "This explains the basis for defilement and purity in terms of its essence; however, it does not imply that the basis for defilement and purity possesses the functional capacity [to produce them], as explained in the *Mātṛkā*.
Guan states: "Ji asserts that the manas of attachment to phenomena serves as the basis for purity for the wisdom of the emptiness of persons. This is the meaning.

"That may be so. Fan said: "Ce’s interpretation contradicts reason, for the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) cannot defile the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*). (This judgment of right and wrong follows the explanation in the *Mātṛkā*).

Regarding those who, after the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), attain wondrous enlightenment or reach the level of the Bodhisattva’s stage of practice and application (*adhimukticaryā-bhūmi*):

they are not necessarily restricted to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Their untainted (*anāsrava*) mental states manifest, or they may reach higher stages; once they have entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), although it is no longer necessary to give rise to the two [types of selflessness],...

They ride upon the untainted (*anāsrava*). They are reborn as Bodhisattvas because they enter into emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If it were not tainted (*sāsrava*) or if one were without mind (*acittaka*), the Tripiṭaka Master says:

"Since this does not exclude the stage of the emptiness of phenomena-in-themselves (*dharmanairātmya*), it is clear that the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) must necessarily entail the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*)."

However, as for the previous statement that the phenomena of arising and their nature are both empty, this was taught in terms of three [categories] rather than three types of formations (*saṃskāra*).

Nevertheless, because they are considered in relation to one another, the term "possible" (*yujyate*) is employed. That is to say, it is not the case that the emptiness of arising can possibly occur within the contaminated (*sāsrava*), except among the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states where the mindless (*acittaka*) states are excluded;

or conversely, it is not the case that the emptiness of arising can possibly occur within the mindless states, except among those with mind (*sacittaka*) where the contaminated states are excluded. This is due to...

This explanation includes the two characters "or" (vā) and "admits" (sambhavati). If both were entirely excluded, such that [the faculty] would necessarily always be manifest, then the word "admits" would be rendered useless.
The three stages of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) should be understood by analogy with this. The *Śūyao* (*Jiuyao*) states:

"The five faculties of the ten stages cannot necessarily give rise to the five untainted (anāsrava) consciousnesses; the tainted (sāsrava) non-common [faculties] must necessarily coexist with their corresponding objects. Regarding the faculty...
Because they are subsumed [within it], as in the stage prior to the bhūmis.
These four types of lineage (gotra) [surpass] the subsequent Buddhas.
The commentary states: This is the fifth cause, the gate of arising.
"Subsumed under the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (up to) the Subsequently Attained Wisdom.

The commentary states: This is the sixth section on the objects of cognition (*ālambana*). The text is easy to understand. As for the phrase "either a single phenomenon or two or many": [it refers to the diversity of objects].

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The objects of the three wisdoms are not fixed; however, because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is constant, it is always termed 'all-knowledge' (*sarvajña*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "If there is no totality that is not exhausted, it is called all-knowledge. If phenomena are boundless, how can they be known exhaustively?"
The answer is: The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable and his universal knowledge is boundless; it is like a large box for which the lid must also be large.
This treatise establishes that wisdom as being exclusively *prsthalabdha-jñāna* (subsequently attained wisdom), unlike the *Asvabhāva-śāstra*, which encompasses both types of wisdom.
"These four categories of wisdom (jñāna-citta-varga) [range] from [the first] to [the fourth], with many varieties of distinctions.
