The commentary states: There are two parts to this explanation: the explanation of the verses and the explanation of the various categories. Within the first part, there are two sections:
the essential nature and the formal characteristics. This is the first [section]. Regarding the essential nature, there are two types, distinguished by wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
"All outflows are eternally exhausted" (up to) "and is purely without outflows.

Commentary: Within the second characteristic, there are six [points]. The first is the characteristic of the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). Master Ji says: Because one is free from the bondage of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*), the outflows are eternally exhausted;

because one is free from the bondage of conditions (*ālambana-bandhana*) and so forth, the outflows do not increase. The term "pure by nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddha*) serves to exclude that which is not so.
"Learning" refers to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*). "Perfectly luminous" (*pariniṣpanna*) refers to learning and so forth being without outflows (*anāsrava*).
*Cai* says: "Because outflows are eternally exhausted, *nirvāṇa* is pure by nature; because outflows do not increase, *bodhi* is perfectly luminous. Regarding the meaning of "repository" (*garbha*):

*nirvāṇa* contains and encompasses unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merits, while *bodhi* contains and encompasses conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) merits. The Sarvāstivādins and others also maintain that the Buddha...

Because there exist the five contaminated (*sāsrava*) aggregates (*skandha*). Question: It may be so for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), but why are the four knowledges (*jñāna*) and the contaminated [aggregates] all uncontaminated?
Answer: This is a further objection. If they were all uncontaminated, it would contradict the statement that fifteen elements (*dhātu*) are exclusively contaminated;

consequently, the Tathāgata would lack the five sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth. There are three ways of resolving this objection. First is the interpretation of Bandhuprabha, as found in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
Jizang said: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* contains this passage: 'The second [type of transformation] has no master and is not that of a Buddha;

it is the coarse transformation produced by the records of other persons, and thus consists of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). That of a Buddha is subtle and is not so. Since there are no five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), upon what would the wisdom (*jñāna*) rely?"
There are two masters’ interpretations: one says it is based on six [factors], while the other says it is based on seven.

Regarding the third master, Dharmapāla’s statement that "it is taught elsewhere that they are not [included within] the *dhātus*," Jñānasena says this refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others; Cien says it refers to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and others.
This refers to the transformation of impermanent aggregates and the attainment of permanent aggregates, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, and so forth.
"This is the fruit of the transformation of the basis" (up to) "because it is that which is illustrated by the illustration.
The commentary states: This is the second characteristic. It is because there are three reasons: [it is] a path where mind and speech are cut off; and it is realized only within oneself.
Because it is not an analogy for omniscience.
Furthermore, this is subsumed under the wholesome (kuśala), specifically the untainted wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*).

[The] Commentary states: This is the third characteristic. As for the statement that the Buddha-fields and so forth are neither suffering (*duḥkha*) nor its origin (*samudaya*), they are included within the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Abhidharma*.
The Mahāyāna and so forth;
this, moreover, is eternal (nitya), reaching to the point of being uninterrupted and inexhaustible.

The commentary states: This is the fourth characteristic. Regarding "because that upon which it relies is eternal," it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher..."

This refers to what is called the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal; this is not an eternity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but is established through three causes.
[Zong]ce states: "All of these are inferences (*anumāna*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 28, says: "The Buddha-body has two aspects:
first, the eternal; second, the impermanent. Furthermore, fascicle 14 says: "The minds of śrāvakas are distinct, the minds of pratyekabuddhas are distinct, and the minds of the Buddhas are distinct."

Because they are distinct, they are impermanent. The formal inference (*anumāna*) is stated as follows: "The Reward Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*) is eternally abiding, because he is free from all afflictions, just like the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*).

The critique states: "This thesis contradicts the sacred teachings, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, because the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and so forth, are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, the reason [of being free from afflictions] violates the distinction of the intended meaning, for it is admitted that [the Reward Buddha] begins to arise and cease only after the Path; thus, it should be [treated] like the Dharma Body."
The body also does not arise (as in the "Fourfold Response to Difficulties" regarding humans, like the record on the golden drum).
This, moreover, is peace and bliss; up to [the point where] both are called peace and bliss.

The commentary states: This is the fifth characteristic. Although it is a ripened (*vipāka*) pleasant sensation (*vedanā*), it is blissful yet not peaceful, because it is permeated by coarseness (*audārika*). There is...

The outflows (*āsrava*) are "light" (*praśrabdha*), yet they are not "peaceful" (*sukha*); because they invite future suffering, they are not called blissful. Awakening (*bodhi*) and *nirvāṇa*, however, are free from coarse afflictions and compulsions;
they do not invite suffering or distress, and they enable sentient beings to experience ultimate happiness, and are thus termed "blissful" (*sukha*).
Because all that is attained by the two vehicles is subsumed within this. The commentary states:

Regarding the sixth, the characteristics of the body (*kāyalakṣaṇa*), there are two kinds of bodies, as explained in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*: the liberation body (*vimuktikāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).

In terms of the liberation body, the two vehicles and the Buddha are equal and identical; however, in terms of the dharma body, it is said that there is a distinction. This refers to the unsurpassed maturation of tranquility.

Regarding the "Silent Dharma" (*mauneya*): in Sanskrit it is called *muni*, which here means "silent and tranquil. Because all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) has been cut off, all untainted (*anāsrava*) states are termed *muni*.

However, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained through the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena is the most supreme and excellent; thus it is called "Unsurpassed. Because it is unsurpassed, it is named the "Great Muni.
It is not merely the body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*) defined by being free from bonds, but [is also] free from... [the objects of... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end.)

It is known as the "obstruction-knower" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and is also called the *dharmakāya*. Since it is said that there are five dharmas, this is not a separate *dharmakāya* among the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Jizang says: "The three meanings of essence-nature (*tǐxìng*), basis (*yīzhǐ*), and accumulation of virtues (*dèqù*) are designated as 'body' (*kāya*)."
"Thus, from the Dharmakāya (up to) all matters of benefit and happiness. Commentary states:
Within the second section on various gateways, there are seven gateways; this is the first of these three, the gateway of characteristics. Master Ji says:

"To be free of characteristics means to be devoid of the ten characteristics. To be quiescent means that the path of discursive thought is cut off. To transcend conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) means—"
It is said that the path of speech is severed. Because it is formed by the various marks of the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), it is called "perfectly complete" (*atyanta-pūrṇa*).

Because its essence is free from all faults, it is called "perfectly pure" (*atyanta-viśuddha*). Because it is uninterrupted and inexhaustible, it is called "perfectly eternal" (*atyanta-nitya*). Because it is omnipresent, it is called "perfectly pervasive" (*atyanta-vyāpin*). The term "continuous" (*saṃtati*) distinguishes it from the *svabhāvakāya*;
"serene" (*sānta*) distinguishes it from the other two bodies, for they are not perfectly radiant and pure, as they possess interruptions. — [Mei] Cè.

It is said: "This [Dharmakāya] does not preach the Dharma, because it preaches the Dharma only to give rise to understanding in others. Alternatively, it may be said that it does preach the Dharma, because it experiences the bliss of the Dharma.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Dharmabuddha preaches the Dharma because it is the sphere of internally realized noble practice.
How much more so for the *svasaṃbhogakāya*; how could it alone not preach? As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "Only Buddhas speak with Buddhas," whether dwelling in the pure or the defiled.

Regarding this, there are two interpretations in the West. The first states that, according to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and other texts, ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) truly are born in the Pure Land.

However, when the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of "intentionality regarding another time" (*paryāya-abhiprāya*), it refers to the Enjoyment Land (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), because it pertains to the third stage within the system of the seven stages.

As for the "intentionality regarding another time" in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it refers to having the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) but lacking the practice (*pratipatti*). Since the root treatise states only "generating [the aspiration],"...

One interpretation states that there is no place of rebirth within the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation) lands. This is because all sutras explain this as being of "intention for another time" (*paryāyābhiprāya*).
Based on a temporary manifestation, it is said that one dwells in the Pure Land; this is as described in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, where the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe to purify it.
This first [interpretation] accords with the various sutras.
"By means of the five dharmas, [up to] all possess true wisdom. Commentary:
Within the second section on the mutual inclusion of the characteristics of the five dharmas, there are two masters' interpretations; this is that of the first master.
Since the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and other texts state that suchness is the *dharmakāya*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "The transformation of the *ālayavijñāna*..."
Because of attaining the body of self-nature (*svabhāvakāya*), the wisdom of equality in speech manifests the Buddha-body for all bodhisattvas within the purely pure land.

Regarding this, the *Two Commentaries* state: "It is unknown which teaching [this refers to]. According to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, when questioning the two types of wisdom, it merely says, "as explained in other treatises," without specifying their names.
As for the statement that "the wisdom of contemplation preaches the Dharma," it cites the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* regarding the transformation of...

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun) concerns the transformation of consciousness; the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She dasheng lun) concerns the drawing forth and gathering [of dharmas]; the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* (Dasheng zhuangyan jing lun) concerns the inconceivable transformations of wisdom; and the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (Weishi zhongbian fenbie lun) also concerns wisdom and its distinctions.
These are likewise included within the *Saṃgraha*.
There is an interpretation [up to] "therefore it is not said that they exist.
The commentary states: This is the second, the correct meaning. Regarding the scriptural evidence cited, the *Śrī-mālā-sūtra-alaṃkāra* says: "The self-nature is uninterrupted and continuous;
the three Buddhas are together in the hall. Since it is stated that the body’s self-nature is eternal, the *Buddhastotra* composed by Asaṅga says:

Because the *dharmakāya* is without arising or ceasing; the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is likewise. Vasubandhu’s *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because it is attained through realization.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The support of all Buddhas; the *dharmakāya* is without distinction. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"It is like empty space," up to "because it is neither form nor mind. To preempt an objection, one says: "It is endowed with boundless virtues."
"How could it be that form and mind are lacking? [Hui]hui says: "These are all unconditioned virtues; they are not actual form and mind.
Regarding the statement that the Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is the Enjoyment Buddha (*saṃbhoga-buddha*), the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* quotes the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* as its source.

Regarding the inclusion of the Buddha’s unique conditioned real virtues, Woncheuk says: "This is proven by reason. "Causing all to possess mind" refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. "Transformation creation" (*nirmāṇa*)... [text ends].
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* speaks of the three types of karma. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* speaks of the dependent mind.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of the transformation-mind that is without roots.
Thus [are explained] the merits of the three bodies up to the marks of transformation.
The commentary states: This is the third section on the distinctions of merit.
Furthermore, from the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body) up to its manifestation for others.

The commentary states: This is the fourth section on the two benefits. The *Shuyao* says: "This is explained according to the increase [of afflictions]. Fundamentally, it is for the benefit of others;
yet by realizing one's own enjoyment, the benefit of others by all Buddhas is itself their own benefit. Therefore, speaking in terms of reality, both are encompassed within the two benefits."
Furthermore, the *svābhāvikakāya* (Self-Nature Body) [up to] "is also without fixed limit.
The commentary states: This is the fifth section, the gate of distinctions in the basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa-mukha*). Regarding that which pertains to the Buddha-dharma, the two commentaries state:

"That which pertains to the Buddha is the 'subject' (*dharmin*), because its nature pertains to the Dharma; thus it becomes the basis (*āśraya*) whose measure is like that of the Pure Land, and the measure of the body is likewise."
Regarding this, Ce says: "The bodies in the desire and form realms vary according to the magnitude of karma, up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where the body size reaches sixteen thousand yojanas.
The Tathāgata is likewise; because he is produced by the drawing forth of boundless roots of goodness, each and every part is boundless.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* states: 'The eyes and other faculties of the Tathāgata all pervade the Dharma-realm.'"
"From the *svabhāvakāya* and its realm (*dharmadhātu*)... because [it] gives rise to all beings. The commentary states:
This is the sixth section on similarities and differences, concerning the affiliation of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). What serves as the proof? It is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Question: If Śākyamuni Buddha extensively delivers beings throughout the ten directions, why is there a need for other Buddhas? Answer: The causes and conditions of sentient beings differ from one another.

As it is said in the *Śrāvaka-dharma*, regarding the specific causes and conditions of a disciple such as Śāriputra, even all the Buddhas together could not deliver him, let alone others. This is explained in detail in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
"These various bodies and lands... because they are associated with meditative concentration. The commentary states:

Regarding the seventh consciousness’s transformation into differentiated forms, there exists an untainted nature (*anāsrava*). [In this case,] the subject and object are distantly separated yet correspond to one another. This is not the case for the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.

This is because the bodies and lands transformed upon the primary mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) belong respectively to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the other aggregates as their objective and subjective aspects. (3)

The same applies to their nature (*svabhāva*). This is because the subjective transformation and the objective transformation each arise from distinct seeds; that is to say, while the contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses possess a mixture of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses are not discussed in this context.
Since the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth apply to both, they are mentioned in both places. Otherwise, there would be no [distinction of] the five, twelve, and so on.
If the subjective and objective transformations were necessarily identical to the aggregates and so forth, then there would be no [distinction of] the five aggregates or the twelve [bases].

Regarding the bases (*āyatana*) and so forth, the eyes and other faculties that are transformed [by consciousness] should be included within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Within the discussion on the distinction between the unreal and the real, there are two masters’ explanations. The first says:

because they are transformed by the two parts—the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)—they are unreal; only the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is capable of transformation, and thus it is real. Paramārtha (Ce) says:
whether they are of the same or different seeds, both interpretations may be adopted according to one’s preference. The second, Dharmapāla, explains the objection through three successive stages.
It should be understood that there are three possible interpretations. One interpretation is that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the others all have consciousness as their nature;
this is the position of Sthiramati, because [he maintains] that there is only self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). However, the intention of the Tripiṭaka Master [Xuanzang] preserves two interpretations.

Regarding the "three sections" and so forth of this treatise, the commentary states: The third part is titled the "Section on the Dedication of Merit. As for the mention of "three sections," there are two interpretations in the sub-commentary (*śāstra*).

One says they refer to the three sections of the root verses (*mūlakārikā*); another says they refer to the name of this explanatory treatise (*bhāṣya*), as indicated by its title at the beginning. All commentators on this treatise [agree with the latter].
The *Ming'en liangshu* (Two Letters on Clarifying Kindness) states: "The essential points say that all places where one may study are subsumed within this;
there is nothing further to seek. Thus, students need not laboriously expend their efforts."
Notes on the Study of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (End)
